Such an incredible performance from Riz Ahmed, and he also, I mean, and this is this is maybe not the point of being in here, but he's so hot in this movie, so hot. Like I dyed my hair blonde and people thought it was because I was having a gay midlife crisis, but in fact it was because of the Sound of Metal.

Couldn't stop in the closet without talking a little bit about Wong Kar-wai. In the Mood for Love is such a, one of his best. I think it's an incredible movie. I will say this is kind of a placeholder for me for Happy Together, which they are giving me on the way out. Happy Together specifically, if I can talk about that really quickly, is I think the first movie I ever saw that depicted love between two Asian men, and it was such a powerful movie for me to see at that point in my life because I'd just never seen that on film before. And it and like I feel like we do get lost in the sauce a little bit when we talk about representation and what it means and how important it is and all those things today, but I for me, like when I think about how powerful it can be to see yourself represented on screen, like that movie comes to mind immediately for me because it definitely, seeing yourself reflected in that way when you're not used to it, it can it's it's a real paradigm-shifting moment for, or it can be for a lot of people, and it was for me. So, In the Mood for Love certainly, but if you have time, check out Happy Together as well, please.

This is incredible. I did, I thought I would really struggle, but I'm I'm having such a good time and finding so many good ones like this. I just looked up and this is what I found: Hedwig and the Angry Inch. John Cameron Mitchell, one of my all-time favorite filmmakers and somebody that I definitely draw a huge amount of inspiration from. And I had the honor of being his husband in the Hulu show Shrill, which was such a full circle moment for me as an actor and as a writer, just like being that close in proximity to somebody who has shaped so much of my creative lens is, was, was really cool. And seeing this in here makes me so happy.

Okay, now it's time. I don't even know if this is going to fit in my bag, but this Godzilla sort of 15 Kaiju Classics. Now if you only have time for one, I'm definitely going to say Mothra vs. Godzilla is my favorite out of this crop. I grew up on these movies, like we would get them and like wear them out from Blockbuster Video, RIP, and I, Mothra was my favorite of these films. I don't know exactly why. I think there was like something, I don't know, like gentler about Mothra. I think like Mothra is, forgive me, gay-coded, and I think I sensed that as a little boy, and I just I love it.

Oh, well, okay. The last thing I watched on Criterion, because Donald Sutherland, he passed, and he is such an amazing actor. But this movie, Don't Look Now, it's such a great film because, you know, it's it seems like it turns into a horror film, but really is a film about grief and about love. I mean, and Julie Christie could not be hotter. Donald Sutherland's amazing. This is how you do a love scene. It's so moving, and you really feel like the way he intercuts it with them just kind of getting ready, you feel like they've been married for a long time, they love each other. It's so beautifully done. I'm really psyched to have this.

Oh, ha! I'm not going to choose this, but Bound, this is the new 4K version, and it's on Criterion. The Wachowskis, I knew they were great filmmakers the second I met them, even though this was their first film. But I'm not I'm not choosing this, cuz I'm going to get this later. I don't want to I don't want to, you know, use up one of my things.

Oh, wait. Hold the phone. Wait a second. Brazil is a must. God bless Terry Gilliam. Terry's imagination is so vast, and of course, this is like one of the many examples of, oh, it's a science fiction dystopic, you know, satire set in the future. You know what? Like, this is happening. You have to watch this because just the plastic surgery scene alone, Katherine Helmond is so fantastic, and it's just so outrageous. This will be always one of my all-time favorite movies.

Here's a movie that is not as well known. I read about her, I fell in love with her story, this is years ago, and I thought, oh, I can play her, I want to play her. What an interesting woman, Lola Montès. This to me is a cautionary tale of what not to have happen. I don't want to end up in a cage. Not—I don't want to give it away, but I'm not going to lie, I got really depressed after watching it, but I love it.

This movie freaked me out when I saw it. I watched this movie in a midnight screening on the way when I was in NYU, trying to look for an apartment, and I thought, oh, I'll meet this weird guy at midnight. It turned out to be a weird guy, whole other story, and I had just come from seeing The Seventh Seal. You know, the guy is coming from war, and there's the bubonic plague. I mean, everything feels so grim, and what's life about? And it's kind of weirdly life-affirming. And of course, you know, all of a sudden he meets the artists, the circus people, and they're so full of life. I don't know, I think there's a it's a real statement of how artists, you know, they're in the moment, they're enjoying life, they bring beauty into the world. Anyway, this is, if you haven't seen this, it's a must.

Do you want to do that random thing I told you about of like, and for my last film, I'll like close my eyes and—oh yeah, yeah, let's do the random thing. It's like picking a tarot card or something. Okay, all right, I'm going to, okay, eyes are closed. Wow, I don't know it. The Friends of Eddie Coyle, a Peter Yates film. I have no idea what this, but it is starring Robert Mitchum, which is one of my favorite guys, who I use as an influence, going back to Bound, he was one of the guys I watched quite a bit. Peter Boyle is in it, who was in my first real movie I did, Red Heat. It's 1970s, I love a '70s Hollywood sort of film. Great. Here's my surprise.

I saw this and I freaked out because I love Godzilla. I do. I'm just going to say it, I love Godzilla. Look at this. Now, these have all the originals, right? This is one of the greatest scores of all time. I think it's one of my favorite scores, you know. When I have to get going in the morning, I listen to the theme of Godzilla. And I love this. Thank you so much. This is a great graphic. Whoever did this, you're a genius.

Okay, I just I just need to be the one to talk about Tampopo just because this is a movie that like I feel like is very much like a reflection of my soul. I love food, I love absurdity, I love yeah, I love the way that it's like really sweet and also really horrific sometimes. The sexuality in it is just bizarre and beautiful. And the one fun fact: one of our good friends, Hiro Murai, who's another music video director who now Atlanta and stuff like that, he's incredible, his father was the composer and he was also at the beginning of the movie. He's the guy who's eating chips really loudly and gets beat up by the Yakuza. So this place, that was when I first heard about it was like Hiro posted online. I was like, maybe I'll watch that, his dad scored it. Yeah, no, this is this is the best movie ever. Yeah, it's amazing.

I have like a I have a problem with movies based on True Stories. Like I feel like it's like just scary, you know, like bad journalism that like screenwriters can just like nudge the facts around. But every once in a while a movie breaks that for me, you know, I'm like, never mind, this one's incredible, you know, like Love & Mercy is one and Malcolm X is one. This is just like such a riveting crime saga, like maybe my favorite crime movie. It just blew my mind when I first saw it like a year ago. And I also like am a pretty big Spike Lee fan as a writer-director and a very big Spike Lee fan as an actor. He just comes in so hot in this movie and in Do the Right Thing, obviously. But like the opening scene is just him and Denzel just walking through this long one-er. Incredible, crazy movie. I want to watch the special features.

Oh, we gotta we gotta do a little shout out for Jason Kisvarday. So our production designer, we've been working with him for about 10 years, this is his favorite movie of all time. And every year for his birthday he forces all of us to re-watch it and make dioramas inspired by the film. And there's like a diorama competition and he gives a winning prize out every year. And I think almost every single film or thing he's ever done he tries to sneak at least one prop that is inspired from this movie. And so you know, anyone who's seen the film knows that they have all these fake products or whatever in the background, but they're like the laziest, most basic thing where the beer can will just say "beer" and the cereal will just say "cereal." And he is in our movie, the Chapstick says "Chapstick." Oh yeah, exactly, I think so, that's like the same kind of branding, that's a Repo Man Chapstick. So anyways, I'm gonna give this to him because I haven't... Oh, you want to go? Okay, I actually want to keep it. Okay, I bet he already has it. I swear, does he have Criterion? I don't know, we'll have to find out. He probably has every version. Yeah, but yeah, I've now seen it like five times because I go to Jason's birthday parties and it gets better.

I'll do a quick shout out to Police Story 1 and 2. This is a very formative... My dad, his whole family, they speak in the language of old Hong Kong kung fu films. Like, one of my uncles is, you know, he's he's on the spectrum and he can basically recite, like he can tell you whatever movie you call it, he can tell you what year it came out, every actor who's involved, and how it's connected to whatever universe. And so we watched a lot of Jackie Chan. And yeah, Police Story 1 and 2 was like way too brutal for me as a kid, but I really loved it. Like the finale in the mall where he's going down the pole and getting electrocuted, and then you see in the end credits he literally has like second and third degree burns on his arms. Is I probably watched some of that stuff a little too early, but, obviously this is why we made Everything Everywhere, is because I, kung fu movies is in the blood. So this is very exciting.

This is like the first movie I ever loved. I actually don't know which Godzilla was the first one, I was I was so young, but like right as a kid I became obsessed with Godzilla movies. And there was something about knowing that it's a man in a suit smashing toys that just like blew my mind. And I was like, this is, can I do that one day? And I still sometimes say that's the genre I'm interested in, is a monster movie, but only if it's costumes and miniatures. I don't want CG monsters, I don't care. Yeah, old school kaiju. Yeah, only if I get to be the kaiju.

These movies changed my life. Literally, The Before Trilogy, Richard Linklater. They're just great, but I sat down with my partner and watched all three movies with her years ago, and we finished them while on vacation in Central America and had like a life-changing discussion about our relationship after watching Before Midnight. And just kind of like renegotiating our relationship because like seeing this mirror in front of us of just like where we were headed and like what it's like to domesticate someone you love blew my mind. Just a big Linklater fan. What's your favorite of the three? Oh, my favorite, honestly, I think Midnight. But it's not my favorite movie, it's just the one that changed my life, is it like fucking cold-showered me. And it was so, it's so brutal. I also did a film festival of this movie last year where I got up, watched Before Sunrise before the sun rose, and then we watched Before Sunset right before dinner, and then we waited till midnight and watched Before Midnight. This is, you put this on yourself? Yes, yeah, yeah, this is like on vacation with my friend Felicia. Shout out to Felicia.

The one that immediately got my eye and that I feel like I have to take is a good Australian classic, Breaker Morant. A great war film, also a great courtroom drama, and this is one that I appreciated much more as I grew older because we used to watch it at school a lot, and at first I thought it was a boring war movie, but the more that I watch it, the more I get from it, and particularly having such great Australian actors like Bryan Brown and Jack Thompson. That's going in the bag.

Oh, what do we have here? I know that probably a million people talk about Eraserhead, but this was my first experience of David Lynch, and I was probably way too young to see it. Freaked me out. I couldn't quite wrap my head around what was going on, but to me, it was one of the gateways into this whole world of arthouse film, just having that idea of there are other things besides Hollywood movies, and the fact that movies don't always have to make you feel a certain way, like always feel good. It can make you feel confused and also maybe a little bit sick, too. So I'm going to take that one. Got nostalgic value.

So this was actually the first-ever Criterion Collection DVD that I got in Australia, and I had built up a pretty good collection in Australia, and then I had to sell everything when I moved to America because I only took two suitcases to come here. So this is my favorite Akira Kurosawa film. I think it's one of his most watchable. If you've never seen Kurosawa—of course you guys all have, but the people who've never been introduced to him—I often cite this film because it's such a human story. It's also a good Christmas tale, almost like A Christmas Carol, and just such a beautiful way of looking at life and someone's impact on other people's lives after their death. So I'm going to take that, and so I can start my new collection.

Lady Snowblood, yeah. That's such a cool film. I remember seeing this on the big screen in Australia, in Canberra, when I was a teenager, and walking out wanting to be an assassin with a sword. She is just awesome.

Weekend, Jean-Luc Godard. Morbid, dark, really great satire, and one of the best, like, long tracking shots I've seen in a film. Biggest car accident that I've seen in a film. Also has that very stylish feel of Jean-Luc Godard, but post-apocalyptic movie that takes really unexpected turns. Love Weekend.

Gilda. Love Rita Hayworth, and she's someone who, the more that I read about her background and things that I never knew when I watched her films when I was younger, it makes me kind of sad for her. And I think Gilda is one of those movies where she could obviously relate to the character because she is kind of portraying this goddess character, she's really insecure on the inside, and so when I watch it now I see the real Rita beneath the Gilda. And obviously I was inspired by her with the red hair.

His Girl Friday, classic screwball comedy, of course. This in particular, I remember watching this when I was really young, and this is one of the examples I always cite about why representation's important, because seeing Rosalind Russell as a reporter, I remember so distinctly watching it and thinking I could be like Hildy Johnson.
One last Australian film from 1970s, Walkabout. A very dark movie, one by Nicolas Roeg, who was British, but he really managed to capture Australian outback perfectly.

Never seen Written on the Wind, which is which is shameful. I'm excited to add this to my collection. It's the original Criterion logo. I like I like having the old little line, little text. Criterion.
This is probably my favorite documentary and this is the movie I've seen probably the most times of any movie. I've probably seen this over a hundred times.
The Horse's Mouth. This is my dad's favorite movie.

I guess I'm going to have to take Pickpocket because I bought this when it came out and I watched it so many times that it's all scratched up now and there's a great thing of Paul Schrader talking about the movie.
Oh, this is something I've always been curious about. The Golden Age of Television because it has the original version of Marty.

Timothy Carey made a movie who's he's one of the guys that killed in the end of the movie. All he was the only actor that that Kubrick allowed to improvise and he made a crazy movie that I love that I don't think has ever been on DVD called The World's Greatest Sinner that everyone should try to see.
Great opening scene. Great last shot, too. Great little moment where Shock Corridor is on a marquee.
The Shooting. This is this I love this movie. Monte Hellman. I stayed with him in his beautiful bed and breakfast.

film_title: Eclipse Series 33: Up All Night with Robert Downey Sr.
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 33: Up All Night with Robert Downey Sr.
quote: I have this already, but this is my one of my favorite things that ever came out. Criterion. This beautiful box of Robert Downey Sr. Movies. I went to a screening of Chafed Elbows years ago at Anthology and I found this thing on eBay. It's this photograph of him directing Up the Academy, the Mad Magazine movie, and he's in a cowboy hat and he's like pretending to direct Alfred E. Neuman. It's like little man in a mask. And I showed it to Downey Sr. And he looked at it and goes, "Sorry about that one." I said, "Oh, I actually really like Up the Academy." And he was like, he just looked at me with disgust. So, I think it disappointed him.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 33: Up All Night with Robert Downey Sr.

quote: Bob Fosse, All That Jazz. So I just watched this again quite recently, actually. It’s a work of absolute genius, in my opinion. And if you want to look at where a lot of modern editing gets its ideas from, just look at the sequences of him taking the pills, which are spread throughout it. I think that’s a great movie. Great, great, great, great, great, great movie. So this is one I am taking home.

So they’ve got Anora, which… To my shame, I hadn’t seen his other movies. And I went immediately after watching Anora, which I thought was just wonderful, and I went back to Florida Project, which is even more remarkable in a way. And I’d missed it the first time around. So apologies, Sean Baker, and chapeau.
They’ve got one of his other films here, which I am going to take, The Prince of Broadway, which I knew about, but I haven’t seen. So I’ll be taking both those, please, if I may.

So I have to give a shout-out to a great and very, very underrated British director, Stephen Frears. Really one of our great craftsmen. And this is a film he made with John Cusack, Anjelica Huston, and Annette Bening: The Grifters. I think it’s based on a Jim Thompson novel or short story, and… who’s a great writer. Incredible. This, you’ve got to see this film for three sterling performances. You watch Annette Bening and you think, “Oh my goodness me, what an actor.”

Yeah, I was looking… I was looking for Fish Tank. And there it is. Yes. Oh, here we go. So this is a British filmmaker, Andrea Arnold. If you don’t know her, you should see her work. True independent. Brilliant filmmaker. This is a wonderful film that she made. Michael Fassbender’s in it, and it’s partly about Essex, which is an area of the UK. And it has the most extraordinary skies. You cannot believe the… They’re so beautiful and it’s shot by Robbie Ryan, who I think shot her new movie, Bird, as well. The casting that she does, the way she finds actors… remarkable. Yeah, wonderful film and a wonderful filmmaker.

So there is a theory that… which I’m happy to say that this is absolute proof of, that your first film is always your best film. And my first film, which is also available on the Criterion Collection, was called Shallow Grave, and it… My dad always used to say… I used to take my dad to all my films, and he’d say the same thing every time when he came out of them. Didn’t matter what it was, whether it’d won Oscars or whatever, he said, “Oh yeah, it was good, son, but it wasn’t as good as Shallow Grave.” So he believed the theory that your first film is always your best film. To say that the Coen brothers have never made a better movie than this is not an insult. It is an extraordinary… It just shows you the talent that’s there, and you can see them learning their craft as they make it. So if you want to watch where it all began, then this is the one to start with: Blood Simple.

Oh my goodness me. So, I was talking earlier about Shallow Grave, the first film, and one of the buzzes when you do films and you kind of like… you get invited to exotic places. And we got invited to Cuba, to the Havana Film Festival. And it was an incredible experience to be in Cuba. And two of the films that we saw while we were there was this: I Am Cuba, which is a staple and is recommended, and everybody should see it really.

But this film is the film with the worst title, I think, probably imaginable. It’s called Memories of Underdevelopment, and it’s a film by Tomás Gutiérrez Alea. What can I tell you about this film? When I saw this film, we were working on Trainspotting, so we’d released Shallow Grave and we were working on Trainspotting, and I can’t remember whether we’d… I think we’d shot… No, we hadn’t shot it. We were working on it, and we didn’t have an ending. And I saw this film, and I stole, frame by frame, the last shot of this film for the last shot of Trainspotting. And if you happen to watch this movie, which is available on Criterion and is available on an extraordinary, proper regrade of this, you’ll see the last shot of this film as it was intended to do, as it reflected the last shot of this film. And you’ll realize how the phrase, “We stand on the shoulder of giants,” is highly appropriate. Yeah.
So immediately I see Cronenberg, Videodrome. I did a movie, Faces of Death, and this was a big, big inspiration. This, Crash, which… I have the DVD, I won’t be… I’ll keep it… I won’t be greedy.
The Vanishing, I also have this DVD. Incredible movie. It’s just… Wow. So scary. And has changed my life in many ways because that last scene, if you know what I’m talking about.
My Own Private Idaho. Gorgeous. Stunning. I’m taking this one.
Drugstore Cowboy, I’ve never seen it. I would like to see it. I want to just… I’ve heard many good things and I’m excited. Gus Van Sant very… very cool guy. Very, very cool guy.
My best friend loves Mildred Pierce. He’s been watching it several times a week since I’ve been away. So I’m getting him the DVD. This is for you, Ben.
Oh, Betty Blue. My favorite soundtrack. Just beautiful. This is a very big inspiration.

Polyester. I have a lot of John Waters DVDs. This is the one I’m missing. Incredible. Also, this cover just… stunning. I love– Okay, so I love the camp of it. I always was really attracted to camp. I watched a lot of Gregg Araki and… which was a big inspiration for me, and I think that John Waters has this insane way of just showing the American filth of it all. And Divine is also like a… just incredible. RIP.
Red Desert, watched this at Metrograph. Hand acting, baby, hand acting. Inspo.

If I could plead to people to watch a movie, it’d be Safe. Julianne Moore. I mean, it is… It’s a tough watch. It’s… For those who are hypochondriacs, possibly a little bit too close to home. But, I mean, the performances are incredible. The film is amazing. I highly recommend. I’d be on the street, you know, just slinging them.

This and A Woman Under the Influence, which is… I know it’s here. I know it’s here. A Woman Under the Influence. Gena Rowlands, I mean, just everything. But I’m going to take the Cassavetes box set because Christmas came early.

Araki. Okay, Doom Generation, big inspiration for me season two of Euphoria. Rose McGowan, she’s everything. So this is going to be really fun. And there’s Nowhere on here too. So fun. I haven’t seen Totally F***ed Up, so this is going to be… it’s going to be a new watch for me.

This is a beautiful, beautiful film: My Life as a Dog, Lasse Hallström. It’s all about the first stirrings of romantic love and interacting with adults that are, you know, a lot older than you. It’s just really great. And the kid who plays Ingemar is wonderful. It’s like he doesn’t know he’s in a movie. It’s like he’s living the film. And it’s director-approved, this print, so I’m gonna show this to my kid because this film was one of my favorites. Check it out if you haven’t seen it.

How could I not? Night of the Living Dead. George Romero basically invented the modern zombie and I don’t think he gets enough credit for it, because a lot of people have taken his idea, myself included, and Edgar Wright, although it was very much a tribute to George, and sort of run with it as if it’s like the public domain, like Frankenstein’s monster or the mummy or whatever. But this was 1968, right in the heart, right in the middle of the civil rights movement. It was a major kind of thing that he cast Duane Jones as the lead, a Black actor. It really, really rings true that this was a time of social upheaval, no more sort of demonstrated than in the final moments of the film, which are the darkest… is one of the darkest endings of any film ever. I remember we showed George Shaun of the Dead. He said, “I really enjoyed the movie,” and I said, “I… I’m sorry because Philip, Bill Nighy’s character, he reanimates quite quickly in Shaun of the Dead and I know in Dawn of the Dead Roger takes quite a while before he comes back.” And I was really sort of like… had this verbal diarrhea, like I was apologizing for messing with his mythology. And he went, “Simon, I didn’t mind.” I was like, “Phew.” So yeah, as a tribute to George, an amazing maverick filmmaker, this is where it all began. And it’s a piece of work. It really is. Black and white. Terrifying. Brilliant.

Quadrophenia. This is one of the definitive British teen movies of the 1970s. Very disillusioned young man who has an awful job in the post office, who at the weekend becomes a mod and fights rockers, as were the two sort of youth cultures of the time. He goes down to Brighton and there’s this massive fight on the beach. And it also features an amazing performance from Sting, who plays this sort of uber-mod who… obviously Sting is beautiful and he’s dressed so cool and Jimmy really idolizes him. And then the disillusionment he experiences when he sees his sort of hero reduced to running around after these rich people is just so beautifully played by Phil Daniels. It has an incredible ending as well, and an amazing soundtrack by The Who. “Quadrophenia,” I think, is a state of being in four minds about something, and that kind of reflects Jimmy’s multiple personalities and, yeah, it’s an important one, this one.

I wanted to pick a David Lynch as a tribute to David, who we sadly lost recently. I got to meet him at the Paramount 100th anniversary photograph. And he was so sweet and so nice and so normal, so not the guy that you thought would come up with stuff like Blue Velvet, which is an insanely disturbing movie. I showed this to my daughter the other day and she hated it. But she hated it for exactly the reasons that David Lynch wanted you to hate it. This really, really, unnerving exploration of Middle America, the seedy underworld that exists just under the surface. What I love about Lynch is that he just leaves so much to you. He throws stuff out there, which is kind of indecipherable, but it’s your job to decipher it, it’s your job to apply your interpretations to what he’s saying. And they’re always there. And… I was delighted that Tilly hated it because she talked about it nonstop that night and then the next day. And I said, “Sometimes entertainment is an overrated function of art. Sometimes being made uncomfortable is the point. Sometimes being repulsed by something is the point.” And I think David Lynch knew that better than most. So I’m putting Blue Velvet in my bag.
Town Bloody Hall. I love nothing more than when misogynists and feminists have a fight at a large event space. That's what this is about. I can watch it for hours and then put it on again.

Love & Basketball. This couple, this romance makes me want to play sports. Everything you want a movie to be, and it's a true comfort film for me and a classic example of a romantic comedy that is not bogged down by the genre. I love it.

Streetwise/Tiny. These documentaries by the brilliant Mary Ellen Mark tell the story of runaways who are making it on the mean streets of the Pacific Northwest in the '70s and '80s. These kids' speaking is better than anything adults could ever write, and Mary Ellen has the most tender, sensitive gaze on their lives. You will laugh. You will cry. These movies are unbelievably special. Trivia fact for you: after his first movie got into Cannes, I got Josh Safdie the biggest Streetwise poster in the world, framed it for him in yellow, and it's still in his office. So if you didn't think it was cool, it is cool.
My Brilliant Career, I mean, this film by Gillian Armstrong, it is touching, it is powerful, it is feminist. Judy Davis's hair, she's going to the Met Gala, guys. It's going in the bag.

Okay, Daytrippers. I love this because when I used to go to Tower Video when I was a kid – shout out to all the cool twentysomethings at Tower Video who helped me pick videos. Greg Mottola introduced me to so many of my indie film icons. I mean: Stanley Tucci, Hope Davis, Parker Posey, Liev Schreiber, Anne Meara. Look at all of that virtuosity in one place. That's like a lot of indie-film inspiration for one little girl. With a big dose of kind of… like, kind of gay panic. It's perfect.

This is a newer favorite for me. This is Okja. I love this for so many reasons, but I am a pig parent and I think that this talks about the beauty of the interspecial bond and the kind of tenuousness of the mycelium network of animal and human interconnections in a way that so few movies do.

And I forgot that I'm also allowed to grab things that I want to see. So, for me, that is Night on Earth. How can I be a New Yorker and have never watched Night on Earth, you may ask. This is something I told a lot of men that I'd seen so that we could make out.

Defending Your Life. I love, love when Meryl goes LOL. We know no one wipes the floor with the drama better, but when Meryl Streep blesses us with a comedy, just like when Albert Brooks blesses us with an emotional scene. So, Defending Your Life: one of the craziest premises, one of the most remarkable films.

So one very particular and interesting film for me was this film: Federico Fellini’s La strada. And the reason that it had a special meaning for me was that in Toronto – we’re talking about the 1940s, 1950s – every Saturday there would be a… like a swarm of lemmings, there were children who would come to a particular cinema called the Pylon. And one day I came out of that cinema, having seen the traditional kind of what for us were kids’ movies, and across the street from the Pylon was a new theater, a very small one called the Studio, and it only showed Italian films in Italian, there were people coming out of a screening that had happened at the Studio, and it was adults only, no children, and they were coming out onto the street and there were weeping, men and women sobbing, crying. Across the street to see what the film was that had that effect on these people and it was La strada. And so, of course, many years later I saw La strada and then I was crying on the street myself and I thought that was the moment that I realized that film had that kind of power. It made a difference to me and my entire film career. So, La strada.

English films were a big influence, too, and they had their own particular tone. They were very theatrical in some ways, but they had a really special power. And one in particular for me was this one: Odd Man Out, with an actor I absolutely adore, James Mason. I would have loved to work with him. He had the most wonderful voice and presence. Directed by Carol Reed. And it was an incredibly powerful, melancholy, surprising film that was… as I say, had a particular English feel that you would not find in the rest of Europe or certainly not in Hollywood also. So, Odd Man Out. Fantastic to have this film in my hand.

But, as we said, there were two poles. And there was a European pole, but there was also the American pole. Now, American filmmaking, of course, was not just Hollywood, and a film that I could relate to more in terms of my own filmmaking was… David Lynch’s film Eraserhead. Very American and saying some really interesting kind of sublime things about American culture and the American ethos and zeitgeist that you wouldn’t see in a Hollywood film, but you also wouldn’t see it in a European film. This is a really special film that had a big impact on me. I can’t say that it was an influence because I had already been making films by this time, but it was… it was significant for me. And I met David and we got along very well. I went with him to Bob’s Big Boy, where we would eat hamburgers for lunch. And we got along very well. And it’s a really… of course, it’s a tragedy that he died so young. Eraserhead.

This immense collection. Quite fantastic and really heavy. And you could use it in your workout. Bergman also was one of the greats for anybody who felt that film was art. And, in particular, Hour of the Wolf, a very, very dark, depressing film, which was great, had a special meaning for me because, when I was making my film The Fly, there was a moment when the Jeff Goldblum character, who has now sort of fused with the fly DNA and has strange physical capabilities, could climb up onto a wall and hang from a ceiling. And I remembered that Bergman had done that in Hour of the Wolf, a scene with a man who is experiencing such anguish that his anguish allows him to walk up a wall and onto a ceiling. And I was wondering, “How did he do that physically?” because now I was going to do the same thing in a science-fiction movie with quite a different tone. And so I watched Hour of the Wolf again. And so I felt a kinship with Bergman and I think John Landis told me when he went to Bergman’s house on his island, his special Swedish island, that amongst his collection of DVDs there was a DVD of The Fly. So I thought, “Okay, Bergman and I, we are… we are blood brothers. We are connected.” So this huge, immense collection will go into this quite small bag.

I certainly don’t hate The Philadelphia Story. Katharine Hepburn I think would be annoyed that she’s only a small figure in this picture, but… And it never occurred to me that I would ever get her to do these shows. She called and she said, “You know you’ve made me a goddamn saint. Everywhere I go, if I go shopping, people suddenly adore me more than ever before.”

Jean-Luc Godard. I remember when I introduced him, some guy in the audience screamed at the sound of his name, and you could see that he couldn’t believe he was going to actually see him in the flesh. So it’s nice that I made somebody ecstatically happy. Well, I’m lucky because Every Man for Himself is the title of… Right there. You can see it. I don’t know what that film is. So I’m glad I came.
You know, I don’t think I’ve ever seen this, but I’m not sure. Only Angels Have Wings. You can’t beat Cary Grant and Jean Arthur. And nor should you try. What a good thing to have.

There seems to be a film called Stagecoach. And I’ve heard of it. I’ve probably seen it at least four times, possibly more. I don’t see how a movie would get any better. And this is the Blu-ray special edition. What a film.

And Odd Man ‘Oot’ or ‘Out.’ Carol Reed. One of the few movies with three words all the same number of letters. God, that must be thrilling for you to know. But it’s also a wonderful film. Yeah, I like it a lot. I wish I had Carol Reed here and I could tell him.

Oh, and this is, in fact, Husbands. That’s the movie that these three guys came on and made total asses of themselves. You can find it online as “The Worst Show Dick Cavett Ever Did.” They goofed around for the whole time and did very funny things, like taking your shoes off and smelling their feet. Afterwards, John Cassavetes himself chewed them out mercilessly and said, “You have just unsold most, if not all, of the tickets to this movie,” and they were like three kids being smashed with criticism. It was sort of sad to say, but it didn’t make up for how crappy they were on the show. Are you taking it home? Oh. Sure.

Wow. Oh, you probably wonder why I’m saying that. David Lean Directs Noël Coward. Whose good idea was that? I hope they were well paid. And the films, if you’re wondering, are In Which We Serve, This Happy Breed. Beautiful. Blithe Spirit, of course, and Brief Encounter. I bet you’ve never made movies that good.
And of course, I see my film here. And it’s the first time I’m seeing Killer of Sheep on Blu-ray. And I look forward to showing it to all my friends who hadn’t seen it. Be something to talk about.
Dodes’ka-den. It’s one of my favorite films. Every chance I… have, I would watch this film. It was such a wonderful film. It’s such a treat to watch and see. Dodes’ka-den. Yes.

A Day in the Country by Renoir. I like his… his choreograph– I mean his… the way he arranged characters. And when he was living in California, he lived quite near UCLA at the time and I would sneak past his house hoping that I would see him out on the street or something like that, but never had an opportunity. Anyway, he was one of my favorite filmmakers. I like his acting and I like the way he presents a community and how he dramatizes it. Another good filmmaker. You can learn a great deal from him.

Il Posto. You got all the best films here. Ermanno Olmi. I remember I was at a… I used to work for Chasin-Park, which was an agency, a talent agency, and some Italian producers came in and I was really excited about– “Oh, some Italians are coming in, so we can talk about Ermanno Olmi,” but it was a… a real sort of… a disappointment because they were very commercial, and… Ermanno Olmi was making films that were really relevant, but not exactly commercial. So he wasn’t very popular among producers who were out to make a lot of money, as opposed to creating a cinema that speaks to humanity. And… he’s one of my favorite Italian filmmakers. And filmmakers period.

One of my favorite film noir pieces. Double Indemnity is this film. It’s really a suspenseful film. I met Fred MacMurray. Because I used to work for this agency that handled him. I had to take scripts over to him and people like that, have them sign it, and that was my job. I was like a messenger. And he was such a nice person. A very talented actor. Good stuff.

And here I have Melvin Van Peebles, who I met years ago after he did… The Story of a Three Day Pass, I forget– it’s been so long. And he inspired a lot of filmmakers, people of color, and I remember him coming to UCLA and speaking to the class, and it was such a treat. And… I’m glad you have this film. I’m glad I can take this away. The classic.

film_title: Three Revolutionary Films by Ousmane Sembène
catalog_title: Three Revolutionary Films by Ousmane Sembène
quote: Ousmane Sembène… Ousmane. And Emitaï is one of my favorite of his films. And… thinking about colonialism, and how they control all aspects of the people that they’ve colonized, and they’re forcing these Africans to go into brutal war for them and die for their cause. Fine film. Tragic, of course. But it’s still… it says a lot about humanity. It’s one of my favorite of Ousmane Sembène.
box_set_name: Three Revolutionary Films by Ousmane Sembène

quote: Okay, do we have… Ingmar Bergman? This is too much. This is very great. This is… The Seventh Seal I liked. I remember that. The Magician… Virgin Spring. You can’t go wrong with this. All of them. Persona was a big hit. Look at the body of work that he did. I look forward to sitting at home watching that on a rainy night or whatever. Or a hot night. Whatever night. Be special. Well, I can’t thank you enough.

The first I’m gonna pick is this one right here: Harlan County, USA, which is an incredible documentary by Barbara Kopple. And I picked this one because, yeah, I love it. It’s terrifying and heart-expanding. And it is about the power of collective action and the importance of union membership. Two things that I believe in very much. We have a lot more power than we think. There are those who don’t want us to use that power, and they try to convince us that we’re powerless and they can do a pretty good job. Watch this film and see that they’re lying and own your power. So Harlan County, USA, that’s going in my sack.

film_title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (Jacques Demy box)
catalog_title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (Jacques Demy box)
quote: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg by Jacques Demy. I have seen this movie… I do not know how many times. But to be able to make a perfect 92-minute gem like this. Oh, I should also say it’s fully sung through. It is technically an opera. There is no speaking in this film. Catherine Deneuve. Look at her. Are you kidding me? So you get to look at her. If you like guys, it’s got Nino Castelnuovo in it, and he’s just as beautiful as she is. You can swap back and forth: who do you like better on a particular viewing? They’re both so beautiful. And this film is not cotton candy, although the pink in it is cotton-candy colored. And the use of colors in this thing are bananas. Probably the most amazing… I mean, it was like this and then you had to wait a while and then you had Kieślowski, and since then nobody’s been doing color like them. To make something that even flirted with the quality of this would just be… is a life’s work. You can spend your life doing that.

This is three films that André Gregory and Wallace Shawn made together. But the only one I’m featuring right now is Vanya on 42nd Street, simply because it was a very important film for me. It just blew my mind because it was the filming of the rehearsal of a play. Like, Wallace Shawn and André Gregory and friends had been rehearsing Uncle Vanya by Chekhov for years. I don’t know if it was even towards the goal of necessarily performing it. They’re just kind of workshopping it. So they did that. Then Louis Malle heard about it and was like, “Why don’t I film you doing this?” And so he films them. And so it’s like a story within a story within a story. So you know it’s not real. And I love films that are open about their artifice. Like, these are not… This is not a Russian landowner. It’s totally Wallace Shawn, who you saw get off the subway and walk into the theater and do the thing. But you immediately forget that because you’re watching Chekhov being directed by André Gregory being directed by Louis Malle. So you’ve got all their stink on it. And it’s just a beautiful, beautiful film that really taught me a lot about storytelling.

Not the whole Before Trilogy, but the final one. Sharon Horgan and I were writing the first season of the show Catastrophe, and my wife said, “Let’s watch Before Midnight.” And so she puts it on and watching I’m like, “Oh my God.” As soon as it was over, I called Sharon, I was like, “Put down your quill. We have to retool everything because the ultimate work of art about a marriage has just been made, and if we think that we’re gonna play in that arena, then we got to study this playbook.” Before Midnight is such a spectacular, horribly accurate picture of a marriage. It made me love being married even more than I already did. Even though people who aren’t married would watch this and be like, “That looks awful.” But don’t… You’re not supposed to be happy. Being married isn’t about– No one’s happy, whether single or married. It’s not about that. But the whole world that can be contained in a marriage is accurately captured in this masterpiece by Richard Linklater and Ethan Hawke and Julie Delpy. I revere the three of them individually. Put ’em together? I mean…

I’ma start over here in this section, with this one. It’s the second movie I remember seeing, or the third movie I remember seeing. And my dad took me to see it. I was… I was very young. I was probably about six years old. I saw it at the Grand Lake Theatre in Oakland, California, projected on film. And this movie changed my life. In my opinion, Spike Lee has made two of the best film openings that I’ve ever seen. One of them is this one. The other one is Do the Right Thing, with Rosie Perez. The way that so many people meet Malcolm X is through audio, through recordings of his speeches. That was how I’d first hear him as a kid. And he juxtaposes it with footage of the assault of Rodney King by members of the Los Angeles Police Department. And he juxtaposes that with an American flag that burns into the shape of an X. And somehow that’s not the best part of the movie. You know, it’s just such an incredible movie. Just loaded with talent and incredible performances. This film will live forever. So I’ma take this one home and add it to my personal collection.

This is Love Jones. It’s a perfect movie. I’m a hopeless romantic, as you can see from some of these movies I’m gonna grab. The performances from Larenz Tate and Nia Long in this movie are exceptional. The chemistry is off the charts. The intricacy of it. The film’s got an incredible dynamic range, like, of scenes of a lot of talking. There’s scenes with none. And shout out to the city of Chicago, man, which is gonna bring me to this other one.

It’s also set in Chicago. Where are you? This is Thief by Michael Mann. And I’m going to grab another movie… that I think has to be in conversation with this. All right, so this is Thief by the great Michael Mann. And this is Following by Christopher Nolan, who’s a mentor of mine. And I do think that, in observing Chris’s movies, I think that Michael Mann is a big influence. And you can feel it quite a bit when you look at this film. If you haven’t seen this movie, holy fucking shit, this movie. What I heard– A rumor about this film is this is the movie that made wetdowns a thing. A wetdown, if y’all don’t know, is when you got enough money to– I mean, this is probably, like, a waste of water. But when you got enough money to have a truck wet your streets down. And what it does is it makes the… for nighttime photography, it makes the streets reflective. And the performance of the villain in this, and how the performance is captured – you’re slowly peeling back the onion about how dangerous and how evil this dude is. Michael Mann just did a brilliant job.

And this is Following by Christopher Nolan, who’s a mentor of mine. And I do think that, in observing Chris’s movies, I think that Michael Mann is a big influence. And you can feel it quite a bit when you look at this film. Which takes me to this. This is my guy. I’ve come to know him, I’ve come to know his wife. Amazing people. First and foremost, they’re just lovers of cinema and lovers of family. The world is richer because they’re making movies. And it’s just brilliant because it’s obviously the most indie you’ll ever see… Mr. Nolan, he finding his way. A lot of the Christopher Nolan trademarks are here in this movie. So it’s great, if you coming up, to get a little taste of this.

When I was coming up as a young man, there were two filmmakers that were making movies at the same time, that were in conversation with each other. That was Spike Lee and that was John Singleton, rest in peace. Both of those filmmakers mean the world to me, as an American filmmaker, as an African-American filmmaker. And their movies taught me things. Some time ago, the same thing was happening in the country of Japan. You have Akira Kurosawa and you have another gentleman named Yasujiro Ozu that were epic filmmakers, making films at the same time. And making very different types of films. Much has been said about this film. What I think he was the greatest at, in terms of things I’ve learned from watching his films, is the art of blocking. The other thing he’s great at is poetic fallacy. Choosing when to use wind and rain is just insane.

Ozu. Ozu is a filmmaker who… He didn’t give a shit about a lot of rules. Most importantly, a rule we spent a lot of time learning about, which is the 180-degree line. This is an imaginary line between conversations. Because film is a two-dimensional, visual art form, if you move the camera across this imaginary line, what will happen in the editorial process is it will look like characters are looking in different directions, which can sometimes be confusing or can put an audience in a state of unease. Ozu didn’t give a fuck about the line. He would jump it all the time. He also was very famous for shooting doorways. But what I’m going to talk to you about with Ozu right now, in this movie, is his capacity for the most emotional endings you’ll ever see in your life. Holding your hand throughout a story and making you fall in love with characters and then just ripping your heart out at the end of the movie in a way that oftentimes leaves you sobbing. But also in a way that makes you question everything that you saw before. Late Spring is a great example of this. Late Spring was the first Ozu movie I ever saw. I saw it before I had children, obviously, I was in my twenties. And it’s a story about a father and a daughter at its heart. Watching this movie, along with making my first film, Fruitvale Station, made me realize that I wanted to be a father.

This is Devil in a Blue Dress by a hometown hero, Carl Franklin. So, this movie’s a masterpiece. Massive influence on my latest picture, Sinners. But it’s a Great Migration movie. It’s about Los Angeles, but the characters are all from Houston. And it’s just beautiful, man. It’s a Walter Mosley adaptation. You know, my admiration for this film has only deepened. But it’s just an incredible… piece of cinema, and an incredible film noir.

Love & Basketball by the great Gina Prince-Bythewood. So look, me and my producing partner and wife, Zinzi Coogler, we both met as athletes. We met on a track field. And… yeah, this movie is about two athletes falling in love with each other, dipping in and out of each other’s lives in their pursuit of athletic greatness. I can’t look at this movie and not see us. I can’t look at this movie and not think about where I was when I first saw it. I was in high school. It just leans into the romance– I love the ending of this movie, the ending of this movie just puts a lump in your throat. Who’s watching who and what professional– I mean, look, this is… This is the one. You know what I’m saying? This is going in the bag.

This was my number one film that I wanted to grab. I haven't seen A Brighter Summer Day, but I'm a huge fan of Yi Yi. And I love Edward Yang's work. I think that he has maybe the greatest eye for composition of any director ever. I just love the stillness of his movies and just the way that the shots are composed and their so kind of melancholic and profound and quiet ways. And yeah, I was told by many people that I needed to also watch A Brighter Summer Day. So I'm very, very excited to watch this probably as soon as I get home.

Still Walking. I'm a huge fan of Kore-eda. The tone of his films and the pacing and the performances are always so incredible. And there's just this real, tactile, kind of naturalistic feeling in all of his movies that I find to be very haunting and stick with you for a really long time. So I'm a big fan of his, and he's one of those directors– I want to see every movie that he's ever made. One of my favorite directors. Very, very excited to check out this film.

This is my final pick. It's The Spirit of the Beehive, which is both a great band and film. This young, six-year-old actress, that, yeah, has these eyes that looks like it's seen maybe 40 different lifetimes. They just have such great depth. And her performance is stunning. It's a beautiful, haunting film, and I can't wait to revisit it because I remember loving it so much. And yeah, I'm excited to add it to my collection.

I do want to start, actually, with this incredible Fellini box set. I came in here wanting to get I vitelloni because I… I saw that film for the first time a couple years ago at a Fellini retrospective in Eugene, Oregon. And I went with my two friends Cordell Stetson and Carrie Mann who really introduced me to film at a young age. I remember having a Eugene Weekly that we tore out and them making me this amazing, comprehensive list of films that I should check out. But when I went and saw I vitelloni, it felt like a really special moment because it's kind of about a band of… slackers that are stuck in a small town, and I feel like that was very much who we were as teenagers. And I think that watching movies was kind of our way of getting out of that small town. And I feel like it's a really underrated Fellini movie, and it's really, really great. And this is an incredible box set that looks like it's filled with records, but is filled with films. So I'm very, very excited about this.

film_title: Martin Scorsese's World Cinema Project No. 1
catalog_title: Martin Scorsese's World Cinema Project No. 1
quote: I just got back from Korea. I lived there for all of 2024 to study the language for my second book that I'm working on. And to completely immerse myself in the language, I decided that I was only going to consume content that was in the Korean language. So I only listened to Korean music and I only watched Korean films. And there's something there called the Grand Bell, which is like their… I don't know, Cannes or their Oscars. And so I wanted to watch all of the films that had won Best Picture in the Grand Bell and learn a lot more about Korean cinema, which is so fantastic. And I'm surprised I never got around to watching it, but this movie called The Housemaid by Kim Ki-young. Yeah, it's pretty much any one of your favorite South Korean directors, they probably will have said that they were influenced by this film because it's very famously one of the greatest South Korean films of all time. And it's a part of this Martin Scorsese World Cinema Project box set, which seems to have a bunch of really fantastic films that I'm sure are all really great. And so, yeah, I'm excited to finally watch Kim Ki-young's The Housemaid.
box_set_name: Martin Scorsese's World Cinema Project No. 1

quote: So let’s start off with something very artsy-fartsy and kind of hard to watch. We’ve got The Mirror or Zerkalo by Tarkovsky. This is great. There are, like, tableaus and vignettes in this movie that are so gorgeous. There’s this scene where she’s washing her hair and then the whole crumbling apartment just– You gotta watch it. It’s really beautiful. Tarkovsky really knows what the fuck he’s doing.

Okay. I’m gay! So here’s the thing about being gay, sometimes it gets sad. And I watched All of Us Strangers probably not at the best time. I think the dopamine level in my brain was, like, subzero. And I did one of those things where you cry so much it gets gross-slash-“Should I go to the ER?” I was like… You know, call me basic. I know I’m… I’m on the Paul Mescal bandwagon. I’m on it. I’m on that hayride. And Andrew Scott is devastating. It’s a really beautiful, poignant kind of ghost story. Doesn’t really make a lot of sense. Doesn’t matter. But it’s just so beautiful, and you just… When Paul’s at the door with the whiskey, just like, “Let him inside. Let him in!” But he doesn’t. Anyways.

Belle de Jour’s a fabulous movie. I love one of Luis Buñuel’s other movies: Le Charme discret de la bourgeoisie or The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie. But this is great. So, Catherine Deneuve, so hot, she plays a bored housewife who becomes a hooker. So many little things from this movie stick out, like there’s a guy at the brothel who tries to pay with, like, coupons or something. And I’ll never forget, the madam is like, “Non, ça ne marche pas ici. De l’argent!” And I always just say that in my mind: “That doesn’t work here. Give me money.” There’s some fun BDSM kind of fantasy stuff. And she’s just so… She’s just so gorgeous. Catherine Deneuve. Okay.

Pina. The thing about Pina Bausch is that her dance theater troupe was kind of like… kind of like a cult, but in a good way. It’s a group of people that were so intensely committed to a singular vision from her, who was revolutionary. She’s really, really, really changed the whole game in terms of dance and dance theater. I got to see two of her pieces in Brooklyn Academy of Music before she passed away, so I’m really glad about that. Long pieces. Two and a half hours. Hard for Gen Z.

Now, anybody who loves film knows that if there’s a really, really difficult problem that you have to solve or an obstacle that you have to get through, cross-dressing is the number one most effective way to do that. I’ve found that in my life to be true and so has Dustin Hoffman in this classic, Tootsie. Dustin Hoffman plays a struggling actor who can’t get a gig, so he tries to get a gig on a soap opera playing this woman. He goes in drag and of course he gets it. And there’s even– One of the older cast members, who’s kind of a pervert, falls in love with her. And it’s this like… Did everybody have glaucoma? It’s, like, crazy but it’s just so well done. And Teri Garr. Tootsie.

And here we go. Happiness, Todd Solondz. This is probably the most fucked-up movie you’ll ever see in your life. I’m so happy that Criterion has it because I couldn’t find it anywhere. It’s not just a black comedy. This is like a rotten black comedy. It’s people at their worst, at their dazzlingly worst. And it’s just like an accumulation of human shit piling up on top… It’s just so fabulous.

Polyester, John Waters. Oh my God, look at that. Look at that cover. Romance. Francine Fishpaw. Tab Hunter. (Gay.) And then… It’s got a whole bunch of stuff. I think this was the one where the daughter gets in trouble for dancing at school. The mom says, “You don’t dance at school, do you?” She’s like, “For a quarter I will!” And it’s just so funny. It’s just so great. Fucking A. So Polyester. The classic.
And I’m going to boost this one because, like I said before, I do happen to be extremely gay. Viciously so here in New York. Querelle. Or “Querally.”
Oh, I have La ciénaga. This is a great Argentine film that you of course know very well, and that I think that I'm taking home.

film_title: To Be or Not to Be
catalog_title: To Be or Not to Be
quote: And here, there's one that I remember that I have to take too, that is To Be or Not to Be. I remember there was a student of mine in Buenos Aires, a Spanish student of mine in Buenos Aires, that he was a big fan of Lubitsch. And I haven't seen Lubitsch at that time, or I've seen one, so I was very ignorant even being a professor. And he gave me a DivX with all of his, of many of his films, and I put it, I started watching one and I watched the whole DVD in one night. And I remember this, the experience of watching To Be or Not to Be, and I thought that the movie was just like beginning and it ended, and it was amazing how the flow, no? There was something about the flow of it that surprised me. I was like absolutely captivated by it. I do films around Shakespeare that I say that they're not adaptations, and so one and I call this sort of genre that I think it for myself alone, that is this the Shakespeariads, no? They're not adaptations, they're Shakespeariads, that I drink from Shakespeare and do my own thing. And somehow I feel that there's other films that do the same, like To Be or Not to Be. It's not an adaptation. Of course, it's a masterpiece.

Another Renoir, let's be, let's have a criteria here. A Day in the Country. This that they have on, it's, I don't know if it's crazy to say that it's as good as the film, but you have all the shots, all the takes that they've done with the clap, and with you have like little children doing the clap. And you somehow you see how they wait till the clouds leave the sun, and so they do the, they start with the shot. And it's all edited as the film is, but of course with all the shots, with the entire take.

catalog_title: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir

And I especially like the, I like them all, but The Golden Coach, if you've seen it and you've been through that ending, it's pretty chilling. And I'm guessing that this is not going to be the only Renoir I will be putting here.

quote: I have to take the Rohmer's Six Moral Tales. Something about how he talks about words, how he has written about words and people talking, and how he's not afraid of doing films with people talking so much. And he's showing that words are photogenic in a way, no? That words are part of the, I like the perspective that I have from here.

So yeah, one more, let's try to find it. I have, I don't know if you've seen Family Plot by Alfred Hitchcock, there's a moment in the end that she finds a diamond that is hidden, and I feel that I'm doing the same thing, but with Jean Vigo. So she does like this with a finger. Here, Vigo, yeah. I'm even putting only the L'Atalante music in order to cheer my day up, so I think that this will make my day.

Naked. Okay. This is one of my favorites. This is David Thewlis at his best. Mike Leigh. I see there’s two editions. I guess I’ll just take both. Such a crush on him from this movie. And Katrin Cartlidge, who’s so amazing, who passed away. But, yeah, don’t watch that, like, if… you know, like, if you pick up a skater, let’s say, in Tompkins Square Park and… I’ll hold the movie again so it has context. You know, you pick up a skater in Tompkins Square Park, you bring them home. Then the morning after, you think, “I think this guy’s really gonna get it. They’re gonna love Naked.” You put it on, you realize it’s, I don’t know, 2020. They don’t have the attention span for that. So watch it alone.
Hoop Dreams. This is a hell of a picture.
That’s fun. Heaven Can Wait. I really always thought that showbiz was going to be more like this. They had a good time in these.
Oh, La strada, of course.

Naked Lunch, that’s a hit. This is good, especially if, you know, you’re trying to figure out if you’re in a good or bad relationship. Remember, it’s not quite so bad that there’s a… Is it an apple placed on the eye and a gunshot? That never ends well for Judy Davis.
Umberto D. Okay, there we go. You need to have some classics in the mix.
Oh, I’m in this one, Uncut Gems. I’m a voice or something. Safdie tried to get me. And I had a real part in this. Said I’m a voice on the telephone.
Devil in a Blue Dress. It’s a hot film.
By Raging Bull. Okay.

Town Bloody Hall. And this one is really great. I had the opportunity to direct the brilliant Jacqueline Novak’s comedy special, Get on Your Knees, at Town Hall. And I had the opportunity to hang out with Chris Hegedus, who was D. A. Pennebaker’s wife and collaborator frequently, and we based a lot of the aesthetic on this, you know, Norman Mailer getting grilled by Germaine Greer and so on. The lo-fi nature of it.
Pickpocket. Is this Bresson? Let’s see. Yes. She gets it again.

And this is one of my favorite movies of all time: Sunday Bloody Sunday. This Schlesinger movie, who also, I guess, is Midnight Cowboy, right? But this movie is so fucking good. Peter Finch. Oh God, he’s good in this movie.
City Lights...
Pandora’s Box.

I think I’m about to have tits out, but let’s see what this adventure is about. Sweet Smell of Success. She’s going back down. ‘Cause James Wong Howe is the cinematographer of that and he’s my favorite cinematographer. So I’m going back. Come on, James, quick. I found it. You know what this is a little bit like? Go Fish. Because you gotta spot it and see it and then retain where it was.

catalog_title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling
quote: So, guys, Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling, written and directed by Richard Pryor. If you’re looking for a double feature, I’d strongly suggest pairing it with the Bob Fosse movie All That Jazz. These are two sides of my favorite coins, my favorite genre. They’re movies that, you know, they start in a hospital bed. And of course, our friend Gideon, he’s in that bed in that middle space and Jessica Lange is upstairs in the rafters, and “It’s showtime,” the movie begins. But it takes you back through his complicated life, and, well, my favorite, our dear friend Richard Pryor. Now, I wouldn’t say that this is a perfect film. But it is. It is a perfect film. I’m not sure if you know about the incident that the brilliant Richard Pryor went through, but, well, he made a Fosse-esque extravaganza of it. And I’m really indebted to these two films for everything I’ve thought of since. So I love these two movies.

I’ll definitely do Pasolini, Trilogy of Life.
