film_title: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman
catalog_title: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman
quote: Then this, Rossellini starring Ingrid Bergman, is a collaboration. You must think, she was she made Casablanca, she was a star, yeah. And then she went to this communist, Catholic communist Rossellini to Italy and they make six movies together. Stromboli, there is one scene when Ingrid Bergman wants to leave the island and she seduced there a man who can bring her out. She's sitting with this guy at the beach and she's walking with her naked feet to his feet. This is such a seductive, sexual scene, I must say. And some years later, both make Journey to Italy, and I think it's about the end of their collaboration and the end of their love. But it's some it's often like this: when something is dying, you can feel for one moment all the enthusiasm of the start. You have to see all these movies.
box_set_name: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman

quote: Oh, Devi is by Satyajit Ray, is just so beautiful. It's one of the greatest films I've ever seen, I will tell you. It's about the wife of a of a man who kind of becomes like a goddess and it becomes it destroys her life, but it's also, but it kind of puts you into a trance almost. It's like really one of the most powerful cinematic experiences I've ever had, and she's just incredible in it. Yeah.

So, The Color of Pomegranates by Sergei Parajanov is just like a unabashedly poetic film that's ethnography, cinema, poetry, painterly, surreal, but rooted, really rooted I think in Armenian culture. Beautiful historical film, like not historical film in the sense of being accurate maybe historically, it's mythic. It's a mythic film. And I remember seeing it when I was on tour with a with The Cherry Orchard in Soviet, what was then Soviet Georgia, and just being just being astonished by it. This was in 1986 or something. Anyway, beautiful film.

A Short Film About Killing, I don't know how to describe it exactly, but it puts you into the occasion of sin along with the person in the movie. It's like a pure film, but very disturbing. There are two films, the two most disturbing, it's one of the more disturbing films I've seen, A Short Film About Killing and Salo, which I was, and by Pasolini, and then the other one was Repulsion, which I couldn't talk for like 24 hours after I saw them in college.

Also, you know what's also great, who made most wonderful movies of that kind was Miloš Forman. Loves of a Blonde by Miloš Forman is an absolutely wonderful, wonderful movie. Tonally it's just so wonderfully free and specific, and very much about a female character, which I loved, and it's really about romance, you know, and it's classic New Wave cinema as well, but there is something about the Middle European slightly depressive humor that I just find so appealing. It's like you can just feel the sadness in the humor.

So, Children of Paradise by Marcel Carné, Les Enfants du Paradis, oh my god, this is I think maybe my favorite movie ever. It's poetic realism as it, but it's also so deeply human, and the woman, Arletty, who play who plays the sort of, who's loved by several different men, is such a wonderfully sad, knowing, wise, sexy, liberated creature. And yet you completely believe that you're in 18th century France, which is really hard to do. I mean, I and I feel like unlike most period films, it doesn't come with its own time. I mean, like you really feel like you, somehow they managed to transport you into the into the period. And it's like funny and sort of wistful, and also the crowd scenes are incredible. The beautifully, beautifully orchestrated crowd scenes, and costumes, and the textures, and the patina of all of the design is really extraordinary. There's something about that that I find very compelling. But the character of the mime is so wonderful, and it's a sort of, it's almost also a philosophy of life in this film, you know, a kind of forgiving.

So my first film is Alex Cox's Sid & Nancy. This one's incredible, and of course, like, you know, Alex must have been a punk. You know, you watch Repo Man, you see his influences throughout his career. So this is my first one.

My second is gonna be this one here, Maîtresse, which I think is a really incredible film by Barbet Schroeder. The best way to describe this film is kind of like what happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object. Like, you have this dominatrix that, through some bizarre like home invasion situation, starts dating this giant ogre of a man. And it just sort of becomes about, you know, despite the fact that that he has this physical prowess, that she has a psychological prowess. So the film's always kind of posing the question, like, you know, who's wearing the pants in this relationship? And, without ruining the ending, just to see where they're driving together at the end, well, it's insane. It's just completely demented.

film_title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
catalog_title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
quote: Okay, I, I mean, you've got me, you've got me stuck between whether I want the DVD version or the Blu-ray version of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, because this I think was the first Criterion DVD that I got in high school. And I remember because it has the little removable outer part of it, which I thought was just an incredible way to kind of showcase Ralph Steadman's work without, you know, without putting the print directly just over it. But, you know what? I'll pick the Blu-ray. You might as well live in the 2020s and embrace the formats.

All right, my next pick is going to be Medium Cool, because I haven't seen it, but I love Robert Forster. He was often overlooked, it always felt like he was in a lot of B-movies. Obviously, you know, Tarantino gave his career another surge with Jackie Brown, but I've always seen clips of this and it looks pretty incredible, so let's check it out.

My next film is David Byrne's True Stories. I, I grew up in Texas, true story. There's very few films that really capture kind of the, the banality and, and the beauty of, of rural Texas, especially in that time frame. It kind of strikes that same chord as something like, you know, like when you watch King of the Hill and you're like, well, you kind of got to be there, gotta be from there to get the joke. And this film really does a phenomenal job of that.

Talk about a music movie. You know, this is, this is an all-time favorite, Jarmusch's Mystery Train. I don't know, I have a strange connection to this film because I used to live in a college town that had a train that would kind of pass through it in the middle of the night, and I was dating somebody at the time that was really obsessed with blues music. So I would kind of be nodding off, you know, listening to Skip James or something, I would just kind of hear that train roaring in the background, and I feel like this film really kind of captures that, that eeriness. You know, I love that in the middle of the night, you know, three people have the same encounter with this one song on the radio. You know, I, I love it when people incorporate like radio as like diegetic audio in a scene. I think it's great, so this one's going in the bag.

This is another all-time fave. This is a Felipe Cazals film called Canoa: A Shameful Memory. And it's interesting because I remember, I think I first saw it in a Mexican horror film programming block, and they included this despite the fact that it's not supernatural. It's actually based on a true story, basically, you know, this, this town that was controlled by this priest who convinced everybody that these three backpacking students were actually subversives from the city that were there to protest, and the three of them wound up basically being lynched. And it's a really intense story that kind of occasionally breaks from the narrative to do this kind of like documentary-style interview with the characters, but it's really amazing the way that it kind of drums up tension. Yeah, I could talk about this all day.

I think my last pick will be Wings of Desire. I remember I saw this movie in high school and my dad had this really beautiful comment about it, where we were watching Peter Falk in that scene where he can't see the angel, but he's talking to him and he's explaining how, like, you know, it's like, oh, you don't know what it's like, you know, you have a nice, you have a cup of coffee and you rub your hands for warmth, see, and you smoke a cigarette. And he's like just basically explaining what it's like to be a human. And my dad, I remember he just, he just kind of, he leaned back and he was like, "Oh yeah, this is what it's all about," you know? And as somebody that I wouldn't necessarily like label as a cinephile, like when a movie is able to just convey a simple idea to someone and, and it just connects on this fundamental level, I think it's done its job.
Okay, I will start by choosing Watermelon Woman. The way this plays with Black identity, Black lesbian identity, what it is to be sort of a Black cinema lover. Very fun movie.

I have to do this. This is like a left-field pick for me, but Bresson I'm starting to get into, so I want to take L'argent. I've seen it once, embarrassingly on a plane, so I want to take this to like properly watch it on the big screen.

A Brighter Summer Day. Yes, let's go. This movie is crazy. What do I say about this movie? I sat for four hours on a Sunday in Metrograph here in New York, watching this and just left feeling like nothing's the same. I mean, this is like a tale of like youth, and finding yourself at like its finest, I think.

Claudine. I just saw a poster for this outside. James Earl Jones. Looks amazing. "A bittersweet, big-hearted celebration of family and community set to a sunny soul soundtrack by Curtis Mayfield." You got me.

Okay, La ciénaga, a game changer. Criterion put me on to it. I would not have known about Lucrecia Martel, the incredible, without Criterion. I don't even know what to—look at that cover image. Like for me, growing up in Georgia with a lot of green around me, with a lot of nature, and this sort of sultry, humid, hot, slow, blood-boiling summer type of image. Watching this, sort of strange Argentinian family's like summer house crumble as the kids are running around and the dogs are barking and the wine glass is spilled. I, I don't know if I want to find myself in that situation, but I connect to it somehow.

The Music Room by Satyajit Ray. A aristocrat who has a opulent music room, who used to show everyone all of his amazing riches and throw these opulent parties. Really a story about indulgence gone wrong, cautionary for our times. And you know what, I want to like do something with this. I don't know what that means, but when I first watched it I had this impulse to be like, how do I, how do I expand or think about these themes now? I mean, amazing stuff.
Oh yeah, Love & Basketball. I'm so embarrassed I haven't seen it. That's it, that's all I'm going to say. I'm going to run home, see it now. Don't, bully me.

Yeah, Punch-Drunk Love. Okay, boom. This movie and all the work of Paul Thomas Anderson. I mean, I feel like I'm speaking on behalf of so many people when I talk about him. Paul, if you're watching this, I'm in the long list of people who would love to have lunch with you, because of this movie and everything else you've made. What a fun, dark, revelational—like this is a movie about finding love against all odds. I love it.

3 Women, Altman, who I discovered from my, like, everyone's hero and favorite, Paul Thomas Anderson, who cited Altman as a favorite. And then when I saw this, I was just like, what a strange and amazing movie. Emotional convergence, jealousy, envy, love, lust, friendship. I, I love this movie.

Okay, Garrett Bradley, Time. Shout out Garrett Bradley. I feel so connected to this filmmaker's voice, the way that she's sort of making movies, and artworks that sort of think through, gaps, missing images in sort of Black American life. What we haven't seen, what we don't know, what's lost in the archive. And then what I also love about Garrett is that she lives in New Orleans. She's working closely with sort of, oftentimes, people from the South, and being from Atlanta, that really connects to me. Love, love her work.
These I'm taking for Dad, Notorious and Rebecca. My dad raised me, on Hitchcock. This always hits, and I'm going to bring it right to him.
These I'm taking for Dad, Notorious and Rebecca. My dad raised me, on Hitchcock. This always hits, and I'm going to bring it right to him.

Ozu box set. Nick Tanis, Language of Film, Ozu. When I moved to New York as an NYU film student, talk about getting shown this in the NYU theater with Nick's laser pointer just dissecting how amazing every single frame that Ozu does, is put together, how intentional it all is, how the framing tells the story. I just didn't realize movies could look like this. I didn't realize they could be so poignant and quiet and subtle and powerful at the same time. It's amazing to be reminded by Ozu and by so many filmmakers that you don't have to do much photographically to, to, to say everything.

film_title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
catalog_title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
quote: One that I is here that is obvious one, Mujeres al borde de un ataque de nervios de Almodóvar. Of course, this is like an all-time classic. This is super important and influential to me, yeah.

Yeah, so another thing that became super important for me when I was a teenager and I saw it for the first time is Cría cuervos from Carlos Saura. I think when you were like a child and you grew up in Spain under Francoism, I think you really identified fully with the way of looking at things of this child in the film. And if you haven't seen it, you really have to. It's amazing.

film_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
catalog_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
quote: My favorite Pasolini, I mean I think the one that I like the most is Salò. By the way, let's take it here. This is the one that I like the most even though it's the most difficult to watch. Making a film as a political project and at the same time like in taking care of each of the details in terms of performance and the visual language, I think it's an absolute masterpiece. Even though I have to say it's a film that I have barely seen fully from the beginning to the end, but it's always when I have questions, this is the film that I came back to very often.

So yeah, another one that I want to take is Antonioni, Deserto Rosso. So I saw the full retrospective of Antonioni when I was 20, and that completely changed my way of seeing things, especially I have to say because Antonioni has this very kind of heterosexual binary way of looking at things, but when the question is how to look at a space, how to look at architecture, that is really like a, you know, amazing, and I think it's like a must-see for anyone that is doing cinema, that is just like walking around in a city to see things differently.
Pasolini became super important when thinking about people that have adapted crazy things, crazy stories, like you know, taking the challenge of adapting Greek theater or Decameron, things like that.

Oh yeah, something else that I have always loved and that I think it came back a little bit with the kind of playfulness and childish way of looking at the world that you can see in Orlando is Tati. So yes, I think this is almost like a visual therapy for the mind. Yes.

Also when making Orlando, I was thinking about authors that have made films like letters that are being written to someone. And so Chris Marker, that was for me like a fundamental. It belongs for me to the films that are made by what I would call philosophers in a sense. So he really finds a completely new form for saying what he wants to say, and it's full of poetry.
12 Angry Men, directed by one of my mentors, Sidney Lumet. It's incredible. The editing, the performances, woo, to die for.

Oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, I didn't have to go too far for this one. You ready? Boom. Cooley High. It's like a little bit of like my old school kind of flavor. Chicago, 1964. It wasn't shot in 1964, just so you know, don't be confused, but catches that era. Cooley High. Okay, moving on, moving on, moving on.

film_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
catalog_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
quote: Dr. Strangelove. Stanley Kubrick, okay? The first time I heard about Stanley Kubrick, I want to tell you, people, was a movie called Spartacus. Can you believe that Stanley Kubrick came in four weeks before shooting that movie and he shot that movie? And he didn't want any credit for it, and it was one of the most amazing movies. But this movie right here, Peter Sellers, wow, George C. Scott, what, you know, James Earl Jones. I mean, all these guys when they were they were young, they were coming into their prime. But this is a great movie. Gave me something to think about.

The Ballad of Gregorio Cortez, with someone who I highly look up to in my industry, Edward James Olmos. First time I saw Edward James Olmos was on the stage here at the Winter Garden Theatre. I was a teenager. He was in the play called Zoot Suit, and Pachuco, his character, that became kind of like my spiritual guide. Great movie, a must-watch. I don't think it got all the recognition that it should have gotten, but I'm giving it the recognition by Luis Guzmán. Edward James Olmos, thank you for this. Love you, Papa.

Dreams come true, they can happen to you. Punch-Drunk Love. Let me tell you, Paul Thomas Anderson, thank you, thank you, thank you, brother, for putting me in some of the most genuine, beautiful movies that you have done. The thing about Punch-Drunk Love, it was the first time that I met Adam Sandler. I was like, what, Adam Sandler doing a Paul Thomas Anderson movie? Yep. After five minutes, you forget that it's Adam Sandler because you get into this guy Barry and his like six sisters and you just feel for him. Showed up every day, kept doing take after take after take after take after take. Made it happen. We became not friends, we became brothers. You know, I even I even shot a scene with his dog, Meatball. But what a great movie, what great performances. Philip Seymour Hoffman, thank you, brother. Thank you for your gift.

My favorite all-time film, I'm going to tell you, On the Waterfront. So I got to find it, I gotta find it, give me a second. Wow. Let me tell you something. When I was a kid growing up, every Sunday afternoon they used to show The Million Dollar Movie on Channel 9, and I would be in my room and my dad would be in the living room, and I would hear that theme song come on, cuz I knew like Million Dollar Movies was like the best of the best, the cream of the crop. And the first time I saw this movie, oh my God, I'm almost going to cry. First time I saw this movie, I was a kid and I watched the performance that Marlon Brando gave. Listen, overall cast in this movie was incredible, you know, the story, the directing, but man, Marlon Brando, oh man, this is beyond a must-see, okay? You got to run an IV and just hook this movie. This is unreal. But many, many years ago, I'm on Ventura Boulevard in Studio City, Saturday morning around 11:00. Me and my buddy Izzy were walking down the street, just talking. This guy comes out of this children's hair cutting place, and my buddy goes, "Yo, that's Marlon Brando." "Get out of here, Marlon Brando." "Bro, that was Marlon Brando." And I went up to him and I said, "Please forgive me, I'm not, I don't want to disturb you, I just wanted to tell you thank you, thank you for what you do." That's it. And as I start to walk away, he said, "Young man, excuse me." And I come back and I go, "Yes?" And he goes, he points at me, "And you do very fine work." He said that to me. Come on, man. On the Waterfront, people.
Eve's Bayou. I watched this so many years ago and plenty of times since. Such a, sensual, very textured film. I adore this film.

Ratcatcher. I'm pulling this one primarily for Small Deaths on the DVD. That short gave me permission to explore form in my own work. I really adore that short film. Also, there's this one shot of a cow's eye in that short that is just amazing.

The Piano Teacher. I remember the first time I watched this, I was just really struck by the viscerality. I'm really drawn to films that bring me into my body and this film really does that in a deep way. And again, it was a film that after I watched I was like, "Oh, you can do that in cinema too," you know? And I'm so, this is one I'm really grateful for.

Amores perros. Similar to Small Deaths, how this film plays with structure opened a doorway for me. And this is one of the ones pre-me knowing I wanted to be a filmmaker, but it really surprised me in the best ways.
Medicine for Melancholy. Got to shout out the legend that is Barry Jenkins. You know, it's only right to own a copy of this beautiful film.
Fat Girl. Talk about this girl.

Weekend. Such a beautiful, slow unwinding of a love story. So many of these films that I'm pulling are ones that stay with me after watching and that even years later I continue to think about, and I, I just really love this one.
Faya dayi by Jessica Beshir. I'm such a fan of her work and I haven't seen this one yet, so I'm pulling it to watch.
La ciénaga. So tactile, visceral. The blocking, oh, it's just, it's in your body. Love this one.
The Devil's Backbone. I watched this film, a few years ago. There are some images as I'm holding it that are sitting in my mind right now, and I, it's really one that I want to revisit.

You know, every time I come to New York City, I tend to think of films that in a way introduced me to New York City even before I came for the first time to this place. And one of them is one of my favorite films by Mr. Martin Scorsese, After Hours. This film taught me a lot about editing and camera setups.

Spirit of the Beehive is something is something special. The interesting thing about this film for me is that I have never owned a copy of it. It has only existed in my head, very much like it used to be in the past before home video. You could not keep a film, you could only keep a film in your head, the memory of it.

I'll just make sure I get Barry Lyndon because my two kids, they are getting to the age I think I can show them Barry Lyndon and they will, I'm sure, feel something because this is such an amazing film and I love the way it takes its time and the way the music comes in and the way you're completely floored by the images in the film. I know maybe so many people have reacted to this film the way I have, but that's pro- that probably explains why it's a classic.

Lost in America is a film that takes me back to 1985 when I saw it on VHS, which somehow disappeared. I'm not sure exactly how and why, but it's happens to some films, some very good films actually, because for every Barry Lyndon, which is has never gone out of fashion or style maybe except for the time it was released, but Lost in America is a film that made many friends, but somehow it disappeared. And I've always liked this film and I haven't seen it in more than 30 years, so I really want to see it.

Yeah, A Brighter Summer Day's I don't know, it's such a it's such a special film that I'm I'm not even sure what to say about this film because I might get emotional. And this now will be part of my collection.

Last one is this. It's probably many people's favorite pick also, Don't Look Now. And it's 50 years old now, which is hard to believe it is, this is 50 years old. And it looks more modern than the latest film out in the multiplex these days. I don't want to sound like a nostalgic, but I'm beginning to sound like a nostalgic.

catalog_title: The Signifyin’ Works of Marlon Riggs
quote: Just last year we did a retrospect- a full retrospective of Marlon Riggs at the Instituto Moreira Salles in Brazil where I am a programmer. And it was kind of sad when we sent back the files, and I'm happy that I now can invite some friends over and show them some of his films and videos.

film_title: Martin Scorsese’s World Cinema Project No. 3
quote: This is a special box with Martin Scorsese's World Cinema Project, and one of the films is Héctor Babenco's Pixote, which happens to be one of the great Brazilian films. It's an incredibly emotional film about the world, I think, and life in society. Pixote also makes me think of Nick Cave. Nick Cave is a big fan of Babenco's film.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: Agnès Varda is someone who, without really planning it, but during the editing stage of Pictures of Ghosts, Agnès Varda came to talk to me many times as an imaginary friend. And this happens many times when you're making a film. Sometimes you're in trouble and you just think of someone and you begin to remember his or her films. And Varda, in a way, she helped me get through the film, and I love her.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: Wanda, I mean obviously not just because it's about a woman trying to find her place, but also like I guess I'm always attracted to women who subvert their fate, but also wanderers. So Wanda will be in my yes pile for sure.

I mean I think Gene Tierney in Leave Her to Heaven is such a magnetic, tragic, but also moving character to watch. Movies where women are struggling with their monstrous sides is something that I find really inspiring. So we have Wanda and Gene Tierney hanging out.

film_title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
catalog_title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
quote: Céline Sciamma's Portrait of a Lady on Fire. I mean not only the performances in this film, but just the visual grammar. Like I don't know that many people who have used reverse shot, like shot-reverse-shot, in a way that it's like, sure, it's spatial and maybe it's geographical, it's supposed to be about like this person is here, this person is here, but in the context of the desire and connection and bond between these two women, looking at how a woman looks at another woman and then coming back. So that the shot-reverse-shot in this, I was just so like, it really struck me. Like the women singing around the fire as like witches. I consider myself a witch, so I think the celebrating of witchery and women coming together to celebrate each other and to see each other and to desire each other, it's a yeah, it's a yes.

film_title: Eight Hours Don’t Make a Day
catalog_title: Eight Hours Don’t Make a Day
quote: I mean I love all of Fassbinder's films and we have a bunch of them, but Eight Hours Don't Make a Day kind of like marks his melodrama, but it was like a soap opera and he has like this softness that is a little bit different from some of his other films. Yet it has this, I don't know, like critical and very awake perspective on German society as a whole. It's a tender film, but I think in like, in tenderness, actually in English that word tender means when you've been hurt. So when you go to a doctor someone says like, oh is that still tender? And that to me means kind of living in pain, which maybe sounds a little bit harsh, and I do feel like Eight Hours Don't Make a Day is a film that reminds us of the tenderness of like everyday life because it is about living, but it's also about accepting that we're living with this pain.

Oh, Flowers of Shanghai. That'll be, and I did see Exotica and I don't want to leave Atom Egoyan. I mean it's funny that I actually picked them together without meaning to, but just Hou Hsiao-hsien's just like the glow and the sort of like lingering, sort of like delirious camera work, but just like how he gets us close to these two characters and this sort of like impossible love.

And speaking of impossible love, just Atom's Exotica. I mean Atom is a filmmaker who both in his cinema, but in his personality, is someone who I find just really inspiring, and just I think the interest, his interest in damaged souls, something that I found really inspiring. This is a beautiful artwork for this.

Bo Widerberg's, I'm probably mispronouncing it, a Swedish filmmaker. The only film here that I've seen is Raven's End, and it's about this man who's trying to be a writer and he lives in a working-class setting. So I'm looking forward to the other films that he made because I think there is harshness, but a softness, like there's a sort of like a humanist approach and a way to look at things poetically, but also looking at things sort of straight up, like directly. So.

Wow, look at this one, Klute. This is actually connected to what we, the story we just finished telling. You should tell them about it. You should tell them about it. I think it's Jane Fonda's best performance, she's so arresting in it. This was a really big inspiration in its lighting design for A Murder at the End of the World, which we just finished making for FX. I love Pakula so much because I feel like he's one of the few filmmakers that it doesn't, there's no ego. You can put it in the bag. Oh, I can take it? I'm going to take one too. No, no, say what you were saying about Pakula. Just that I admire him because he, I don't ever feel like his ego is involved in the filmmaking. I feel like he is using exactly the shots that need to be there to communicate the story correctly, and there's something very effortless about that.

Time Bandits. So I haven't seen this. Okay, well, this is an interesting film. When I was a kid, my grandmother had just died and my mom and dad were very sad. I was sad too, but I was doing what I did when I felt sad, which was I was watching a TV in the hotel, and this movie, you know, like when you're a kid and in the old days you would flip channels, and this movie showed up and it was three-quarters of the way in, and this movie blew my mind. What was it about it that moved you so much? The freedom in the story. It's not limited by anything. And of course, time travel. Okay, so I need one too. I need to catch up with your childhood.

Oh, what are you seeing? Blood Simple. Yeah, get it for you. Oh my god, Frances McDormand. If you've not seen this movie, her performance in this at like, how old was she when she did this? Like really exciting also to see something that's not made for an enormous budget, but feels big. One of the things that we always use this film as a reference for is there's a wall of photographs, yeah, in Blood Simple. And all the photographs are real 35 millimeter prints they must have taken. And so whenever we make a movie these days, we say we've got to take real 35mm photographs. We actually show the scene where the 35 millimeter photographs are on the wall to our collaborators, and we're like, it has to feel this real. Because there's something about when people are captured in film grain, and you took the time to shoot it in a real location and then develop it and then print, it's not photoshopped, and then put it on a wall, and then when the camera is passing over that, you completely believe in the history of the characters and the world that led up to this moment.

Oh, Brit. Double Life. Oh, wow. So my parents showed me, The Double Life, maybe I was 13, they showed me The Double Life and I was blown away. And I, you know, I was really drawn to a female lead, to the metaphysical aspects, but also the groundedness and the beauty. It's so beautiful. And then though we would write something and call Irène Jacob and be like, do you want to come play with us because we love Double Life of Véronique and Red so much? And she did. She was amazing, yeah. And you know what's interesting about Irène is that as I get older and we get more practice, you realize more things. You realize that like this film works because the actress, the actor at the center of this has such a purity in their soul. It's a film that captures soul, really, and it's her soul that you're watching and you're so moved by. She was my favorite actress growing up. I never thought that we would spend time with her that way, but spending time with her is like watching the movie. There's no gap.

And it's kind of obviously shot, in the middle of all this realism outside, it's kind of obviously shot on a stage, because I'm sure they got it wrong and he has to cock his gun and appear perfectly, so they took it and did it on the artificial stage so the depth of field is really small. A photo of my stepdad's truck is in her phone right now. From one Carhartt and pickup to the next. Yeah.

And I found Down by Law. I love this movie. This is Jim Jarmusch? Yep. I haven't seen this one, but I, anything Tom Waits does, I'm going to watch. It's so good, and John Lurie's in this. Yes. This one too, here, right here. Great. One for you, one for you and one for me. Aw, our little besties Down by Law Blu-rays.

So the film I'm picking for Erica is actually her nickname, because I was called this by, if you watch this and spend any time with her, you will see it. We love you, Greta, we love you so much. I'm going to happily take this. I love this film and I love her performance.

I don't know why I'm going to get this for you. I didn't have the ability to like thoroughly look, and so I saw this and it just like immediately was like, this is a Lily movie, The Adventures of Baron Munchausen. This film is beautiful and wacky and wonderful and so imaginative, and so if you haven't seen it— I love all of those things. I think you're going to like this. I can't wait to watch it, thank you. Yay, okay, something you haven't seen.

catalog_title: Rolling Thunder Revue: A Bob Dylan Story by Martin Scorsese
quote: There is one more that I wanted to get in here, Rolling Thunder Revue. I've got to take one of these. You should, you got to. When I was filming Killers of the Flower Moon, actually, I had this just on all the time. It was always playing in the background, 'cause I wanted Marty, I wanted to just like, you know, be immersed in Marty, but I didn't want to be influenced by other narratives, so I just had— You mentioned that one. Yep, and Robbie's in this, and yeah.

La notte of Michelangelo Antonioni. It was one of my favorite of his film actually and I remember watching it on the screen on the big screen last time in '90s again in San Francisco Cinematheque and he was visiting that. He was there and he was sitting in the back of the screening room and I was like passing next to him and he was watching his films and he was crying, so that image will stay with me. So La notte.

Parasite, I think I don't have the video. Very revolutionary film. I think it tells about the modern world, about the contemporary world, something extremely disturbing and very, very true. So I would like that film to stay with me as also as a reminder who we are.
Very recent films, Perfect Days by Wim Wenders, which I have say I missed in the theaters and I wanted to see it in the theater and I missed it, so I will screen it in my private theater.

And Anatomy of a Fall, which was one of the most surprising movies and again the great example of women director's point of view, and we have more and more like powerful and very outspoken women directors and that is good. And I feel a bit like when I was talking to Agnès Varda, she was telling that she is the mother of those directors and I will say she's maybe grandmother of those directors and I can be mother.

My last pick will be about the film which I'm rewatching practically any time I'm preparing the film, and especially I did it on the Green Border, and that is the Diamonds of the Night by Jan Němec, one of the auteurs of the absolutely wonderful Czech New Wave, who unfortunately was forced to immigrate and he never achieved the power when working in the West of his early film, but that is a absolute masterpiece. But also it has incredibly long shot when two young men, two boys who escaped from the transportation to the concentration camp, they are running through the forest and through the valley, and it was before drones and kind of the, you know, incredible cranes. It was just made with such a energy and talent and the innovation, personal innovation of the filmmakers, and it's so effective and so incredibly engaging that, as I said, I rewatch it before any film I'm doing.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: So first I will pick, it will be the box, very heavy one, of Agnès Varda. Two films of her which I was watching as a teenager in Warsaw made such an impact on me that I can say that it's also because of her that I became a filmmaker. One it was Cléo from 5 to 7, but second one was the revelation to me and till now I'm advising it to the young filmmakers and especially women filmmakers to watch and to see how it is possible to say so much with such a little, little means. That is Le Bonheur, Happiness. It's my favorite. I hope that I'm following her path.

quote: So I saw this and I'm so excited Criterion did this, La Bamba. Pretty much one of my favorite, like, music biopics, so great. The music is killer, it's got commentaries, so even more exciting, great. La Bamba.

So actually the cool thing about this too is, when I was a kid, my dad worked in VHS distribution, which means, like, we would get sent, like, VHS tapes every week. And so we had, like, a closet like this in our house. Actually it's like a rental store of just, like, VHS promo copies of blockbusters and arthouse films and, documentaries, like, you know, classics, like we had everything, it was pretty wild. The cool thing about that, though, is it showed me a lot of films that I would have never seen, you know, had it not been for that closet. When I was in high school, they put out a VHS of this movie, The Last Picture Show, and this movie just blew me away. Just so beautiful, takes place in Texas, a little dirty too. So this film is, like, you know, kind of one that I feel, helped me mature and helped me, like, appreciate different things. Peter Bogdanovich is like one of the best, to listen to for commentaries, so I'm excited to hear him talk about this movie too.

film_title: The Worst Person in the World
catalog_title: The Worst Person in the World
quote: So we got to talk about this movie, talk about something newer, The Worst Person in the World. This is probably my favorite romance of the last five years. This movie is just so wonderful, feels really, like, raw and honest. So I'm really glad Criterion did this, it's amazing.

Okay, Risky Business. The soundtrack is killer, Tom Cruise is killer, Rebecca De Mornay, unbelievable. And also has one of my favorite, love scenes, the scene where, like, the wind is blowing and there's a TV on and everything, it's really dreamlike and kind of knocked me out. So this is really exciting, Risky Business.

The last little story I have, revolves around this movie, Tales of Hoffmann. Let's see, I had a girlfriend, like, mid-2000s, we were both obsessed with the Criterion Collection, and, there was this video, store, like a chain called Hollywood Video, they were going out of business. And so I thought, wow, like they're selling off all the Criterion DVDs, like, super cheap, like we got to go get, like, all of them. So what we did is, like, we went together and went, like, all around town and bought, like, as many Criterion DVDs as we could get. And, like, each, like, store had, like, different ones, it'd be like, cool, like we found Picnic at Hanging Rock or we found Diabolique, but I found my favorite movie then, from Criterion, The Red Shoes. But I've always wanted this one because this is the follow-up to The Red Shoes, and I consider The Red Shoes ballet like the most beautiful sequence in film. That when I first saw that sequence, it like moved me to tears, it was so beautiful. And I think they thought, like, hey, like that was so great, why don't we do, like, a whole movie like that? And so The Tales of Hoffmann is pretty much just like, hey, let's do The Red Shoes ballet, but like a bunch of them, and it's pretty wild. And I've actually never had this, like always wanted it, it was like elusive. And so it feels like cosmic that I'm finally getting it now, like today at the actual Criterion Closet.

catalog_title: Eric Rohmer’s Tales of the Four Seasons
quote: Okay, let's keep going. Tales of the Four Seasons. Tales of the Four Seasons by Eric Rohmer. His films are just very simple, like, romances with, like, you know, a group of people kind of just get entangled in their little romantic situations, and they just take place in beautiful exotic locations. I thought that's the way to do it, just go deep into that and do it. These are cool though, because these are all like, his '90s stuff, which I really don't know, and watch it when I get home.

quote: I already see the first film that I like. Fellini’s 8½. Fellini is my god, my hero... Fellini made it... Made it possible for me to think that I was a filmmaker. Because none of his stuff makes sense really, really, at the end of the day. But it does make sense. And I don’t make sense. Yeah, I love it.

When I think of my work, you know, I... I think it's, like– Do the Right Thing. I think of myself as... I don't know, I feel like I'm a... Definitely influenced by European directors, by, you know, Spike Lee– Black directors, by gay filmmakers. A little Euro, a little ghetto, a little homo.

Whoa! Whoa, whoa, whoa. Querelle, baby doll. Querelle, man. Insane. Brad Davis was a god here. I think Jeanne Moreau's in it, too. Yeah, Jeanne Moreau is a beast. This was exciting. This was an exciting film for me.

“I've got lots of trouble... Female Trou–.” So I took my mother to see John Waters– and my aunt, to see John Waters's film. I think that was another turning point. I think I was 19, in Philadelphia, and I took my mother and my aunt to see this. And at the end of it, you know, my aunt a little old Black lady, slapped me in the face. And I knew at that moment that I want– I knew for sure I wanted to be a director, because that's– I wanted to make people feel the way she felt. To me, it's not about just Feeling Good. It's about, “What have I experienced?” And it made my aunt experience something she had never seen before.

Pickup on South Street! Yo. This is another one that just threw me into a loop. Thelma Ritter is off the chain. Fuller. Sam Fuller. Let me tell you something. Yo, this cat right here... He had the lead guy punch a woman in the stomach in the subway. I've never seen anything like it before. Again, risk-taking that... That you just don't see. Yeah, don't get no better than this one.

Jane—Jane's The Piano. The Piano... You know, taught me to be quiet. And Jane does that. She sits with people. Where Cassavetes is moving it, moving it all around, you know, Jane is still. And, you know, taught me to be still with the camera.

Oh, my gosh. So, Claudine... Claudine reminds me of my mom. My mom was elegant– is elegant. She raised five kids on her own. And, after my dad was shot and killed– he was a police officer– killed in the line of duty, my mom took us to see this in Philadelphia, West Philly, at the Locust Theatre. And... It– I couldn't believe I was seeing my life on screen. We all walked out of the theater holding hands. And I didn't understand what filmmaking was at the time, I think I was probably nine when this came out. But I saw my mother smile after my dad's death, and I wanted to make her... Smile. So I think that this is it. It's very dear to my heart. And Gladys Knight's and the Pips' soundtrack, Curtis Mayfield's soundtrack on this is just a beast. I play it. It's my workout to this day.
Spartacus! Oh, man.

And guess what, they said in case I'm interested... Ha! I'm taking this one home, y'all! Okay? Whoa! Fellini is my god, my hero... Fellini made it... Made it possible for me to think that I was a filmmaker. Because none of his stuff makes sense really, really, at the end of the day. But it does make sense. And I don't make sense. Yeah, I love it. Thank you.
Oh my gosh, Destry Rides Again. I mean, come on. Marlene Dietrich, Jimmy Stewart. Nothing like it. I'll definitely take that one.

Cary Grant, Katharine Hepburn. Holiday. It's not Philadelphia Story, it's Holiday, and it's also just fantastic. Who is the beautiful daughter in this? Doris Nolan. Philip Barry, one of the greatest playwrights. I got to take that.
Quadrophenia. You know, I don't think I've ever seen this movie all the way through. It's The Who, and I'm a nut about Tommy, so I've got to, I've got to get that and watch it.

catalog_title: It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World

Christ Stopped at Eboli. I know nothing about it, but somebody told me I had to see it, so I'm going to take a look.

Oh, Local Hero. I have not seen this since I saw it originally, and it still lives with me every single day. Written, directed by Bill Forsyth, and, Peter Riegert is amazing in this film, and Burt Lancaster. That's right, okay, Local Hero.

I know there was one that I saw, that I saw, Cate Blanchett say, "Oh my gosh, this, this film is just so amazing." I literally wrote it down because it was like, well, I've got to see that. The Ascent. There it is, right there. Okay, so I know nothing about this film, The Ascent, but Cate Blanchett said it was really good, so I'm going to take a look. Thank you, Cate.

For my last pick, I'm just going to reach down here. I, I haven't even bent down to look down here, but I'm going to just come down here, pick out something. Let's see what it is. This is Ride with the Devil. Ang Lee, Tobey Maguire, Skeet Ulrich, Jewel, Jeffrey Wright, Simon Baker. Yeah, I, I need this.
Amores perros, Iñárritu. 100%.
WALL•E, magic.

Mean Streets. Mean Streets is also my neighborhood where I live in New York since 14 years. Later on I started working with Robert De Niro and, walking those streets with him and understanding where I live, of a neighborhood that I have only known since it's already hype and not what it used to be. Seeing it through his eyes, it's something that really, moved me and I never look at the neighborhood the same way. And because we started working in a very different way that I've done with Agnès, but we've started the last couple years working on a very deep project, where I'm often thinking what Agnès would say about this or that. I know she would be super happy cuz I reconnected the two of them 25 years after they've worked together and, and so, it's an incredible journey that I'm in that I'm only ready to do because I think Agnès prepared me for it. So that's something I have to, I have to take.

Oh yeah, there's one that's very important to me by Mathieu Kassovitz, La Haine. Because I, I didn't grew up learning about movies much. I think I was just, you know, watching TV and knowing about, you know, just, classic blockbusters. And so I saw that on television, one day, when I was 14 or 13, and it really like moved me because it was the world I knew, but at the same time it was, in an approach, black and white, and there was an artistic approach that hit me. And at the same time I had never thought of being an artist and you know no artist, I didn't even know it was a possibility. So I didn't know there was a world of film and way of creating differently than just, entertainment of what I was seeing as a kid.

Louis Garrel, one of my best friends, but also one of amazing actor and director and, this movie, The Innocent, is incredible. Maybe his best. He got also a lot of success for it, so he doesn't need me to say it, but it's really like, if you haven't seen it. So I have to take it.
And this one also, a incredible film that really, when you think you've seen everything or you know how a story could be told, this one of the point of view of a donkey will really blow your mind.

Roma from Alfonso Cuarón. Roma is a masterpiece. It's just, I don't know what to say. It's just every frame is such a beauty, the story, the depth, all of it. It's just one of my favorite movie ever, director approved, so have to take this one.

So of course I have to get this one.

quote: Then, Cassavetes.

Okay, this is one of those things, it's fine, I'm not going to get embarrassed about it. You always want to say that you saw all these movies like at least a decade ago, right? But I just saw this a few years ago, All That Jazz. I had that feeling of like, why did no one tell me about this? You know, when it's like a movie was like made for you, and it feels like it's been in your bones your whole life, and you're just like, I can't believe I've just been wandering the Earth and none of my friends are good enough friends to have told me to watch this movie. I'm sure they did.

Klute is one of the coolest [ __ ] movies. I remember watching this, I think I had my laptop and like a little external disc drive on the set of one of the Twilight movies, 'cause I spent a lot of time in my trailer on those movies, 'cause I was barely in them. You know, toward the end, like Donald Sutherland is like rushing in to save Jane Fonda, and I'd get called to set, and I would be like irrationally unhinged, like on edge, and just like wanting to get back to my trailer. Yeah, wanting to get back to your trailer makes you sound like a dick, but you know, when you're halfway through Klute, I think that's a good excuse.
Stalker. Beautiful, stunning, hypnotizing, and really kind of deals with the nasty business of looking at oneself and how devastating that can be, and thematically, that's my [ __ ].

film_title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
catalog_title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
quote: Passion of Joan of Arc. I will say, I think that sometimes I fall victim to that thing where certain scores for silent films take me out of it. And I will say, like one of the cooler cinematic-going experiences I've had is they were showing a print of this at the Silent Movie Theater on Fairfax, and there were these two guys who did like a modern experimental score to this, and I was weeping uncontrollably almost the entire time.

I also just saw Saint Omer. It's a French courtroom drama, take on the Medea myth, but also, can I say, between this and Anatomy of a Fall, what's going on in the French court system? This is not a joke, this is not like a jokey thing I'm doing. I would really love for like someone who knows the French legal system to like, I don't know, hit me up on Twitter, I don't know. It seems a lot more like a like a family therapy session than a than a legal structure in both films, but yeah, if there are French lawyers who speak excellent English, because my French is [ __ ], that would be so amazing.

Okay, I will say, I did, I feel incredibly special, and I did not just pull this off of the shelf at random. This is like a kind of a comprehensive Bergman collection. I think when I was like maybe 18, somebody gifted me the Fanny and Alexander Box Set, and it was one of those experiences where sometimes you watch a movie and you immediately love it, like All That Jazz, where you go, this is like someone's looking inside my brain, and that was not that experience, but it was something challenging, like it was something that touched a part of me that was untouched, or that was too sensitive to touch. I remember even watching interviews with him where he would talk about, late in his life, talk about how he still was terrified of death and had not resolved that, and particularly as someone who was like a teenager at the time, that was very unsettling to hear, 'cause you want to hear that people, as they get older, become okay and accepting of death. And it's like even in his interviews, and certainly in his art, it's like he's incapable of telling lies to keep himself comfortable, and certainly to keep you comfortable. And it sent me down this journey, and now he is one of, if not my favorite directors. I think Winter Light is probably my favorite Bergman film, if I had to choose. I also particularly adore Cries and Whispers. The production design, the performance are wonderful, but there's this scene where these two sisters have this kind of come to Jesus, and then at the end of the trip, as they're departing, one of the sisters is like, I'm so glad that we had that moment and we've kind of had this breakthrough, and the other sister goes, I mean I'm translating from Swedish so it's not this, she's like, oh God, I know, that was so silly, that was ridiculous, anyway, it was so good to see you. And it's just, it makes you want to never speak to another human being, and then it also makes you realize that that's the only thing worth doing, like to curl up in a ball out of that fear of being distanced and rejected is not a way to live. I just, I love this man, I love this man, and I love you guys so much for pulling this out for me.

Let me start with Do the Right Thing, Spike Lee. Such a great film. Reminds me of New York, of how I studied here. 1989. I came in 1991, so the movie just came out and it was like a revelation of a film. So, so that one I'm going to take. It says director approved, so Spike Lee approved it. It's wonderful.

This is a movie I absolutely adore. Downhill Racer, Michael Ritchie, 1969. This one, I've seen it many times. It's the best movie. I mean, if you love skiing, watch it. Or if you love sports, if you love Robert Redford, watch it. But also, sound. Sound is incredible. And I remember having, like, watching this and thinking like the sound is so good, it's so crisp, it's so precise. Every, like, you have these downhill racing scenes and it goes like you hear the skis fluttering on the ice and you hear his breath. And I remember asking my sound designer, Frank Kruse, a German guy, how they did that. And he said it's mono. That's why it feels so, it directs your attention to the sound, directly to the screen. And this mono, I'm thinking I'm gonna have to make a mono movie at some point, because this is the best sound design ever.

Cold War. I'm sure you know it. I adore it because it's so emotional while being so restrained. And it's, you know what, it's when you watch it, you think this is like Doctor Zhivago, this must be like three and a half hours. It is 88 minutes. It is really, it's really short, but it has the emotional impact of a massive epic. So this is a masterpiece that will stay forever in the canon of movies.

The Exterminating Angel. Great film. People are stuck in one building, in one room, they don't leave. And all I remember from this movie, I saw it a long time ago, so there's one character who keeps saying like, "And suddenly I lost all my hair." And so I, for some reason, I remember that. So, and it's very funny, so I think that's a great movie.

catalog_title: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman
