quote: But I'm kind of torn because it is Germany Year Zero, it's in the War Trilogy. I think I'm going to take that, the War Trilogy, because sometimes, I live in Berlin, and I walk through the city a lot thinking, "God, look at that, look at how beautiful it could have been, and this is what happened." You know, a country that self-destructed, basically gave in to its sort of destructive impulses. And we have that so much now again that you see. And in Berlin you go through it, it makes you sad sometimes, and you see all these streets and they're all destroyed and been built up quickly. And sometimes they're old and they're beautiful, and then you go to the next street, it's just destroyed and reconstructed. And this movie captures that incredibly. I mean, he went to Germany right after the war, made this film. So I'm going to take both.
Oh, and here, last one. Fanny and Alexander, Ingmar Bergman's masterpiece. I'll take this.

Okay, have you seen this crazy film? This was actually Häxan: Witchcraft Through the Ages, a huge inspiration for Babadook. It's about the devil and about witchcraft. It's also about women going nuts. Fantastic, so I'm going to have to take that with me.

Okay, love this one, Australian from Peter Weir, it's The Last Wave. I didn't see it for a long time because I'm embarrassed to say I thought it was a film about surfing. It's not a film about surfing, it's a film about the end of the world perhaps, and, it's one of his most sort of mystical and spiritual films. An amazing performance by David Gulpilil. Love it.

Okay, this is an amazing film, Kuroneko. Actually, I saw somewhere here Kaneto Shindo's other film, Onibaba. It's very well known, but Kuroneko is maybe lesser known, and it's the most haunting, sort of spine-chilling ghost story. I really can't explain it, but I think if you haven't seen it, you need to go and watch that. So I'll take both those.

Actually, I saw somewhere here Kaneto Shindo's other film, Onibaba. It's very well known, but Kuroneko is maybe lesser known, and it's the most haunting, sort of spine-chilling ghost story. I really can't explain it, but I think if you haven't seen it, you need to go and watch that. So I'll take both those.

Oh, Mulholland Drive. I mean, David Lynch is really up there with one of my absolute favorites. I've seen this film about, I don't know, 10 times. The first time I saw it, I was, I didn't really understand it. It made me really angry, and I thought I've wasted my time watching this stupid film about nothing, which is embarrassing to say. But as I, the second time I watched it, I sort of fell asleep midway through and woke up, and then I started to understand it. The third time I watched it, I really felt a sense of what it was about. And then the fourth time I saw it while I was in L. A. And I thought, this is a documentary on L. A.

I only discovered Robert Bresson recently. This is A Man Escaped. What a genius. I mean, he really invented a new form of cinema. One interesting thing about this is, all that I learned on Criterion, is that all of the sound was post-synched, everything: sound effects, dialogue. And I didn't even realize, but what it gives you is this kind of incredibly real, but also slightly surreal world. Just a stunningly beautiful and tense film.

Tokyo Story, absolutely beautiful, Ozu. I watched this sort of around the time my mom passed away, and it's a really affecting and subtle and sad film about not appreciating your parents. I, I can't recommend that enough.

All right, this goes back way back to way my way back machine, René Clair's I Married a Witch. Now I have married a witch, my wonder witch, which you know my wife Karina is my partner in my Jingletown Films company and we just rock and roll together, but she definitely has that magical, I'm already rich out. In this film is Veronica Lake, who I just adore, and this film was a pre, like, like, Bewitched was made after this. Now if you haven't seen anything with old special effects and you know, you know, just a 1940s feel of sauciness and witchery and comedy, this is great, this is great stuff here.

All right, okay, so I go back way back to where I started at Rutgers in New Brunswick. I studied, video art and we studied experimental makers, Barbara Hammer, you know, a few others, Buñuel's in this collection, but I'm not going to go there right now, but another person whose work that I really loved was Hollis Frampton, and they have his collection here of his shorter works from '66 to '79. He did films, he did, he played with time and speed and just questioned cinema and the totality of it and what it means with representation. This is really something if you want to like learn about form, which is very important to learn about how to, learn about narrative. So there's moments between people talking and what you see, and Frampton gives you a lot to see here, so this is something I'm, I'm going to take as well.
There's Mudbound here, my gosh, shout out to the other queers.
The Cameraman, look at this, oh my gosh, early cinema, huh, Buster Keaton comedy. You know what, I'm just going to add to the bag anyway, huh, I have the opportunity to do that.
Yeah, one of the more recent adds to their collection is To Die For. All right, I mean, Gus Van Sant. I, I'm going to my heart here.

I, I'm just going to shout out to find myself in the collection, so look, Watermelon Woman, and I, I guess I'm really into the collection as well, here at Criterion because I love cinema and, I've always loved cinema, it's the seventh art, and it really allows me to express myself, allows me to be a storyteller, allows me to invent, to reinvent, which cinema is about reinvention, take things off the wall and put into the world, but I'll put it back here so others can take it, you know what I'm saying.

Look, I'm just saying Chantal Akerman, beaucoup Chantal Akerman. We know what it means, I know what it means, Jeanne Dielman, which you know is just the tip of the iceberg of what Akerman has done. I mean, I don't want to go through it all, but you should, and, I'm taking it with me.

film_title: The Signifyin’ Works of Marlon Riggs
catalog_title: The Signifyin’ Works of Marlon Riggs
quote: Now, as a Black queer filmmaker, I must say we have few mentors, few people's work that we can look up to, to find ourselves in, to, even speak to, to figure out who we are as filmmakers, and I was fortunate enough to meet and speak with and be encouraged by Marlon Riggs, and they have the Marlon Riggs collection here. When he passed, he left a lot behind, and he left most importantly, his work behind for us, and this is a collection of his work, and it's always so hard to find, it really is always so hard to find streaming or anywhere, and it's here in the collection, so, I'm going to take that, and I would say you should take that, and find it here and add it to your collection because there's very few, again, Black queer makers', work, as so important as Marlon. Had to take a breather on that one.
box_set_name: The Signifyin' Works of Marlon Riggs

quote: Oh, my box sets, don't forget my box sets. My box set of the BRD, Fassbinder, who, I mean, he was a postwar, German young filmmaker with radical ideas and really reinscribed, invented, infused a new sort of life force into melodrama, family dramas, postwar dramas, living, how do we live, talking about the kind of core of life and its values, but, this has Lola, The Marriage of Maria Braun, Veronika Voss in it, so this is a real great special collection of that work, and it's a great introduction to, German cinema from this time period, that's in my special collection I asked for.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: I told you I was going deep and hard, and Varda is the one. I'm here for all my homages, I'm here for people whose cinema I just can't live without to help me make cinema and continue to make cinema and go back to again and again and again, and this is the box set of Agnès Varda, and I'll have everything of Varda. Varda has passed, but her work remains alive here, and it's in my bag. Hear that? That's a box set right there.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: So I'm just going to start, Allen Baron's Blast of Silence. And what I love, about the Criterion Channel is that you can discover movies on it, and, I love noir. I'd never heard of this movie. It is one of the best hardboiled, unsentimental detective movies shot with mostly an objective, camera, not a lot of compression. It's like 35 to 50 millimeter lens most of the time. But what the best aspect of it is, is the voiceover. It's some of the best voiceover I've ever encountered in a film. This one is not to be missed.

And then, a movie that could not be more different, Topsy-Turvy by one of my favorite filmmakers, Mike Leigh. This movie is exquisitely acted, which is true about all Mike Leigh's films, because he develops his movies with actors. It's a, it's a long, long, meticulous, involved, research-oriented process. This is a rare period movie made by Mike Leigh, but he still applied all the rules of making sure that his incredible cast—Allan Corduner, Timothy Spall, Jim Broadbent—that they researched, the world of, in this case, Gilbert and Sullivan. But what's amazing in addition to the acting and the writing in this movie is the production design. It is as good as it gets, in any movie. I'm, I'm just gonna say this, in any movie you'll ever see, and my buddy Joel Coen agrees. This is one of his favorite movies as well.

film_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
catalog_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
quote: Okay, so, you know, I'm just going to be completely cliche here and I'm going to pick a Cassavetes. Here is my favorite Cassavetes film, The Killing of a Chinese Bookie. You have everything that one comes to love in a Cassavetes movie: incredible extras casting, but then also incredible casting in the actors around, Ben Gazzara. Seymour Cassel, of course, is in it, another, Cassavetes muse. And the photography, you can see the focus pulls as the, as they're trying to improvise, the movement with the actors. So the, The Cameraman is dancing with the actors in, in a, in a really jittery way. That's the way Cassavetes achieves immediacy, and you don't feel like actors are acting, you feel like you're present in a room. And an exquisite, exquisite portrait of a small-time loser who gets in, way over his head.

All right, I'm going to go there and I'm going to do, I'm, I'm going to do not one, but two Coen brothers movies. And yes, that is, pro domo, very, you know, selfish of me, because without Joel and Ethan I probably wouldn't have much of an acting career. But what can I say? How can you not do the Coen brothers when you're in this closet? They're two of the most important filmmakers not only alive, but who've ever lived, in my opinion. So, among those that are available here, the first one I want to talk about is Inside Llewyn Davis. And it tells the story of a guy named Llewyn Davis, a fictional character, inspired by Dave Van Ronk, who just misses the boat. He's a down-on-his-luck, talented singer-songwriter who makes bad choices personally, irresponsible choices personally, and is always, like many Coen brothers characters are, just a step behind the inimical forces in life. And he's trying to catch up and just impose some measure of control over life's haphazard, Topsy-Turvy, unfair forces. That's the quintessential, to me, Coen brothers character. Even when a character is talented or optimistic, or is just sure of success, they're, they're always going to get smacked down.

So another Coen brothers film, that's here, absolutely one of my favorites is Miller's Crossing. This is a movie, I'm just going to tell you, you need to watch it not twice, but you need to watch it three times, at the very least, because the, the story is so intentionally, almost willfully, convoluted. And Gabriel Byrne is incredible. Marcia Gay Harden is, phenomenal playing the character of Verna. Albert Finney, extraordinary performance. But it's Turturro. John Turturro plays a character named Bernie Bernbaum. And what John does, in, in this performance in terms of what I like to call, as an actor, taking a dive. When an actor takes a dive, they just allow themselves to be ugly, to be humiliated, to be unappealing in every way without any vanity to it. Because of course you can be unappealing and it can be vain at the same time, because you're saying to the world, "Look at how unappealing I can be, aren't I a wonderful actor?" That's not what's going on in John's performance. He just embraces the notion of being, the aesthetic of being unappealing, and it's a gorgeous performance. It's one of my favorite character actor performances in all of cinema, and it's certainly my favorite performance by John Turturro, who has given performance after performance worthy of nothing but praise.

I've been presented with the option of just picking something randomly off the shelf. Probably I'm not going to know what the movie is, and here we go. Okay, well already I want to see this. It's Ozu's Tokyo Story, but look at this cover. There you go. Bye.
Bamboozled, probably the best movie about television ever made.
Spike Lee double feature. Malcolm X, best biopic ever made.

Víctor Erice's El Sur. Second film, maybe not as well known as his first film, which is equally beautiful, The Spirit of the Beehive. Honestly, every film he's ever made is one of the best films in cinema history. This film is gorgeous. Along with Spirit of the Beehive, these two movies taught me how to film people watching, which is such a huge part of my own cinematic language.

Peeping Tom. When I was working on I Saw the TV Glow, a lot of people told me that I was sort of operating against like a century of film history where kind of like the protagonist being a loner, not able to look you in the eye, weird guy. And in fact, in my film, that character acts this way, I'd say risking spoilers, because of queerness. And so revisiting these films and thinking about them through the lens of queerness is always something that I'm really interested in.

Werckmeister Harmonies. I watch Béla Tarr films when I have the flu, because they make you feel bad in the way that having the flu makes you feel bad. And sometimes when you're feeling bad, turning on a movie that's going to just meet you right there is about all you can ask for.

My dear friend Angel asked me to get them Autumn Sonata. Angel's my queer fam, family. I spend most nights at Angel's house watching movies on their couch, and I told them I was going to bring them home a Criterion that we could all watch, and so here is Autumn Sonata for Angel.

Wes, hey, it's me, it's Jane. The Grand Budapest Hotel, maybe becoming my favorite Wes Anderson movie. I was obsessed with Wes Anderson in high school, and then I had like 10 years where I was like, you know, I've got I've got like much snobbier taste than that. And then I'd say in the past 5, 10 years, I've just like fallen way back in love with the man. I don't think there are any American filmmakers out there who are building their own language and have been doing it for as long as he has and as beautifully as he has. And I feel like this is the movie where his style becomes moves from like maybe early to late or mid. It's just like he starts becoming obsessed with like nesting doll storytelling, and he starts building these like increasingly complex devices in his filmmaking, until the film itself is almost this like hyper elaborate and beautiful like nesting doll of a world.

I like thinking about David Lynch before he was David Lynch, when he was just some dude in a warehouse or wherever the fuck he filmed this, you know, using all of his savings and essentially abandoning his family to make a movie that at the time I can't imagine that too many people understood. Filmmaking is an act of faith, and I think it's like beautiful to imagine, you know, someone like Lynch before he was the brand David Lynch putting it all on the line to make something as insane as his first feature film, Eraserhead.

Got to go for the box sets. I've wanted this forever. I love Jacques Tati, and honestly, like I love him. I feel like the more I make films, the more I am like just like in love with any film that feels like it was just like sculpted as its own universe. I rewatched PlayTime recently, and it's just like it's almost like a music video before music videos existed. It's so ambitious and so gorgeous. So I'm very happy to have now my Complete Tati.

Okay, this one. A Face in the Crowd. This is a movie by Elia Kazan, and I have always thought that this would make a really incredible remake except for the fact that we're living it. And Patricia Neal is incredible in that, and I believe it was Lee Remick's, first movie.

So, this is a good one. Céline and Julie Go Boating. It has this very, you know, Alice in the Looking Glass feeling. But it's also two women who are, who are friendly with each other, you know, as opposed to a lot of movies where there's so much friction between the women. These are like, this is a real, I think, women's women kind of movie. So I'm going to put that in there because I like to watch it when I need a little boost.
I would really love to get some, Godard films. I've seen, I mean, I did wear my, my Godard Masculin Féminin sweatshirt, so, so what do you have? Oh, here. I love Band of Outsiders.

This is the first movie by Bruno Dumont, called La vie de Jésus. It's, I remember seeing this in the movie theater actually in France and being very, struck by it. He didn't really use any actors, I think these are all pretty much, nonprofessional. And then I met him later at the French Film Festival in Sarasota because I really wanted to work with him, but he told me at the time that he could never actually see himself working with an actor. I'm glad that he's gotten over that. I still hope to be able to work with him one day, but I'm really, I really want to see this again.
And then also I see that, Love Streams, which is not in the collection, but I'd like to have that as well. This was his, this was his last movie that he did before he died.

So now I am going to close my eyes and just do a random pick. I'm going to try to do something that I have not, have not seen. Ooh, Umberto D. A film by Vittorio De Sica. I have not seen this one. It's a neorealist masterpiece.

film_title: Dietrich & Von Sternberg in Hollywood (box set)
catalog_title: Dietrich & Von Sternberg in Hollywood (box set)
quote: Well, the first thing I think I'd like to get is the, the Dietrich and Von Sternberg, and I have seen some of these, but I have not seen all of them, so I think I'm going to go for that.

film_title: Eric Rohmer’s Tales of the Four Seasons
catalog_title: Eric Rohmer’s Tales of the Four Seasons
quote: To that point, I have to get, Eric Rohmer's Tales of the Four Seasons. These are movies that I've seen a bunch of times. It really is like my comfort viewing, whenever, whenever I'm feeling a little bit down. And I feel like March is definitely one of those months where you think, in New York you're like, is this ever going to end? It's so cold, it's so dreary. I also love Rohmer because he is, for me, he's one of the most bookish filmmakers that there is. You know, there's tons of dialogue, the, the, the, the camera angles are not complicated at all, but, but it really, it just evokes a feeling, and it's a feeling that I, that I really like, so going to put that in there.
box_set_name: Eric Rohmer's Tales of the Four Seasons

quote: Lubitsch Musicals. Lubitsch combined his love for European operettas and his mastery of film to create these elegant, bawdy, pre-Code delights. Okay, yeah, fun. I love watching pre-Code, like what they got away with.

So one of my favorite, favorite movies is The Nights of Cabiria, which is in this set, which is the Essential Fellini set. Yeah, so this, if you're a Fellini fan, this is, this is definitely. I actually got to meet Fellini when I was 13 years old when I did my first movie, which was Paul Mazursky's Tempest with John Cassavetes, and Gena Rowlands, and we filmed a month at Cinecittà. And, this guy came in and, 'Bellissima,' kissed me on the top of my head, and I was like, 'Who's that?', it was Fellini. So really excited about watching all of those because I haven't seen all of those.

Oh, the John Cassavetes: Five Films. I'd really love to take this because, I love John Cassavetes. I mean, what he says is all of his movies are pretty much about love: how people love, why they love, you know, why. He's like, 'I just basically keep making the same movie again and again,' because that's, that's what obsesses him, that's what obsessed him. And, excited about that.

I'm gonna take The Cremator. I love this film because it's very disturbing and kind of sick, but funny at the same time. And when I find myself laughing at things that are pretty disturbing, I, you know, I think the directors, you know, they did what they wanted spot on.

I was introduced, and I'm going to drop a name now, by Benicio. Introduced me to Kaneto Shindo. He did the commentary on The Naked Island, and he gave me that movie as a present, and I loved it. I loved it because of the simplicity of it, and the visuals of it are insane, you know, about this family going, taking water and food to the island and all that. So I love it. So I haven't seen this one, but, you know, I want to explore more of Kaneto.

Oh my God, this is Amores perros by the master Alejandro González Iñárritu. The script by Arriaga and him, and cinematography by Rodrigo Prieto, which is amazing. And I just worked with him in a film, and watching him work, the detail, the obsession in detail with the light and everything, you know, it makes it more special. And I think for every Mexican this film is really big. I mean, when it came out to see, you know, and all these great actors in this story, and it was, it's so, so visceral, you know, the way the camera movement, it kind of feels for me as a, you know, as a kind of documentary kind of way. And I think Alejandro is a master and a true artist because he's always, for me he's always one of those artists that are always trying to, you know, to find the truth, either in their characters or in the stories that he tells.
Another Mexican film, Canoa by Cazals. This is such a, this is such a good movie as well, and I think it's one of the greatest, if not the greatest, you know, my favorite Mexican film.

I love Terrence Malick. I think he's the poet of cinema, and I love this film, The New World. When he matches with the cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, I think they do pure magic. They capture moments that I wish I could be there to see how they do it, because, you know, they, it feels like very instinctual the way they use a camera, and they grab the moments of the best moments of the actor with the best light, natural light, and it feels like they're improvising, and it's just so beautiful what they do.
My favorite film of the last years, Cold War. It's just, it's just beautiful, the everything about it. I love it, it made me cry. He's a master. I love this.

There's oh yeah so there's one up here. Christ, I have to get up in this stool now which is going to be a bit of a pain with these fucking heels, but do I want to take it with me? Yeah, I suppose I do because it means a lot to me, this movie, Night of the Hunter. It's very, I bet you know, loads of you know it. It's this very famous movie and Martin McDonagh, when I first met him, was like, "Night of the Hunter this, Night of the Hunter that, you have to watch Night of the Hunter." And I remember watching it and having a big effect on me, and I remember didn't he have tattoos on his hands? That really stuck out to me. So I'm going to take this one and maybe I'll give it to Martin for a present, or maybe I'll keep it.
Oh, Fish Tank, Andrea Arnold, that's a great one. And what's his name, Michael Fassbender's character's a real bollocks in it.
And Kes, Ken Loach, is another one I love.

George Washington, that was brill. And that was your man's first film, that guy David Gordon Green. It captures youth and childhood and it makes you remember like when you were a kid and what that was like. And I think that's kind of hard, like first of all, acting with children and directing children is really hard. You have to be really delicate because it's like they're kids, but it's also you know to kind of put yourself in what your mind was like as a kid. That was a really, I remember that movie being brill.

Let's see what... The Tin Drum. You know, I will say this: The Tin Drum, I remember seeing this. There's a good few movies that I've seen when I was in my early twenties and I'm not going to lie, like I was kind of stoned, so I vaguely remember them and I've seen them. So there's a lot of movies I should rewatch. Actually, I'll take The Tin Drum because I saw it when I was very young and maybe it'll all come flooding back to me.

Oh, Secrets & Lies. I won't take this because I've seen it loads, but when I was young and I wanted to be an actress, Brenda Blethyn in this was so inspiring. She was nominated for an Oscar, I believe, at the time, and Mike Leigh, his method of his style of... Actually, I'll take it actually, because I want to work with Mike Leigh and I don't want to screw myself out of a job. So I love Mike Leigh and I loved Secrets & Lies.

Oh, there's one up there that I'm not going to take, all right, because I can see it. A, it's high up, and B, I have it already, but McCabe & Mrs. Miller. Will I get it? Do you want me to get it? I'll get it and I'll show it. But the reason I'm not taking it, because I have it, is because an ex-boyfriend gave it to me and I started watching it and I was like, "Do you know what? Turn it off." So there you go, McCabe & Mrs. Miller. I'm sure it's great, but he did a bit of a number on me, so. I feel bad now, McCabe & Mrs. Miller is probably brill. Maybe in time, you know, time heals all wounds, as they say.
Oh, Valley of the Dolls! Valley of the Dolls is brill. That's one you'd kind of watch all the time, it's so entertaining.

My favorite, and I see it, and it's my favorite movie and I've mentioned it before so I hope I'm not like repeating myself: Dogfight. Oh my god, Dogfight. There's so many reasons why I really like this movie. I watched it when I was very, you know, a teenager and I really wanted to be an actress. So Lili Taylor in this movie completely affected how I thought about acting and how I thought about like what kind of actress I wanted to be. Because the movie is basically about these bunch of young lads are heading off to fight in Vietnam the next day, but the night before they go they have this game called Dogfight, where the challenge is to bring the ugliest girl to a party, and the guy who brings the ugliest girl wins. And River Phoenix, oh he's so brilliant in it, and he looks so young and innocent to be going off to Vietnam, and he's trying to find someone and it's late at night and he can't find someone, and then he goes into a cafe and he finds beautiful Lili Taylor. But in the story she's not beautiful, you know, she doesn't look perfect or whatever people think is beautiful. And, but anyways, he takes her out and there is a scene, she finds out it's a Dogfight—I'm not giving the whole story away, I'm just giving you the first bit of it—but there's a scene where she's playing the piano and she's singing a song and he's watching her and there's no dialogue. I'm going to start crying just thinking about it because he's smoking this cigarette and he's watching her, and he was such a pure, beautiful actor that like he starts to realize that, "Oh, hang on, she's really sweet and she's really deep and beautiful, and actually I don't want to hurt her." And it all happens just in his face while he's smoking, watching her. And it is so beautiful because it affected me as an actress, but also about love. It made me think that like, you know, love is like so personal and how someone affects your soul. And lads, this movie is amazing, and like it was directed by a woman too. So it's all, you know, "women directors this, women directors that"—this movie was directed by a woman a long, long time ago and I don't think it got the recognition it deserves.

Oh, this is tricky. It could either be All About My Mother, amazing, but then it's between All About My Mother or The Prince of Tides, which is super romantic, and I worked with Nick Nolte, and he was like, you know, one of my favorite people to work with. He really influenced me, and he was just wild and amazing to be around and to work with. So Jesus, lads, it's a tough call here. We got Pedro or we got Nick, and so I have to take both of them, and I love them both.

But then it's between All About My Mother or The Prince of Tides, which is super romantic. And I worked with Nick Nolte and he was like, you know, one of my favorite people to work with. He really influenced me and he was just wild and amazing to be around and to work with. So Jesus, lads, it's a tough call here. We got Pedro or we got Nick, and so I have to take both them, and I love them both.
Okay, so where to begin? I think I'm going to start with John Waters classic, Female Trouble. This is the best thing in the world. John Waters forever.

film_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
catalog_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
quote: Oh, do we have The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant? We do indeed. Oh my God. Okay, so this film, first of all, oh, it takes place all in one set and the set is perfection. She's, Petra is on the bed and she's in love with this younger woman and she's just, just all kinds of everything. Oh, I've referenced this movie so many times, I can't tell you. And behind her is this like blown-up mural of this flower and it's just like, it's so, it's so grandiose and like it just looks so good and, and so dramatic and, and it's tragic-queer. Bless her, Petra, bless her. She just, she's just looking for love, you know? We're all just looking for love.

film_title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
catalog_title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
quote: Okay, Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown. Pedro, I love you, I love you, I love you so much. You know, you, when you see movies by people who like, I don't know, like love women, like love their mothers, you know, this is a gift. Like he loves his mother and I love that for him and for us. I can't, I just [__] [__] can't, I cannot.

To Die For, Gus Van Sant. This movie is so funny. Nicole Kidman is so [__] funny in this movie. She's psychotic. She is like icy and just about to crack. She is absolutely terrifying. I mean, even just like look at Nicole Kidman's face on the cover of this, just... So there is some kind of through line happening here, I'm realizing, between John Waters and Pedro Almodóvar and, and Gus Van Sant and Fassbinder. It's a real like pantheon of queer cinema. You can draw a line, I think, around some of these aesthetics that are, you know... She knows how to code-switch 'cause she's got a lot of things going on all at once. Oh, she's perfection. I love it. I can't, I just can't, I cannot.

Okay, where do we go from here? Okay, I'll, I'm going to go, I'm going to go Guy Maddin on this. This is, I remember buying this film, Brand Upon the Brain! At Kim's Video in the East Village circa two... Who's counting? This is like, Guy Maddin is a freak. Just watching this black and white like bizarro world that he creates, I've definitely ripped him off as well. It's wild, it's wild in that, in that sort of like full dream state. What am I looking at? But you, but it feels very intimate at the same time. You're like, oh, I know exactly what he means. So I'm going to take it.

Oh, here's a good one. Okay, Dazed and Confused, classic Richard Linklater film. I saw this movie so many times on a VHS, in Dallas, Texas, growing up in Dallas. And oh, first of all, oh, the soundtrack is so good with, "Summer Breeze", Seals and Crofts, and, it's got Rick Derringer on it, it has Aerosmith, it has, who else? Black Sabbath is on it, or no, yeah, because "Paranoid" is in it. It's one of those movies where you feel sad when it's ending, like you feel like, oh my, the party's over, like you really feel like you don't want to leave the party, and the, the characters and the people. And so the final scene, they, the sun is rising and Lynyrd Skynyrd, "Tuesday's Gone" plays and it's just like, it breaks my heart. Also again, War, "Why Can't We Be Friends?" This is my first introduction to War, which is one of my favorite, bands. Shout out Long Beach scene. Oh, I put it in my bag, I get to keep it.

Okay, so I'm going to, I'm going to, spin around, like a piñata. No, the piñata doesn't spin, the person does. This is starting to hurt. That I'm going to get this, and it is Diamonds of the Night. I don't know this film. Okay, well, fate led me here, and I'm taking it.
Hey, can I take this Chantal Akerman? Can I take this? I want this, so I'm going to take it. You know why? 'Cause I don't know her work and I should. That's why I'm taking it.

I am going to start with this classic, Bringing Up Baby by Howard Hawks. One of my all-time favorite movies. I used to write papers on this movie a lot when I was in film school. And, for people who've seen my films, particularly The Living End, Doom Generation. The Living End is actually called "An Irresponsible Movie by Gregg Araki" because of this movie. There was some Robin Wood essay called "The Lure of Irresponsibility" that I read when I was in film school that, dubs The Living End "An Irresponsible Movie."

Something Wild by Jonathan Demme. I'm actually screening this movie today at—tomorrow at IFC Center. I picked it as an oldie, but a classic. The reason I picked it is Jonathan Demme, he was sort of making, you know, hitting his stride right as I was in film school, and a big inspiration to me. And he was very much, influenced by New Wave music the way I was, and also very much like a film school kind of director. Like, Something Wild is, like The Living End and Doom Generation, very much related to Bringing Up Baby, the movie I just picked.

film_title: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me
catalog_title: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me
quote: David Lynch, Fire Walk with Me, I think is his masterpiece. I know it was critically attacked when it came out, and my story about it is we actually got the Showcase Theater on La Brea in Los Angeles for The Living End because Fire Walk with Me was such a commercial disaster. It opened and closed in L. A. Like in like a day or two, a week or whatever. So we got a better theater in L. A. Because of the flop of Fire Walk with Me. But to me, just that amazing, perfect movie. I love it so much, and it has recently been critically resurrected, so thank God for that.

Of course I'm gonna pick this, Masculin, féminin by Godard. I mean, Godard is a huge, huge idol of mine, and I took a Godard class in my senior year as an undergraduate, and it was life-changing for me. And it's such a profound influence on my, like, voice as a filmmaker and what I wanted to do, when I started making my own movies.

Pink Flamingos by John Waters. John Waters is the original godfather of everything to me. I just want to really pay tribute to him, and this movie, I remember just being blown away by, how intensely punk it was and how outrageous and shocking it was by '90s standards. And, this is for John. I mean, I just, you know, he is a national treasure and thank God for John Waters.

I just have to pay homage to this. Stranger Than Paradise by Jim Jarmusch, 1984. I was in film school, like at the peak of "Who am I? What am I gonna do? I'm just this weird, arty, artsy Godard punk kid, this queer punk kid, like where's my place in, you know, the filmmaking world?" And this movie came out, and I just remember seeing it and being so stunned by it and so inspired. And it's like thinking that—if I remember, this played in like a, you know, one of the little art houses in West L. A. And I was like, "It's so cool that this movie is in theaters in America and people are paying attention." It wasn't that, you know, it wasn't a huge blockbuster, but the idea that there was this indie cinema that could exist was, for me as a young filmmaker, life-changing.

I'm going to start with the film that actually I shot and the reason is that we recently did this remastering of the movie, so it's a new color grading. The original video color timing was done without our supervision, Alejandro González Iñárritu and myself, Amores perros. So one of them that was a great inspiration, I'll pick here, I'll pick On the Waterfront by Kazan. This was quite fascinating because Kazan was the theater director in New York, and the first couple of movies he really was just shooting as if it was theater. The cameras were still, he sort of didn't know how to, you know, what the camera could do in terms of enhancing the action. And you see he evolves as he starts to make more movies that there's an enormous change and how he starts to master this relationship with camera and movement. And in films like East of Eden and On the Waterfront, and then you start to have these incredible films where the physicality of the actors is, is, you know, in the relationship to a camera that's never, you know, never self-conscious, that's never there just for virtuosity, that's really, really, you know, these choices are always very, very specific to each scene. He actually, if you read his biography, he really recommended directors to, to, to go take dance, to watch choreography. He, he really understood the importance of, you know, analyzing, you know, how to move people in time and space and how the camera could, could, could be an incredible partner in, in that movement.

So now I'll pick Tree of Life by Terrence Malick. And so that's for, you know, for different reasons it has to do with, with dance. You know, in dance we always say, you know, you don't want to be, you know, you want to make dance look like you're, you're, you're just coming up with it in the moment. I mean the best example of that is Fred Astaire. Fred Astaire always looked like he was improvising, right? It's just like yeah, these, these, these moments of grace and you never know what's coming next, coming, you know, and it just had this, this, this is sort of what you want to achieve. Terry has a way to capture that magical moment I think better than, you know, anyone else. And he does it by just his continuous shooting. I've been on set, had the opportunity to watch him work on set. You know, the camera keeps rolling and he sort of lets the actors walk in all kinds of directions, and he's just, you know, it's, it's him, but it's also the camera operator who has the sensibility to the action and just has this, this ability to, to, to, to catch these moments that are completely graceful and completely unexpected and, and catch, you know, take your breath away.

So interestingly, a totally different approach to, to movement here, because obviously Fosse, choreographer, director, isn't someone who really where the, the movement isn't about how he moved the camera on, on, on in scenes. You know, the dances are complex and they happen on stage and he would essentially capture all these different angles, and the choreography for me happened in the editing room. You know, the editing of Fosse is what's absolutely phenomenal. There's a rhythm, there's a, the choreography, he literally creates choreography with the editing. For that reason it's, it's a really important director to watch that I also, also love. Obviously Cabaret is a masterpiece and so is All That Jazz.

I think it's also interesting to talk when you, when you think of, of movement and also of, of the importance of stillness, to talk about Antonioni, which is a director that, that I love for, for the, the, the tension, the mystery in his films, the things that are unsaid. I think what I admire here is actually how so often he decides to, you know, not move the camera, and also not necessarily see the character from the front, but experience the character from over the shoulder, the back. If you're doing it to show that you can create a, you know, a moment of virtuosity, I think it's, it's you're missing the point. I think the idea is that how these elements come together really beautifully, and in a way you need to be immersed in the picture and the emotion and not feel like the camera is moving. And, and Antonioni is a really great, great director to watch because of these choices actually of not moving the camera.

God bless God for making Peter Sellers. That'll this, if you're ever down and feeling like I can't go on, just put this on, it'll cheer you right up.

Bob Rafelson, Five Easy Pieces. There you go. There you go, Bob Rafelson and Hal Ashby, they just don't make them like that anymore. They really don't. I mean just so rich and complex and easy, it almost feels like it's just happening, you know, but not in like a slow way. I wonder if you have King of Marvin Gardens because I like that one too.

catalog_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
quote: I wonder if you have The King of Marvin Gardens because I like that one too. What? Oh my god, well there you go. That kind of ticks a lot of boxes. I've never seen Head, Easy Rider, Five Easy Pieces, Drive, He Said, A Safe Place, The Last Picture Show, and The King of Marvin Gardens. Yeah, this makes up for all the Christmases where I didn't get much of anything. I guess I'll put that back.

quote: And I'm picking out Naked City. It sort of relates to stuff that I love like Sam Fuller and kind of really great B-movie stuff of the, you know, 40s, 50s, and 60s. Okay, I'm gonna put this in for now. I said I would take a lot and then maybe select, sort of like when you're shopping you do triage.

film_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
catalog_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
quote: My favorite John Cassavetes film is Killing of a Chinese Bookie. I look at it over and over for the way he filmed this. It's so present and real, and there's an amazing scene in a back room of a restaurant where something bad is about to happen, and the way it's filmed is incredible.
Sid and Nancy. I knew Nancy, not well, but I knew her a little bit, and I knew Alex Cox because we were at college together. This is a great movie.

Mala Noche. I think Gus Van Sant's work, in the 80s had a big effect on me. It was when I was working in television in Britain and I was, I think I had started to write scripts and I was trying to get to direct film, TV. At that point I was a researcher, and I think this and then seeing Drugstore Cowboy, just told me that there was a different way to make films, you know, that outside of Hollywood and outside of the classic films that I loved and or the kind of experimental European, you know, art house European films that I sort of also grew up on. But this was like, oh, this was happening now, and it was really unsentimental and quite harsh, and it was a different way of making a movie.

This is a really underrated movie, Lost Highway. It's got a lot of sort of 40s noir femme fatale sort of mythology in it, but it also has this crazy like metal soundtrack. And I really like the way David Lynch kind of counteracts his, and I wouldn't ever call his filmmaking nostalgic, but it's steeped in certain images of the past, but then he'll combine it with this really like jarring modern thing. And it is like your craziest dream. It's funny, I just had a dream last night where I was walking down a road through the woods and I realized that I'd been in a car with my mother, who actually died not long ago, and I couldn't, and I didn't know how I got out of the car, and I was like, I've got to call her, and I realized I didn't know her number. And I was thinking after, I thought, oh, David Lynch movie. You know, and I was thinking about him this morning about how well he captures that, you know, the world of dreams, the complete disorientation of suddenly you're in one place and the other. And I think with Lost Highway people minded the way it jumped around and people changed identity, but you know, that's the life that you have and I have every night in dreams when we can remember them.

This is My Man Godfrey. It's the wonderful Carole Lombard and it's set in the Depression and it opens, under the Brooklyn Bridge, but there's just a lot of fantastic, rapid-fire 30s comedy. And a lot of the time when I'm trying to direct people, the main piece of direction I give usually is "do it faster." And sometimes I say "do it like 30s comedy, just rapid-fire," because you know, comedy is pace, and you know, they knew that. And some of them came from theater and they couldn't mess around and they couldn't do a lot of takes and they couldn't, you know, do a lot of coverage. So it's like get it right, you know, in one, you know, shot. It's bang, bang, and I just love that.

I'm not gonna pull my own because it's tacky and because Criterion gave me about 10 copies of it. But this was a big moment for me in film school, out of film school, being obsessed with the Criterion Collection, knowing what it represented, how much I learned from it, and then to get that call that they wanted to do Love & Basketball was a pretty great day.

Black Orpheus. I actually have, I have this poster, this movie poster in my room. It's an incredible inspiration. It was really one of the few, may have been the only black love story that I had seen, and really spurred me to, I want to see more, and so I come back to this movie actually a lot. So I'm glad this is the first one that I picked. You're gonna see me pull a lot of love stories.
In the Mood for Love is so beautifully shot, it's so heartbreaking. I love this type of story that gives you that ache.

Broadcast News. Anytime anybody asks what my top five is, this is the first movie that comes up. James Brooks, the way he's such a good writer, he just makes you feel, and this movie, absolutely an inspiration to me in working with actors and getting performances. I'm actually excited about the extras on this to keep learning from James L. Brooks.

A Dry White Season, Euzhan Palcy. There are three people that I looked up to as I was discovering my voice as a filmmaker: Euzhan Palcy, Kasi Lemmons, and I know Kasi just got Eve's Bayou as part of the collection, which I'm excited about, and then Kathryn Bigelow. Those are the three that were doing it, making movies, and people I could look up to, and they were all so cool and supportive. That was a beautiful thing, to meet them and get inspired by them and know that I had their support, so excited about this one.
All right, I have not seen Ratcatcher, but I've heard people I respect talk about this, so go ahead and check that one out.
Know there's another, Andrea Arnold's Fish Tank. So yeah, I'm eager to see this, Ryan Coogler recommendation.
Devil in a Blue Dress, man, this film, it was so smart, it was so well shot. Carl Franklin killed this.

Claudine. Okay, like I remember like it was at least 20 years ago that I saw this and I can remember like faces and lines and emotions. Where I grew up it was, you know, it was very difficult because there was nobody that looked like me, and so, and certainly when you watched TV and film as a black woman, you're not seeing yourself reflected. And it's crazy what that can do to your self-esteem, and so much of what I do as a filmmaker, I hope, is fighting to put black women on screen so that we can see ourselves, and this was one of those movies. Seeing Diahann Carroll like changed me. I've never forgotten this movie.

film_title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
catalog_title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
quote: For my last two I'm just gonna randomly pull two, whatever I get, and I'm gonna just watch. Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas.
An Actor's Revenge. Is this a good one?

Come on, and the way that he works with actors, it's so inspiring. I guess my favorite thing of the filmmaking process is building characters with the actors. I've been so fortunate to work with some great actors who have chops and who love digging in and going deep. I mean, Sanaa Lathan, where it all started, Yale Drama School, someone with such incredible depth, work ethic, to then Gugu, same thing, incredibly dope, to certainly the folks that I just worked with on The Woman King, and this again is going to be film school for what I'm I'm writing next.

Stephen Sondheim, Company. It's kind of to me Sondheim at his most challenging. If you're not a person who's already drawn to show tunes, some of these ones will absolutely make you run screaming if you're an anti-show tunes guy. But then you can sit with it, you'll be very happy you did.

Salvatore Giuliano. What is this? "On July 5th, 1950, Sicilian bandit Salvatore Giuliano's bullet-riddled corpse is found face down in a courtyard in Castelvetrano, a handgun and rifle by his side." Friend, honestly, if you don't relate to that description immediately with a feeling of extreme desire, you and I are different people.

This is Sir Laurence Olivier doing Richard III. I'm going to take the controversial position that Laurence Olivier probably does a really good Richard III. And I haven't looked at Shakespeare in a long time. A big defender of Shakespeare. Joseph Fink and I have had—Joseph has a position that everybody should stop doing Shakespeare for a while and let other people in theater get some air. It's a good position, but at the same time it's like, I don't think it was it was some mysterious cabal of Shakespeare defenders who made him famous, it's that these plays are astonishing. Olivier, come on now.

So this is the Shadow Warrior, Kurosawa. I mean, everything he ever did is great as far as I know, but he also is one of those great artists who is still trying to find new ways to do what he does in his old age and is embracing grand themes. Speaking of Shakespeare, he's super Shakespearean. He's very into the big Shakespearean questions of life and how it should be lived and what are how do we atone for past actions and all these kinds of things. It's quite long, Kurosawa is not shy about taking as long as he needs to, but I will absolutely watch Kagemusha, and so should you.

Do I need Youth of the Beast? Oh man, come on, what are you trying to do to me here? "When a mysterious stranger muscles into two rival Yakuza gangs, Tokyo's underworld explodes with violence." It's now in my bag. There is room for it. I'm putting it there.
And I'm going to put The Ballad of Narayama there and bid you a good day from the offices of the Criterion Collection.

film_title: The Signifyin’ Works of Marlon Riggs
catalog_title: The Signifyin’ Works of Marlon Riggs
quote: Let's see here, The Signifyin' Works of Marlon Riggs. "There has never been a filmmaker like Marlon Riggs, an unapologetic gay Black man who defied a culture of silence and shame to speak his truth." I'll absolutely be checking that out, that sounds great.

film_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
catalog_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
quote: Let's see here. Well, you know, I know there's something I'm going to take before the bag gets full. It's the Bruce Lee collection. I think about Bruce Lee a lot because when I was a child, Bruce Lee was known by every kid on my block to be the coolest man alive, right? We were just kids, you know, you didn't think about what that meant in terms of representation, and Bruce Lee was an incredibly important figure in this. And my children are Asian American and my younger son, when he when he first saw Bruce Lee, was like extraordinarily excited to see this guy. He was so—it was so clear and obvious that we—we've watched these movies and you can give these readings to Bruce Lee movies, or you can just watch one of the greatest martial arts artists of all time wailing on dudes, and that's what I like. So I'm taking the Bruce Lee collection.

However, on the other hand, we have here a thing that says The Samurai Trilogy. Do I really have to explain to you that I'm taking home The Samurai Trilogy? Oh man, what is it? This is Hiroshi Inagaki, starring the inevitable Toshiro Mifune, one of the greatest actors of all time. It's funny, there's a book about Fellini called Fellini's Faces, because he has such an eye for the face, but Mifune is the other side of that, where you can bring a face to the camera that the camera just naturally can't resist. Obviously, you're in the presence of one such face right now.
Amarcord, one of my favorite movies of all time. Just atmosphere, Fellini, coming of age, fascism, wonderful. It's one of my favorite Fellinis of all time, so glad to have it.

Wages of Fear. What can you say? One of, you know, not only the, the time of France, Yves Montand, some of the most tense, nerve-wracking scenes I've ever seen, but really captures the post-war existentialist, it's a, it's an existentialist epic adventure.

But Crumb, Terry Zwigoff's Crumb. I've seen this many times. It's one of the films I can see over and over and over again. It just, it's, it's a great, it's about families, it's about San Francisco, it's about art, and it's about lunacy.

Battle of Algiers. Well, you know, I use the music from this often as a temp track. And you know, but the vitality, you know, of, of, Pontecorvo's film. I mean, it's, you know, it's a unique film, it's a unique political film, but, vitality is extraordinary. And I can remember being in little theaters in Los Angeles, and I've saw it a number of times, and there'd be revolutionaries photographing off the screen how to create a revolution, literally, 'cause these were revolutionary times. I mean, this was the primer, for a lot of people. And, you know, it, it's a film that transcended the cinema, really.

Just look at the, what a great still. The, the children, you know, the seeing, I mean, the eye. That is a marvelous still, isn't that? The way that Fanny and Alexander are looking around. Just also has the best fart scene I've ever seen in a film.

film_title: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir
catalog_title: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir
quote: Once at a screening down in Los Angeles, I came late and I walked into the screening room and I stepped on somebody's toe and I sat down next to him and just as the film was beginning somebody came in front of us and the man next to me said 'Hello Fritz' and Fritz Lang turned around and said 'Hello Jean' and I was sitting next to Jean Renoir with Fritz Lang sitting in front of me. They're great films, inspire me and all of us to get started.
box_set_name: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir

film_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
catalog_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
quote: But I can find a lot of Rainer Fassbinder movies that I really, really like. I really like Petra von Kant's, The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant. I think I will pick that one.

I mean, I have seen so many films. I actually like this one a lot, Catherine Breillat. But I don't like this title that much, Fat Girl. I actually like À ma sœur! To My Sister, that is the French title. And I think that she had an approach to sexual content that was totally new for me when I watched her films. But this one, I actually have this edition also, so I won't take this one.

But I saw over here, it was Love Streams. And this one I will take for my producer, Erik Hemmendorff. He said, "You have to take Love Streams." I haven't seen it, but I love a lot of John Cassavetes films, and the approach of his filmmaking. And of course, Gena Rowlands, the way she acts is just fantastic. So this will definitely be one for the bag.

And I also saw Bicycle Thieves by Vittorio De Sica. And this film was a film that Roy Andersson was talking a lot about when I was in film school, and that has been a really, really important film to him. And it was nice to see that you have the right title on the film here. For many years it was called Bicycle Thief, and I think Bicycle Thieves is a much better title for the film. So that's the film that I definitely will take. I will give this to Roy Andersson.

Viridiana of Buñuel, and The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie of Buñuel, which I think would be the perfect title for my new feature film, Force Majeure. It should have actually had a name of The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie.

No, but I can talk about Ingmar Bergman, actually. I can talk about him because I think that what he did when it comes to the Swedish film community was that everybody talks about him like the demon director, as someone that is so in control and knows everything about the films that he is making. And maybe when you went to film school as a film student, you were a little bit afraid of exposing that you sometimes are not 100% sure what you are doing. And when I shot a short film that is called Autobiographical Scene Number 6882, I made an experience that had been extremely important for me as a director. We were shooting this film on a bridge, a high bridge, and there was only three shots, and we had one camera position each day during this shooting of the short film. And on the second day of shooting, I had big plans for the camera position. I have built up a, or me and the crew have built up a big tower, a large tower, high tower on The Bridge, and on the top of the tower there was like a jib arm in the air above the water. We have placed the camera, and it took like half a day of building this construction to have the camera in that position. And immediately when I put in the BNC cable into the monitor and I could see the image, I realized I will never use this shot. And I ended up with a struggle, because should I now tell the film crew that I have made a wrong decision, or should I just like continuing and pretend like this is exactly how I want to do it? Because I could feel that the history of Ingmar Bergman, that you should be a demon director, you should know everything you are doing, was relying on my shoulders, or on my shoulders. And we went to go and eat lunch, and during that lunch I had this inner conflict: "Yeah, maybe I should tell the crew everything is right and we just continuing the shooting, and then I call them back three weeks later and say we have to reshoot it." But after lunch I actually gathered all the people in the crew and I said, "Okay, I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I made a wrong decision. We have to take down the tower, and I have to find the camera position myself." So everybody was like, at that moment I thought that, okay, there will be a mutiny, people will not trust me anymore. But instead there was a very experienced sound designer that came up to me and he said, "Okay, now I really, really trust you." Because I think that's what filmmaking is about. When you are a director and you are on set, you have a lot of pressure on yourself, and if you are leaving your own instrument, if you're looking at something in the image and it's something that is not exactly how you want it, then you have to be very, very sensitive to your instrument, and you have to follow that instrument. And as soon as you are leaving your own instrument and you are just doing things to avoid struggle during the shooting, then you're also leaving the reason why you are a director.
Jules and Jim, my first three-way. I haven't even looked back here. I can't take all what this is like. How do you choose?

Okay, this, this I've recommended. Preston Sturges' Sullivan's Travels. Just, I really hope you people get to experience Joel McCrea and Veronica Lake in this movie. It's just so joyous and it so speaks of, you know, the human experience of wanting to be important and be counted, forgetting the fact that you might also want to entertain.

I think my love of movies started with just my mom. How much of, if I couldn't sleep because I was a little bit of an insomniac as a kid, she would, she said, "Watch, let's watch this movie together." Heaven Can Wait. Anything by Lubitsch, just brilliant. But it was kind of a time for me to be with my mom, and for her, movies, she was an usherette in a theater in Liverpool. I always thought that she wore this little uniform and she had her hair, she had a little beret, and she would sell ice creams at intermission as well, cigarettes and all the rest of it. And she was always going up to the balcony and they couldn't find her, and that was her escape. Books and movies were her escape, so they kind of came, became my escape too.
Limelight, just because it's Charlie Chaplin.
Oh, childhood favorite: A Taste of Honey. Great film. I fell in love with Rita Tushingham in that film. And Tony Richardson.

Wanda. I really have to thank Criterion about this, for this, because I didn't know about this film. And to have it, to bring it back, was such a treat. I didn't know that Barbara Loden, I know her as an actress, but I didn't know that she was a director. And this was such a, it was a labor of love, and over many years, and coming back to it, and being so, so focused and persistent. I can't imagine, I mean it's hard to get a film made now, what it was like then as a female director without any track record. And she came out with a masterpiece. I mean, I read the reviews and saw the documentary on the DVD, and what was extraordinary about it was just the commitment. And that at a time in her life where you think she had so many offers, that this is what she decided to do with her life, is to make this film about a woman who was invisible, and she made her more than visible: viable. You really care about her and feel for this, this kind of woman who was a pawn to men's schemes. And, but gee, you'd think, well, why would I feel for somebody like that? But she's so, so lost, so at sea, and Barbara Loden gives her voice. Great film.
Tony Richardson.

Well, I was kind of channeling Nashville on this last project that I did. It was just Ronee Blakley in that last scene, and Geraldine Chaplin, and great, great American film, that film. The narrative was so different. I remember seeing it, I saw it in Calgary in a little tiny town, and it just blew me away, how political it was without being. And I know there was a lot of criticism, excuse me, from the country and western people when it came out because they said that's not what it's like. I think he really put his finger on something.
Repulsion, okay.
Cat People. Meow.
Fanny and Alexander. This was an extraordinary experience, just the evolution of a family and the way change and loss of a parent affects everybody.
With my tote bag reaching up to get Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing. This is so hard because like you know everybody wants like the whole closet to come home, but one must choose.

film_title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice
catalog_title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice
quote: Okay, so this is an Ozu film I haven't seen, but I saw the title and it just washed over me. The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice. I'll let you know, I'll let you know what I think about that one.
And I am really happy to have this. Stalker, Tarkovsky. It's like you know, but Stalker is my jam, my jam.

Blow-Up, it has like a crazy energy and the mystery is like just hovering and there's just so much like tension and misunderstanding. And it's like a film I watch, it's like a train wreck. I don't even know like what I'm waiting for sometimes. So I'm gonna take it home and watch it again and try and figure it out.

So this is a visual poem, this film. I don't know, I think I randomly found it in a library, took it home, watched it, didn't know what I was watching. Definitely changed my understanding of how to make an image for a film frame. And then like a few years ago I was in Rotterdam at the film festival and they had like his outtakes of stuff that's not in the film. Oh, it just took my breath away all over again. So I'm really excited to revisit Parajanov's The Color of Pomegranates, because man, there's this film is like nothing I've ever seen.

Whenever someone asked me like which Sembène film to watch, there are many, but this one I think is just so close to my heart. I just thought maybe like the first film I ever saw that really focused on a Black Girl, period. And so I just absolutely love this film and its biting commentary.

And in that vein, I remember like the title sequence of To Sleep with Anger is ridiculously cool. It is just enthralling, exciting, and sets you up for like this incred- this really intense, thoughtful family drama. Which the entire the acting, the performance, it was so exciting when it came out to see this, such a breath of fresh air. But for some reason it's the title sequence that is just seared into my mind.

This film, Symbiopsychotaxiplasm, is that I'm a teacher and it is always my great pleasure to introduce my students to this film to talk to them about 1968 and like a different time. And their responses every year as I grow older and they grow younger change. The language gets like uncomfortable, people have to do trigger alerts and stuff. And I love this movie. I love the way people talk to each other. I love the mutiny, I love the crew struggling, I love Bill Greaves doing this thing like.

Oh, where's Princess Bride? So you know like whenever someone starts quoting from this film, it's like you know you've met family, right? This film, this is like this is the bonding comedy. I've seen this film 25 times and I'm always sent into like total fits of giggles. I don't know what it is about this movie, I wish someone could explain it to me, like why, why it never stops being funny. But it just looks like it was fun to make, fun to be in, like it's just the fun is just so contagious. I'm really excited about, look at this beautiful storybook cover.
And so I'm gonna go back to my school days and get a Chris Marker, La Jetée. This is important.

film_title: Eclipse Series 31: Three Popular Films by Jean-Pierre Gorin
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 31: Three Popular Films by Jean-Pierre Gorin
quote: I'm taking home Jean-Pierre Gorin because I worked with the guy at UC San Diego for several years and I'm quite fond of him and I think his films are like nothing else I've ever seen. So I'm really happy to have them in my collection.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 31: Three Popular Films by Jean-Pierre Gorin

quote: Well, look, I'm an actress, okay, so All About Eve is required watching because, you know, probably at any given time you're either, you're, you're either like Bette Davis or you're Anne Baxter. I mean, I don't really love seeing women pitted against each other type movies. If there is one movie where I will watch it, it is this one, because it is clever and sharp and clearly of a time when women gave as good as they got.

I mean, here's the thing, you just, I again, like, what year was this? So '86, so I was 15 when I watched Betty Blue. Like, Béatrice Dalle was like, like somebody, like somebody drew her and she came to life, like this embodiment of everything that I wanted to be as a woman. Something about French, French movies when you're a teenager as well, they kind of let me down when I grew up, when I realized that life wasn't like that. Like, I really did think that it was that beautifully lit, it was that hot, there was that much sex and that much power. And that also, I was disappointed that there weren't more women like Béatrice Dalle in the world, but I think perhaps there can only be one.

An Angel at My Table by Jane Campion. It is about New Zealand's probably most famous author called Janet Frame and her apparent madness, even though she wasn't really mad, and the landscape of New Zealand, this power and grace and beauty of this place, and the experience of this brilliant artist who was just treated so appallingly. One of my first jobs out of drama school was this really beautiful, strange four-part series for the BBC that Danny Boyle directed called Mr. Wroe's Virgins, and Kerry Fox, who stars in An Angel at My Table, was in it, and she is a rare, deep, beautiful actress.

Uncut Gems. Uncut Gems. I do not understand why Adam Sandler was not nominated for an Academy Award and why he did not win. What I found so arresting about this film, apart from Adam Sandler's performance and the direction and the horrifying music, which is literally like you think there's something wrong with your ears and you need to go to a doctor, is that the female characters are so fully drawn. They are so full of blood and life, and it makes this very kind of dirty male tale so centered and so, rife with life. I love this film. I could not believe how hard it was to listen to it.

This film, this along with Withnail and I, Down by Law and Withnail and I are probably the two movies, maybe Betty Blue as well, the three movies that I would watch when I was a teenager, and it was exactly what I dreamed being an adult would be like. This slightly surreal, you can do anything, but you may well end up in prison, that maybe I could fall in love with someone as cool as John Lurie or Tom Waits or indeed Roberto Benigni. I mean, "I scream, you scream, we all scream for ice cream," like I've, I've cackled that on so many occasions like as a kid. I mean, Jim Jarmusch, I don't know, he just captures this part of that unbridled imagination that you have when you're young, that everything and anything is possible, that everything can be cool and funny and also tragic and broken. I feel like there's, there's a line between Jarmusch and the Safdies, like I, I, I do maybe watch these together while, you know, having a drink, you know, or not, just watch them totally sober as well.

So La Cage aux Folles, I guess I did, I did, I mean, who didn't love—I love The Birdcage, I love the remake of this film, but this, this, this is, this is the one to watch. Really, like in 1978, to be telling a story of, of a gay couple and like this big caper, it's like a, a gay caper movie. It's, it's a "gaper" movie. It makes you laugh at the absolute kind of mortification of the way in which people behave, at the deep love that is at the center of it. It's a really brilliant film. It was, it was one of my father's favorite movies.

Oh yes, and just like from an acting point of view, Robert Bresson, or Robert Bresson in America. I just saw Pickpocket and Bresson, Bresson is really interesting because he's very progressive in his acting because there will, there will always be acting, ways of acting that are more fashionable for, I guess the time you live in, but yeah, this was, he believed that all our actions are mechanical and you don't really choose what you do, like your arm goes there and here and then, it just does that. So his, yeah, the actors in his movies are really special. They're very, open because they are not doing very much. And we tried to with Joachim's film, Joachim Trier's film The Worst Person in the World, we tried to play around with how little we could do.

Oh, this is like the best combination and, I, this is, White Material. Yeah, I just love the sensibility and the sensuality of Claire Denis and the way she elevates kind of everyday moments is to be very sensible and very like, I'm always almost there, you know. I can smell stuff, I can feel stuff when I, when I see her films.

Oh, this is I think my, because I come from a place where you don't really see films, and it's, it's a very, very small place. It's called Solbergelva and it's nothing there, and I wasn't exposed to films and art until very late. But this, you can imagine, Mulholland Drive, David Lynch, when I was young and I was in shock, and I saw it maybe like 20 times and I read all about it, and I read like people try, have tried to understand it and actually going crazy trying to understand it. I just love him.
