When we were children, we couldn't watch, I don't know, a lot of films, but this is one of the films that was screened very often, showed very often on TV, so I know it by heart. And I still, it still has a few scenes which I consider to be memorable. I still like to watch this from time to time with my children, especially that moment when they bring this machine which is supposed to feed people while working. I find that to be a great moment, especially because every five seconds there is that thing that serves to clear his mouth, which I like a lot. So I think that in order to, I don't know, have a little bit of an education for children before they just watch American cartoons, it's good to start like this kind of silent films, which I like a lot.

A third film which I was, I could watch back home when I started, started, you know, watching a little bit of older cinema was Bicycle Thieves. At some point they started having this Cinematheque in Romania and there were always like the same films, not too many, that we could watch, I don't know, Tarkovsky, Fellini, Antonioni, Visconti, stuff like this, a few Japanese films. But for me, what was important was to discover the strength of this Italian Neorealism. And later on in the film school, I watched this film several times and I think that somehow it became part of my education about, and desire just making very realistic films in which most of the tension is coming from things that could happen to everybody.

And then the other thing I wanted to talk about, about my childhood, is this Dekalog. In the '80s they were not having enough funds, so many, enough money to keep on buying films, so they started trading films with the other socialist countries. So for a period we couldn't be watching a lot of cinema in the theaters, we could only watch TV, and this became a cult film with us, the Dekalog. And when I got to the film school, the decisive question was to comment a fragment from the Dekalog. So it has a very special meaning to me. I still remember that moment because it brought me to the film school.

And then two films that I like a lot. I don't remember when I've seen Blood Simple for the first time, but I liked it a lot and I became, I became a fan of these people. And it was very funny for me to get that old that I met them later on in Cannes years after watching this film, which I can still consider to be very, very strong and very good. And I was even in a jury in Cannes when they were having a film, which I thought is very funny in closing this kind of circle.

And last but not least, this is a film, Easy Rider, with a special kind of impact for me and history because at some point something strange happened to me. I finished my first film and I was flying back to Romania from some festival in Karlovy Vary or somewhere, and once I got to Europe I got this million messages on my telephone that Dennis Hopper wanted to meet me, which at that moment looked as a very funny piece of information. So I flew back to Romania and what was happening is that Dennis Hopper was shooting as an actor a film in Bucharest, and he stayed so long there, he met the local community of expats and somebody gave him a screenplay just for an opinion. But instead of just delivering this opinion, he decided he wanted to direct that thing, and he gave it to his Romanian producers for which he was working, that it was a piece in his film. And they told him, "Look, this film is about the Romanian Revolution, so the screenplay is not very good. You need a local writer that could write in English." And they checked into their telephones and actually there weren't too many writers who had written something in English, and they found me. I had written a screenplay which got an international award, so it was translated, and Hopper read the screenplay and we met in 24 hours, and he watched my first film. So I think that a week from that moment I was in Wilmington, Carolina here, and for two months I spent time with him rewriting that screenplay. And I think the experience was better than the screenplay, but it brought me closer not only to his films, but to him as a character, and he was a character.
This is one of the first films that I remember seeing when I went to film school.
Miloš Forman, Loves of a Blonde. This is amazing. This is a simple, heartbreaking film. Very, very lovely, well worth seeing, not a film a lot of people know about.

The Graduate, another amazing film, Mike Nichols. This is another film, you know, I, I started out as an editor when I went to film school. I ended up focusing on editing and I started my career as an editor. That's actually how I came to Pixar in the first place, was to edit the first Toy Story film, and I still edit on all of the movies that I make. So I'm, I am directing now, but my first love will always be editing, and there were a number of films that kind of blew my head open having to do with editing and, and the power of editing, and The Graduate was one of them.

Punch-Drunk Love, Paul Thomas Anderson. This is, I think it's in my top five movies of all time. I'm friends with Gary Rydstrom, who was the sound designer on this, and he talked to me a lot about, about how Paul Thomas Anderson talked to him about this idea that they were kind of like aliens observing everything going on in the story from kind of outside the frame line, and it's nothing that's implicit in the film, but when you watch the film there's kind of all this kind of odd stuff with lens flares creeping into the frame, and, and I think he had, if I remember correctly, he had Gary do kind of sound design that was specific to that, to that notion, and again has nothing to do with the film, but I love hearing things like that where the filmmakers are kind of thinking about ideas and expressing ideas that are kind of outside the bounds of the, of the film itself.

An Angel at My Table, I believe was originally made as a TV movie in Australia and then it ended up getting released theatrically around the world. Not many people have seen it. It's a beautiful film. This is probably the most quoted movie in my household. My wife and I saw this years ago, we loved it. I got to meet Jane Campion when we were releasing Finding Nemo in Australia, and it's, it was maybe the most nervous I've ever been meeting a filmmaker because I just adore her so much. I remember she looked at Andrew Stanton and myself and she just said, "Oh, you're babies. You're just two little babies. You've made this beautiful film and you're babies." Not a baby anymore!

Seconds, John Frankenheimer. This is an awesome film. I first saw this in film school at a screening, and I think at the time that I saw it, Seconds wasn't available on video anywhere. So I saw this one screening of this amazing film and I for a few years was telling everybody about it. Rock Hudson, beautiful black-and-white photography by, is it James Wong Howe? And a lot of really innovative camerawork that you would see influences from later on. Ernest Dickerson, who would shoot for Spike Lee, a lot of that kind of locking the camera onto the character thing that, that Spike Lee used to do really came from Seconds. It's essentially a feature-length Twilight Zone episode, but shot really, really beautifully.

Another one of my probably top five favorite films, All That Jazz, Bob Fosse. This is an amazing film, also very '70s, but that's not a bad thing. This was one of the first films that really showed me the power of editing, and it's amazing that Bob Fosse hadn't been a filmmaker in his career. I mean, he was a choreographer and a stage director, and to see the command that he had over filmmaking and editing and using it rhythmically the way he used dance and movement was really remarkable.

I will start with something that I have never seen that I feel very guilty about, which is The Three Colors Trilogy. My friend Andrew Stanton loves these films and he's been trying to get me to watch them for years and, and I haven't, so I'm gonna fix that now.

Great film. This should be this should be wallpaper.
You know, I never saw Kiss Me Deadly. The Greyhounds rocking out tonight, which of course was a great Generation X song. When two punks choose Kiss Me Deadly tonight.

It's tough not to love. That's the pigeons and the pigeon coop. I used to live in Hoboken and would recognize pretty much every street that this was filmed on. It meant so much to me. I just love Kazan.

I think this is one of the few films that truly got punk rock. But I also loved my dad actually loved this film because the repossession of cars. My dad worked for the Hertz Corporation and cars were a big thing.

This movie, The Rose, Bette Midler. I don't know what year it came out, 1979. So I was like 13 and I really absorbed it. I was so bullied, and I always had this idea that if I could prove I was enough somehow by being famous that then it would make, they would be sorry. And my mother always told me you can't shine. And how she goes back and tries to fix her pain and you can't do it. You can only move forward and be with the people who are of your family and your tribe. Some say...

catalog_title: Pigs, Pimps & Prostitutes: 3 Films by Shohei Imamura

quote: Ace in the Hole, love that. This is one of those movies with an evil character that is so much fun. And Billy Wilder, another one of those people that had to leave Nazi Germany, come here, learn English, and learn to write in an entirely different language, and be a director, and be the best, most American director there ever was, 'cause he seemed to like it here. And Kirk Douglas, he makes such a great badass.
This is my friend Marty Brest's favorite movie. So amazing. The idea that people love you, they hate you, they love you, they hate you, and he made it so funny, and it's so heartbreaking.

What can you say about this one that hasn't been said before? This is the ultimate explanation of creativity, where it comes from, how it makes you a jerk, how wonderful it is, how ridiculous it is. It's somebody laying bare their soul and being more entertaining than anybody could ever be. Yes, cool. Yikes.

This is Mean Streets before Mean Streets and Scorsese will definitely tell you this was a big influence. About a bunch of schnorrers that are of the age when they should grow up, hanging around the neighborhood up to no good. Sadly lacking in Ronettes songs, but other than that, it's awesome.
That was a sick movie, but fun if you like pesticides to get high on.

Tokyo Story. This is the most heartbreaking, and you know, if you're somebody that is obsessed with World War II, and then wants to see what happened afterwards, and what was life like, and how do people get over such a devastating jolt, and the beginning of a completely different world when, you know, youth and modernism are just kicking out all the old ways and the older people, and it's just completely heartbreaking. And the daughter-in-law character, who is the one nice person amongst all the children, is just amazing. She will blow your mind. Anyhow, this is, this is an awesome movie everybody has to see.

Oh, M. Peter Lorre, one of the best actors in the universe. When he is caught by the thieves and has his speech, like, "M! M!" and you just go, oh my God, you can understand the worst behavior because, you know, he makes you understand it.

Oh, well, the first thing I see is this. Oh, it's only DVD, which is a shame. The Horse's Mouth. Now, I saw this on TV in the UK and it's an incredible movie about an artist and I think it's John Bratby does all the drawings and the artwork in it and it's Alec Guinness and for me this is like a kind of a almost like a side-by-side piece to something like The Ladykillers which I would have watched quite a lot when I was a kid, but I remember taping this probably off, it might have been off Moviedrome actually, the Alex Cox show, and I loved it a lot. And as I've walked around the Criterion offices, I saw a poster for it and I thought, "God, I love The Horse's Mouth. I hope I run into it in the cupboard," and I have. So, that's going, that's number one pick.

This is one of my favorite films, Grey Gardens. But I have it so I'm not going to take it. But, yeah, it's such a brilliant movie. And Laurie Rose, the DP that I've shot all my films with, and I will often watch Grey Gardens before making a movie, just to remind ourselves how to move the camera as if it's an inquiring eye.
Two-Lane Blacktop, Monte Hellman. This is possibly I mean, my hand is getting cold by holding this 'cause this is probably the coolest film that's ever been made anywhere.

Now, Things to Come was a film I saw when I was a kid and saw it on TV not knowing what it was and started watching it just thinking it was a normal war movie and then it slowly became a sci-fi film and then completely freaked me out and I was like I thought that basically I'd slipped into an alternate reality where this might have happened and I haven't seen it since I was like 12 or something. So, I'm looking forward to getting back to that, one of the most, one of the original sci-fi movies.

This is one that will make my wife Amy Jump happy. Fishing with John, which is a particular favorite in our house, but we've only seen it on you know, to my shame on slightly crappy YouTube rips. So, we love this. If you haven't seen it, you should see it immediately. It's one of the funniest things.
Seven Samurai. It's one of the greatest action films ever made. And it's also Criterion Disc 2, which is going to be quite exciting for my collection at home.

Seconds. This is a brilliant film. And again, I remember seeing this completely blind, not knowing what it was and being completely spun out by it. And like the kind of in just in the first 10 minutes of it that the plot is so twisty-turny and the use of wide-angle lenses is especially brilliant. Yeah, this is like meeting up with an old friend. Hello.

This is one of my favorite films, Sweet Smell of Success. And I love it also because it's like a this is the actual proper sister film to The Ladykillers that you know that you can go from making that Mackendrick can go from making The Ladykillers to go to making this. So the quintessential English film to the quintessential American film in one in one leap. And also Mackendrick wrote one of the greatest books on filmmaking and if you haven't read it you should read it immediately because it's the only book you need basically.

So, a slight change of pace, Crumb, which I remember seeing at the cinema at the time. I'm a huge fan of Crumb's work and this documentary is fantastic and kind of tragic as well and sad, but I could listen to Crumb's voice all day long and listen to, he's got a brilliant taste in music as well.

I saw Rumble Fish when I was a kid and I only had a black and white TV so the certain scenes of it were completely lost on me. And I remember going to school the next day and going, "Yeah, Rumble Fish was brilliant." And they go, "Yeah, that bit with the goldfish, the Rumble Fish was amazing." I'm like, "No, I don't know. Was it?" Yeah. So now finally I'll be able to see it with that tiny bit of color in it. So that's exciting.

When we got a video recorder in our house, the first rental I made was Watership Down and Death Race 2000. When there was no control over what you could get from video shops at that point at whatever age. Watership Down didn't work. But Death Race 2000 did work. And I think that's probably, sums up my whole career really. Thank you.

Now, speaking of samurais, I'll go for The Blind Swordsman here. Now, this is one of two things that cartoonist Geof Darrow told me to pick up. And I was chatting to him in Chicago the other day and he's going, "Have you seen this?" And I was like, "Damn it, Geof. I haven't seen it." Oh, it's like embarrassing. He said, "You should definitely see it." So, now I can. Wow, that's a nice one. That's big.

Tarkovsky. This is not my favorite Tarkovsky. I would say Stalker, what do you call that in English? Stalker, Stalker. Stalker it's called in Danish, is my favorite Tarkovsky movie. But he is, he's a master. I've stolen many things from him, we all have.
Quadrophenia. This is the fucking best. This is rock and roll and it's a great film.
And this is also great. I have this, but I just want to make a point that this is an absolute masterpiece by Nicholas Ray.
Insignificance, Nic Roeg. I'm actually going to have lunch with Nic Roeg in London in a couple of weeks.
This, Alex Cox, come back, we all miss you. Please make more movies, make more movies. We miss you, Alex Cox.
Oh, this one. This is, this is worth the whole day. Now you have made my day. See this, Things to Come, William Cameron Menzies. Master.

On the Waterfront. What's unique about—I had dinner with Elia Kazan when I was 24 and had just done my first movie. And we were having ice cream, me and him, in Stockholm. And of course I had to ask the question that we all want to hear at that age, which is: what advice would you, would you give a young filmmaker? And so I asked Elia Kazan, so what advice would you give a young filmmaker? And he said, "My advice to you is do it your way." Which of course had a meaning, specific meaning when I was 24, but I also understood that it would have the same meaning, but a different way, the older I got. And it's been the only thing I can ever give myself, because I realized that he was saying "do it your way" meant that your way will change over the years, because it is a bizarre industry, and just every time remember to do it your way. So that was a very important piece of advice from Elia. Thank you very much.

So yeah, I guess I'll start with Good Morning because this one kind of made a big impression on me and it was I think the first Ozu movie I have ever seen, and I've seen a few of them since then. And it sort of deals with all the familiar themes that he deals with, mostly concerning parent-children dynamics and shifting dynamics and generational gaps. And have you seen this movie, actually? Yeah, so there's a lot of fart humor in this movie, actually, which was unexpected. And you know, the kid shits his pants and all that, and it's it's really cute. And it's such a simple story, actually. I think he made this movie in as a silent film first called I Was Born, But... Which is another really special movie. And I had a very special experience watching that movie with a friend that I hadn't seen in years, and actually now our friendship has taken root again since we saw that movie together. So he's a powerful filmmaker. And it's a pretty simple story of the kids want a television set to watch sumo wrestling and stuff, and the parents don't want to buy the television set. It's sort of like, you know, industrialization and the future, and like the Western world creeping in this post-war Japan. And the parents are against it, but they realize that they can't win that battle, and the kids take a vow of silence against them to get their ways, and they win. And it's just a beautiful film. And I really love Japanese films, which is something I learned about myself a few years ago, and so I wanted to put that one in my collection just to because it's like the first thing that got me started down that road, I guess.

Yeah, so the other movie that's really special to me that I wanted to mention is Close-Up. And I guess probably it's a it's a very widely appreciated film, but I think some people don't know it. And I actually got some friends of mine to watch it one night. Some friends of mine asked me for a film recommendation. I said, "Watch Close-Up, like there's no way you won't have a great time." And they were like, "No, we didn't kind of like, wasn't the right vibe." But anyway, it's an incredible film, and it's like the most incredible use of real people reenacting something that really happened to them. You can't believe that what you're watching is not real, that it's a reenactment. He used the real people who were in these situations to create the feeling of those situations again, and it's it really feels like you're there in this in these moments, and it's just full of magic. And I don't know, I guess it's probably him at his most powerful, Kiarostami, with this film, that and Where Is the Friend's House? Which is it's just beautiful. Yeah, and it's a very sad film too about, you know, film love and wanting to be someone that you're not and wanting to kind of disappear and, you know, things that we all deal with on a daily basis, I guess. So there's that one.

And then I also kind of wanted to just mention Tootsie since I saw it in here and didn't realize that it was coming out on Criterion, and that's a great film. This is like kind of a special thing, this movie, that there's this incredible, powerful director, Sydney Pollack, making this kind of seemingly light comedy, but doing it in this really intelligent way. And a friend of mine told me a Sydney Pollack quote that is, "A film, a good film should be two sides of a good argument," and I think this movie is a good example of that, you know? And of course Bill Murray's like incredible in this, and Jessica Lange's beautiful, and Dustin Hoffman's also beautiful. And Straight Time is another great movie, might not come out on Criterion, but another good movie, Dustin Hoffman performance that everyone should see.

film_title: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King
quote: And then yeah, this Allan King collection. I'm Canadian, so I thought I should put a Canadian in there, and I wanted to just find a collection that matched my shirt perfectly. That's odd, actually. But anyway, yeah, this whole collection is incredible, and we were talking about Come On Children, which is a really great film with great music too, Arlo Guthrie music, and Warrendale is also a great one, but the one that really, really got me is A Married Couple, which is so funny and so heartbreaking at the same time. But I mean, the language of this couple is incredibly comical and feels written almost, the way they're talking, you know? The husband is so kind of sardonic, and at the same time you're watching this real thing, which is this marriage disintegrating in front in front of a camera, and maybe partly because of the camera. You kind of get a sense that they're like not able to hide anymore from their problems. And yeah, it's sort of like a real-life Scenes from a Marriage in a way, kind of feels like that. You're watching them try and fail at putting the pieces back together. It's a really great, great collection. Yeah, those were the ones I was going to pick.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King

quote: And then I was also gonna take WALL·E. Also quite, you know, silent, kind of a modern silent film almost, but very, very visual. So I think even my little baby boy might like this one.

Okay, I would like to talk about Hobson’s Choice a little bit because, like I said, I really don’t get to watch movies at the moment, just with my life, the demands of my life. But I did watch this sometime in the last year and I had such an amazing, magical viewing experience that I made my wife watch it with me a few nights later and had just as much fun watching it through her eyes. It’s like a Disney movie almost. It’s, like, wall-to-wall orchestral music, flourishing every… every physical gesture, and Charles Laughton’s so incredible, but, oh, so are Brenda De Banzie, who’s his daughter, and this other– John Mills. Oh my God. Those three are all so perfect in this perfect little movie.

Take The Mother and the Whore. It is, like, a long movie, so you make an afternoon of it. You make, like, a rainy afternoon of it with a friend. It’s so wonderful. The conversations and the dialogue. It’s just very voyeuristic and fun to get lost watching this movie.

Oh, yeah, well, my very, very, very favorite guy: Abbas Kiarostami, The Wind Will Carry Us. What an amazing movie. I’m so happy that Criterion is putting this out because it’s been hard to get a good version of and hard to find in general, and one of his most special. I mean, every Kiarostami movie is just a complete beautiful poem. But this is so, so amazing. For the longest time this has been, and it still is and will remain, my, like, desktop image on my laptop. Just because it’s so beautiful.
I will– yeah, I’ll just end with these two Sean Baker. 4K and the Blu-ray of Anora. I have not seen this movie, and I was– I’m just so ashamed of that. So that’s exciting.

And then while I’m there, down here in the Sean Baker corner, I’m gonna take Prince of Broadway by Sean Baker as well because I’ve also not seen this, and… Very important guy doing very, very, very special work in a very exciting and unusual way, finding his way through the trappings and the restrictions of making movies now, of this, you know, specificity, and doing it like… He’s just got it figured out, so love him.
Oh, right. I was gonna take 8½ too. I’ll pay for it. I’ll take the 4K / Blu-ray of 8½ because I love it. It was a great friend of mine’s favorite movie, who I love. And I’m gonna take it.

So I was gonna take this Jacques Tati Complete, which is amazing. My son is three and a half, my older son, and I did start showing him some Charlie Chaplin stuff and he really liked it. And it’s great, I mean, if you have kids. There’s hardly any language, so there’s not a language barrier, which– I would love to show him, like, Zazie dans le Métro, but, you know, he wouldn’t understand it. But this is great because it’s like a cartoon almost. I was gonna show him Mr. Bean as well, so this’ll be a good… this will segue us into Mr. Bean.

Okay, we’ll do the Gregg Araki. Teen Apocalypse Trilogy. Love Gregg Araki. Wish he would hire me. I have to admit I have not seen Totally Fucked Up. I’m assuming that the stars… that ‘f***ed,’ I’m assuming that’s the word ‘fucked.’ But Nowhere is incredible. Anyway, Gregg Araki’s Apocalypse Trilogy.

Let's talk about Following. Okay, he made this film over a $7,000 budget. He shot it on weekends. It took him I think about three years in the making because they would just shoot it on the weekends, whenever anyone had time to shoot. It was no plan, it was he just had a script laid out, a schedule all planned out, but he would his actors, his actors are one of his best friends that he I think met it through work or something, some job he had, and his girlfriend or wife at the same time, Emma Thomas, produced it with him. He edited it, shot it, directed it, and wrote it at the same time.
Okay well Rushmore. Where's Rushmore? Okay, I'm getting everything on Blu-ray.
The only Hamlet there is, the great Sir Laurence Olivier. That sounds good, we'll have that.
Else do we have? M. We don't have M, do we? We don't, let's get this.
Where's Rules of the Game?
Ooh, Rosemary's Baby with everything.
The Killing and they include Killer's Kiss.
Close-Up, we don't have. Do you have Close-Up with you at all? No, we'll take Close-Up, yeah.
The Human Condition, all three. All three movies. So, yes.

Oh, remember when we first saw this? Oh, wasn't that, is that our first Criterion film? It's yeah, it's the first Criterion film. I think that was our first Criterion film. No, first, no, first Criterion film we bought. First one I ever saw was Jeanne Dielman.

Well, let’s start with Inland Empire. I rewatched it recently after David Lynch died. I was looking forward to meet him one day. What he said about one of my films is my happiest moment in my film career. He had seen Dogtooth, and he said in an interview that he thought it was really funny. And I’m trying to find the actual clip of the L. A. Times and frame it. If anyone has that, please send it to me.

Yes, Carnal Knowledge. Mike Nichols, in general, I think he’s an incredible filmmaker, both visually and the performances in this film. It could be quite tricky because the characters play themselves over a long period of time. It could feel kind of silly, but they… they do a great job out of it and they’re all incredible in this film.

And since we talked about Mike Nichols, Elaine May. We actually watched this film with Emma Stone before we made Bugonia. Not right before. It wasn’t like, “Let’s look at this film as a reference to Bugonia.” Well, first of all, John Cassavetes is one of my favorite filmmakers ever, and this film by Elaine May has somehow both of their geniuses combined. And, of course, Peter Falk, also incredible. There’s something about this film, it feels so raw and crazy and intense, and I think it’s just, like, the perfect collaboration. Mikey and Nicky by Elaine May.

Oh. Black God, White Devil. I have heard so many things about this film and this filmmaker. And I haven’t watched any of them. I mean, I’ve watched clips, and it looks tremendous, unlike anything I’ve ever seen before, so I’m looking forward to watch this.

I mean, everyone knows this film, Persona, by Bergman, but I have a very fond memory watching a print of it in his theater in Fårö, in Sweden, with his chair there kind of having a very strong presence. So it’s a film I always go back to and always remember that day in his cinema.

Oh, my favorite filmmaker ever. I couldn’t leave him out, Luis Buñuel. It’s The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie, The Phantom of Liberty, and That Obscure Object of Desire. I mean, I watch them often. And I guess Phantom of Liberty was quite inspiring for Kinds of Kindness, the structure of the three different films that are not necessarily related. And this looks like a bargain. There we go.
Ali: Fear Eats the Soul. It's a good Fassbinder. Fassbinder. Fassbinder. It's a good Fassbinder to start with.
12 Angry Men. Oh, I watched this twice to show it to Ariane in one day. It's a brilliant film.

Salesman, one of the best documentaries ever made. I mean, I can't believe how they managed to do that, and he's like the greatest actor that ever lived. He's so, he's so moving. This documentary is so moving. I mean, you couldn't have put it together if you, you know, worked on it for years. It's unbelievable.
Oh, Mike Leigh's Naked. My favorite Mike Leigh film. David Thewlis is just unbelievable in it.

Man Bites Dog. That's a very funny film, but in French it's totally different, so it's not the proper title. What's the proper title in French? And it means 'It happened next to you,' or 'close to you.' Yeah, I remember watching that when I was, you know, I was quite young. It's '92. I just had finished school and I just saw this film and it was like unlike anything I've seen before, like a documentary. I didn't know if it was, you know, they were doing these things for real or whatever was going on. And it's so funny and violent and dark.

Le Samouraï. How many versions of that do we have? Jean-Pierre Melville, an amazing filmmaker. So contemporary still. You watch these films and you think they were filmed yesterday. And Alain Delon is always great.
Have you seen this film? It's a great Jack Nicholson film, again from the '70s, and it's a little bit like Chekhov, isn't it? Yeah, it's, let's get that.
Let's get that Buñuel, Viridiana. You remember that? Yeah, of course. I love all of Buñuel's films.
I want to watch this film, I've never watched this film: Things to Come.

I watch this film every time just before making a film. Just how, you know, how he's structured those scenes and how it's filmed, and it's so, it looks like it's not narrative, but it is. It's just the way he's editing and he's filming. Remember that film? It's just one of a kind.
Polanski, Macbeth. I haven't watched it for many years and someone was telling me yesterday that it's brilliant. Josh Safdie was telling me that this is a brilliant film.
I want to get all the Bressons. I have them in every version that exists: VHS, DVD, now I'm collecting Blu-ray.

Great Bresson, one of my favorite filmmakers ever. The most moving film I've ever seen. I'm ashamed to say, but I cry most of the time that I watch a Bresson film. It's just so moving, you know? It's my favorite one.

Pierrot le fou, of course. And that was a very happy film too in a way. Even though the film is a little bit sad in the end, but we had great fun doing it. Jean-Paul, Jean-Luc and me, we went to this island called Porquerolles and we said, "Well, we're going to get so bored, you know, on this island by ourselves." And, we never laughed as much as on this island.

Also Jacques Demy, Agnès Varda, of course, we did a little film, a little piece of film inside the Cléo from 5 to 7, Cléo de 5 à 7, we did a little scene, you know, like a silent movie inside the film. Very funny. He was a kind of Buster Keaton type and I was, you know, with all blonde hair, little, little dress like this, little sweet. And yes, we knew, I know him since a long, long time. She was doing the pictures for when we got married with Jean-Luc because she was a, she used to be a photographer before, before she became a, a director. So...

Hey, A Woman Is a Woman. Well, it's a film that, by Jean-Luc Godard with Jean-Paul Belmondo, Jean-Claude Brialy and me, and it was great fun to do it because I think that Jean-Luc didn't think about me to begin with because he saw a lot of actresses before, but then he saw me in a film called Tonight or Never made by Michel Deville, and he said, "Oh, I liked you so much playing comedy. So would you do A Woman Is a Woman?" So we did it.
That's Made in U. S. A. But yeah, that's me.
The Kid. That's one of my favorite films. Charlie Chaplin. Oh, it's so good. So lovely.
I'm going to try to pace myself, but I'm I'm already screwing up at that because I have a Blu-ray in my hand. I love this movie.
Also, Wings of Desire. This was the movie that made me want to make movies, seeing this.

Y tu mamá también, this I love this movie because it's just not afraid to sort of be almost genreless, you know. It's funny, it's also a coming of age movie, it's also just a great honest portrayal of sex. I just made a sex movie and this was one of the films that we watched in preparation for that.

Thief, I think this might be the only Michael Mann movie, I guess The Keep, that's the other one, yeah. I haven't seen The Keep, but this I haven't seen either and I fucking love Tangerine Dream. They did the score for this, right? Yes, yeah. And I love Manhunter and I love James Caan, so I'm sure I'll love this.

So this is a film that I for some reason I always avoided this and I think it was just because it was like a like I thought it was like a dance movie and for some reason, you know, or like a I don't know, just even the title All That Jazz. It just it was something that always I don't know, I just and it was never shown to me also. But I finally saw this maybe two months ago and I was like just a fucking mess by the end of the movie, just like in tears. I think it's one of the best movies ever about being an artist and it's definitely one of the best movies ever about time management and its effect on the human body and trying to do too much.
This is just one of the most beautiful movies ever made. I got to give respect to the man.

This is I love all of his movies, but this is still my favorite Wes Anderson. And this was another movie that came to me at a really crucial point in my life. There was just something about the characters and the way they were interacting with each other and the sort of casual, like lived-in feel of the relationships and just and the and the humor that just resonated with me so much and it made it feel possible to make something.

L'Eclisse, the, the very first, next to my first movie. L'Eclisse is the one I wanted to have, that's what I came for. And, and as it is sitting next to Young Törless, it makes it even nicer. Isn't it an honor? Michelangelo, he took me to a palazzo once in Venice to watch the parade of the boats. Well, you see, L'Eclisse is really the one what I, why I came for. And isn't it magical that you come in, there hundred, hundreds of them, and the first one I see where I stop is the Eclipse? I might just as well leave right now. But I'm very, very happy with L'Eclisse and All That Jazz.

Well, I'd like to have All That Jazz because when we were shooting Circle of Deceit in Beirut, once a week we got dailies sent from the lab in Paris, and we went to a still-working local cinema in the mid of the civil war. And all the time they were playing All That Jazz. I get that the only print they still had in war-torn Beirut, and we always had to sit through the last 15 minutes of the movie before we could screen in our dailies. And it became like our leitmotif during the shoot: "Bye-bye happiness, I think I'm going to die," which was exactly how we felt like often.
I'm proud because I see a few of my own. The Coup de Grâce, again with Margarethe von Trotta, then married to me.

I've been flooded with good movies. I mean, I have to start with Boyhood because it was somehow so unexpected and was so wonderful. It was already six weeks ago. A miracle of a movie. How could he in the casting, especially with the boy, have the intuition that 10 years or 14 years later this boy would still be wonderful? And same with Arquette and everybody else. Hawke's is just fabulous. To see people really age on screen, no fake makeup, and still remain in their character. A miracle, a miracle of a movie.

By Claude Chabrol. I remember the very first screening of this in the Grand Auditorium of the Sorbonne. It was the first film of the Nouvelle Vague that kind of, you know, with, screen was so different from everything else. Actually, I at the time working with Jean-Pierre Melville, I thought it was a bit amateurish, and I didn't quite understand how great it was just because of that. Wonderful. And the pharmacy in the province, in the French province.

Like Le Havre, another great one about the French province. Actually, maybe the French movies set not in Paris, maybe even better than the ones set in Paris, more authentic. Certainly true of French novels like Stendhal and Flaubert.
I'm glad you have Ace in the Hole, Billy Wilder's film maudit. They tried all kind of titles. I thought the last release was called The Big Carnival.
Sunday Bloody Sunday. It came out the year of The French Connection and was nominated with The French Connection.

film_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie

quote: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie. I just got that, Cassavetes. These are all the Cassavetes films. I mean, I'm sure he never thought they would have an afterlife, you know. quote: Oh wow, there's another film that I love that you can almost never see, occasionally on television, one of Walter Huston's greatest performances: The Devil and Daniel Webster.

There's M, which I believe has the short that I made, the interview I did with, yeah, it's here: Conversation with Fritz Lang, a 50-minute film by William Friedkin. This used to be distributed by the BBC. Very humbling to see some of these pictures.

Brute Force was, I think, Lancaster's first film, by Jules Dassin. This was one of Dassin's first crime films. Of course, most of you will know him from his later films that he made in France like Rififi and He Who Must Die, both of which are masterpieces, and he was kind of a expatriate because of the belonging to the Communist Party, so he lived and worked out his life in Greece. But this is this was made in 1947, Brute Force, and I remember it as being a stunningly powerful film. I never thought I'd see this again. 1947, I hate to admit it, but I remember seeing this when it first came out. I'll I'm going to take this one, thank you.

Oh, let me just tell you, Casey and Peter and all of you at Criterion, surrounded by all of these riches, all of the great history of international film, this is the one for me. This is one of my favorite films ever, and I'm not even going to look for any more past this, because just to walk out of this building with this film on Blu-ray makes my day, my week, possibly my year. Thanks to Criterion, and thanks to Federico Fellini for one of the greatest film experiences I've ever had. Thank you.
Sisters was one of the first ones I remember having. I think yeah, maybe might have been Sisters.
And The Magic Flute I really love.

I'd say Zazie dans le Métro was a as maybe with Persona my favorite film. This is like I watch this probably every month this film embarrassingly. And so, it's just consistently, it's just every thing in it has just so many ideas and just you see the same extras in the background recur and the music's beautiful and she is so good and charming and it's so I don't know, it's just so light on its feet and it's just such a pleasurable world to be in that this was a big, influence I guess on Submarine.
Aki Kaurismäki I love. He was a I guess a big influence on The Double that's just come out.
And in a way Les Cousins I guess was on The Double just the idea of you know these two characters and in that you know one's this meek field mouse and the other's the kind of city rat.

I had Jesse watch some Buster Keaton which he found incredibly unhelpful and it probably in retrospect wasn't that helpful but it was more the sense of someone acknowledging that everything bad that happens to them shouldn't come as a surprise.

I want to take I want to take Down by Law because I'd never I didn't know who Roberto Benigni was, but I saw this in an Italian version in Rome in about 1986, and I remember him being the funniest man I've ever seen. And he and to a Roman audience he just had to walk into shot and they laugh, but he never said anything, he just, and they didn't understand what he was saying anyway.

I have to have this movie because I guess if people say what is the first movie when you became aware of movies, and I would have to probably say The Robe when I was about 12, but I remember this film, Bicycle Thieves, and I remember it was made by an aristocrat, and this aristocrat was making movies about poor people, and that seemed to be a, you know, I can kind of understand that. I don't even know why I knew he was an aristocrat, but I did, but I remember this beautiful film. I remember the emptiness of their lives and the central performance of this actor who, I'm sorry, I don't even know who this actor was or is, but I remember De Sica showed me something I've never seen before, which was, I guess, in a post-Second World War Italian poverty. So it's wonderful.

This was a complete revelation to see this movie. I'd never seen I'd never seen a pure world, which is like mid-19th century Sicily. I was look I knew I was looking at something that was so the quality of what I was looking at was so special, and the evocation of a period was so vivid and so really, you know, it wasn't some boring old reproduction, and yet it was probably the most carefully researched movie I'd ever seen. And it introduced me to the world work of Piero Tosi, the costume designer, who those of us that know his work, incredible work, not just actually not just the costumes, but particularly the hair, that you've never seen hair that's kind of oiled and controlled in this way, because most of the costume designers' work is often jeopardized and sabotaged by the work of hair and makeup departments. And so to see a man incontrovertibly in control creating this world, creating the world as much as the sets and the lighting of the costumes and the way they literally wear the, and you know, most time actors just wear clothes, but when they when they're in this movie they inhabit the clothes. And so it's I guess it's the first film I want to show people that are interested in costume design, and that's not just, you know, it doesn't mean whether they follow the modern fashion or anything else, this is a very, very special movie. And I remember people have said to me, you know, that when they think of Tosi and they think of this movie they think of this huge tyrant that was, you know, somehow managed to whip everybody into submission. When you meet Tosi, you know, he's this gentle, modest, beautiful man who did it by guile or by being just being so brilliant, you know. So this is for you, Piero. Okay.

You really, Naked. And this is the first Mike Leigh film I ever saw in my life. And it just, that came out while we were at college, didn't it? And I think we were at college, everybody's, yeah, it just kind of like just, '93. '93, yes, oh yeah, about a year before. So this kind of defined our time doing film degrees, British filmmaking, but it's just so great that I felt good about where I was, you know, and that I didn't feel so embarrassed, and that it, because it was such an amazing film that it was really, like if you're in a council flat, that it just kind of, it gave you some sort of, I don't know, it's difficult, it just made you feel good because it's so clever. And then you were like, wow, our poor people down and out, like begging in the street, can also be smart, you know. And it's celebrating the outcasts, and it was really great to watch.

Okay, since I'm mad, oh good, since I'm called Missing in Action, I'm gonna choose, and also I talked about Costa, I'm gonna choose Missing by Costa-Gavras. Yeah, this kind of resonates for what's going on in Sri Lanka right now. We have a lot of the stuff that I talked about and the reason why I'm called M. I. A. So this is like the first film that connected with that, though it's based on a situation in South America. You should watch it. Have you seen it? No, I know, it's incredible, the cinematography, and like it's kind of like real, but the aesthetic is very Born Free. Like if you've seen the Born Free video, oh that's more what it's better look at, then I thought maybe you should watch it.

I am gonna pick Kes just because I've just moved to Sheffield in England, and the whole—tell everyone where you live—the whole of the city of Sheffield runs off the fumes now of Barry Hines, who wrote this, and Ken Loach, who directed it. And I went to the local like art cinema for the first time, watched three different films that they'd made together as a team. This wasn't one of them. There was one called The Gamekeeper, and one called Shouts and Whispers or something like that, and one called Threads that was insane, about what would happen if someone dropped a nuclear bomb on Sheffield in the 1980s. And it was so extreme, like there was like flesh hanging off, people screaming, it went on for hours, and like saw the whole thing right through to like 35 years after, where the kids of the people that had got radiation poisoning were like getting through it in the potato fields. But this film is probably the best thing that they did together, and it's just incredible. Like everyone of our age in the UK has seen this film. It's just such an iconic bit of British culture, and it really like captures the heartbeat of the north, and yeah, it's just amazing.

When I came in I saw Badlands and now I can't see it. Oh, you can't choose Badlands, and promise me you won't choose Badlands. My favorite film. Yeah, cannot choose that. Whoever finds it first gets it. Where's Badlands? Give us a clue. It's order of release, and since it's a great film, they would have released it way earlier than anything else, and be up there. It's my favorite film, by the way, so I showed it— No, I think I saw it first and recommended it to you. This is why Terrence Malick is a genius, like this is just like the most unique thing. Do you know the budget for this? It's like 300 grand or something, it's ridiculous. I can believe that. Yeah, I just find it really dreamy. Remember seeing it the first time and then forgetting what it was and what it was called, but remembering like a shot of a piano on fire, and then that xylophone tune that's all the way through it, and just individual images, like dreamlike. That's an absolutely beautiful film. I want American movies to get back to this moment, and I don't know if it would ever do that, but this is just like, I mean, I could watch this all day. Have you shown Ikhyd it yet? Yeah, I have. I put it on and I just force him to watch it, because every time he is watching like, watched Transformers, like just noise and CGI world, then I put this on to be like, this is real filmmaking. And he's always so like blown away by it, like when he watches a very like subtle kind of a beautiful film that's just got a perfect storyline, and it's a little bit intense for Ikhyd, but I sort of narrate through it for him so he understands it. Mm-hm, and yeah, it's just so beautiful. All right, cool, that was mine, that was my last two.

I want to choose Dheepan, which is right here. Yeah, was it there? Dheepan, just because it's the first Tamil film story in this whole closet. So Jacques Audiard actually sent the script to me before he made it, to cast me as the girl, and then I got fired off the job because they said I was too good-looking to be a Tamil in the story. So they ended up casting a woman in it who was actually Indian, she's South Indian, she wasn't Sri Lankan at all, when I am the actual Sri Lankan refugee, and I didn't get cast for the film. But he did ask me, I was the first person he asked. But it really, you know, he was the first director to bring it into the serious film space, a cinematic space, so I just respect him enough that, and he's a great director. A Prophet was one of my favorite films ever, so I just found it extremely flattering and amazing.

Okay, you know it just feels like I should own 8½. I love it. Earlier this year, or no, last year I interviewed Geremy Jasper who wrote and directed Patti Cake$, and he said that for like months on end he just watched 8½ every night and that was like his film school. So I would be remiss not to take this right now.

Election is one of my favorite movies. Tracy Flick is one of my favorite characters ever, and I love Matthew Broderick in that movie and Chris Klein. Oh, it's like it all comes flooding back. So I obviously need to take this one.
Dressed to Kill, never seen, seems fun. Brian De Palma, great.
Fox and His Friends, have also never seen, so that's mine now.
I love Metropolitan. I have the Criterion edition of Last Days of Disco, so actually for that matter I could just take the Whit Stillman trilogy, except it has—...
Oh yeah, I've never seen Barcelona. Alright, I'll take that too.

High and Low by Kurosawa. Yeah, these you'll never get tired of.
Simon of the Desert by Buñuel. That is a brilliant movie. That is nuts. Have you ever seen it? Yeah. 45 minutes long, fantastic.

I Married a Witch, René Clair. Okay, just for fun. Do you know this one?

I think I have to do this because of Wally Shawn, and, he helped me so much on, a project that I just finished called Habeas Corpus.
Trilogy of Life. Great Italian poet. Okay, I can't resist.

So, The 400 Blows, a film I've seen over and over, but which I love. I wrote to Truffaut, actually, when I was, when I was young, and, and he, he sent me, he wrote back, he sent me a poster and, sent me some stuff back, and it was really, it was really nice. I love it.

Okay, Stranger Than Paradise. I love that. It's a long time I haven't seen it. I, I used to love it, and I remember it being really simple. Scarlet Empress, that's that amazing scenery and the set decoration, it's incredible. And Josef von Sternberg was in love with Marlene who was magnificent in the film. Look at this photo. This is great.

That's the thing also, that films, you, you know, sometime they're in your memory and it evolves and you have to see it again. Like, I saw Brazil, which is amazing, Brazil, and, and, and each time I see it, you know, it's kind of different. And sometime, the first time I saw it in theater when it was released, and it was like, it was total magic. It was really total magic.

House I will get, because I saw the, the poster and, and it looks, looks really weird. And that's also the good thing, you know, so many films I discovered on Criterion that I didn't know nothing about. And it's good to, you know, when you, it's like in film festival, you see films you don't know nothing, you haven't read anything, you just discover the film, you don't even know what it's about, and it's like, it's great. So, so House I'll get for the, I saw someone with a t-shirt that's really scary, the big eyes.

We're gonna pick an obvious one, In the Mood for Love. I, our obsession with Maggie Cheung led us to Hong Kong at one point. We got to have, you know, spend five days with her and we made her sign all of our DVDs. We carried them over to meet her and she was just as wonderful as you could imagine. And her films with Wong Kar-wai were, I don't know, they were probably the most important films that we've watched in our lives. I think that all of his films should be in museums, they need to be the most celebrated films ever made and he is wonderful.

Oh here's a good, this one's, do you love this? The Double Life of Véronique. It's the, actually I have, we have a great Criterion Collection story. When we had our first show in 2000, 2005, we didn't really know what it meant to have a show and we called up the fashion show, got in contact with someone at Criterion and said, you know, I think we have this collection and we're really inspired by Double Life of Véronique and we'd love to give out the DVD and they let us do that. And it was really, you know, so I have a long history of connecting with this film. And interesting again, this goes along with if you want to watch this, Persona, Sisters, 3 Women, all about I think fractured identity. Yeah, great films to look at together. And I would say that we actually really believed when we were giving this film out, this is the homework assignment to our audience, everyone's going to watch it. Now 14 years later doing fashion shows, I'm not sure if that's exactly what happened, but I hope so. It did speak to the fact, maybe we, I think we gave out Fanny and Alexander the extended like the real length version with it. So well, it did speak to how much we love movies. Yeah, wanted to share that with people.

Oh wait, wait, what about this one? To pick a David Cronenberg film for keeping things wild and if you're wanting to take risks, remind yourself to do it. He's the person to make yourself trust your gut.
And then we need to pick this one because we're Sisters. Oh yeah, and this is also one of my favorite films about identity, shared identity.

In a Lonely Place. If you're a fan of Humphrey Bogart, you will be surprised by this performance. It is very tense, it's incredible, and it is something that is thrilling from start to finish and as well it's impeccably made. So this is something to see. And I haven't seen it. So she hasn't seen it, so she will watch it and be very happy. I will say that Laura sees things first and then tells me to see them, so we could have done this whole closet thing with that theme.

These two together, Multiple Maniacs and Polyester. I'm the person that has too many drinks and I sit down and say to someone, 'We need to talk about how John Waters is like one of the more important filmmakers of all time.' And I have been my diatribe about why I think he's just incredible, so.

Shampoo. I picked this right away. I was like, oh it's great that I first saw it because when Laura and I both went to Berkeley and when we were in school there was one costume design class that we managed to figure out how to take somehow through the theater department just because there weren't a lot of classes there for things like that. And one of our first assignments was to you know pick a Shakespeare play, but then put it in a different context. And I remember that I said okay, I forgot what I actually forgot what the play was because I quit midway through, but the idea that I had was to do it as if it was all characters in Shampoo, which was interesting because we did go on to do some costume design work with costume designers, so I picked this movie.

These two together, Multiple Maniacs and Polyester. I'm the person that has too many drinks and I sit down and say to someone, "We need to talk about how John Waters is like one of the more important filmmakers of all time," and I have been my diatribe about why I think he's just incredible, so.

Well, this is one that by all obvious points I should have seen this film. I know it's one of the great films ever made. I know that when we did Black Swan this was, we were doing the tutus and stuff for that movie, it was one of the things that you know clearly we should have watched. My sister has seen it millions of times and for whatever reasons I haven't. So I, I've now changed my mind, this will probably be the first one that I watch. That is, it is embarrassing that I haven't seen it because it doesn't really make sense when you piece together all the things that Laura and I do. But that being said, it's also sometimes amazing, I sometimes feel like you see things at the right point in your life. It's like when you go to a new place you've never been, you think, well maybe I'm coming here now for a reason, so this is my movie for that.

Let’s go for Black Narcissus. This movie is, I think, one of the greatest color movies of all time. There’s one particular shot towards the end of the film with Kathleen Byron, which, in my head, that is probably minutes of film, when in reality the shot is only on screen for less than two seconds. And it’s a shot of Kathleen Byron coming through a doorway, and it’s part of an incredible climax, which I won’t spoil if you’ve never seen the film. But it’s one of those shots in cinema that is ingrained on my brain. Like a lot of Powell and Pressburger films, I think it’s just a… picturesque quality to it, which is just somehow difficult to pinpoint exactly what the magic of Powell and Pressburger together is. But, I think, the thing is sometimes these are the films that you keep returning to, is you can’t kind of define exactly what it is about the film that keeps you obsessed, you just keep coming back. And this is one of those movies. Okay. I already have it, but it’s going in the bag. I’ll give it to someone else. I’ll be like Santa, I’ll just be… I’ll just go up to somebody in the street and say, “You should watch this, Black Narcissus.”

Let’s talk about this film, Something Wild. Jonathan Demme, in his career, excelled in many genres. I think this is a particularly striking film to me because, tonally, there’s something about this film that I think is… is really special, jarring, but also makes complete sense in terms of the story it’s telling. Also there’s just amazing things like… even just the end credits of this film, with a live performance over the end roller, is something that I find really inspirational in terms of Jonathan Demme, in the best way, seems like he’s having so much fun making a movie and, like, including everything he loves. Extremely memorable, and this is a film I return to a lot and I love it.

Let’s talk about A Hard Day’s Night. This is not my hot take on the Beatles being a great band. I think that what I’d like to say here is that Richard Lester is a vastly underrated director. Part of that British New Wave, post-French New Wave, people inspired by European cinema and just breaking all of the rules. And Richard Lester, in all his films, is very experimental and joyous in his use of music and comedy. And then this film is capturing lightning in a bottle, manages to get the Beatles at the height of their charm. And it’s more than just a collection of musical set pieces. I just think Richard Lester is somebody that deserves a lot more love from film fans. So if you’ve seen this and like this, you should also check out his other films.

Let’s talk about The Earrings of Madame de... By Max Ophuls. Ravishingly made, and so sort of delicate and detailed in every aspect. And yet, even though there’s this kind of sort of Fabergé-egg feeling to Max Ophuls’s films, they’re also really funny and really playful. And this film in particular, I think, kind of breaks the… It doesn’t quite break the fourth wall, but does a lot of interesting sort of tricks throughout, one of which is that you never find out the Madame’s actual name. So if you haven’t got on the Max Ophuls’s train yet, I highly, highly recommend it. One of the greatest filmmakers of all time for me.

catalog_title: The Three Musketeers / The Four Musketeers: Two Films by Richard Lester
quote: The Three and The Four Musketeers by Richard Lester. Highly, highly entertaining, and I’m definitely going to steal this at the end of this session.

film_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
catalog_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
quote: I’m going to bring out this, The BBS Story: America Lost and Found. On this you have The Last Picture Show, you have The King of Marvin Gardens, you have Five Easy Pieces, you have Easy Rider. But the film that I’m sort of obsessed by is Bob Rafelson’s debut, the Monkees’ film Head, cowritten by Jack Nicholson, no less. Eighty-five minutes long. And I’ve already picked Hard Day’s Night, Head is a very different proposition. It’s a fascinating film. The Monkees were coming off the back of two massive kind of seasons of their TV show and several hit albums, and then Head was a very bold and potentially kind of suicidal attempt to completely deconstruct the myth. It is a movie about four young men trying to escape from their network contracts, but then there are incredible musical sequences throughout it, one of which– The performance of “Circle Sky” on stage with the double exposures is just like… is just pure cinema to me. I really, really love this movie, and I love the Monkees, so I highly recommend this box set. I mean, an incredible box set, but I really recommend watching the Monkees’ film Head.
box_set_name: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story

quote: And last but by no means least, I love that the Criterion Collection included the work of Jackie Chan. This is a box set of Police Story and Police Story 2. Oh, I’m on this. I completely forgot about this, actually. Yes, I’m actually on this DVD. But Police Story 1 is one of the greatest action movies of all time. And what’s interesting about this film is that Jackie Chan had come to Hollywood twice at this point and had not had a good experience because he felt compromised and felt that his attempt to break into the Western market had not gone so great and he hadn’t been allowed to make the films in the way he usually made them. And so he goes back to Hong Kong, he makes the first Police Story, and it really feels like Jackie’s revenge. And the climax in the shopping mall is an incredible set piece. But that wasn’t the reason I picked it. The reason I picked it is because I heart Jackie.

Oh, Eyes Without a Face. This is an amazing film which my father used to talk about this movie. Well, he used to talk about a movie and he could never remember the title of it. So he used to say, 'cause he knew I was into horror films, and he would say, 'Oh, the scariest film I ever saw was this black and white film. It's a French film and it's about a plastic surgeon who is like taking the faces of car crash victims, and it's really gory and it's really scary, and I cannot remember the title.' So, and then cut to like five years later, I see Eyes Without a Face and I'm at art college and I call my dad and I say, 'Hey, I know the name of that film, the French film, it's called Eyes Without a Face.' And my dad says, 'No, that's not it.' I'm like, 'That's definitely it.' He goes, 'No.' So I might have to get this one for my dad just to prove that. So I'll take that one. Eyes Without a Face, amazing movie.

Let's see what else we got here. Oh, is that Alex Cox? Oh yeah. I've never seen this Alex Cox film. I do like Alex Cox and he was a big deal when I was a teenager 'cause he used to present this show on BBC2 called Moviedrome where he used to introduce cult movies.

Throne of Blood, so I finally saw it on the big screen and it was fantastic. And I think I probably would have watched it sooner if it kept its Japanese title of Spider Web Castle. Throne of Blood is a good title, Spider Web Castle is an excellent title. If Kurosawa had stuck with Spider Web Castle, it would have been the first Kurosawa film I watched. But this is fantastic, don't own it on Blu-ray, now I do.

Don't Look Now is genuinely in my top 10 of all time. It's just a hypnotic, incredible movie. Some of the best editing in cinema. The opening sequence alone is just I think one of the greatest kind of like put together sequences. It's a big influence on me because I like to do lots of kind of foreshadowing and omens of like doom, and the whole of the opening is incredible. It's kind of most famous probably for an extremely naturalistic, some would say almost documentary sex scene. Apparently Warren Beatty, who was going out with Julie Christie at the time, was so convinced that Donald Sutherland was actually having sex with his on-off girlfriend that he tried to get Warner Brothers to not release the movie. That's true, that's in Peter Biskind's book, which is an amazing story. So if like Don't Look Now didn't get a great release in the United States, Warren Beatty might be the person to blame. It is incredible, it has an amazing twist ending. If you don't know anything about it, don't read anything about it before you see it. But Don't Look Now by Nicolas Roeg is one of my favorite films of all time and I'll show it to anybody who's never seen it. Now I have the Blu-ray, anybody coming into my house will have to watch Don't Look Now.

Wow, wow, wow, wow. Blood for Dracula. I, let me tell you the story. I was in an airplane from Rome to Munich and there was a man sitting next to me, and you know in planes you talk, and he said, "What do you do for a living?" And I say, "I'm an actor." And I had already a picture and showed him my headshot and he said, "Interesting, give me your number." Took out his passport, wrote my number, and I said, "Who are you?" He said, "My name is Paul Morrissey and I work for Andy Warhol." And, and I remembered at the beginning it was Trash, Flesh, very artistic movies with Joe Dallesandro, and, okay, nice meeting you. So then a couple of weeks later I got a call: "Hey, it's Paul, you remember the man in the plane? I'm doing for Carlo Ponti, you know, the husband of Sophia Loren, I'm doing Frankenstein in 3D, and I have a little role for you." And I said, "Wow, thank you, great. What do I play?" And he said, "Frankenstein." And I thought that's not true. Anyway, it was true and I became Doctor Frankenstein. And at the end of the film, we shot the film for, we had $100,000 in three weeks in 3D, and at the end of the film, there was Fellini was shooting next door and in the cantina where all these, wonderful figures, and I was sitting there having a glass of wine and I thought, well, Andy Warhol said everybody is famous for 15 minutes, my 15 minutes are gone. So I was a little sad, and then Paul Morrissey came in and he said, "Well, I guess we have a German Dracula." And I said, "Who?" He said, "You, but you have to lose a lot of weight in one week." I said, "No problem." So I had only salad leaves and water, and when we shot the first day of Dracula, Dracula, and I was so weak that I had to sit in the wheelchair. And they were famous lines: "I, I need the blood of a virgin. The blood of these whores are killing me." So that was that.

I was in an airplane from Rome to Munich and there was a man sitting next to me, and you know, in planes you talk, and he said, "What do you do for a living?" And I say, "I'm an actor." And I had already a picture and showed him my head shot, and he said, "Interesting, give me your number." Took out his passport, wrote my number, and I said, "Who are you?" He said, "My name is Paul Morrissey and I work for Andy Warhol." And I remembered at the beginning it was Trash, Flesh, very artistic movies with Joe Dallesandro. And "Okay, nice meeting you." So then a couple of weeks later I got a call: "Hey, it's Paul. You remember the man in the plane? I'm doing for Carlo Ponti, you know, the husband of Sophia Loren, I'm doing Frankenstein in 3D, and I have a little role for you." And I said, "Wow, thank you, great. What do I play?" And he said, "Frankenstein." And I thought that's not true. Anyway, it was true, and I became Doctor Frankenstein. And at the end of the film, we shot the film for, we had $100,000 in three weeks in 3D, and at the end of the film, there was Fellini was shooting next door and in the cantina were all these ex, wonderful figures, and I was sitting there having a glass of wine and I thought, well, Andy Warhol said everybody is famous for 15 minutes, my 15 minutes are gone, so I was a little sad.

There we are. Another story, another story. I was in Berlin and a young, director came to me and he said—, I was there to see movies—and he said, "Well, my name is Gus Van Sant. I have a little movie here, Mala Noche, I made for $20,000, but my next movie, My Own Private Idaho, I'm preparing now and I would like that you play." And I thought, well, directors are always very lonely at festivals. But he wasn't lonely, he meant it, and we start writing letters to each other, and then, he got me the work permit, I became member of the union, and I went to, Portland to shoot my first film in America. Dracula and Frankenstein were American productions, but not in America, in Rome. So I made the movie and, and then I liked America, and River Phoenix was amazing and Keanu Reeves. And I came back for the premiere and I stayed with a girlfriend, Anna, and she said, "Why don't you stay in America?" I said, "No." So after a few glasses of wine I said, "It's not a bad idea." So now I'm 30 years here. So that was My Own Private Idaho, very important for me.

I'm a lucky man. I'm a really lucky man. I never learned how to act. I mean, I learned from great actors, but I never went to acting school. And in Germany, of course, I was very lucky that I worked with Fassbinder, who was one of the directors who showed Germany how it really was after the war, so it wasn't kind of craziness. And I went to Mannheim, is an intellectual film festival in Germany, and I had a little short film called Last Trip to Harrisburg, and it was the Opening Night film with a film of a new young director, Lars von Trier, called Epidemic. And when I saw—he wasn't there, there was a lot of directors sitting in one row with me—and when I saw The Element of Crime, I couldn't get up my seat. And I said to the directors who were invited from America, said, "We all can go home, because whoever made that film is going to win." I expected somebody like Fassbinder or Kubrick, dressed in black, scratching themselves, being in a bad mood, the eyes are closed, and there comes this student-looking young director. And we talked, we had a beer, we talked, and we exchanged a telephone number. And again, lucky man, couple of weeks later I got a call: "Hey, Lars I'm doing Medea from Carl Dreyer, and I want you to play the husband of Medea, King Jason. But there is a problem." I said, "What is the problem?" He said, "You don't look like a Vikinger. Don't wash your hair for three weeks, don't shave, and come to Denmark because I have to sell you as the king of the Vikinger." So I went, very smelly and strange looking, I went to Denmark, I got the part, and we became friends, and his wife got a baby and he wanted me to be the godfather of the baby, and now we work together 30 years.

Some Like It Hot I saw I think when I was five. I… I remember watching it in the bathtub. I watched it twice in a row in the bathtub, and it was very cold and I was very pruney by the end of it, but it was just, like, revelatory. It actually makes me really, really want to watch it with my own kids. I have so many kids now. And, I mean, the three of them together, it was just magic times a million. The best. So, Marilyn, it’s the three ‘M’s, I call it...

And Molly. I mean, I was born in ’79. I’m a child of the ’80s. These John Hughes movies, holy moly, were they everything to me. But this movie is a masterpiece. And Anthony Michael Hall, oh my God, so vulnerable and so hilarious, and just a throbbing, beating heart, all of them. The Breakfast Club. The Breakfast Club.
And then Defending Your Life and… So, now, what a love story and what an imaginative way to, you know, contextualize a love story. So, okay, they go in there.

Okay, Dogfight, River Phoenix and Lili Taylor. And those actors are some of the finest actors that have ever lived, but certainly, like, of my generation. Handsome boy meets, you know, we’re not supposed to think very beautiful girl, but come on, who are we kidding? Star-crossed lovers and empathy and love where you least expect it.

Yes, A Woman Under the Influence. Okay, this I talk about kind of in relationship to Streetwise because I watched it, like, for my work. I should have just seen it because it’s a classic, but when I was starting to think about Carrie Mathison, I’m pretty sure it’s never explicitly stated that she’s bipolar, and I was playing somebody with that condition as well, but it is so… authentic. She’s working so hard to make… to make full sense of what’s happening. And she’s always just falling short of that. But it’s just, like, drenched with love. It’s just brilliant. God.

I’ll do The Grifters because I saw this much earlier than I should have seen it. It’s when I discovered Annette Bening, I think, and she was so dangerous and super raw and so hot. What a good cover, too, like the glasses, it says it all. But everybody’s brilliant in this. But I remember just thinking like, “Ooh, that’s naughty.” So that would be, I guess, my final one.

film_title: Tiny: The Life of Erin Blackwell
catalog_title: Tiny: The Life of Erin Blackwell
quote: Okay, we are now going to venture here, to the streets of Seattle. Streetwise. I discovered this movie not too long ago when I was shooting Fleishman Is in Trouble and one of our PAs, who was brilliant, this guy Eli, loved him, real cinephile, was wearing a T-shirt that kind of referenced this movie, which is about street kids, and when I was thinking about the character I was playing, I was working with my friend who, when I was starting to put her together, he had really a helpful insight as I was trying to explain to him who she was and what she was… why she was suffering, and said, “It sounds like she’s like a runaway, like a teenage runaway, and there’s something kind of feral about her, or just– like there’s no support, like the ground is falling out from under her.” So I watched it with that in mind, which is a funny connection, but it was the key into her, and this was a wonderful resource. But it’s just heartbreaking. And they’re so tough and cool and resilient and also, you know, vulnerable. Amazing movie.
box_set_name: Streetwise/Tiny: The Life of Erin Blackwell

quote: Oh, Princess Bride. Gotta take that. That’s an amazing– This is one of my favorite movies of all time, and it will be useful for the movie I’m about to make. So I’m going to take the 4K UHD of that.

A Blu-ray of this, The War Room. This is an unbelievable documentary. Chris Hegedus, D. A. Pennebaker. Maceo and I watched this religiously to understand how they filmed everything, the way it looked, the way the camera moved, the way the extras were blocking the camera, literally everything about this movie we studied. And it’s just incredible. And I cannot wait to have a Blu-ray version of it, because it’s also shot on 16mm and it was part of the reasons why I shot Smashing Machine on 16mm.

When We Were Kings. This is a great one. This is another documentary that we watched, just in preparation. Such a beautiful portrait of a fighter getting ready. There’s nothing like seeing George Foreman hit the heavy bag and dent it the way that he does. Oh my God. And, oh, Kelefa, he writes the… He writes the essay. Kelefa’s the best.

Oh, wait, you have Carnal Knowledge? No way. Yes. Done. I love– This is an incredible movie. Every single person’s performance is completely unique and individual, and then seeing them all combine and combust, it’s just wild. And Art Garfunkel is unbelievable in this movie. And Jack Nicholson is… There’s just something really… I can’t even believe it.

Flow! Oh, yes. This is… Literally, this is one of the best movies I’ve seen in such a long time. I was watching it the other day with my kids and our cat who loved the movie because the actual sounds in the movie are real animals and they can tell. So, when you’re playing it on your screen, they watch too. So it’s a truly full-family affair, and so deserving of all of the accolades and awards. I love this thing. And I can’t wait to see what it looks like in 4K UHD.

Husbands. Done. I’m going to take this. So, yeah, this shot, specifically, this is very inspiring, just for a lot of things that I’ve done recently. But the… Specifically how it kind of captures the actors free in the frame, long lens, is just, like, remarkable. And the performances here are just out of control. I remember actually, the first time I saw this movie, it was in 4:3, and then when I finally saw the widescreen version, it was the scene of him on the telephone, and I didn’t realize that they were on the other side of the telephone, joking around while he was on the phone. I think you can hear them, but I didn’t see them, and I’m like, “Oh, that’s such a better shot.” So it’s why you should see things in the original way it was intended.
Oh, Great Escape. Done. Sorry, last one.

Oh, Wim Wenders, yes! Okay. This is incredible. Literally every single… I have not seen Wrong Move, so I’m excited to see that. But Kings of the Road and Alice in the Cities are two of the greatest movies ever made, and I like to think of Kings of the Road as the adult version of Alice in the Cities, and Alice in the Cities is, like, kind of a kids’ movie, I think. Two of the greatest title shots, Alice in the Cities and Kings of the Road. The actual titles, when they come up, are unbelievable. And there’s an awesome shot from the train in Alice in the Cities which is amazing. So, that’s… I’m looking forward to seeing Wrong Move.

film_title: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse
catalog_title: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse
quote: Oh, The Red Balloon, that’s… Oh, wait. Okay, what other stories? Because I’ve seen White Mane. I’ve not seen these other ones. This is an incredible, beautiful movie. It’s one of those movies as a kid that you kind of watch and you don’t even really remember if you saw it or if it was part of your own memory. And the same with White Mane. He’s just… They’re really special, so this is… I can’t wait to watch this with my kids.

quote: This movie I've been waiting Yes, I've been waiting for this to come out. It's I'm just talking about I just want to say I'm taking one for myself. This one, I've been saying I've been dying to see this I've seen it a million times. I've seen it on YouTube. I've seen it in a class, but I've never seen it actually on Blu-ray. I know. I came in here just for this movie, really. That's That's it. I can't have enough of it.
Yeah. It tells you It tells you exactly what happens, and yet, the whole time, you're like, "Oh, my God, is he gonna get away?" It's like, yes, he escapes. Man Escaped.
Oh, my goodness. Wait, what? On 35 millimeter.
It might be, yeah. Anything for that title, that title shot alone.
