I have a dance background, ballet background, and the metaphor in the movie, the passion for the craft and the art, and how it can drive you insane or like to, you know, desperate, desperate lengths, and so... I won't talk about The Red Shoes for the whole thing, but we have to move on.

Love & Basketball by Gina Prince-Bythewood. This film. Okay, so I probably saw this film... Height of puberty. Suddenly you're interested in, you know, I was, you know, like, "Oh, look, that boy's kind of cute." And I'm– you know, that's just peak teenage angst. And... It's so good. The chemistry. Omar Epps, Sanaa Lathan. Just beautiful. Just such great performances. And Gina... I feel like I just rinsed this DVD so much that I broke it. How many copies do you have? Because I might just need all of them.

I have to pull this movie. Paris is Burning. I remember seeing this movie and just being like... I just didn't know this existed. And this is what's so powerful about movies, is that you can get pulled into worlds that you didn't know about, and you see how cultures that start in these small ways, and then it just becomes really normal. Everybody knew what voguing was because of Willi Ninja and, like, the way that we do our makeup now is influenced by the amazing people that are represented in this film. And... The fashion and the lingo and the slang that we all use, I mean... Yes.

film_title: The Worst Person in the World
catalog_title: The Worst Person in the World
quote: Worst Person in the World. I absolutely loved this film. I think women are often just taught such a limited... We're socialized to have such a limited view of what we can be or what our lives can be. And I just love this woman who's got so much agency and so much, like... She makes choices for herself. Like, whether they're right or wrong, she has the courage to just make them, and... You know, she deals with the consequences of them, but... There's a real courage that I really loved, and yeah, Renate Reinsve, she just gave such an amazing... I mean, look, if best actress at Cannes... I mean, it makes perfect sense. She was so good in it. So, yeah.

This box set of Small Axe by Steve McQueen. This one has a very... Significant and important connection for me because it's about, you know, Windrush Britain, the Caribbean community coming to the UK after the world war to rebuild the motherland, or whatever. And the experiences of those people that came. And I am a direct descendant of those people who came, and it was really important that somebody told these stories. And Steve McQueen has an amazing, clear mission to tell stories from people and communities that we don't often get to hear from. And so I felt so seen by this. And so many of my amazing peers are in it as well, and I just loved watching them be great. So happy to receive and, like... Hold this with me for as long... For forever. So. Get in there, you.

Okay, this one, The Blob. So this deals with like a whole town of teens that are trying to warn the community like this alien, like blob is taking over, and it's basically going to, consume all of us, so beware. So, a super campy. All the actors and everybody involved, they, they were imagining this. Like it was them that sold it, because The Blob itself wasn't that scary, but it was how they reacted to The Blob that made it scary. It's one of the godfathers of, of horror. And then I love the opening music, "The Blob" of this, like, oh, if you guys didn't know, in addition to being an actor, I also make music.

Eraserhead. This is David Lynch's debut, but I remember watching this and getting to the end and being like, I have no idea what the this film is about, but I love it. It's so bold, it's surreal, it's fantasy, it's, you're in a dream state. It feels like you're probably on five different drugs at the same time. Like I don't know what David Lynch was thinking about when he wrote it. I, I, I heard an interview with him that he doesn't even remember writing it. If you're a lover of horror and you're looking for a new language, this is going to give you your new language.

Yep, we are going to get into 1984. This film, 1984, along with Metropolis, Fritz Lang's German Expressionist film, both of these films have absolutely inspired my work, as a concept artist, especially on the music side. I try to have work that celebrates and uplifts, marginalized people. And so when I think about 1984 and what it said then to what it says now, it is still relevant. It talks about surveillance, culture, it talks about the totalitarian societies and what happens when power goes unchecked.

Oh, wow. Yeah, we have to do this one. Brazil. Look, you think it's all that, but it's so much more. Oh my goodness. There's a connection between 1984 and this film, but I think they use different, a different tone to talk about it. Like humor is used in this. How it's shot, the zoom-in, shots, the color palette. Everything about Brazil to me just represents creativity at its finest, and it has something to say, and you're rooting for the protagonist the whole time.

When you think about ghouls, when you think about, zombies, when you think about The Walking Dead, none of that would have existed if this had not come out in 1968: Night of the Living Dead. This is one of the most iconic horror films, of its time and even now. And it talks about, our environment and how our environments, I think it has something deep to say about, radiation and what that does to our people, what that does to communities. The radiation in this film made all of the people in the cemetery who were dead come alive to eat other people and then infect them. So it did have something to say, and I think that it, you can't talk about Halloween, you can't talk about horror without Night of the Living Dead.

Oh, now I have been wanting to show you this my whole life. In fact, I've brought this on 19 vacations and you guys never wanted to watch it. It's so good. Oh, watch this. War and Peace, amazing. I mean, and it's animated. No, it's not animated, just joking, the cover. War and Peace. Yeah, you can get confused here at Criterion 'cause the posters are so cool, are so beautiful, yeah, that you think everything's animated.

Frances Ha, favorite Greta Gerwig performance. Oh, amazing. Though I also really liked the romantic comedy that you guys did together. Oh, thank you. You're welcome. Somehow I bet that's not. Watched it on a plane and it really got me through a long flight. All right, all right, well that picks a dad up, you know, it puts wind in his sails.

When I picked up Stranger Than Paradise I thought it was going to be Children of Paradise. You got to show everybody Children of Paradise. I constantly recommend it to people. I was so grateful that you—you're doing the Lord's work when you do that. For those of you out there at home, you can't go wrong, Children of Paradise. But I highly recommend being patient. Like Sunday morning, like cup of coffee, just chill out, sit down, enjoy the ride. A Good Morning watch. Yeah, it'll change your life. Great.

Have you seen this movie? 3 Women, Altman. Oh, right, 'cause when I fell in love with Nashville so hard I like checked this movie out. It is a confounding movie. I love it. It is so profoundly strange. Anything with Sissy Spacek is a winner as far as I'm concerned.

I took your mother to see this movie on our first dates, yeah. Husbands. Husbands, Cassavetes. Cool. So I think she liked it. She did, she didn't like the chairs at the Film Forum. She complained about the chairs, but I think she liked the movie.

The Magnificent Ambersons, I've actually never seen. Like people who say Orson Welles was a one-hit wonder, then there's the others who say, "Have you seen Magnificent Ambersons?" And I'm like, "No, I actually haven't." And they're like, "You're not really a film fanatic if you haven't seen that."

This movie has inspired me to no end. Pina. I don't know, I don't know this. Really? Put it in your bag. Okay. Wenders' documentary on Pina Bausch, the incredible choreographer. It sounds like it's going to be a dance documentary, but it's like it, I don't know, it's so moving. You know that one of the high points of my life was when we showed Wildcat at Telluride and I actually met Wim Wenders. I said Wenders and it's obviously Wim Wenders, I just. But you sounded, said it with such confidence that every, I even thought, "Do I pronounce his name wrong?" No, no, you're right. Anyway, we bought a cowboy hat together and that kind of made me— Changed your life. Well, it made me feel something must be going all right.

I'm looking for some of the movies on our list of our Wildcat inspirations, but I'm having a hard time finding An Angel at My Table. Do they have that? Oh, there it is. 'Cause what it does is it, An Angel at My Table is, it's yeah, it's a biopic, but it's a great film. You don't need to know who Janet Frame is, you don't, you don't need, you just Jane Campion knocking it out of the park again. And it's so patient. Even though like very little ever like quote-unquote happens in a scene, every moment that happens, every exchange, like every raised eyebrow is the, is the happening of the scene. And it's just, I don't know, like changed my brain, this movie.

Oh, Tess. I learned a little bit about how it was made and that they like shot every scene at golden hour, and they would just like prepare and rehearse all day and then go shoot at golden hour and then be done for the day. I was like, can we bring that back? I know. Like is anyone still doing that? 'Cause I'd like to volunteer as tribute to be in that movie.

Where you— Well, that makes me think, I mean it feels like when we watched Days of Heaven together, I felt like that movie must have been done that way too. They probably shot at, you know, 5:00 a. M. And 6:00 p. M. It's so beautiful. Where is Days of Heaven? The wall behind. No wonder we couldn't find it. Bright eyes, every now and then I see a Terrence Malick film and it burns my eyes. Okay, beautiful, Days of Heaven. It's a classic worth revisiting. It needs to be done.

Speaking of Terrence Malick and beauty, this is Peter Weir, and he directed my first, the one of, well the second movie I was in, Dead Poets Society, and he just retired, and you know, his whole canon is worth revisiting. But Picnic at Hanging Rock, we all owe a lot to this movie. This movie is one of those weird movies where you watch it and you're like, oh, people have been ripping this movie off for generations.

I also haven't seen Kicking and Screaming ever, and I would really like to. Is it, is it, is it, am I just, am I just seduced by the title or is it also— Well, the reason why you're seduced is Josh Hamilton is in this movie. Really? Yeah. I love him. I know, and the reason why it is my favorite Noah Baumbach film is because it stars Josh Hamilton. Note to Noah Baumbach: give Josh a great part again, your career will take off, dude. Yeah, he needs a lot of help. Yeah, he needs a lot of help.

I'm starting with Moonstruck. I think it's my all-time favorite movie. I think it's one of the greatest screenplays ever written. I think every performance in this movie is pitch perfect, and whenever I am in need of inspiration I put it on, and anytime I meet someone new and they haven't seen it, I will sit down with them and watch it, and that I think is the joy of movie making and movie watching. So we move on.

Tokyo Story. If you have not watched it, watch it. I watched it when I was very young and didn't understand it, and then the older I get the more I do understand it and the more I love it. Just a dream, one of the greatest movies ever made.

So, The Piano Teacher. It's not a comedy, and when I worked at a video store I would often recommend it to people, because I thought it was like an impressive movie to recommend to someone as like a young person. Oftentimes I'd recommend to families, not quite knowing, I hadn't seen it at the time. So I was kind of like, the cover looks, you know what I mean, it's like an, it looks like an important movie, and then I saw it and was like, oh no. Not kid-friendly. It's as good as I hoped it would be. I would now not recommend it for family viewing, but unbelievable performances and it is, gosh, it packs a punch. Wish I could take back some of those recommendations, from the video store, but you know what.

Election. This was one of those movies that made me realize that actors make very, very smart choices. Reese Witherspoon's choice to make this movie coming off of everything that she had been previously known for, I thought was so great. It was such a smart move, she was so brilliant in it, and it also showed a kind of like professional fearlessness, which I think as actors you hope that you get the opportunity to express. So Election. Reese, I love you.
One of the great love stories ever told. I could watch this movie over and over and over again. I mean, it goes without saying, Love & Basketball, always and forever. Watch it if you haven't.

Weekend. This was probably one of the first films that I saw that really spoke to like gay storytelling in a way that didn't feel heavy-handed, it didn't feel kind of we were telling the story. It was the first time that I just saw people existing in a way that felt so real, and, owe a lot to Andrew, and this is apparently director-approved, so Andrew, thank you, in advance for letting me take this home and for this beautiful, beautiful movie.

The Daytrippers. Parker Posey is someone who, I mean, I have tried in my life to watch every single one of her movies. One of the great actors of her time, our time, my time. Anyway, watch this movie, watch the entire Parker Posey catalog, frankly. You can start here, it's a good, it's a good place to start.

So The Virgin Suicides has a very special place in my heart. I was, taking a film production summer camp in Toronto, Canada, and we were asked, whether we wanted to go on a field trip, and the field trip was to the set of a movie that at the time we didn't know, we didn't know what the movie was, but it turned out to be The Virgin Suicides. And I remember like sitting, I must have been like 16 or 17, sitting with my film summer camp talking to Josh Hartnett, who was about to shoot that scene in the pool, and I remember him saying like, "It's really nice to meet you all, I am now going to come out in the tiniest pair of swim shorts you've ever seen in your life.", which I was like, you know, you got to do what you got to do, I guess. Anyway, it was like the first taste of filmmaking, and I never got to meet Sofia on the set of this movie, but I remember thinking like what a generous thing to invite a film production camp to your set. And her support funnily enough has like carried through my whole career. When Schitt's Creek was in its last season, we got, like a letter I guess from her saying how much she loved the show and wanted to send us champagne for the last day of shooting, and this full circle moment of like being on set for this movie, being so affected by her work, and then having her kind of congratulate our show on its last day with champagne, it was like, it was a pinch-me great moment. And I've only met her once and it was in passing and I didn't get to quite tell her how I felt, but Sofia, thank you for your generosity and thank you for playing like a big part in the inspiration of my career.

I think for my last, I mean I could be here for quite literally seven hours, so I think what I'm going to do is just close my eyes and pick, but I think I'm going to go on this wall because there are some older movies that I have not seen on this wall, and so I'm going to just close the eyes, I'm going to just close the eyes and... Kagemusha, Kurosawa. It's time. I have not seen it, it is time I watch it.

And I suppose I better pick out a film to start with, A Touch of Zen. It's really martial art movie making of a superior and poetic way. I think this is the first film I'm going to see when I get a chance to look at the DVD, because it'll thrill me.
Il Gattopardo. The Leopard. This is magnifico. This is really a masterpiece.
Beau travail. Claire Denis. Goddess. She got masculinity better than any man. Thank you, Claire.

The Last Wave, by the master Peter Weir. Peter Weir is a good friend of mine, and we share a beach in Australia where I go. And it's got David Gulpilil, who was in my first film I produced, Mad Dog. I'm looking forward to seeing this again. I remember all the water pouring out of the radio is a magnificent shot.

The Rules of the Game. La Règle du jeu. I'm choosing this film because I haven't seen it maybe for 50 years, 60 years, and it was one of Bertolucci's very favorite films. He loved this film. He was talking about it all the time. Anyway, I'm happy to have this. I'm very happy to have a very beautiful film by Jean Renoir.
One last. I've just seen it. There you go. The beginning of it all. What can I tell you? It'll be wonderful. Fellini, Federico, my hat's off.

The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie. In fact, I like that, but I've got three films here, and The Phantom of Liberty and That Obscure Object of Desire. Now, Serge Silberman, who was my inspiration as a producer when I was growing up as a young producer, I was looking at this man, and then I met him, and he gave me advice, you know, and he said to me, "Jeremy, you can only do well by using your own taste in choosing your projects. Never let anybody else choose your projects for you." And that was a very, very good piece of advice from this wonderful man.
I couldn't have a bag full without a bag of Wim. Kings of the Road. It's got the best poo in any film, all I can tell you. It's got an incredible, recommended poo. It's the most poetic poo in cinema.

Well so here The Killers, the version that I'm familiar with is the Don Siegel version. There's a movie that I just made called Asteroid City and without getting wasting your time, an aspect of it has to do with acting and the things actors do and sometimes overdo. One of the things that was a was like Wes had suggested I look at is Clu Gulager's performance in this film. I watched it so many times and needed it so much as a reference that I ended up just filming my television, which I shouldn't say, so that I had it on my phone at all times. Like he'll just do some stuff like this and then he'll just destroy something and it's like okay, how early, how many seconds ago was he prepping that move, you know what I mean? He's just he's great in it.

I like the making of things. I like to see how people communicate and express ideas that are sort of hard to explain what they're after or what they want and people trying to understand what someone else is trying to get at, and two big, big, big examples of that. Not only do I love these movies, but this is Under the Volcano and this is Straw Dogs. On top of Under the Volcano is great to watch John Huston watching the actors, seeing the shot, the way he talks to the actors, the way everyone is listening to each other, the way he's responding. You know, someone who's you know made these masterpieces and then while everything's happening, he's just sit here, he can just like sit there and read a paper and I go that's because he knows if he's doing.

Straw Dogs, the takeaways I take from watching this are silly, but one, that Dustin Hoffman, you see him shaving with an electric razor in his trailer. It looks like the kind of thing would just eat your neck up. But he's really talking about the movie, "I'm a mathematician," but the thing that I found really, that that stays with me is this I guess it has to do also with Under the Volcano, like John Huston reading the paper, sort of what people do, how they budget their focus and energy over the course of a shoot and what they do between takes, and, Sam Peckinpah doesn't read the newspaper. He has a knife that he, is a pretty big knife, and he throws it at this door that's like a broken door piece of wood leaning against his house until they're ready to shoot. I've never been around a knife-throwing director. Don't know how I'd feel about it, and I guess in that case I'd be more afraid of the razor shaving one.

An Unmarried Woman. Jill Clayburgh I think is just one of the greatest actors of all time. Wonderful, beautiful performance. I don't know, she's like showing you a maze, but without solving it for you. When my wife and I first started dating, I think we were dating, I don't know if in my mind that's when it started, but you know it doesn't matter if you didn't know we were I was dating you, we were dating around this time. We were giving each other music and movies and things, and my wife gave me this. Looking back, when it's someone that you love and have a family with, it's amazing that they gave you this thing because it's saying like, "Here's me, but I don't know why I can't, here's things like I can't say." Like it's a way to invite someone to know you in a way that you can't really articulate. I've kind of have been talking about that and thinking about that, with my new show, The Idol, coming out and, you know, clogging up the TL with controversy. We can't deny that women have unorthodox and naughty desires like this, even if they reflect the rules of the patriarchy or are like wrong desires to have, they still exist and thrive and burn, probably by the nature that they're forbidden. Buñuel was looking at this decades before the current discourse around sex scenes and post-MeToo feminism, all of it. It's hard to watch, it's challenging, it's scandalizing. I mean, imagine the conversation we're having now, 1967. I love this film and I also love watching Catherine Deneuve just go so bravely into that.
Grey Gardens, Maysles brothers. One word: staunch. Happy Pride.

The Red Shoes is one of my favorite Technicolor films. It's one of like the weirder, darker films that I've seen captured on Technicolor. When I was shooting Barbie, Greta was shooting on a custom color cast, which was on the slate called Techno Barbie, which I loved. She wanted to recreate the look and feel of classic Hollywood studio Technicolor, and, for Technicolor, I think this is as good as it gets.

Black Narcissus, my favorite Technicolor film. Sexually repressed nuns in a convent in India. Bad vibes, great visuals. I feel like Deborah Kerr never really got her due. She, she had kind of a more subdued, straightforward approach in an era where kind of the more theatrical performances of someone like Bette Davis or Joan Crawford, who I loved, were kind of like more Oscar bait. Deborah was just kind of holding it down. I feel like, I feel like Deborah would have been like an even bigger star, later in the 20th century.

Design for Living, Ernst Lubitsch. Pre-Code romantic comedy farce, basically about a throuple. I don't know, this film just feels like home to me. This feel, this film just feels like Thursday. I saw somebody on Twitter recently talking about how the Hays Code and the censorship that emerged after this film in Hollywood in the '30s going into the '40s, how like that's kind of the root of culture getting messed up in America. Last Days of Disco with Whit Stillman. And that's why we watch movies. Thank you, goodbye. You're never getting these back.

The films that help me to really think about how I would like to do the cinema was Mandabi of Sembène. When I saw that film I, I just really, really see for the first time someone who was looking at me, someone who was looking at my culture. I was looking, when I was child, a lot of American films and French film also, but it was open me to the world, but not connect me to my reality. It was the first time that I was seeing a film that really connect me to my reality, yeah.

And, Black Girl. I grew up in Cameroon and wanted to do cinema without having any legacy about cinema. My parents was just a modest family in Yaoundé, Cameroon, living their life and offer us something good by sending us in school. But I wanted to do, to dream, to dream about story. And Black Girl really putting in, putting in my face my own colonization, because I went to Belgium study cinema and hoping that in Belgium I would learn how to tell my story. But I, I, I discovered that I already have it in me, and what I really learned in Belgium was just some tools or how to think about that cinema. And it's when I watch Black Girl that I really, I have that, that phrase in my mind: "What do you want to say, Rosine? What do you want to say?"

Bicycle Thieves. I don't really, in my way of doing, I don't create something, I just find it in the daily life of people and organize it, because I really hope that we all have a part of cinema in us and I just have to find it, yeah. And the Bicycle Thieves really help me to just see that, that yes, that reality was possible, that just to capture the reality as it is, as we are seeing it.

And then we have Close-Up. The mixing of fiction and documentary was so powerful that I was, like Safi Faye said, there was no boundary between, as African we don't have no limit between fiction and documentary. And, and Close-Up, it's really in alignment with that. It also opened me to the work of Makhmalbaf and, and how, how I was connected to, to people that I don't even know or imagine before, and how I was so close to that reality only because they, they frame it in a certain way and they show it in a certain way. Also free me, free me to just say to myself: I don't have to choose between documentary and, and fiction, I just want to just tell story as I really felt it, yeah.

The feeling that you've dropped in the room and you're right there. You're just, you're like in there, you're just not being able to join in the conversation. They're so, not only visually beautiful, but unique storytelling, and the voices of the characters, you almost feel like they're ad-libbing their dialogue, that's how real it feels. Renoir really has, you know, his father was a painter, and he has a great sense of mise-en-scène and where to put the characters within the frame. And it's a phenomenal, if you're talking about blocking and staging, this is a phenomenal film. Scenes from a Marriage. I did a talk at Brooklyn Academy of Music and I introduced John Singleton's, to me, one of his great films, Baby Boy. And one thing that was interesting is that John Singleton was at the, the Canadian Film Centre, and they asked him, thinking it was maybe in 2004, if he passed away, what would be his favorite movie, and it was Baby Boy. And I mention this with Bergman because sometimes John Singleton was looking for the truth of character, and in Baby Boy you see a lot of tension, you see maybe some violence with the characters, especially with the relationship between male and female, but you see that in this, too. So it's not just, you know, sometimes we get pigeonholed, Black directors get pigeonholed, and we think the violence is just about our culture, but this shows that their marriage is just as tenuous, and sometimes just as violent, and emotionally violent.
I love this movie, if you want to laugh, Divorce Italian Style.

This is wonderful. This is Agnès Varda, she's one of my favorite directors, too, a woman. And her really great film, Cléo from 5 to 7, is wonderful. I also love Vagabond with Sandrine Bonnaire. It could actually inspired me to do my movie, Vagabond, because it showed a woman who was a complex character. She wasn't just a good girl or a bad girl. She was really complex in this movie, and it was a realistic portrait of a woman going through, oh, called homelessness and despair, but still having a sense of who she is as herself. And that was kind of a great inspiration for my film, Just Another Girl on the I. R. T. Great director, Agnès Varda.

Being There. We named a record after this movie. So that record, that means a lot to me.

Over the years I found the world to be weirder and more unpredictable than fiction is, and both of these movies blur the lines between documentary storytelling and completely made up, which I find exciting.

Melville. I've not seen this one. This man's movies are personal favorites. I think some of the greatest film noir ever made, and I can't wait to see this. I love the look and the gritty feel of Melville's films, and even a film like Le Doulos, which doesn't actually make complete sense, is completely captivating to me.

film_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
catalog_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
quote: But John and I grabbed the box set, The BBS Story: America Lost and Found. This film, The King of Marvin Gardens, is a real favorite of mine. It's beautifully photographed, I'm pretty sure it's László Kovács that was the cinematographer, and just it's absolutely gorgeous to look at. It's a very lonely film, very kind of slightly surrealistic, takes place in Atlantic City in the early '70s as Atlantic City is kind of in a state of decay, and it's just it's just fascinating. There's a scene in the middle of the movie that takes place in the abandoned convention center in Atlantic City that is one of my favorite scenes in all of film. So excited about this.

catalog_title: Eclipse Series 9: The Delirious Fictions of William Klein

Serge Gainsbourg works in it, and just completely unpredictable, wild movie, and I love the way it looks, and I'm excited to see what else is on here.

quote: When I was in college in Washington, D. C. A good friend of mine worked concessions at the Key Theatre, and which was an independent theater in Washington, D. C. So she basically let me get into movies for free, and also gave me a free bag of popcorn. And one of the first films, so it was all indie films, and I didn't really care what it was, I had no money, I just wanted to go to the movies all the time. And one of the first films that I saw was, Cronos from Guillermo del Toro. Didn't know anything about the movie, I gradually discovered that it was a horror vampire film. I found it really, really fascinating. I mean, Ron Perlman speaking Spanish, which I, you know, I've seen the actor before, but didn't know he spoke Spanish. And it was really a great twist on the, the vampire mythos.

Oh, well, I'll start with one of the basics for me, which is 12 Angry Men. I, one of my favorite films of all time. I guess I always describe this film as an action movie of words. In many ways, the reason why I thought that I could write the play version of One Night in Miami was because of seeing 12 Angry Men and saying that there was more excitement in this battle of ideas in this room than anything I'd ever seen. So, very, very inspirational film for me.

Oh, one of my favorite animated films of all time, Watership Down. It's, it's very interesting because I first saw Watership Down, it aired on television when I was a little kid, and it kind of terrified me when, when I first saw the film. And I loved that about it. So for me, I never saw animation cartoons as something for, for kids. I always just thought of animation as an incredible medium for a certain kind of storytelling. And I always, I don't really see animation as for young adults, or children, or adults. I see animation as for everyone. And it's a lot of that philosophy, I think, that, that brought me to, to Pixar, and was something that we always kept in mind when we were making the movie Soul. So Watership Down was, is always a film that I, that I bring up as something that it might scare kids a little bit, but they can also enjoy it. And it's a, it's a very special, very important film for me.

Matewan. It's about union organizing, in West Virginia coal mines, which I know sounds like super duper exciting, but it actually is, if you Google, look up the, the Matewan Massacre, to see how, you know, the, the coal mining companies, did their union busting. And there's a, there's a great scene, there's a great speech that Chris Cooper makes in this film when James Earl Jones's character shows up and wants to join the, the union, about how, you know, how the, the corporations often separate people along racial lines or, or ethnic lines, and, and, and that's how they keep people from power. And I think that that's a lesson that we could, learn a lot from today. So it's a really, really great film, Matewan, and I'm happy to, to have a copy of that.

Bill Duke's Deep Cover. Love this movie. Most people know that this film, it's most known because it was the first appearance of a song featuring Snoop Dogg, Snoop Doggy Dogg. The, the Deep Cover, soundtrack is really, famous, but I, I just love this film. Laurence Fishburne and, Jeff Goldblum. Laurence Fishburne is a cop who goes undercover, and Jeff Goldblum as a lawyer slash sleazy, drug dealer. And this was just a really great, just like crime noir film, that, that I'm super excited to see added to the collection.

This is super exciting. I did not expect this to be here when I got here, but, this is my first time getting my hands on the Criterion Collection copy of One Night in Miami, that I'm the writer of, based on my play, directed by the incredible, Regina King. We're, I'm so proud of this movie. Talk about like a labor of love. And I cannot wait for everyone to see all the additional materials that both Regina and I, and a lot of other folks involved in the film recorded for the, the Criterion release. So yeah, One Night in Miami, make sure you, you check it out.

I know everyone's seen this one. I know you've all seen Naked. How incredible is this movie? I can't even, I can't even tell you the plot. Like if you ask me what's the plot, I'm like, it's hard to explain. But it's just, it's amazing. I mean, you want to kill the guy, but you love him, you know? I mean, it's, it's nuts.

This is one of my favorite movies of all time, but I want to take it. Mona Lisa. I'm not taking it because I've seen it too many times, but it's, it's amazing. Bob Hoskins. The Long Good Friday, Mona Lisa. That Bob Hoskins was a beast.

My Life as a Dog. You ever see this movie? This is one of the great movies of all time. If you haven't seen this movie, you, I promise you, I mean, it's amazing. There's no way to describe it. It's Swedish. The beginning is him with his family, his family dies, and he's trying to pick up a glass of milk at the family table. Even if you just watch the first five minutes, you're going to be glad you saw that movie.

Well, what I really want to talk about is Roma. Now a lot of you people are saying, Roma, it was all over the place. No one's denying that. But what a beautiful, like, love story to the city of Rome. Even though a lot of people said it doesn't remind them of Rome. But if Fellini says it's like Rome, who are you to argue? Fellini said, this is my Roma. A lot of critics were like, well, we didn't really. Let, listen, I'd like to make this about New York. I mean, I'd like to make my version of Roma, New Yorker, you understand?

This, Le petit soldat. And I know you people are saying, oh, look at him, he's being pretentious, Le petit soldat, but, but anyway, I've always wanted to see this movie because I've heard amazing things about it, and I just watched the other movie about the Algerian, The Day of the Jackal.

So, Something Wild. This movie, Carroll Baker, she was in, where her husband and her made this movie, but it's got all these shots of New York, like all these New York shots. And by the way, the most brutal, it's a movie ahead of its time. She gets raped, doesn't tell anybody, and has PTSD. I don't even know where the whole plot, but anyway, but it's a very small movie. It's really, it was ahead of its time. It was, you know, I watched it, I was like, nobody thought about this stuff until the '90s, really, what happened. This movie is like 1960 or 1959, but anyway.

Susan Seidelman's. Here's the thing, when you're from New York and you're old like me, you love to see old New York. Like Smithereens. Who would have ever thought this was old New York? But when I watch it, I'm like, oh my god, I miss New York, you know, the way it was.

Claudine, by the way, another, another amazing New York movie. It's like Edgecombe Avenue or something. It's the whole, all these shots of New York in like 1971 just bring back my little childhood, so that's why I always love it, you know. And, that was another good one. James Earl Jones, the garbage man, Claudine's working, she's a cleaning lady, and their kids, and it was really good.

Could you do one of these without a Cassavetes of some sort? Why not Husbands? Why not? Because I can't think of anything more fun than the thing of the clash of acting styles that go on in this. Everybody is fighting for territory. You can almost, if you listen closely, hear John Cassavetes's maniacal cackle watching these guys go nose to nose, tear duct to tear duct with each other.

How about Dexter Gordon in his film debut in this film, who was one of the most decent people you would ever meet, such a wonderful soul. I had many dinners at festivals around the world with him. And Tavernier tells a great story about casting Martin Scorsese in this film, saying, "You know, I said, 'You know, Marty, I want someone like you who is the soul of decency, but ruthless.' And Marty goes, 'I can do that.'", so he's sort of an impresario on this. But the Dexter Gordon performance, and Bertrand was smart enough to let Dexter shape the performance because he had written one thing on paper and Dexter kind of goes, "Black people don't talk like this." "Dexter, how do they talk?" "Let me show you." And it works in performance. And Oscar win for the Herbie Hancock score.

Oh, To Sleep with Anger. Every Burnett film feels, has a sense of being lived in, but nothing feels staged. You can feel that intersection of American Black life and Italian neorealism and also the Nouvelle Vague. I can't think of anyone who's more masterly about that kind of thing, about unobtrusive, generous filmmaking than Charles Burnett.

Here's a film that finally exists on home video. You talk about a film that probably has impacted as many filmmakers of color as any movie the last 40 years, it would be this one. And, just the chemistry between the two leads and the way music is used, and maybe probably one of the first big budget films that really bring the sort of slam poetry as a kind of emotional evocation. The director should have surfaced again. You can't help but see this title and think, what was in the establishment that kept him from working? Because clearly he had the stuff to make many, many movies, and I'm hoping there's a big one from him around the corner.

My hands are shaking because I think that spirit of anxiety passes along when you're holding up The Parallax View. I got the title in that time. It's the Pakula film that to me feels the least studied. You sort of feel a kind of control of the camera in a lot of his films, and this one feels like he's really trying to bring the filmmaking of someone like Fred Wiseman or D. A. Pennebaker, a lot of the documentary filmmaking. He wants us to feel the anxiety in each frame.

Would you say, Miller's Crossing-wise, would there be a, a Criterion Closet without a Coen brothers film in it? I have a specific love for this movie because, as a comics person, I always thought it was kind of the version of Will Eisner's The Spirit. That if you did The Spirit, this would be it. Gabriel Byrne's always being punched in the head, he wears his hat low covering his eyes, and at the end he turns out to be a little bit smarter than almost everybody else, except for Marcia Gay Harden. There's an action sequence in this, a violent sequence actually, that's almost like a musical number, where a group of thugs think they're going to take out Albert Finney, and he puts his cigar down to dispatch them. At the end of the sequence, he picks up his cigar and finishes it. As someone who likes both Will Eisner and cigars, I can't recommend Miller's Crossing more highly. By the way, when I asked them about that, they went, "Who is Will Eisner?", they had no idea what I was talking about. And I said, "Well, it seems kind of Three Stooges." "Oh yeah!" Because he's getting dope-slapped all the time. "Yes, of course it seems like The Three Stooges."

The Essential Films of Melvin Van Peebles is appropriately this. If you're looking online to pick up one of these things, that you should have it. But also what's really great about these movies is that they're really about the spirit of independent filmmaking. That Melvin recognized the way to, if you were a person of color, to promote your film was to make it independent rather than a Black film, which means you'd be left in the margins. Instead, he made it about the selling of the film. And of course, the great thing that we talk about in the documentary I just made, which will be on Netflix, it's called, Is That Black Enough for You?!? Is that Melvin was smart enough to realize that rather than pay to submit his film to the MPAA, the X rating wasn't copyrighted. So he just slapped it on himself and said, "Rated X by an all-white jury," and effectively hijacked it, and also in effect created the XXX rating because everybody would say, "Well, we'll put an X on ours too and call it triple X and quadruple X."

Okay, these last two that I'm taking, I'm taking, one, I haven't seen either, but I also think the packages are really cool. So of course I've seen The Before Trilogy and other films by Richard Linklater, but Dazed and Confused, oh my gosh, I'm in love with how cool the packaging is.
The Cranes Are Flying is in my Criterion top 10, and it's just one of the most swooningly romantic and expressionistic films I've seen. It's by Mikhail Kalatozov, who also did Soy Cuba, I Am Cuba.

catalog_title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters

I'm getting a Blu-ray of Black Narcissus. We discussed this on one of our quarantine film club meetings. So when lockdown started, I started a film club with a few of my friends, and this was one of the movies that we talked about. Although some of us did not like it, I loved it though.
Is it silly if I do one where I just close my eyes and pick something random? Quadrophenia, a film by Franc Roddam. I've never heard of this filmmaker, I'll be honest, but I'm excited to watch this.

I remember watching The Devils in the Lincoln, at Lincoln Center when they did a retrospective of Ken Russell, but I never got to see Women in Love, which is considered, I think, his masterpiece or one of his masterpieces. So I'm going to grab a copy of this.

I'm getting a copy of The Age of Innocence. I've seen the film of course and love it, and I also think that the source material by Edith Wharton is one of the most perfect American novels ever written, and Michelle Pfeiffer is just gorgeous in it.

I also have this Cassavetes box set, and funnily enough, I, my film Lingua Franca is nominated for John Cassavetes Award at the Independent Spirit Awards. And A Woman Under the Influence is of course a very, very influential film, is also formative for me as a filmmaker.

catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: I'm definitely not leaving the Criterion closet without this box set of the filmography of Agnès Varda. She is a hero and a champion, and I've only really seen a handful of her works, Cléo of course, Vagabond, and her later ones, but I really want to dig, dig deeper into her body of work.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: Oh, okay, so this, obviously fantastic. Naked Lunch. Howard Shore, Ornette Coleman soundtrack, David Cronenberg, Burroughs. This is a full package.

Okay, Grey Gardens. This is a perfect example of kind of where I grew up. Like, these ladies remind me of women in my family. Not just with, like, the sort of New England, Northeast quality, but also the, family versus family and, slight lovable insanity.

Oh, and then of course one of my favorite films of all time, and I'm so glad—I actually looked online to make sure you guys had done this before I came here, because Repo Man. Harry Dean Stanton, amphetamines, Emilio Estevez, punk rock. This is a great flick.

Is this Graham Greene? Odd Man Out. Carol Reed's fantastic. Really like, anybody that would put Orson Welles in a movie and have him do the Orson Welles rule, where you talk about the bad guy for the whole movie and then meet him in the last, like, 30 minutes of the movie. It's like a real payoff kind of thing, but they're like, you know. So I felt like Carol Reed always came from the same school of cinema as Orson Welles, and they worked really well together, and this is a great flick too. It's psychological noir, perfect. Also, the line, "A robbery that goes horribly wrong." It's classic cinema.

This movie is upsettingly good. I make my girlfriend watch movies with me constantly to the point where I think she's sick of watching movies and probably sick of me, but this was one of the movies that I think made it all worth it. Watched it together, she was like, "That's a great fucking movie." And like, after that, like, every now and then I'm like—like, to get her to watch a movie, I'd be like, "It's Frankenheimer," and like, reluctantly, like, "Okay." But yeah, this is, this made me dig into all of Sinatra's other films as well that he acted in, like The Man with the Golden Arm. And, you know, Sinatra's great because he is exactly what he is when he's emulated, and everyone loves his music, but this was his finest work. Like, Frankenheimer really got a great performance out of him, and I already own this, but this movie is perfect.

Fantastic. David Byrne, True Stories. Great music, great movie. I just—the Talking Heads sort of started in my hometown. I'm from Providence, Rhode Island, and there was a, like, there's all this mythos. I grew up—the first apartment I lived in when I was 17 was with, like, two people I barely knew. It was a nightmare, it was a shithole, it was in the basement, we got robbed. But right around the corner was a place that they called the Vault that apparently used to be—I don't know if this is true or not, but it used to be an old bank, and apparently the Talking Heads used to live there and practice there. And I remember hating the Talking Heads when I was a kid just because it was too twee for me and I was into, like, punk and metal. Now I love the Talking Heads and I have a little point of pride, so I've been buying all this stuff and I bought this. This is fantastic. And, you know, I just saw David Byrne play recently and he was great, and I can't say enough good stuff. And now I'm, like, reading about them working with Brian Eno and, like, looking into how they wrote music and even taking a little bit of that for our band and emulating something that I hated when I was a kid, which is a very strange thing to do, but there it is.

Okay, this is the one—this is one of the ones that I actually came, in, and totally in love with this flick when I was a kid. This was probably one of the first black and white movies I saw. I'm a huge horror fan, and it kind of blew my mind that somebody—Night of the Living Dead, that somebody, sorry, that somebody would have made this film, and it kept my attention as a hyperactive kid, you know, black and white. Like, if you look on Amazon now, I was like looking up, just, just for morbid curiosity. Looking on Amazon reviews of films is a terrible idea, and I remember reading somebody's like three-word review that just said, "Ew, black and white," you know? And I was like, really? But then I was like, wait, I think I actually might have felt like that when I was a kid too, that like if it was old, it wasn't good. But this movie was the first black and white film I saw that actually kind of like kicked open the door, realizing that a lot of old movies are better than movies now, frankly. And this is a—this is a perfect piece of cinema, and because of that, I just love everything George A. Romero does. I still have all the Fangoria magazines that have interviews with him and stuff, and this was Tom Savini? Maybe it might be too early for the two of them. But anyway, I'm very excited to see that Criterion did a fat collection of this flick, because it's a statement about civil rights and war, and also happens to just be a zombie flick, which is awesome. So, perfect film.

What immediately jumped to my face is the Dreyer box. I remember when I was working with Jacques Rivette, we went to see Gertrud together and we organized a screening of Ordet, and we had long discussion about what was so important in Dreyer's work for so many filmmakers. So because this is in my hand and because it made so much effect on me, I think, may I put it in the bag?

What I immediately jumped to my face is the Dreyer box. I remember when I was working with Jacques Rivette, I we went to see Gertrud together and we organized a screening of Ordet, and we had long discussion about what was so important in Dreyer's work for so many filmmaker. What immediately jumped to my face is the Dreyer box. What is Gate of Flesh? Yeah, it's Suzuki's film, Gate of Flesh. I knew it under another—, come on, this is so great. Okay, what a beautiful title in English. Oh, Gate of Flesh. Okay, let's turn because this is too attractive.
Tout va bien! I remember I have not seen Tout va bien for a long, long time, the film by Jean-Luc Godard and Jean-Pierre Gorin. Well, Tout va bien, it's great.

Summer with Monika. I've been dreaming of it, I've been dreaming of it. I've been dreaming of that pure, splendid momentum of youth. And of course, each time I see it I am desperate, as if through the film you know that this youth and this light of summer is not going to last. And I think I would like to finish there.

I think all of this film, His Girl Friday. Howard Hawks, very important and very—I'm very shy when I'm watching Hawks. I feel like I'm such a failure. Hawks is always giving a lesson of how bad I am somehow. He's magic, yes.
The Importance of Being Earnest. This has one of my favorite one-liners in it, The Importance of Being Earnest: "If you are not too long, I shall wait for you the rest of my life."

Lady Eve, okay, Lady Eve has one of the best love speeches ever written. His, his speech about, you know, "When I look at you, I see, I see two children coming towards each other. They're eight years old," and keeps on advancing it. One copy of The Lady Eve.
Sullivan's Travels. Everything by Preston Sturges.
Okay, Shampoo, because everybody in the cast hit it out of the park.

Albert Brooks is one of the, you know, I mean a specifically original and great comedy talent. And Julie Hagerty was the perfect person for him to play with. And this has one of the, I guess one of the most famous comedy monologues in film. And you know, and you know, Albert wrote, I think with Monica Johnson on this, yeah. Wrote, directed, starred in. I think, was I in this? I think I was. Did they go that far down, far enough in the cast? Was I in this? I think, yes, I was in this. I think I was, I was in a few of Albert's films. He always said, he always said, "Be in the film and I'll make it fun." I always said yes. It was never fun, because I became that, but it was, this is the most valuable thing I got from the experience. And, and, you know, and, and, and Albert's, you know, just a comedy genius, the most original stuff. The, you know, he, it, it's, he's this very specific figure in American comedy and is, and I became, you know, the thing I got being in front of the camera for the only time that I was ever in front of the camera, and once I was, had a, had a real part I think in one of them, and, and I became the worst actor a director can have. I was the guy who was outside your trailer when you got there in the morning: "I can do it again, let me do it better." I became that guy. But it's only when you feel the vulnerability of being like that, it helps you, you know, it, I think it helps you direct.

Before I directed my first film, John Cassavetes and Elaine May were on the studio lot, and they were improvising a play. They were writing a play by improvisation. And it was the most amazing thing I've ever seen in my life. And just before I, never directed before, I'm getting ready for my first movie, and he was so generous and just hanging with him, you know, there'll never be a spirit of film like him. I mean everybody, everybody expected to do it for the love. I remember there was one actor who was involved in it, it was going to be Christmas, and we were all at lunch together. I was just there every day in the audience, and sometimes they'd turn to me and they'd direct comments at me. I didn't know whether it was part of the improvisation or whether it was real. You couldn't tell reality and improvisation, eventually you didn't know what was real, what was unreal. But the, the spirit was extraordinary to be around. And then there was one day during the Christmas holiday where everybody, he took everybody and me, the audience, to lunch. And, and one of the actors said—well, they've been at it for several weeks—and one of the actors said, "I had to take a paying job." And, and it wasn't only that John said no, he said to the guy, "You better not let Elaine hear you said that." Because that was it, everybody was there for passion. Anyway, he's in, you know, I'll make a case for him being one of the great men ever in film, and started independent film. I mean, you can't be more important than him.
Great artist. I heard this film is amazing and this has just been recommended to me. Never seen this, I'm very curious about this.

The first film that that I saw in my life that changed my perception of film and basically made me believe that I could someday make a film was Altman's Nashville. I saw it in the theaters when I was when I was a teenager and there was something so epic in the scope of it, something so a spirit of also mischievousness which I would later learn is one of the best things about working with Robert Altman. Oh, there it is.
This is a great film, Sweet Smell of Success.

This is an amazing film. There's a reporter that goes undercover in a mental institution and try to solve a murder. And there's a scene in it that is shocking even now where a African-American inmate stands up on top of a box and starts giving a speech, a histrionic speech. And it's about this black man is talking about Negroes and how they have to be stopped. And I asked Sam about it, he says, "Yeah, that's that's that's not, I didn't write that." He said, "That comes from Congressional Record." That's direct speech by a congressman about a black men and the blacks in our country. So that he did that kind of subversive that subversive writing and filmmaking.

Okay, another movie that changes your life. There's that great part in that where he talks about living in New York and how he's questioning whether New York is just one big jail and we don't think that we can get out of it. We've convinced ourselves as New Yorkers that we can never leave it. I haven't seen that for 30 years.
I haven't seen that for 30 years.

quote: And right now I'm holding Jules and Jim, which I'm taking with me. I was kind of, the first time I saw it, I kind of like, I was, you know, I put on blah, blah, blah. Oh, I see, I get it. And then when she's walking with the other two guys and they're involved in a conversation amongst themselves, totally ignoring her, and because she doesn't like that, she just out of nowhere jumps into the Seine. I was like, oh. Oh, now I'm interested.

Oh, well, let's just, you know, in the interest of being like fully completing, let's take Rules of the Game, shall we? Right? It's one of those things, it's a film school thing, you know what I mean?

Notorious. Hitchcock's Notorious. I think it's a masterpiece. It's funny what you can do, what you can get away with in a movie from that era. Outside of the obvious that, you know, the, that the Nazis guys are smuggling is literally being kept, and Grant spills it out onto the bottom, to the floor, and it's, this is prior to the detonation of the atomic bomb, so we give them a little pass on that, but, you know, Grant falls in love with Ingrid Bergman in like a shot, right? Like they're in Rio, and there's like a scene on a hill, and that's, and that's the movie going, okay, they're, so they're in love now. Okay, they're in love, and can we move on with the story? Okay, good, we can move on with the story. Let's just move on with the story. I'll give you one scene where they fall in love, and then we're moving on with the story, and the audience just accepts it. Whereas now you could never do that. You'd have to, you'd have to detail them falling in love, that would have to be a part of it. And for him, it was just a pipe to get past so that the rest of the story could function. Kind of miss those days.

Blind Chance, I think I have, but I'm taking it because it's Krzysztof Kieślowski. And as long as you have The Dekalog and Red and perhaps Double Vie de Véronique, as long as you have that, you're good.

Oh, Deep Cover. Now this was a movie that was very influential to me. I love Fish in this movie, I love his performance. He's so commanding and spare and charismatic as this guy. It's a real, for me, it's a real movie star performance. And there's some elements in here that I actually stole from for Love Jones. The sort of toast poetry, kind of like Iceberg Slim kind of toast poetry that's in the voiceover of this movie, I nicked a little bit of that for some of the dialogue in Love Jones. I thought this was fantastic.
And then it would be nice to come back to the Ozu, now that I'm, you know, way older than I was in film school, and see how I feel about it. That'd be cool.

quote: Oh, the movie, the movie who really confirmed my desire and encouraged me and make me say, "Okay, I am going to be a filmmaker." Black Orpheus, Camus, Marcel Camus. Oh gosh, Marcel Camus, he doesn't know what he did to me when I when I saw that film and I was a young girl in the Caribbean. And that that day the theater was packed and I would never forget, it was so rare to have a movie with Black characters and in positive role roles. So the distributor decided to increase the cost of the ticket because the characters, there was, they were Black, and people were fighting to see that movie. They were so starving to see themselves, people like them on screen. So that man, he said, "Okay, the ticket will be more expensive because there are Black folks on the screen." And people wanted that, and I think that I saw that movie, that story, at least 50 times. Orfeu Negro. Oh, wow. Love it.

Yes, yes, yes, Mr. Hitchcock, Alfred, of course. I learned a lot from him. Now, when The Lady Vanishes, yeah. And I remember with my brothers when we were watching a Hitchcock movie like Psycho or others, you know, in fact we used to play a game. We were, I have three brothers and myself, watching the movie and we will try to imagine the who is the villain, who did the coup, what will happen next. And of course we will fail because he was, oh, it was impossible with Hitchcock. He will take you all over the place.
Oh, Guillermo del Toro, he's a genius, my dad! Everybody should see his movies, he's great, I love him.

I'm happy because very few people, you know, know that movie, The Naked Island. They call it L'Île nue in French, has the same translation. That movie has no dialogues, and the way that that filmmaker told the story with those two characters, a wife, a man and his wife on a boat. They live on an island and then they have they do the crossing to go to town to buy food, water, and all kind of things. And no dialogue, and it's a feature film, and you have to sit there and then you just like, you get into that movie, and not one minute you feel bored.
Oh, Guillermo del Toro, he's a genius, my dad! Everybody should see his movies, he's great, I love him.
Oh, Guillermo del Toro, he's a genius, my dad! Everybody should see his movies, he's great, I love him.

Okay, then The 400 Blows from Truffaut. I was very fortunate to meet Truffaut through his daughter Laura. I was a student in Paris and I was I was working on my first movie, a screenplay, I was writing the screenplay Sugar Cane Alley. And Truffaut read the script, he gave me some advice, and at the end he became my godfather. And when the movie got the best film, the César for Best First Film in Paris, what we will call the French Oscar for Best First Film, Truffaut was there in that room because he was getting the César for his for all his work. And I talk about it with a lot of emotion because he was very sick, and that was the last time they saw him in public because he had a tumor and he died shortly after that.

quote: I just want to like, one of the first Criterion DVDs I ever bought was Knife in the Water. It was for a paper I wrote on Polanski. I'm afraid to watch this. I'm afraid about how offended I'll probably be, but I worship this film and I worship the short that comes with it, Two Men and a Wardrobe. This is spectacular.

I mean, this is just the, like the fight sequence in Do the Right Thing is one of the best things that's ever been put on film. It's flawless. It's just a flawless sequence. The opening sequence is great. I think if there's anything that has been a mainstay in all the films, it's like dancing, and if you get those things right then you're fine. This is gonna be a good movie.

It's yeah, The Spirit of the Beehive. I saw this in film school. I don't remember what happens in it, but I remember feeling so caught up in this girl's world. I remember feeling like the film matched the world and that's really rare, that like the pace of the film and the unfolding of her narrative matched childhood in a way, which is how I feel about Ratcatcher as well.

But then you have a film like Ratcatcher and a filmmaker like Lynne Ramsay and you're like, yeah, I'm here for what she has to say. Ramsay as an artist, paintings, there's some dance, gorgeous. I'm really touched by everything she does.

So we've got Cassavetes. I was in a class with Ira Sachs and it was like the best directing class I've ever taken because it's funny with directing, there really isn't a way that you can teach it. It's sort of like how do you teach someone to have a personality or like have a taste? It's like you just are you and go make something. But Ira Sachs was really great because he showed us films by auteurs and then we've read about like interviews with the auteurs and then the whole point of that, the end of the class, he was like, well, just make something and I booked this room, we're gonna screen it here for your classmates. And one of the filmmakers he showed was Cassavetes. And when I look back at Cassavetes, it felt like whenever I was watching his stuff, like he was making his own rules. I'm like, whether it worked for me or not on a personal level as a viewer, I was like, you're not following anything prescriptive. And so much of film school felt like prescriptive, like this is how you line up the shot, like this is how you get inside the emotional like language of that character. And I don't think it's that straightforward. I actually think a lot of filmmaking is throwing the rules out the window and being like, this is what turns me on, like this is where my instincts are taking me, and that's what it felt like with all of the Cassavetes films I've seen.

I have to take Tiny Furniture because I've never seen Creative Nonfiction and I think that's part of this DVD, right? Yeah, and an interview between Lena and Nora Ephron, so I'll start with that. So Tiny Furniture, it's where I'm gonna start.

Safe was a really huge influence on Cameron Post. There are like several sequences and a shot that I like straight up lifted from this. When I watched this, when I was about to do my last pass of the script, and it kind of just blew my mind open. I was like, oh, there's a whole 'nother element of institutionalization and group therapy here that I haven't addressed yet.
I just got a really good pitch: I Knew Her Well, which I'm taking 100% because of the cover.

This is a really great cover for Day for Night. It's hard. I'm kind of mad at Criterion Channel right now. I became a subscriber recently and so I revisited a bunch of films I really loved and it turns out they're all super problematic. I started with Jules and Jim, which like was kind of the film that made me want to be a director, and at the time I was like, this just taught me everything I know about love. And I just revisited and was like, oh, that sucks, that film is not anything I should take seriously about love. I feel like, I think for all French New Wave though, that like the thesis statement could kind of be like, bitches be cray.

And this is Life Is Sweet. I've never seen a more honest depiction on screen of bulimia, but it's not about bulimia, it's about this family. It's Mike Leigh. It's my favorite Mike Leigh film. It's really good.

Like, I've been reading about Fellini's 8½, and, and I don't even know if there's a connection between what I'm doing and 8½, but I, I find there's something about, and I did see 8½ there, that's an amazing, edition of it. But, yeah, just reading about the making of it and the design of it, and, and that just, that sometimes gives me a lot more ideas than, actually watching the film itself. And even the film itself can be disappointing when you've read so much about it. So I, I, I mean, certainly not the case of 8½. I, I really love that, and I think, yeah, that's gonna have to be another one I take.
La strada I haven't seen, I haven't seen, for a long time. I'd love to have another look at that. I think I'm going through a bit of a Fellini phase.

I'm trying to get The Red Shoes out. The Red Shoes is, I don't know, maybe if I had to pick one film above all films, it would be The Red Shoes. This is reassuringly heavy, so I think there must be a really good notebook in this one.

Bad Timing I had a, had a look at, maybe about a year ago. It's, it's, it's an incredible film, talking about editing and rhythm. I think it's, for me, maybe his best film, if there's such a thing as a best film. I, I, I think it's one of his strongest films, more so for me than, than even Don't Look Now.

First, All That Jazz, which is one of my all-time favorite films. It's, it's wonderful in every way. I mean, it's a, it's got an incredible, incredible sense of rhythm in the way that it's edited, but it's also the musical numbers. It's the fact that it's autobiographical, it's sort of very present in the way for Bob Fosse. I've got a, I'm completely, I'm going to have to, I'm going to have to take that. It's just, I love it, and I don't own the DVD. And, and one of the things that I adore about Criterion DVDs, I don't know if it's the case with all of them, is it the case with All That Jazz? Because I love the, I love the notebooks that come with the DVDs. I almost enjoy reading about the films as much as watching them. It's my favorite thing.

The Age of Innocence, that's another one I'm going to take. The Age of Innocence is, is the most beautiful of Scorsese's films. I, I mean, I love all of Scorsese's films, but I like, I particularly like the two films that are not typical of his body of works, The Age of Innocence and, and also New York, New York, is, is one of my favorite musicals, made the same year as All That Jazz and One from the Heart, which seems, all in 1979, or they came out in '79. It seems interesting that these three musicals all riffing in their own way off, Hollywood musicals of the golden period, and, and, and yeah, just so different, sort of, yeah, in each and different ways, but I love all three of them.

Short Cuts. I watched Short Cuts. I do love Altman. I do love it. It's no surprise there. I remember watching Short Cuts while I was trying to stay together with my first love and it was our last weekend together. We decided, alright, it's over after this, and we spent and we watched Short Cuts together, and I thought to myself, man, that movie was long and I could have been spending quality time with her, but we just watched a screen for three hours. And I remember more about Short Cuts than I do about why I loved that person, so I think I made the right choice then. I, what, this is essentially High Maintenance. It's a, it's just short stories connected by an earthquake, I guess, is what connects everybody in this film. It's funny how things slip into your consciousness.. Thank you, Short Cuts. And, and Lindsay, I miss you, I hope you're okay.

Have you guys seen Bad Timing? Whoa. So here's the story. I moved into this apartment, it was on Grand and Graham, there were five bedrooms in it, I didn't know anybody. It was supposed to be a sublet that lasted from mid-September to the end of October, at which point we were told by a note slipped under our door that we'd all have to move out. And then so we all moved out, but one of the only friend I made there was this guy, he was a total cinephile who made me watch Bad Timing with him alone in his house. And then when Art Garfunkel fucks the corpse, I'm like, oh my god, this is a lot. And then it turned out that we all moved out, but it was because one of the roommates in the place pretended to be the landlord and got us all to move out so her friends could move in. And while I didn't feel good about being tricked, I was really like, good job, good job. That was great timing on her part.

We have Close-Up. So this movie, eh, we use this chromatic aberration font for High Maintenance. I, I stole it from Close-Up. Also from Close-Up, I stole a moment where there's a, a can rolling down a hill. It's just a moment where there's this can rolling down a hill and it's just like a little pause. I stole that moment directly from this film and put it in season 4, episode 6 of High Maintenance.
Somebody told me that Punch-Drunk Love, I heard a theory that it's actually the story of Superman.

Being John Malkovich. I look like John Malkovich. It's true, if you do this, I get really angry and I enunciate. I don't, I don't speak like him. This movie rocked my world when I first saw it. If you read the, the original screenplay for it, it's much more bananas than the film was. I think they made, where they, the Kaufman experience reached a nice middle ground with this film.

Michael Haneke, huh? Really puts people through it, this. I, I would be interested in going on a road trip with this person and, and not letting him go to the bathroom and being like, what does it feel like, Michael? What does it feel like when somebody is making you feel constrained like this, you know?

Old Joy, Kelly Reichardt. If John Malkovich, Will Oldham, and I were on a road trip together, and Michael Haneke was in the back, that's a lot of energies. That's a lot of different energies to deal with. I would like to make, and, and maybe like in Old Joy, which is a road trip movie, we will all give each other massages in an outdoor bathhouse somewhere in the Northwest. Kelly, you make a good film. I'll take it.

I just want a copy of The Princess Bride for myself just because, look at that, dude. Look at this box. It's like a fairy, it's literally like a fairy book. This is incredible. Good work, guys. Whoever thought about this really was putting their, their thinking cap. I know it's not like the most esoteric choice, but I chose Close-Up, so I get one for me, one for you.
You know, Midnight Cowboy. I love this movie. Art, look at that art. God damn it.

Oh, speaking of Dave's Video, so Turner worked at a at a video store when we were growing up in Ohio, and that is where we found Jim Jarmusch. So let's get a Jarmusch film. Got to. All right, you want to talk about Dead Man? Go ahead, go ahead, talk about Dave's Video. Hi, so I worked at Dave's Video in Sidney, Ohio, which—and I hung out with him while he was working—it's now Davis Meat Market, which is—he didn't need to do an ad for that—very apt. Well, it was also the only porn store in town, so we watched a lot of art films though, and from the $1 bin, cuz there was a dollar bin. There was a dollar bin in the that we grew up in, the movies that people didn't watch, that included movies by Jim Jarmusch. I'm sorry, Jim, but it was the dollar bin. But our entire film education initially came from the dollar bin at Dave's Video.

I would like to get the Touki Bouki one, cuz I don't I don't have that. You got it? Okay, there's only one. All right, Touki Bouki. This movie has inspired every movie we've ever made. Djibril Diop Mambéty. And very, very, very, very much inspired Gasoline Rainbow. And I wish I wish that we were able to pull off the trick that Mambéty pulls off, where the film just feels like it's floating, and that's always an aspiration for us. We'll keep trying, we'll keep trying. But this, this film.

You got like the [ __ ] Les Blank box set? Oh, I mean, I already got that, so you're right, I'm good, I'm good. Well, you wore the T-shirt to the, to the show. I wore the T-shirt to the show. I'm that guy. I'm all right with it. Yes, hell yeah.

All right, so our good buddies made this movie Time that totally, totally [ __ ] me up when I saw it. Lauren Domino, who actually—, that is really rad—so who produced this—go ahead, go ahead, what do you got? They got the Dekalog. But anyway, Time, Time, Time. This like, this renewed my faith in cinema. Garrett and Lauren [ __ ] made something brilliant here.

The Dekalog. Oh, [ __ ] yeah. Well, talk about it, talk about it, that's the whole, that's the whole idea. It's a reference point for everything that we've ever done, and we've still never made anything like it, but also everything. We have time, we have time, we have time. Time, and we have The Dekalog.

The Cameraman. I think more than any one specific film, Buster Keaton as an entity, as an experience, as a kid who grew up and came out of Vaudeville and then just was this personage. My daughter's most cutting critique of anything is, "Well, it was good, but it's no Buster Keaton." I'm gonna take that for her.

And Close-Up, the greatest movie ever made. We'll end on that one. Okay, why? Have you seen this? Kiarostami. Yeah, yeah, but you got to speak to the people. It's, I think Godard even said it, where it was, it was just like he ended cinema with, by making this film, the understanding of what cinema is, we don't really need to keep going.

Grand finale: Harlan County, USA, Barbara Kopple. When Turner and I were first starting out, when our first movie came out, I think she was like the first famous person I ever met. It was at a film festival and I was like starstruck, and I saw her across the room, I was like, "Holy [ __ ], that's Barbara Kopple, she made Harlan County, USA, one of my favorite movies of all time." And I literally like, I went up to her and I, I said that, and then I walked out of the room and like cried, burst into tears. Anyway, all-time, all-timer of a film here.

I have to say this is the film that we remade with Little Men. So this is one of two films that Ozu made. This was in the '50s and in the '30s he made another film called I Was Born, But... And they're both about kids who go on strike against their parents. So we took that plot and we wrote our own film, Little Men, and these are better.
Francesco Rosi, great, great, great filmmaker who should be in the list of Pasolini, Visconti, Fellini, but no one knows Rosi except thanks to the Walter Reade, I do.
This film and The Soft Skin, which you also have somewhere, were both these love triangles that taught me everything I need to know about pain.
I have not seen Shoah since I took a class from Shoshana Felman, who wrote a whole book on my class in college. We studied only Shoah for a year and she wrote a paper, Psychoanalysis and Shoah.

Do you know there used to be a time in New York when you could see a Samuel Fuller film any day of the week that you wanted at one of the 12 rep houses in this city? There was always showing a Samuel Fuller double feature. Now who's seen Samuel Fuller anymore? You guys, right?

I'm working on a Montgomery Clift film and we keep think going back and forth between Raging Bull and All That Jazz as both biopics. Actually, if you think about them, Goodfellas is also a biopic that, and they're each somehow, you kind of because you don't know the person that they're about, you kind of have this freedom of storytelling that is incredible. This film is obviously the manic version of an individual's life.

In Love Is Strange, there's we were shooting a scene in a concert hall with John Lithgow and he said to me, in this movie The Magic Flute, Ingmar Bergman begins the film with a series of close-ups of the audience. And I'd never seen the movie, but I thought it was a really great idea. So on the set when we were in production, I stole from Ingmar Bergman, never having seen the movie.
Great. I'm going to complete my Rosi, my Rosi collection right here. Thank you.

I do not have Sirk. This should be preserved. When I saw Imitation of Life for the first time, I was probably 12 and I watched it in my house. It was like on at night, late in the evening, and my parents were asleep. And I just never having heard of melodrama, never heard hearing of Sirk, but growing up in Memphis and knowing about racism, I wept. I just sat there and I guess it also should have told me that I was a gay man. Like I should have known right then that my future was going to be told in a certain way.

I wrote about Playtime when I was in college because I couldn't get a print of Killing of a Chinese Bookie, which is what I wanted to write about, because the only copy was in Gena Rowlands' bathroom and she wouldn't send it to me, though she thought about it.

I’m going to start at 3 Women. I worked for Robert Altman for four days. And he was stoned, I will say, and… But what I did for him is I went to his warehouse in Queens and I sorted things out, and I stole a poster of 3 Women, which I still have, but it was one of about seventy-five copies, so I don’t feel bad. But it’s unforgettable. That’s all I would say. It really is one of those films that seems like part of your body after you watch it, so this is a really good one.

I love this movie: Night and the City. And I made a movie called Keep the Lights On, and I thought for a while of calling it Night and the City. I also thought of calling it Compulsion, which is, I think, what this movie is about. So, whether it’s gambling or drugs or sex or love or… this film is just fueled with energy of desire and need that is insatiable. I guess it’s one of the best films about addiction, I think, for me.

This film and another, I picked Cold Water. These two films together were transformative to a generation of American independent filmmakers living in New York City in the early ’90s. They are cinema as poetry and as pain and as beauty. They were also films about youth, Beau travail in a different way than Cold Water. But they were films that somehow spoke to the yearning of our lives, and I guess I would say that there was this back-and-forth: there was Cassavetes and the influence of Cassavetes on French cinema in the ’90s, and then there was French cinema in the ’90s and its influence on American independent cinema. And this one has a 30-minute sequence in the middle, which is a party that… like the end of this film, these are things that you can’t forget you’ve seen once you’ve seen them.
