I want to talk a lot about Michael Roemer. He made a series of features, several of which are some of the best American movies made in the 20th century. This is a film… It’s a film about a couple who are together, madly in love, and by the end of the film, something has been destroyed by the environment. It’s a perfect metaphor, in a certain way, for the experience of living in a culture which is hateful and demeaning and destroys something. So this is a film– It’s almost like a Fassbinder film if made by a man like Michael Roemer who survived the Kindertransport, came to America, became a wonderful filmmaker, and made these extremely human films. Nothing but a Man. A great one.

This is The Heiress. Amazing is all I would say. There is something about the desire of the central character, Olivia de Havilland, and its failure to be realized which is breathtaking. Again, I weirdly keep coming back to Fassbinder. This is like a Fassbinder film made by William Wyler, based on a Henry James novel.

film_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
catalog_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
quote: I’ve been in this Closet before, but I cannot believe that I did not speak about The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant or that I did not speak about Rainer Werner Fassbinder at all. Thank you, Richard Meyer, my art historian friend, he quoted this for me, that… that Andy Warhol says all art is copy. And I think probably no one knew that more than Rainer Werner, who was in conversation with the entire history of… of Germany and of cinema in such a beautiful way. It was also this time when there were groups of people who could make art together in a community and over a sustained period. And there was that cohesion and that trust, even if it included violence, which certainly with Fassbinder it did, that was beautiful. I think it’s not dissimilar to what happened in the studio system, it’s not dissimilar to what happened in New York with certain theater companies, or what comes out of these people who commit to each other to make art and beauty collectively. And this is a testament to that.

This is Minding the Gap by Bing Liu. Bing was actually in my class of Sundance writing lab fellows and directing lab. We got to know each other there and I saw his film there for the first time. And I adored it. It feels like a really nice first pick. It's very cool that this is in the collection. And it's the quickest I've ever made a decision in my life.

I have the French poster to A Woman Under the Influence in my office. It's the image of Gena Rowlands in bed with her hand held up. Gena Rowlands is in my mind best actor that there has ever been. The sequence in this film where she is out on the street waiting for her children to arrive home is one of my favorite scenes in any film that there has ever been, and so strikingly reminds me of my grandmother both in appearance and in mind, in the best ways actually. I think I might take an individual copy of this because I adore it.

This is David Lean Directs Noël Coward, which includes Brief Encounter. I actually haven't seen the other films in this collection, which is exactly the type of thing I wanted to take on today, so that's really cool. Brief Encounter has one of my favorite strings of dialogue of all time. She says, "I've fallen in love. I am an ordinary woman. I didn't know such violent things could happen to ordinary people." which is devastating, and that's generally how I like my cinema.

film_title: Eclipse Series 19: Chantal Akerman in the Seventies
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 19: Chantal Akerman in the Seventies
quote: This is Chantal Akerman in the Seventies, which is a part of the Eclipse Series. When I was invited to come in here, this was the first thing that I knew I wanted to grab. La Chambre, which is a short she made in New York in 1972, was the inspiration for the last shot of my film, which is kind of 360 degree. And there is a tracking shot down a hotel corridor that is very directly inspired by Hôtel Monterey. News from Home was definitely on my mind while I was making this, and in fact there was a original poster on eBay for 350 and it was beautiful, and it sat there for six months. And one day I decided I just, this is it, I am feeling egregiously irresponsible enough to purchase this poster, and I went online and it was gone. And I was chatting to a friend recently who told that exact story, but from her point of view. I'm not sure, but instead we're both equally devastated that neither of us own the News from Home poster, which is this gorgeous grainy image of New York. So every single film in here means a great deal to me, and I'm so excited to finally own it.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 19: Chantal Akerman in the Seventies

quote: For example, here I see 3 Women from Altman and I remember I absolutely loved that film, but the only thing I really remember was that there was the dress of the one woman, I think of Shelley Duvall, it was always caught in the car, in the door of the car, and that is all that I remember about this woman. So I take that definitely, I haven't seen it in a very long time.

Oh, and right next to it is Ingmar Bergman, Scenes from a Marriage. Fantastic film. And I have to say Ingmar Bergman is my greatest professional regret, because I met Ingmar Bergman in Munich. He saw me in the theater and he wanted to do a theater play with me and possibly a film, and I turned him down. I don't know why to this day. I think I was influenced by the man I was living with at the time, he discouraged me. I think he was afraid I might fall in love with him. But Liv Ullmann is just one of the greatest actresses ever.

Oh, here is The Leopard. I was doing a film with Cimino, The Sicilian, and so that's why I watched The Leopard. And Cimino had this weird idea, actually great idea, that all the actors in the film, they had to socialize with the people that they were playing. So I remember Joss Ackland had to go in some remote village in Sicily and socialize with the mafia, and I played an aristocrat and I socialized with the aristocrats in Sicily. And so The Leopard was wonderful to watch for that. Yeah, I take that. And Visconti is, of course, visually everything is so, so beautiful.

Oh, Husbands. I love that film. It was for me a whole new kind of film when I saw that for the first time. In fact, I used to show that to my students because I was teaching acting for a short time at a conservatory in Germany. I think our film acting in the '70s was still very much influenced by theater, and this was so new, this improvising and a bit gritty, and I really loved that and I wanted my students to see that. And I one day I when I came one of the first times to New York was in '84, I heard that Cassavetes was rehearsing, and a friend of mine here in New York said, "You can come, I can sneak you into the theater." And so I snuck myself into the theater and was sitting at the very end somewhere trying to hide, and I watched the rehearsal and I was really, was very excited. And then they had a break and all of a sudden Ben Gazzara and Cassavetes kind of moved in the direction where I was sitting, and I was saying, "Oh God, oh God, now they're going to discover me and they're going to say something why I'm here." And then Cassavetes said, "Hi, Barbara." And I thought, "What?" And they asked me if I wanted to have lunch with them. And then I had lunch with them, and he was like I imagined he would be, very personal with the actors, very, you know, gave them a lot of space. I liked the way he worked, and he said at the end he would like to work with me, but I think then he passed, you know.

Mike Leigh, Naked. That was also an experience that was very new for me, to see that kind of acting, that that kind of going really to the edge. And I met him later because I was with him in the jury in Berlin, he was the president of the jury in the film festival, and I heard and I was talking to him that he did these very, very long rehearsals, which was the opposite of Fassbinder with whom I worked.

And I see that there's Berlin Alexanderplatz, that is when I met Fassbinder for the first time. And yeah, he had this thing that he did only ever one take. There was a situation that I remember, I had a scene with Hanna Schygulla and we were in a car, and they had to rig the camera on the car so he couldn't be with us, and so we did the scene without him. I think we were sitting in the car reading a letter, laughing, something like that. And so then the scene was done and he asked us, "So how was it?" And we said, "Yeah." And he said, "You want to have another take?" And we were, "What, another take? We never have the chance to do another take." So we said, "Yeah, of course." We did another take and then we came back and then he said, "So which one do we print?" So we had to decide. It was a way of working that I loved, but very different, I think probably the opposite of Mike Leigh.

La strada. Fassbinder told me to watch before we did Berlin Alexanderplatz, and I think he wanted me to see Giulietta Masina and maybe her clownesque way of acting, that is something that he thought had something to do with the role that I was then playing in Alexanderplatz. What I love is the simplicity of this film, the simplicity of the story, the I you don't need any special effect, you don't need any fancy cameras, it's just to look into the eyes of this person and to see these people interact with each other. Yeah, Giulietta Masina, also one of the great ones.

Midnight Cowboy to me is sort of like the Mona Lisa, like Midnight Cowboy is the most beautiful movie from a cinematic standpoint. John Schlesinger, and it's somebody who's not from New York coming to the New York of 1968 or '69 and like filming it in its most sort of absurd, weird, dirty version of itself, and then inside of it are these like really extreme characters, but filled completely with such great performances from Jon Voight and Dustin Hoffman, who are bring so much emotion and depth to something that could otherwise be sort of like a fascinate, like a novelty piece about these weird guys and all their, or almost like making fun of them. I feel like the version of this now would almost have like more of a satirical slant to it. And it's a miracle of a movie and was rated X and is important and is really great and I love it a lot.

Oh, Destry Rides Again. It's Jimmy Stewart, who's like probably my favorite actor, and Marlene Dietrich, and that alone, if you know what like their energies are, is a weird enough combination that it just makes the whole movie so wild. And there's these great fight scenes with Marlene Dietrich and I forget who the other actress is, like brawls, but Jimmy Stewart's just the most beautiful person on screen and there's this like heart and, fear and rage and just kind of everything. And, and, and so this is like a Western that's a old Hollywood studio system Western, but has just a weird other energy to it that I can't really describe, but it feels like there's something just really unique and special about it.

Okay, His Girl Friday, Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell. Pre-Stanislavskian acting taking over movies, pre-Brando movie. One thing I think about with this movie is the power of having actors who are that good with really kind of stage acting, in the sense that they're able to sustain takes for 10 minutes and stay on, and actors with that level of craft, but who, who are still very real inside of that and have to do, you know, crazy, crazy technical things and pull the hat down and then throw the cigarette over to the other side of the room and say the line right at the same time. And it's just, magnificent. And, you know, I think that having really good actors in your movie is really important because then you can cut differently.

Yi Yi, where'd it be, Yi Yi? Here we go, Yi Yi, Edward Yang. His, eye for these little moments with children or families or turning points in people's lives or sorrows, it's not just beautiful things, it's also the sad things that people go through. It's all shown in this really gorgeous way, almost a little like Wings of Desire, where it feels almost like somebody is outside of life or there's like, an angel or something watching life itself and all of its, I want to say enumerations, but I think that's probably the wrong word, so all its different colors.

film_title: The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp
catalog_title: The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp
quote: My final pick is The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp. This movie is so beautiful and pans, spans over this big period of time, almost related to Yi Yi in the sense that it, you really feel the span of these people's lives over time. And there's something really beautiful about that effect because, you know, my favorite movies, which Yi Yi and this and It's a Wonderful Life do, is that you walk out of the movie and it's not just, oh, I liked that movie, it's that you have a better, you, you want to savor and appreciate the life you have more deeply. And that's to me like the power of all these things at their best is that you leave, you know, looking through different eyes a little bit.

film_title: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King
quote: This is The Actuality Dramas of Allan King. The one I've seen is A Married Couple, which is one of the most stunning documentaries I've ever seen in my life. It's, I think it's 1969, 1969, and you're watching a couple basically get divorced. And it's an era where there is no real television and people don't really understand what it means to have a camera crew with them all the time, and so they let the camera, they forget the camera's there. From an acting standpoint, getting to like watch these events happen with people in a documentary, it is the bar. Like a great performance is a bar, but a higher bar is what do real people look like when everything's melting down around them.

quote: I'm here, so I'll do this. I said to you before, I think everyone probably does this, but it's worth it, John Cassavetes. I was 15, I went to the Aero Theatre in Santa Monica, which is a spectacular repertory theater that I saw a lot of first films at, and saw A Woman Under the Influence, and then I kept coming back to it. And it, there is, there is a reason that he is, you know, sort of the lodestar for so many people now. There is an imperfection to it, there is a wildness to it, a sort of refusal to be anything other than his, his himself at the edge of who he is, at the, on pushing the envelope of everything he had in him and putting it into all of these films, and defying both external and internal hesitation or guardrails against, you know, him being anything other than his fullest self. I wish that more film artists were as fearless, basically.

I kind of want a bunch of movies that I just haven't seen, which are not interesting to talk about, like The Before Trilogy. I've never actually seen. That's where they walk and they talk and they like each other a lot, right?

I'm going to start with The Age of Innocence by Martin Scorsese. The Beast is a film that has three periods in it and one is 1910, and I've done a film called House of Tolerance that had took place in 1900, and every time I do a period film I rewatch this film, because for many reasons. One of them is that he made like the past so contemporary, since for The Beast I really wanted to find a film that in which the emotions are so strong and so hidden at the same time. And the portrait of this free woman played by Michelle Pfeiffer is so heartbreaking. So I rewatched this film just before the shoot.

Another film very important to me is David Cronenberg's Crash. The way he mixes like reality and dreams, the way the body affects the spirit, and it's all these themes are very important to me. The mise-en-scène is so minimalistic and precise, and the tone, the tone of the voice and the music of Howard Shore in this film is amazing. It's like a sex of electric guitars, I mean something I've never heard before and that I copied in a way for some music I do.

What else did I pick up? This one, Clean, Shaven by Lodge Kerrigan. Lodge is a director that's very, very strong, very precise, and I picked up this film, not it's not actually my favorite of him, but because I just miss Lodge's film, you know. I know it's hard for me, for him to make films, it's hard for everyone, but I think he's an amazing director and I'd like to see more of his work, you know. And come on, Lodge, if you if you see me, if you listen to me, go back to work.

Another director very important to me, and when I discovered him in the '90s that was a shock, it's Abbas Kiarostami, and my favorite of him is Close-Up. He was supposed to make another film and then he saw in the paper a story that someone pretended to be Mohsen Makhmalbaf, another Iranian director, just to be able to talk to people and say he was doing some casting, and people invited him home and he could, you know, have relationships with people. So he pretended he was someone else. One of the most beautiful sentences that the guy says when he asks him, "Why do you do that?" and he says, "Because I was alone." "And, but alone is not a pain." And the guy answers, "Do you want to talk about pain?" That made me cry. And this film is really, really fantastic, and the last scene Kiarostami goes and picks him up at the prison, they go on the scooter and they talk, and when he was in the editing room he just took a knife and all the soundtrack, he just ripped it up so we cannot listen to all the words. And this gesture is just like a huge movie maker gesture.

Okay, this is one of the most important directors for me, Pier Paolo Pasolini. My first short movie was an adaptation of his book called Who I Am. And, but it's not only the films, it's the whole man, the thought of a man, this mix of pure, pure, pure intelligence and poetry. I've never seen the mix so high in anyone else. And very often I ask myself, what would he say of the world of today? I would love to see like a film of Pasolini today, or just writings or thoughts, or he's missing, his intelligence is missing, his point of view on the world is missing because it would be surprising, you know, and everything today is so not surprising. But yes, I miss his thinking. This is like the '60s films. If I have to pick one up, it's difficult, but I would say it's The Gospel According to Matthew. And he says about the film, "Even if you don't like the film, you cannot say that I am wrong about the casting. Look at the faces I picked up, I never go wrong on a face." And this is so beautiful.

And first of all, The Lady Vanishes. I'm not an Alfred Hitchcock fan, I'm just going to tell you that. Yes, he's a genius, but his early movies I like the best and this is one, and I don't haven't seen it in a while and I can't wait to see it again.

Straw Dogs. Pauline Kael called it a fascist work of art. I don't know what she was talking about, but it is a powerful one and a disturbing one, and I need to see the Criterion Blu-ray special edition because I haven't seen it in a while, 'cause I need to be disturbed a little this week.

Oh boy, this is one of the all-timers: Badlands, Terry Malick's first movie. And this is one of the great examples of the unreliable narrator, which is hard to pull off in movies. Sissy Spacek is telling a story that is different than the one we're watching. She's telling us a romance in a way; we're watching a murder of a psychopath crossing the plains of America. A stunning movie, I think it's my favorite Terrence Malick movie still. Charles Starkweather, that was the actual killer. Horrible, horrible man. The disc is made in Mexico, it says, so supporting our Mexican economy there.

Oh yeah, got to have Billy Wilder. I met Billy Wilder once. The best review I've ever got: I was in a restaurant about six months after Bull Durham came out, and a man came over and said, "Somebody would like to see you." And I looked over, it was Billy Wilder. And I went over and he said, "Great fucking picture, kid." And, I thought that was as good a review as you could have. So, Some Like It Hot, one of my favorites.

Oh, this is a good one: His Girl Friday. These movies I play for my kids, who are 18 and 22, and they love them. Showing fast dialogue, kind of crazy screwball stuff, and amazingly timeless that all these generations later they can play. Cary Grant, Rosalind Russell, thank you.

And the final movie for my bag: the classic, Elia Kazan, Budd Schulberg script, Marlon Brando, On the Waterfront. 108 minutes. Notice how many of these movies aren't long. My little speech for today's filmmakers: short is good. 94 minutes, 108 minutes, we don't need to tell the story in three and a half hours. I met Budd Schulberg once and he wanted to do a new On the Waterfront in the Long Beach Harbor in L. A. It was just too big of a project for me to get involved in, but it was an honor, and of course one of the great performances ever.
I don't know if I had Brazil on Blu-ray. Oh yeah, Brazil. Yeah, this is great. I love this movie. I'm stealing this.

I've never watched Rushmore. I know it's supposed to be the one. Oh, here's a Carnival of Souls. Take that. And Rushmore, I never finished that. Supposed to be a hipster, haven't seen every Wes Anderson movie. Fucked up.
Naked Lunch, of course. I want to get double for this. Yeah, no, I'll leave it. All right, someone else needs that more than I do.

Oh, you did Jellyfish Eyes! Oh yeah, this is the one. I didn't want to watch this one, the Murakami movie. Yeah, steal! I didn't mean I don't try to find this. Where the hell wouldn't this come out? Yes!
Oh, here's a Carnival of Souls. Take that.
Boom, Dreams, yeah.
Masculin, féminin do I have this don't do blue with it no way I need it I don't have it...
A Touch of Zen. Oh, oh, okay. This looks like it's up my alley.
Yes, I should. Where is that? Thank you. I've not gotten through it. I have to do that on an early one, you know, wake up and watch that. He's like the nap master. Makes me makes me dream, you know?
Ooh. Oh, I've only seen this once. It's good.

Yeah, Trouble in Paradise is for me Ernst Lubitsch's ultimate masterpiece, even much more than To Be or Not to Be and so on and so on. It's the best critique of capitalism and a wonderful reversal of the usual logic of transgression, because the point is that the hero's life as a robber and so on, crime life, is normal life, and then transgression is precisely the idea to marry and so on.
Sweet Smell of Success, well, it's a nice depiction of the corruption of American press.

Picnic at Hanging Rock, I simply like early Peter Weir movies, especially those centered around some mystery, like there is a certain—it's like his version of Stalker, you know? You have an area which is the Zone, and then you never really learn what happens in the Zone.
Murmur of the Heart, it's one of those nice, gentle French movies where you have incest which is portrayed as a nice secret between mother and son. I like this.

Ice Storm, I have a perfect personal attachment to this film. When James Schamus was writing the scenario, he told me that he was reading a book of mine and that my theoretical book was inspiration. So it's personal reason, but I also love the movie.
Great Expectations, I'm simply a big fan of, of, of Dickens, and all the great classical Dickens movies, I like to have them.

City Lights, what is there to say? This, it's one of the greatest movies of all times, the most sublime ending. You know that I have a photo, even Charlie Chaplin here at Radio City Hall in New York at the premiere, he cried. It's simply one of the absolute movies.
Okay, this is for obvious personal reason, I do the comment. Although I must say that my favorite, Cuarón is Children of Men, which is otherwise a failure.
And Antichrist, I will probably not like it, but I like von Trier and it's simply part of a duty.

quote: Dreyer, it's more out of my love for Denmark. It's nice to know that already in the '20s, '30s, Denmark was cinematic superpower and later declined, and I simply like Dreyer.

John Cassavetes, well, I had a very interesting experience with him because you know, I discovered Ben Gazzara in The Strange One, End as a Man, and John used him and John was very concerned because he wanted me to make another film. He loved my films. I ran into him one day on Wilshire Boulevard and he said, "Jack, how come you don't make another film?" I said, "Well, you know, you," I said, "you're an actor, you earn money. So you get money and I admire you because you use the money to make movies, but," I said, "I don't get that kind of money. So I can't, I haven't been able to do it." "Okay Jack, I'll call you tomorrow." He calls me and he says, "All my cameras, editing room, it's all available to you, Jack. Go ahead, start making your movie."

film_title: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir
catalog_title: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir
quote: Jean Renoir, one of my favorites. I met him. I had dinner with him and we talked about acting. And Renoir said to me, which he later repeated in a film, he said that he learned the most important thing about film acting from Michel Simon and Louis Jouvet. He said what they did, what they taught me, he said, is that the actors mustn't start acting, they must discover the character and they do that by talking and listening to each other and see what emerges. And I, these films I've never seen, so I'm looking forward to seeing that.
box_set_name: Stage and Spectacle: Three Films by Jean Renoir

quote: Carl Dreyer. One of the great influences on my life. When I saw The Passion of Joan of Arc, astonishing film, a silent movie, and then Day of Wrath, which I remember very well. The Passion of Joan of Arc and Day of Wrath, one of the great films ever made.

And I met David Lean because I, he, he did, he directed for the same producer, Sam Spiegel, that did End as a Man, did The Strange One. And David Lean didn't like him very much. We met, we had dinner one night and we discussed the unhappiness with which Mr. Spiegel put both of us through. In my case, as he said, he would never let him interfere with his work as a director with the actors. And, but you know, I was very young when I worked with Spiegel. So he came to the set, started to talk to the actors, and I called George Stevens and I said, "What do I do about him?" He said, "Throw him off the set, Jack." So, you know, I was all of 25, gonna throw Sam Spiegel off the set. So I went and I called Elia Kazan. I said, "This is what George Stevens told me." Kazan said, "Jack, don't worry about it. He's been thrown off bigger sets than yours." Okay.
Barry Lyndon, if you can stay awake through this entire movie, you have a sleep disorder.

Shampoo. As a single guy, I can relate to this movie a lot. In the book, Easy Riders, Raging Bulls, there's a story about how Warren and Jack Nicholson were gonna send a kid to med school to be their own private doctor. It's one of my favorite anecdotes about, about Hollywood excess and like a legit good idea.

catalog_title: Me and You and Everyone We Know
quote: Bang, Me and You and Everyone We Know, it captures the loneliness of childhood. Truly like no other book, video, television show, just a fucking masterpiece. Let's see. Of everyone involved, I take it.

Oh my goodness. A Face in the Crowd. Andy Griffith. Yeah, Andy Griffith. Matlock. He's so goddamn good in this movie, and apparently he yelled at the director at the end that he'd make him, he'd made him lose his mind.

Paris is Burning. The Comedian John Mulaney can do entire monologues from this movie in their entirety. He will sometimes text them to me 'cause I said, it's giving businessman or something. And then he does the entire, Paris is Burning. A true masterpiece and a really well made, documentary.

Spike Lee, Bamboozled. Spike Lee, one of my personal heroes, could take or leave me, but, he's one of my, he's the reason I went to film school because he was doing press for Do the Right Thing in 1989. And he mentioned film school. And I was like, film school, you say. And, and then I applied and somehow got in. Oh, interesting. Side note about Spike Lee. I, I did, I created Chappelle's Show with Dave and, Spike did a sketch one time and in the middle of the take my cell phone started ringing. And, Spike charged me 20 bucks. He has a thing on his set. If a cell phone goes off, you pay the director 20 bucks. I was technically probably the director on the sketch, but I paid him 20 bucks 'cause he's Spike Lee and he is great.

Bringing Up Baby. A great illustration of how men interact with women. He, here's what I mean, Baby is a leopard that she brings with her everywhere she goes, just on the street in New York at a newspaper, it's ba and The Leopard represents femininity. And Cary Grant is just trying to figure out, how am I gonna deal with this woman? Ba it's a baby, it's a tiger. It's like a triple metaphor, basically. It's like a metaphor thrice removed. It's fucking insane that this, 86 years ago, they made a movie where a woman brings a tiger everywhere she goes. And that represents femininity and a man interacting with it. Excellent. Good job. Who wrote this? Dudley Nichols and Hagar Wilde. Pretty great. Old, old timey names.

Menace II Society. Allen, Albert Hughes. I now am buddies with Allen. He told me an anecdote about this movie one time that at one point it was so bad, he had a rag in his car to wipe tears with. It was, he would just go to editing. It sucked. And he would drive home and cry the entire way that he needed a rag to, wipe his tears. And it's actually a good, like, lesson in filmmaking, which is, and then he just said like, and then they would just do sections at a time. And just the parts of the movie that were good were like spread, like manifest destiny of quality, where it was like, okay, that's good. This part's good, this part's good, this part's good. That's like as a advice of a good filmmaker. Just you just want as many good parts of any artists of any kind, as many good neighborhoods for your work as possible. And then you just hope that the weaker sections are short and forgivable.

Agnes Varda, Bergman? I've always been a fan of Bergman. I especially love Cries and Whispers and was greatly influenced by it. Hour of the Wolf, though, is a Bergman film I haven't seen. So, I'll pick this one first.
Red Desert is one of my all-time favorites. And I can't leave this out. It's my favorite movie.
As someone who really wants to make a Western, Stagecoach is essential material.

This movie, The Makioka Sisters. This film evokes complex emotions in Koreans. It captures the essence of Japanese aesthetics, but at the same time... As a Korean who has experienced colonial rule... There's a very instinctive rejection of that aesthetic. So, I feel both love and hate for it at the same time. The original novel is also a masterpiece. The depiction of World War II in it is a bit uncomfortable. So, I re-watch it with these complex emotions. I haven't seen this on Blu-ray.
I haven't seen this on Blu-ray. Blow Out is a masterpiece by Brian De Palma, a director I deeply respect. Is Sisters his best work? It's hard to decide which one is better.

Les Cousins by Chabrol. I feel a sense of kinship with Chabrol. He was fixated on the thriller and crime genres and created many works over a long period. I respected Hitchcock, and I also respected Georges Simenon. So, he's a representative of that.
I like Mike Leigh's films, but I haven't seen this one. I need to learn about how Mike Leigh casts actors, rehearses, and directs. Someday, I want to learn that and try to imitate it.
Another sudden one by Antonioni. It's the kind of movie I definitely want to make someday.

Don Siegel is a director who, in my opinion, hasn't been fully appreciated for his abilities. I've even written three lines about Don Siegel's great films, he's a director I really respect. I hope you definitely read his collected writings.
Le silence de la mer, another director I deeply respect. It's Jean-Pierre Melville's collected writings.
Finally, it's here. Before I wrote Decision to Leave... I recommended that my co-writer, Jeong Seo-kyeong, watch this once. It's a film that really influenced me when I was young.

There's another world I don't know. I don't know much about the world of Japanese monster movies. But I know how many cult fans it has. And I've heard a lot about Honda Ishiro. I'll try to get into it this time.

[Translated] In Korea, when I was in junior high, there were so many Nastassja Kinski fans. Based on Thomas Hardy's Tess. It was a big hit in Korea. I'm so happy with the Roman Polanski movie gets out with Blu-ray Criterion.

[Translated] And I love many Japanese classics. This is really classic of classic. Tokyo Story, Yasujiro Ozu. I already have this movie by DVD, but yeah, first time with the Blu-ray and also amazing special features, many documentaries, many making-of.
[Translated] I love this, also. Of all the Kurosawa Shakespeare adaptations, this one (Throne of Blood) is my favorite. Throne of Blood.
[Translated] Oh, there's so many up there, too. Black Orpheus. When I was young, I saw this on TV in Korea, and it made a big impression on me. I can see it again on Blu-ray now.
[Translated] This is my favorite, Henri-Georges Clouzot's masterpiece, but I already have it.
[Translated] This is one of the greatest movie of Peter Weir, Picnic at Hanging Rock. Oh, it comes with the novel.
[Translated] When I was going to school... When I was in film school, I watched the movie, Koyaanisqatsi. And I'm so curious about the other two. It's all in one box set. Great.
[Translated] Medium Cool... I used to have the DVD a long time ago, but Park Chan-wook borrowed it, he swiped it and never gave it back...

[Translated] Repo Man, Alex Cox. Recently I saw Ed Harris in, I worked with Ed Harris on Snowpiercer, a film called Walker by Alex Cox, which I enjoyed. Repo Man is one of Alex Cox's best films, and I'm happy to see it on Blu-ray.
[Translated] Japanese master... One of the most controversial masters... Oshima Nagisa... It's a compilation of his 1960s films...

[Translated] So I look around... And I see Bicycle Thieves here. I want to take this one. This one film had a major impact on my cinema. It was when I saw this film that I knew what I wanted to pursue, what type of films I was after. It opened my path to social cinema. In fact, my film Circle could be just like it, in a way. I mean, like how in Bicycle Thieves, Ricci's bicycle is stolen, and he goes out into the chilly air. His son follows him. In the end, he sees a bicycle and gets close and wishes to steal it to end his misery. I projected the same thing in Circle, in a different form, where the news of a child's birth is given through a window... Which opens, and that window in the prison then gets shut. I mean the scene repeats in a way, and it seems as if it's impossible to get out of that circle. Of course, my society's conditions have been such that you really set out from a place only to circle back to it, as if there's no way out. But it's different in my latest film, It Was Just an Accident. It's as if you can step out. The circle is breakable. My film has more of that hope. Anyway, this is the film I'm choosing. I already have a copy at home, but given this occasion I'm taking this one with me. Thank you.

[Translated] Well, I really loved Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, of course, because it was at a Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers movie that my father met my mother. That was in 1935 or 1936. And a few years later, it was Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers who presented me with the Oscar. So, since I'm a little superstitious, I think Fred Astaire is around here somewhere... Here we are: Swing Time. I'm taking this one.

[Translated] I think Chaplin invented everything. He invented everything... Well, he was lucky to be among the first, but I think all of Chaplin's films speak to today's world, Modern Times... And love, as in City Lights. He talked about politics in The Great Dictator. I think, all while having fun, Chaplin opened so many doors. And I think he's a dad to all of us. The Circus. I think that's one of Chaplin's most beautiful films. An absolute masterpiece. A marvel. All of Chaplin's films are amazing, but this one...

[Translated] Do you have Il Sorpasso? I love it. It's because of this film that I cast Jean-Louis Trintignant in A Man and a Woman. It was because I saw this film. Trintignant and Gassman... They complement each other so well.

[Translated] So in Italian cinema, of course... There's Ettore Scola. A Special Day. A marvel. Mastroianni and Sophia Loren, I would have loved to have them for A Man and a Woman. They could have replaced Anouk Aimée and Jean-Louis Trintignant. This is a magnificent film. It's about politics, love... It's about everything. And they're so beautiful! So...
[Translated] If I may, I'll take all of Tati. Because you can't skip any of them. This is perfection. He's our Chaplin. I was lucky enough to meet him, and to speak with him briefly.

[Translated] and I was also pleased to see that the picture or the sound restoration was going on — restoration of the film Lost Highway, by my dear friend David Lynch. It was very nice to see that when I arrived, to see it being worked on.

[Translated] The Asphalt Jungle. Each time I come to New York, I think about The Asphalt Jungle. That bridge that they cross. I like this film a lot, because it's a bit unsettling. With unsettling people. But there's a scene I've never forgotten, which is amazing, with a girl dancing by the jukebox near the end of the film. And the old guy who has pulled off this job masterfully gets caught in the end because he's mesmerized by this girl dancing in front of the jukebox. And that's how the film ends. There you go. That'll show you!

[Translated] Teorema. Teorema, by Pasolini, which is a tragedy. It's wonderful. It's a love story. Several love stories. Stories of madness. Magical stories with magical people. And of course Terence Stamp. In the end, the whole family falls in love with him. The whole household falls in love with him and we understand why. We understand perfectly. I also fell in love with him when I saw it.

[Translated] So, I've chosen Cul-de-sac, because I haven't seen it for a long time. But it's a film I like a lot. And Françoise Dorléac, Catherine Deneuve's sister, who died in a car crash. I have a soft spot for this film. I really like the spirit of it. The way it's shot. The story. Check it out!

[Translated] The Night of the Hunter. A film that influenced me so much. It's so wonderful. It's about childhood and I really like childhood. I actually have a show in Paris right now of my collection about childhood, and this is the film that made me dare to write and film My Name Is Hmmm... The film I made, which was at Venice seven years ago. Of course, it's beautiful. The music. When he sings on his horse at night, it's frightening.

[Translated] I also wanted to talk about Almodóvar, of course. My dear Almodóvar. Pedro. He calls me tesoro. So Almodóvar. Long live Almodóvar! He's never won the Palme d'Or. It's shameful. I recommend All About My Mother. It's fantastic.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: [Translated] Look, I received a wonderful gift, this is my friend Agnès Varda. She liked that we were both called Agnès. Agnès V by agnès b. Agnès b. By Agnès V. She had ideas like that. She was wonderful. I had dinner at her place a short while before she sadly left us and I'd seen her at the Venice Biennale, dressed as a potato. It was 108 °F. The poor thing. I even gave her my hotel room, because she staying at an apartment with some friends. And I was so happy to be able to give Agnès... I had an air-conditioned room. I think she remembered that whole story for a long time. Anyway, she was a wonderful woman and a wonderful film director. Really.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: [Translated] Pickpocket was a passion of my youth. I've always greatly admired Bresson, and this film in particular. It's a rather short film, but an absolute masterpiece.

[Translated] Finally, Umberto D. Is another masterpiece. Not always, but as sometimes happens with such a tragic film, it's certainly not happy, it wasn't appreciated by the public. But as always with certain masterpieces it holds up over time. I think, maybe it won't be immortal, but it will endure, maybe not centuries, but decades.

[Translated] Throne of Blood, because Kurosawa is one of the greats, and also because the tragedy of Macbeth has always struck me when it's performed in the theater, too. This Japanese version of Macbeth is really incredible.

[Translated] Of all these — these are all masterpieces — but what struck me about Othello when I was going to the Centro Sperimentale was not only the greatness and genius of Orson Welles, but also his ability to edit films. He was always a master of editing. Even more so because this film had so many problems. He had to stop down and restart. He never had enough money. I heard they changed Desdemona, too. They had two or three different Desdemonas in the film. This ability, this endurance, this desire that allowed him to complete it in spite of all of this has always fascinated me.
[Translated] Barry Lyndon is a film I saw in Italy... The dubbed version. I'd love to see it again in the original version.

[Translated] This one: Happiness. I love this film. I think it's a masterpiece. It's one of my favorites. What I like about Todd Solondz— I've heard people say he doesn't like his characters, and I think there's real cruelty, but there's also something beautiful in the way he views all of our perversions, and all the twisted parts of human nature.

[Translated] Here's WALL·E. I haven't seen WALL·E, but I really want to, because I love Pixar in general. A friend of mine recommended it to me, she said it was very funny and very moving. I want to see this little science-fiction robot, and how moving he can be.

[Translated] Then there's my favorite movie. This one here. I think it remains my favorite of all time. Mulholland Drive. What I really love about it, and David Lynch in general, is the way the American Dream turns into a nightmare. I love that.

[Translated] I haven't picked anything French. Here's Pickpocket. For the gestures in it. I remember this film for these shots that were very... Well, I was going to "choreographed," but it's that cinematic choreography, like the moments when they steal the wallets on the train. It feels very much like choreography. Yes, it's an essential French film.

[Translated] Yes. Buñuel. The Exterminating Angel. I think it was thanks to Buñuel that I started to love a different kind of cinema, than what I'd seen before. I discovered this in high school, when I was 16 or 17. I was used to seeing movies on television. This was the first movie I saw at the film club, where I discovered a whole new world of cinema, between realism and surrealism.

[Translated] The War Trilogy by Roberto Rossellini. I have very positive memories of these. All three of them, but especially Paisan. I re-watch that one regularly. I already have a DVD at home, actually. I think it's one of the most beautiful films I've seen, It has that... Is it poetic realism? No, there's a great deal of realism. Some of it is like a fairy-tale, but always grounded in reality, which I've always liked about Rossellini.

[Translated] I prepared a little bit. Let's start with this one. Let's start with Lang. M by Fritz Lang. For me, Lang is synonymous with silent films, even though he continued far past that era, and I think that M is the first major talking picture. It has such a particular use of sound and music, and as with all of Lang films, incredibly dense images. In short, Fritz Lang is the master. I'll put this in my little shopping bag.

[Translated] Here we go. I just found Notorious. Hitchcock's Notorious, with Ingrid Bergman. For the lucky ones who haven't seen it yet... When you watch the scene with Grant and Bergman on the bench, or the kiss in the room, well, you can think of me! Aesthetically, it's simply splendid. The set design is exceptional, and it's all done with rear projection, which is extraordinary. Honestly, I just made a studio film and I thought a lot about Hitchcock. Two for two!

[Translated] L'Avventura, of course. Antonioni is... Well, this is pure modernity and in a way, he invented modernity for 1960s cinema, just as Godard also did, in his work. They're all worth rewatching: L'Avventura, L'Eclisse, and so on. They make you want to make films. I make films because others make them, otherwise I wouldn't be interested.

[Translated] What did I set up here? Oh yes, Tarkovsky. When I discovered Tarkovsky, I must have been... Fifteen. I was at the movies with my mom. The feel of the landscapes. The feel of the light. And of the faces, too. Mirror is very beautiful. The colors are magnificent.

[Translated] I don't know if people still talk about Robert Altman these days. For this film, he adapted Raymond Carver's short stories, and he did it so skillfully. His narratives are so free. They're almost like these surrealist, exquisite corpse exercises. It's very profound. It has Carver's depth and his levity. Very beautiful.

[Translated] Max Ophüls, of course. He was an incredible director. He did La ronde, Lola Montès... He had a genius for soft movement, this Viennese sensibility... There were other Viennese directors in Hollywood, but he was exceptional. La ronde is a series of sketches. Pay attention to the first one, in particular. It's incredible.

[Translated] I love Claude Sautet. Classe tous risques is a remarkable film. Claude's career took a big hit. It was a notorious flop. It took him five or six years to get over it. He had to go back to being a screenwriter. He had this expression: he said he wasn't a true screenwriter, but that his job was to re-sole scripts. Like a shoemaker. Classe tous risques is a very beautiful film.

[Translated] Now we're getting into the hard stuff. This is an era I like a lot, the very beginning of sound. Vampyr by Dreyer. An exceptional film. This inspired Bergman, all Nordic cinema. Especially Bergman. Wild Strawberries by Bergman, for example. Films like that. My friend Gaspar Noé shares my love for Vampyr... And silent films in general. Gaspar, if you're watching this: I'm thinking of you.

[Translated] This is my buddy Federico. La strada feels like a silent film, actually. It's a totally expressionist film. I vitelloni is the story of these young bourgeois idiots in small-town Italy. I think it's pretty autobiographical. Beautiful. Il Bidone, the story of a total failure. I think it ends in a garbage dump. I could go on... I was saying that Lang had these dense images... His framing... There's no room left in the frame. The frame closes in on the characters. Fellini is the opposite. There's this depth of field around them. That's the depth of life itself, and it's... It's devastating.

[Translated] Here's one of my great icons, Buster Keaton, The Cameraman. Definitely one of the directors I love the most... For his courage, his vision, his instincts and purity. I couldn't find this anywhere, and here it is.

[Translated] Then, I also saw Andrei Rublev... Which is right here! Tarkovsky is another one of my favorite directors, and this is definitely a film that's been very important in my career, because in every artist's career there are moments when things are going well, and others when they go badly, moments when you feel more insecure, when you question your own talent. And in those moments I revisit this film. It's a profound reflection on the meaning of art, on the purpose of the artist. It's a film I recommend to everyone, at any moment in life, but especially for those going through a rough period. So let's also put this masterpiece in the bag. I know you must be envious of this, I'm sorry.

[Translated] here's Mizoguchi. Mizoguchi is another director I love very much, Especially Ugetsu, but here I have A Story from Chikamatsu and The Story of the Last Chrysanthemum— two films of his I don't know. So I'm taking the opportunity to put them in my bag, hoping they won't stop me. I'm taking a lot! But Mizoguchi is another director I've loved forever, for his poetry, his ability to penetrate the human soul, always finding original, visual approaches. One of my favorites.

[Translated] And at this point we should see if I can find any David Lynch. Fantastic! Mulholland Dr. Is one of my favorite films. Here we enter a type of cinema that goes straight into the subconscious. It really seems like he's staging Antonin Artaud's philosophy: a cinema which aims to arrive at an experience, and to let the public live that experience. One linked to emotion rather than linear narrative. So it gets right to the raw emotion.

[Translated] Here is one of my fathers. Being from Italy, I was lucky enough to grow up with artistic fathers who were among the most important directors in the world. Because the Italian cinema of the '50s and '60s represents one of the most important cinematic bodies of work in the world. And Rossellini was of great importance to my formation - and still is. And Gomorrah, which is here somewhere. There it is. I have the honor of being part of the collection too. That film is connected to a masterpiece of Rossellini's, Paisà. So Rossellini is definitely a foundational director in my formation, to whom I owe a lot. And surely the goal for Italian directors— if I may also speak for my colleagues— is to make films that in some way serve as a bridge to the great masters of the past. So I'm happy to also put the great Rossellini in the bag.
[Translated] The Lady Vanishes...
[Translated] Seven Samurai...
[Translated] Amarcord, of course.
[Translated] Beauty and the Beast, yes.
[Translated] So... Love Streams. Every human being should have this in their collection.
[Translated] Time Bandits. The best that could happen to anyone's childhood. Just look at this. I wish my life were like that.
[Translated] These two brilliant classics: Eyes Without a Face and Cat People. These are the kinds of films no one makes anymore -- intelligent horror.

[Translated] Naked Lunch -- my favorite for its tone and dialogue. I love this film. Could you say a bit about Cronenberg too? Well... He epitomizes the affliction of the '80s. AIDS, inner angst. I love his work. I think he's more understated... Than David Lynch, for example, but he achieves a depth of his own. I'm quite a -- I won't say “fan,” because that sounds stupid. Anyway, I love it. I always get something from this film. I watch it over and over.

[Translated] Carnival of Souls is brilliant. This is what all us filmmakers need to remember -- that to make just one film like this is enough. It has everything that frightens me most in life. I know I can't watch it alone.
[Translated] And The Red Shoes for my mom. It's her favorite film.
[Translated] These two brilliant classics: Eyes Without a Face and Cat People. These are the kinds of films no one makes anymore -- intelligent horror.

We have to talk about Robert Altman if we’re going to talk about acting. He is the gift to actors: to find truth in everyday circumstance. I had the privilege of working with him. And 3 Women is such an influence on me. These performances are so incredible. Just staring at Sissy Spacek’s face makes me want to cry.
Also, McCabe & Mrs. Miller, Warren Beatty and Julie Christie.

But also, while we’re at it, Tanner ’88. I was just thinking how many series and limited series watched this to discover the intimacy of storytelling, by being on the road with a political candidate, in the way he did his hand-held work, and the performances are incredible, like everything he gave us.
And therefore you have to talk about Persona, two of the greatest female performances of all time. I talk about these performances, I think and dream on them.
And a great hero of mine and a deep hero of my mother’s is Simone Signoret, and you have Diabolique. Please see this film, see all her work. Every cell is true.

film_title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (Jacques Demy box)
catalog_title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (Jacques Demy box)
quote: Since we’re talking about French actresses and we’ve covered Simone Signoret, let’s talk about Deneuve, who all of us want to be when we grow up: that cool, that amazing. But let’s talk about her masterful performances, like in The Umbrellas of Cherbourg, which has influenced, obviously, so many films. The vulnerability of her, all while in song, is just extraordinary...
Only opposed with Belle de Jour. Oh my God, this film. She brings innocence to brokenness and she brings innocence to sexuality in a way I had never seen, and was such an influence on me as an actor.

If we want to talk about geniuses in performance, think about the gift that Jimmy Stewart gave us. We always think about him in It’s a Wonderful Life, and we talk about his purity and being all-American, but in Philadelphia Story, the greatest screenplay. I don’t even understand this writing, it’s so brilliant. It’s insane. Every performance is perfect, and it’s so radical, slightly mean-spirited. Everybody’s a mess. Frankly, a total shit show. Jimmy Stewart is raw and sassy and amoral at moments and yet we fall madly in love with him, like everything he ever gave us. Jimmy Stewart is such a hero, and I speak for my beloved David Lynch, who loved Jimmy Stewart so much, and we talked about him so much.
David Lynch, The Art Life, which I’m staring at right here, which I started to watch and had to stop because I wasn’t quite ready, but I cannot wait for...

And Inland Empire, which speaks to his radical reinvention of cinema. He wanted to use the crudest camera possible, so he grabbed a Sony camcorder and a couple hundred thousand dollars, and for three years we made this movie, at times just the two of us, with a camcorder, in Poland and France and LA, and it was one of the great gifts of my life. And thanks to you all, I also have the gift of so much behind-the-scenes and doc discoveries about David at work. That will be amazing to get to get to be back in those spaces with him, so I really thank you from the bottom of my heart, and I hope everyone will see his bravery in this and, of course, all his films.

You guys have Smooth Talk on Blu-ray, and I made this movie when I was 15 years old, directed by Joyce Chopra, an amazing filmmaker, with Treat Williams, who’s so brilliant in this movie, and I think a fascinating movie. I’m really, really lucky to be part of it. It was, I think, my first lead in a film.

Let me talk about a filmmaker that means the world to me, as an actor, to get me through life, because he is the person that can make me laugh every time, but the acting is always perfect: the gift that is Albert Brooks. Real Life, the mockumentary, which… I mean, honestly, I want to do lines from it. Nothing is a greater gift...

Except top-five favorite movies of my life: Defending Your Life. When I told Meryl Streep this may be my favorite performance of hers because she’s so perfect and he’s so perfect, and it’s the most romantic film. It makes us reconsider our lives, and it’s the funniest idea of what happens to us when we go. Albert Brooks, I love you. Thank you for everything you give us.

I asked when I came in if you had Scorsese Shorts. The Big Shave is such a brilliant and radical short in his political subversion and all that he has always said with his films. And of course, the performances mean everything. But if you want to see great actresses, soon Criterion is bringing us Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore, working on it now with Scorsese. It’s the best female performances ever, including my beloved mom, Diane Ladd. So everyone must see Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore, one of my favorite Scorsese films.

Okay, guys, I heard that sometimes they let people close their eyes and do a random pick, so I’m going to do it. Irene Dunne, my grandmother loved Irene Dunne, and I chose The Awful Truth with Irene Dunne and Cary Grant, and screwball comedies have meant everything to me, as you heard. Amazing that I got to choose this.

And I got a Spike Lee movie and this makes me so happy. This, we all know, is a masterpiece, a masterpiece in acting, a masterpiece in filmmaking. And like all the filmmakers I’ve talked about, if you want to see the essence of culture and community and truth, like Bob Altman, Spike Lee, I think, is the comparable master of creating the world of truth in space like no other filmmaker. He is such a genius.

I just found– Give me a break, I’m going to do it really quick: Night of the Hunter. It is absurdist, it’s incredible, and my godmother, Shelley Winters, is so incredible in this movie, as she is in every performance. You must see this movie.

If you have not seen all of Bogdanovich’s work, you better. And you better read everything he gave us on film and about other filmmakers, including John Ford. The greatest teacher about film, and The Last Picture Show is one of my favorite movies of all time. Such incredible performances.

So I want to talk about some actresses that have inspired and moved me so much. So we have to start with Bergman. The first movie I saw in the theater with my grandmother, of Bergman, she took me to see Fanny and Alexander, and I will never forget being such a little girl and saying to my grandma, “I’ve seen the color red for the first time.” Everything was so vibrant and so powerful and taught me about life and grief and love.

If I’m talking about actresses, I have to talk about Giulietta Masina. And I see this… extraordinary gift of Fellini, but within Fellini’s work with his amazing wife and muse, we have La strada, one of the most important female performances of all time. I was in a restaurant in Rome when I was 19, and they walked into the restaurant and he walked in and they sat down, and, as they sat down, she walked in and everyone in the restaurant started clapping, and he sat down and he asked her to stand and we gave her a standing ovation in the restaurant, was one of my favorite memories to just be part of that.

Two friends making a movie together, and it’s so raw and beautiful, and if you love basketball, you have to see the movie, but if you love Jack Nicholson and if you love Bruce Dern – I happen to – also an amazing movie. quote: Dance, Girl, Dance. Dorothy Arzner, she was one of the… or maybe the only female filmmaker making movies in the studio system in the ’30s and ’40s. And also this movie has a scene-stealing Lucille Ball.

And I’m going to also get her other one, Merrily We Go to Hell. And this is just… She’s working in pre-Code, and does some very radical feminist storytelling, in both of these films. I would recommend them highly.

I gotta give a little shout-out here to Frownland. My husband, Ronald Bronstein, this is his first movie, and this is the movie that I met Ronnie on. My whole life is due to this movie. This movie was also my film school. I’m not going to take this film because we have many, many of them, but I just needed to discuss that...

One of my other idols of all time: David Lynch. My favorite of his is a little movie called Inland Empire. David Lynch is one of those directors who spent his career really focusing on one idea and trying to get at the heart of an idea, and I think he does it in this movie. And then also, at the end of the movie, which I won’t spoil, it’s a celebration of his whole body of work. It’s beautiful.

So this movie, Spinal Tap, is so seminal to me as far as… as far as a comedy without jokes. What I mean by comedy without jokes is every single line that is said, every single vision that is shown, is for comedic effect, but it is real. They are playing this as if it is the highest drama that has ever been made, and that is why it succeeds so heavily as a comedy. And I recommend it to anybody.

quote: And now I’m going to get a little silly. I grew up in the Tri-State area, PIX Channel 11. It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World, always on television when I was a child, always loved it, no matter what point– I mean, you got Ethel Merman, you got everybody. You got the Three Stooges as practical… They’re like corpses, propped up as firemen. It’s all… It’s everybody. It’s Sid Caesar, it’s Mickey Rooney, it’s Spencer Tracy, it’s Jonathan Winters. It’s everybody that– Young people don’t know who they are. But it’s insanity in film form. I have not watched this since I was probably a teenager, and I cannot wait.

One of my idols of all idols: Chantal Akerman. I love that this is called Masterpieces. We have everything in here. Hanging Out Yonkers. Oh my God, I’m so… The film-school tests. I’m so excited. I’m so excited about this.

One of my favorite things as a set, as a piece, is Rohmer’s Six Moral Tales. I would say Love in the Afternoon is my favorite of the Tales, but they’re all stories about women and men and the different dynamics that… really complicated dynamics that can come from women and men encountering each other in different ways. And again, I love a guy who sets out to make a set of movies that are all of a piece, that tell a story if you put them all together.
Jim Jarmusch. I don’t have that. I don’t know it. It’s great. -I love his work. -Down by Law. I know of it. I’ve never seen it. Oh, this is great.
This I’ve never seen. I’ve seen Citizen Kane. I’ve never seen Magnificent Ambersons, to my shame. -It’s... -In the bag. In the bag, yeah.

Have you seen Amores perros? Can I put it in your bag? -Oh, yeah! With the dogs. -Yeah. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, I’ve seen it, but I’m happy to have it. Yeah, DVDs are great because you can share them with your friends, your children, your parents.
Anthony Mann. I wanted to see some of his films because he inspired Wim Wenders’s films. Are you interested? The Furies. I want to see landscape, large... Spaces. Don’t you?
Michael Haneke’s... -Favorite film? -favorite film of his, named... Au Hasard Balthazar. -Do you want it? -Okay. Yeah.

I see I’ve got all the Tarkovskys. But I guess I can take them as a present for someone. Is that allowed? -Where are they? The Tarkovskys? -Well, I wanted to take... Mirror is somewhere here. Mirror. Oui. Well, actually, I know from... Andrei Konchalovsky who wrote... -Andrei Rublev. -Andrei Rublev with him. He said to me that Andrei spoke to him and said, “You know what? I found a new way to edit films and to put the end at the beginning. The beginning and... And that’s my new way of making films. What we call the beginning is often the end. It’s... With Mirror– The end is where we start from.
There’s some big box sets, Juliette, at the end. -Look, I’ve already earmarked... -Oh, yeah. -this. -Oh, wow. -That’s amazing. -There’s only one.

Pasolini, I would love to have it. Would you think it greedy of me if I took this? -No. Go ahead, go ahead, have it. -Thank you. -I’m now taking... -It’s your Christmas-birthday... Christmas present for myself.

quote: Here, A Woman Under the Influence. I love Cassavetes. We love Cassavetes. We love Cassavetes. And then also, I mean Gena Rowlands's performance in this is just one of the best things I've ever seen. Also when we watched it recently, I was didn't like, the ending is so crazy. Like it's kind of wild. Like it gets funny. Yeah, and music that comes on, and then I start thinking about my family and I'm like thinking about my Mom and Dad. Yeah, there's like, I didn't, I don't think I ever realized how like incredible the ending of that movie is, where it's just like, and that's what this family is, like da.

Just saw Barbara last night. This is Harlan County. Super punk rock at the time and she directed my very first movie. Oh, Havoc. Barbara Kopple. She's, Havoc, she's a, yeah, Havoc, Havoc. Shout out to, shout out.

Okay, Paris is Burning. The best documentary of all time. Actually, all time. Oh my god. Oh, look at this cover. quote: This is Jo Jo Dancer, a film by Richard Pryor. quote: This is Melvin Van Peebles: Essential Films set. The two films I want to highlight in here are Watermelon Man and Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song. And you learn from your mistakes, your connectivities with people, the disconnect with people, and you take something and try to create something holistic that will be free of regret, that’ll be free of fear, that’ll be free of just anxiety. We all heard of the term blaxploitation, we’ve all heard of Coffy and Shaft, I’m Gonna Git You Sucka, all these things that ended up deriving from a film called Watermelon Man that didn’t quite have the best reception. And he’s a founding father, and that movie gave him the ability to create what he did later down the line, which gives us the ability to create what we do now. I won't spoil it, but the soundtrack of this was incredible with the little clinking, chips. He's a gambler and, and it deals with the gambling houses, and this movie is gorgeous, gorgeous. Yeah, I'm grabbing the Dekalog box set, yeah I am. I saw this, God, years ago over a couple of nights. Like all great art, when you're done watching it, it makes you look at and react to the world differently, and I love that. I love when they can do that.

One False Move. This, look, the '90s was an amazing time for films, great films came out in the '90s. This is my favorite film from the '90s, directed by Carl Franklin. An amazing Bill Paxton, should have gotten an Academy Award nomination just for the scene where he is talking to the two cops after he has overheard them making fun of him, and he has to put on this brave face, and they know that he's overheard them. It's one of the best shot scenes. This is one of the best crime films ever made, and I just got to work with Carl Franklin last year, and all I wanted to do was talk with him about One False Move and Devil in a Blue Dress. So again, Carl, I'm ending on you, because I love you.

I think this is an absolutely brilliant film, but I cannot watch it, 'cause I've got, two little children, and I found the scene at the beginning with the boy falling, and it would seem to be shot like Bill Viola or something, really super, super slow motion, and it's got a, like a Handel aria or something, which is so utterly moving. It's so—I found it so manipulative and so, I almost couldn't cope with it at all.

I saw Lynne Ramsay's film Ratcatcher here. That's absolutely, completely brilliant, that film. When I first saw that, it was amazing. I saw her short film, I can't remember what that's called, beforehand, before that, and, and then Morvern Callar after that. It's amazing.
