catalog_title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
quote: The Passion of Joan of Arc. I found this—, well, I've just written some music with my friend Will Gregory for this film, and this is the most amazing thing. A friend of mine showed me this because we were looking for a thing for music to, to, a film to write music to, and, I was, I looked at about 20 silent films with Will, and, this one just stuck right out.

Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence. I'm really interested to see this again because it, I remember it really well on TV, like again, the BBC always showed really cool films, and I found that so brutal, so absolutely vicious, and I'm intrigued to see it again, and, yeah, it's amazing.

The 39 Steps. Yeah, I love this. I, I love all versions of this story, but I particularly like this one with Robert Donat, Donat, Donat. Amazing. I, it's just because I love Scotland as well, and it's shot in Scotland, and the story is so, exciting. It's completely brilliant, and, and it's a bit cheeky as well. It's typically Alfred Hitchcock trying to get his camera up as many women's skirts as he can do.
Oh man, Gomorrah, wonder why.
You look at Marlon Brando, boy, was he soft on the eyes right there, man. That's the dude, you feel me?
Hunger. I heard this dude Steve McQueen is an amazing director. I haven't seen it yet, but I've been hearing about it. Got to check this out.
Oh man, this is a classic. The Night of the Hunter. This is one, this is a staple in your video library. Got to have this. This is a must-have.
And last but not least...

Oh, oh, oh, got it. Yeah, this movie is so... I saw this movie when it came out and thought, "Jesus, this is amazing. And look at this about show business, and what a great world to be in." And how unbelievably romantic it was, and unbelievably like, you know, everything in it is incredibly sexy. Even his death is incredibly sexy, Scheider's death. And so that was my takeaway of when I was, I don't know, 13 or 14 when it came out. And now I happened to watch it recently, and it's just terrifying to watch it as a middle-aged man. It's absolutely terrifying, 'cause nothing is romantic, and the death, you're like, you also feel like you're having a heart attack when you're watching the movie. Like your left arm starts really hurting and you're like, "Oh, God, this is it."
This is a cool, oh wow, The Vanishing. I feel like I'm in this corner too much.
That's very funny. Whoever in art decided to do that deserves, you know, an award. That's really good for Videodrome.

Oh, this is such a fantastic movie, The Friends of Eddie Coyle. This is, this is just, it's one of these movies, Peter Yates directed it, but it's one of these films that you can sit and watch it, and if someone is watching it with you and they aren't completely paying attention, the movie will end and they will have no idea what the film's about. This, by the way, I know has an amazing commentary track. You can, cook a fine, fine spaghetti sauce in the time it takes to listen to that.
Pickup on South Street is just a spectacular movie, and you guys did, I have your version of it. It's fantastic, it's just great.
Oh, Night Train to Munich. This is a Carol Reed film that I've, you know, I think it's on TCM apparently, but I keep missing it.

I had a request. My wife knew I was coming, of Contempt. She said, she said, "God, the, the, you know, when you see that marriage falling apart, and they don't even really talk about how it's falling apart, but you can just watch it falling apart." And she really held forth on this. And I was like, "What, is there something we need to talk... Do you really care about Contempt, or is there something else we need to chat about?" She's like, "No, I just care about Contempt." Like, okay, great. Where is, do you guys have that one? It's, it's out of print? Linda, take that! Aha! Two years of marriage and we're still going strong. No Contempt for you.

All right. Today is the release date of Paper Moon, so I am excited that I get to be one of the first people to talk about it. Paper Moon. Probably one of the strongest, most economical openings. In, I’d say 10 seconds, you are interested in character. In about 30 seconds, you are intrigued by the dilemma. And three minutes in, you’re rooting for the plot. And then ten minutes in, you are blindly allegiant to this relationship. I mean, I can’t think of a movie that does that more impactfully, more powerfully, more entertainingly. This is just a great, great, great, great, great, great movie. So, putting that first in the bag.

Brazil, 1985. It’s kind of known in the lore that he had a cut of this that he wanted to release but Universal didn’t, and that he took the film hostage. So he got in a van and he drove up to CalArts, which was where I was with my fellow students that some became coworkers with me at Pixar. My production designer on Toy Story and Finding Nemo and WALL•E was Ralph– the late, great Ralph Eggleston. He was the student projectionist. And he told us that Terry Gilliam was coming up and he was going to show some film, and it just made such a difference– I mean, I was already a Monty Python fan, already a Time Bandits fan, but this film has just... And I think you can see it in WALL•E, just the influence this had. I can’t say enough about this film. I love this film. Love, love, love, love, love, love.

Okay, Local Hero. I come from a small fishing village and I just totally got it. Every line is quotable. It was probably, to me, one of the greatest things Burt Lancaster did near the end of his career as Felix Happer. But this, this movie is– just speaks to my heart. I mean, if I could ever be involved in a movie that had this feeling that Bill Forsyth captured, I’d finish. I’d be done.

film_title: The Worst Person in the World
catalog_title: The Worst Person in the World
quote: Worst Person in the World. This is a more recent film, ’21. This is going to sound weird. It’s a great movie on its own. But my favorite film in the world is Lawrence of Arabia. And people think it’s for the spectacle, the scope, the scale. But it’s because the theme of it is, “Who am I?” And it’s really the closest that you get to a novel, where it’s the internal desire to figure yourself out. So, you’re– all your choices as a protagonist are seemingly reactive to things happening to you, but what you’re invested in as an audience member is, “What will that person choose to do based on just trying to find their identity as they encounter these choices and obstacles?” And this is very similar in that respect. And I just found this the most amazing internal journey of somebody just trying to figure out their place in the world.

It’s staring right at me, so Defending Your Life. This is a perfect comedy. Came out in ’91. We were a year out from really getting serious writing Toy Story. So all the movies that came out around ’91, ’92, ’93 really– like Midnight Run, things like that, had a big influence on our learning curve of trying to put comedy into a feature-length movie. I want to believe it’s why I fell in love with the concept of Albert Brooks being the voice of a fish. To have had the chance to be a front-row audience member for a one-man show in the recording studio with him for close to four to five years total was one of the biggest privileges of my career. And... But this movie is just, it’s just flawless in my mind.

Probably saving the best for last. Matewan. My senior year of film school, I remember seeing an ad for this in the LA Weekly, and... Just– and I think it was a poster looked similar to this, and just kind of being intrigued and took a chance, that’s how I saw My Life as a Dog, it’s how I saw Jean de Florette, Manon of the Spring. Took in a matinee by myself. And I did this and was blown away. John Sayles has a way, I would say Richard Linklater has the same, just a way of doing multi-protagonist movies. He just loves to make the worlds sort of greater and richer than just the singular protagonist or multi-protagonist that you’re following and you feel it everywhere. The other thing that was huge is that he published a book then, in the same year, called Thinking in Pictures. And it was so hard to find a how-to book about how low-budget movies were made, and just– and it was real nuts-and-bolts and practical and spoke in a common man’s language, and I’ve kept onto that book. So, if you only take one movie away from this whole pitch: Matewan.

Yeah, I was hoping I would find a Tarkovsky. So Stalker, I think Stalker was my introduction to Andrei Tarkovsky. It was my discovery of stillness in film and Andrei Rublev of course. But that's that's a real favorite of mine and I haven't seen it in years, so I'm happy to have found it.

So this holds a very special place in my heart, Purple Noon or Plein Soleil, which was the first realization of The Talented Mr. Ripley, or Patricia Highsmith's Talented Mr. Ripley. And of course I was recommended this by Anthony Minghella. A little like the series that's on at the moment, Ripley, it demonstrates how this incredible character from this book can be interpreted in so many different ways, because it's very different to The Talented Mr. Ripley that I made with Minghella. If anything, to choose Delon to play Ripley himself. And they don't change it from the book that he's a painter, in the film what I did, we made him a musician. It's got lots of twists and turns, the same color blue in the sea as our one, and not quite as dark as the Ripley on TV at the moment.

This is a wonderful film. I was turned onto this by another filmmaker who wanted me to see it as inspiration for a film I made with him, The Wages of Fear. Now if I'm really honest I didn't even know... So it's a Henri-Georges Clouzot. You'll probably learn from me I don't remember names, but I remember experiences. This film is about men in desperate, desperate situations who will do anything for money, anything to survive, and they go on the darkest, most dangerous journey. And it's it's just brilliant, it's moving and incredibly... Shamefully I don't know any of these other films, but this one is brilliant.

Oh, this is an interesting film. I remember seeing this in the '80s. My mom, my mom showed me this, Local Hero. It was an interesting time, this and My Beautiful Laundrette were two films I remember seeing at a time in my life when film felt very other, very distant, really about worlds I didn't know about or didn't live in. And this felt very much on my doorstep, it felt like a Britain that I knew, I mean set in Scotland, but a Britain that I knew. And My Beautiful Laundrette was similar in that it felt like a London that I knew. And it really moving, and then this incredible performance at the end by Burt Lancaster who shows up like sort of, you know, a knight in shining armor. That's a wonderful film.

Oh, this was a this was a film that introduced me to Bob Hoskins, who I luckily got to work with, Neil Jordan's Mona Lisa. Which again at a very formative time in my life showed a side of London that I sort of saw and felt around me, but hadn't necessarily seen on film. And Bob Hoskins demonstrating his brilliant ability to be incredibly tough, plausibly real of the street, and yet with this incredible heart of gold, which was kind of Bob himself. And Cathy Tyson gives a great performance in that, and there's a there's a great there's a great supporting role by Michael Caine, who no surprise steals every scene he's in. But it's Bob's film.

So one more, should we say one of my favorite films. My children always joke that I never have favorites, I always say, "Oh, I like I like all sorts of films and all sorts of music." But this film really has stuck with me since being shown it by my mom when I was, gosh, very, very young, maybe 12 or 13, The Night of the Hunter. It's a fable, it's a terrifying nursery rhyme that literally by the end, halfway through, sort of dips into the fantasy of a child where you get this macro images of lizards and spiders, and the most incredible performance of Robert Mitchum. With this, I remember one image that always sticks to my mind is him going, he's just got out of prison and he goes to see, he goes into a strip joint, puts his hand in his pocket and his flick knife appears through his trousers instead of an erection. It's the most shocking image and kind of sums up the threat that this man has. Anyway, that's a classic, and if you haven't seen it you must.

Okay, obviously I know Monika, and I think I have a quite strong relation to that movie like everyone, not Bergman, and also Wild Strawberries. And, but I don't know, I don't know him yet, I know him through Woody Allen strangely, because if you watch, the last time I was watching Scènes de la vie conjugale, but it was too tough for me, because it's too, it's too hard, you know. And I said, okay, I need a Bergman, but lighter tonight. And I put Hannah and Her Sisters, and it's the same, it's a Bergman, but a sense of humor.
Loves... That's the most, one of the most wonderful movies in the world, Loves of a Blonde. This is a very good movie.
Somebody told me that Cuarón came and took a lot of DVDs.
I want to take Jules and Jim. The matrix of so many French movies.
Amarcord. Amarcord, that's fantastic, no? It's very fantastic.

Okay, Pierre Étaix, movies of Pierre Étaix, because Jean-Claude Carrière is a friend of mine, and I'm going to give it, he's going to be very happy, because he works on it, on all the movies of Pierre Étaix, because they are very friends.

Somebody told me, you know, I want to, there is, if there is one movie on Earth, it's a Jacques Tati's movie. And this is a Blu-ray collection, and I have a projector on my apartment, and it's, and with the Blu-ray it's going to be fantastic. Complete Jacques Tati, fantastic.

catalog_title: Eclipse Series 31: Three Popular Films by Jean-Pierre Gorin

film_title: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman
catalog_title: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman
quote: Well, this, because if you don't take it, you're a stupid guy. Because I think is a more than a filmmaker, is also, I think, a light to follow sometimes, Rossellini.
box_set_name: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman

quote: [Translated] The first film I saw in my life was Bergman's Sawdust and Tinsel. And the second film I saw was Viridiana. I was twelve years old and oddly enough, as much as I saw Harriet Andersson as my fictional body... The actress in Viridiana was not my fictional body, but I must have had an even stronger connection to her because in all my memories of the film, it's always my face that I see. It's still very strange. It's absolutely wonderful.

[Translated] David Lynch is someone else I love, and his power over images, here as a very young man. This is his first film, and we see it clearly. He's inspired by the poetry of silent film, with its phantasmagorical lighting. And I draw a lot of inspiration from that too. I think Eraserhead totally inspired one of the shots in Anatomy of Hell.

[Translated] So, Elia Kazan, Marlon Brando, On the Waterfront... The film which allowed me to make cinema again, at a time when I was a pariah in France, its worst director, the shame of the nation... I went into a movie theater, and at the time they played films on a loop. So I went in at noon, and stayed until midnight watching Baby Doll on repeat. And the next day I wrote 36 Fillette. That's the way it is. I find that great geniuses, great works, reach out to you and help you to live, to become an author, to become yourself, really.

[Translated] I'm not familiar with Vengeance Is Mine. But Imamura is an immense master. This Japanese approach, which is not at all popular in France, where films are still very psychological, and things must follow a logic, a flow of facts, of characters and their evolutions. What I love about the Japanese is that things creep up suddenly, and it's so much better. So much more life-like. I think it's absolutely sublime.

[Translated] So this is my childhood. And we always want to revisit our childhoods, especially their myths. I know I loved this movie, and it's funny because we need to revisit the things we saw in our childhood, it's like rereading the books you love. I think it's better to watch a masterpiece 100 times than to watch a film once that distracts you, but has no use. But "distracting" in French has two meanings. It also means to take away. It takes away one and a half, two hours of boredom. But an essential film transports you to another dimension, where we feel so good.

[Translated] Andrei Rublev is obviously Tarkovsky's masterpiece. And Tarkovsky... I met him, I even cooked for him at my house, if you can imagine! He was so modest, and he said that to torture him, they had cut off his phone. The entire negative of a film he'd made was supposedly damaged in the laboratory. That is totalitarianism. It's not necessarily about eradicating you, but about slowly consuming you. And he was so, so beautiful. He told it so simply. He was so deprived of freedom, sometimes of access to his work and everything else. And it's true that he was extremely moving and simple.
[Translated] And, well, there you go. I have the complete Bergman in my hands, as I completely owe him my entire career, because without him, I would've never become a filmmaker.

I’m first pulling out The Lady Eve. It’s hilarious and also really touching. I love… love this movie, I love Preston Sturges, as did John Hughes love Preston Sturges and Mike Nichols, who I worked with, said, “You gotta watch Preston Sturges movies,” and that’s how I first started watching those.

The 39 Steps I saw recently. Black-and-white, you know, British, more British-y Alfred Hitchcock and, like all his movies, there is something absolutely special and magnificent about it. It’s just a great plot that just… Surprises keep coming to poor Robert Donat or… I think that’s how you pronounce his name. There’s a helicopter in it, and one of the worst special effects I’ve ever seen is the helicopter flying overhead. And that’s another Hitchcock trademark, in my opinion, is to have some very fake-looking shot somewhere in his movies. I don’t know why, but he seemed to like that.

My Man Godfrey. You know, Carole Lombard, the most… God, the most gorgeous… You can’t not fall in love with her. And William Powell, too. The two of them are magnificent. And I don’t know the other actors’ names so well, but… that guy with the big… you know, the scratchy voice is in it who’s fucking fant– Excuse me. Fantastic. The… There’s a guy who does an impression of a monkey in it. And it’s a very funny and also very great, clever plot about the need for help after the Depression.

Now I’m picking Now, Voyager. It’s Paul Henreid and Bette Davis. It’s the one where Paul Henreid puts two cigarettes in his mouth and lights them both and gives– “Shall we have a cigarette on it?” And I’m leaving out Claude Rains, who may be my… one of my very favorite actors ever. Great character actor. A little taller, he would’ve been a leading man, but he got better parts because he’s a little on the short side, I guess. In this he plays her psychiatrist, and he is so touching and warm with her. I love him. I love Claude Rains.

So I have a noir: Double Indemnity. This movie is… Everybody talks this very clipped, short, stylish noir way that… there’s no other film quite like it. It’s perfect. And Barbara Stanwyck, no collection is complete without Barbara Stanwyck. One of the best film actors ever.

And this is The Cameraman, which is Buster Keaton. And I think this is one of his best ones, one of his most… It’s not like episodes of stunts. It’s like a real good story and a good character, and… I saw it at a movie theater with a live band and the audience was dying laughing. It’s funny to watch these movies in… with other people and realize that they’re still funny, which after a hundred years or ninety years is kind of amazing.

This is David Lean and Noël Coward, both of whom… nobody better. And the fact that they came together, some people don’t know because you know other David Lean movies and you might know Noël Coward plays, but Brief Encounter is very famous. Brief Encounter. There’s no more heartbreaking, yearning, regret-filled movie, but ends with a certain amount of happiness and peace somehow, brilliantly, even though it’s… it really tears you apart. In Which We Serve you might not have seen, but is magnificent. Noël Coward is in it. I believe he hated making it and decided he didn’t want to do movies anymore after that. He said, “I’m going back to the theater.” This Happy Breed I have not seen. Blithe Spirit, Rex Harrison. I haven’t seen that in a long time, but I can’t wait to see it again. Can’t believe David Lean directed those. Because you think of him as this enormous epic guy, but these are more intimate.

First thing I see up there is The Lady Vanishes. Hitchcock. Which is one of my favorites of his. There’s a looming threat. Psychological thrillers I think are so much more interesting. I think a lot of modern filmmakers could take a leaf out of his book, that he’s never gratuitous. The violence is always implied. It’s left to your imagination, which I think is much more compelling and engaging than just showing, you know, extreme violence, which I think is dehumanizing. And Hitchcock doesn’t do that. And also he laces it with humor.

12 Angry Men. Well, that’s Sidney Lumet, someone who’s workmanlike, who doesn’t mystify or mythologize his process. He’s written a very good book about it, on directing, and he talks about it in a way that feels like he’s talking about how to build a bridge or something, almost like he’s an engineer. It’s really refreshing. It’s very honest and direct and unambiguous and very accessible.

film_title: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
catalog_title: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
quote: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold. Okay, so The Spy Who Came in from the Cold. There’s a lack of color to this film, which is… Well, it’s black-and-white, but… I mean in the way it’s rendered, it’s… it leans into that monochromatic world that we imagined the Cold War to be in. There’s a speech in this film that Richard Burton gives, which is, I think, the best speech he gave as an actor, about what spies are. It’s the counterargument to James Bond. It’s a John le Carré… Based on the John le Carré book, of course, and really… really it’s worth watching just for that speech. And it has a bleakness to it I really like.

film_title: A Matter of Life and Death
catalog_title: A Matter of Life and Death
quote: Matter of Life and Death. Okay, so… Powell and Pressburger, they managed to embrace the surreal and the avant-garde and still make something accessible and popular. And that is such a hard thing to pull off. And they do it so well. But A Matter of Life and Death is wonderful. David Niven. Funny, witty. Deals with mortality and love in a… in a fun way. I love them for that. And that’s… This film in particular is a great one that deserves repeated viewing.

Okay, The Servant. Cracking movie. All about the British class system. Full of tension and microscopic attention to detail. It’s about power play. The shift of power in a relationship. Really stands the test of time. Very interesting that Joseph Losey, this American… It takes an American, an outsider, if you like, to sort of see the British class system objectively, because he’s not part of it. So he can see it as an outsider, as a witness. Yeah, I love this film. It’s fantastic.

Klute, Alan J. Pakula. This is very morally ambiguous. Jane Fonda gives, I think, the performance of her career. And it’s disturbing and unsettling, and the way it’s framed, it makes you a voyeur. Sometimes the screen will be… there’ll be a big wide screen and half of the screen will be black and the other half will be black and it’s just a narrow gap in a doorway that you’re looking through. Plays the whole scene like that. It takes real confidence. And it’s not just there to be different or experimental. It actually serves the narrative. You feel like you’re pulled into it. You feel you’re eavesdropping. So you lean into the screen and listen to it more. Fantastic film.

His Girl Friday. Okay. Often these films, it’s best to always see them on a big screen because they don’t go in for close-ups. They just rehearse it, almost like it’s a play. And they stay on the wide. And they just have these characters who… your eye goes to them, the way it would in the theater. Someone gives a performance, you just check them out and then you look over here. You sort of do the edit yourself. But they’re so well rehearsed that all the cues are really fast. It’s like they’ve rehearsed it to within an inch of its life, so it’s very tight, very disciplined. This is Hollywood at its best because it’s smart, savvy, there’s an emotional dynamic to it. It’s… Yeah, they don’t make them like this anymore. They try, but they don’t.

This is Rififi. It's a jewel heist. My husband loves any movie about a heist. Rififi, it sounds like it could be a great movie or the name of our next door neighbor's poodle. Rififi, here, here Rififi. Oh don't Rififi, don't.
This is one I love. I always—this is another one, if I see it, I have to watch it to the end. And it's directed by the great Ernst Lubitsch.

You should all see Night of the Hunter. And sadly, the reviews were very mixed, and he never made, he never made another film again. He felt so defeated by the reviews—that's why you shouldn't read reviews. But Charles Laughton, one of our greatest actors, and based on this, could have been one of our greatest directors.

I'm just, I'm I'm sort of going with the classics, but I love this movie. Sweet Smell of Success has some of the greatest dialogue ever. Burt Lancaster is fantastic as this sort of horrible Walter Winchell columnist. "I love this dirty town."
The Kid. Well, there should be one Chaplin.
Bitter Rice. A neo-realism with a heaping dose of pulp. And we're not talking orange juice, ladies and gentlemen.

Oh look, this I don't think I've ever seen this all the way through. This is, and it's written and directed by the woman who wrote The Birdcage, the genius known as Elaine May. One of the first of three women directors in the in the Directors Guild. It was Ida Lupino, Elaine May, and some other woman who I'm sure was wonderful. But Elaine, and now we realize how brilliant she was. A New Leaf, The Heartbreak Kid, the original Heartbreak Kid, that's the one to see, Charles Grodin, Jeannie Berlin, it's genius. And this is Peter Falk and John Cassavetes as small-time hoods.

Here Comes Mr. Jordan. Yeah, that's that, Here Comes Mr. Jordan was the movie that Heaven Can Wait, is that the other Heaven Can Wait? Oh, it's so confusing. How about this? Look at this. This looks very gay. This gives you, this is like a an older man, younger man, a young saxophone player, a gay relationship that's not going to work out.
Odd Man Out, directed by Carol Reed. I'm gonna give this a shot. I don't think I've ever seen this. James Mason, one of my favorite actors.

Valley of the Dolls. I was in a TV remake of Valley of the Dolls that starred Jean Simmons in the Susan Hayward role, and I played the stage manager at the Academy Awards. Look, my career could change if I was this tall. I could be a leading man.
The In-Laws. Yeah, it still holds up. It's still one of the funniest movies ever made.

This film, I sort of retired from musicals, but I went through a period where I thought if I was going to do a musical, I would like to do a musical of Being There, because it would be an interesting challenge, because he's the central character. Sometimes I asked Sondheim if he would be interested in doing it, and he said, "But the central character is a cipher, he doesn't sing." And I said, "I know, but people, it forces other people to sing at him." I said, "That's an interesting dynamic, don't you think?" I just thought, for one thing, with a character like this, I wouldn't have to sing for a while. I wouldn't sing until the end of the first act when the President of the United States would turn to me and say, "What do you think, Mr. Gardiner?" And Chauncey says, "Well, it's it's like a garden." Ding! And you would hear the musical cue, and then he would sing this childlike song about gardening, and yet the President would see all of these like it was a great analogy for the country. And then other people would start singing it, it would be on the news, and then and then children in schools would be singing this song, and then it would build to this huge, almost frightening anthem that would end the first act. That's that was my concept. Watch Being There. Peter Sellers, perhaps his greatest performance.

"Seized by customs upon entry into the United States, subject of a heated court battle, banned in cities around the world." I'm sold. "Vilgot Sjöman's I Am Curious-Yellow is one of the most"—why do you need the dash?—"it's one of the most controversial films of all time. This landmark document of Swedish society during the sexual revolution has been declared both obscene and revolutionary." In the bag.

Heaven's Gate, I'm fascinated by it. You know, it has a lot of, it has a lot of baggage with it, but I've never really sat down and seen it. The parts that I have seen though are a lot of texture of clothing. It looks so period. I think, Isabelle Huppert is in it. Yeah, and, I'm dying to see it. I'm really dying to sit down, get the popcorn, and watch the whole thing. I can't wait.
Okay, The Damned. The costumes are by Piero Tosi, unbelievable designer. I try, try to emulate him, but I will never reach the level of Piero Tosi if, if I live to be a hundred. So, one can try.
Here's another one, Barry Lyndon, that, Milena Canonero, another genius, designed. And I use it often for inspiration.

Aha, The Leopard, from my buddy Piero Tosi. And I've seen some of these clothes up close. The shapes, the fabric, the details. There's a, a thing with some of these films too, that you get a sense of when the film was made, but you also are, are just in love with the, how period it all looks and how exquisite it all looks. And so that's the kind of thing that wets my appetite to watch and, and to enjoy, and to just luxuriate in the, the beautiful artistry of a designer.

Oh yeah, okay. Jules Dassin, Naked City. I use it for research because Bill Daniels drove around New York and photographed real life people from like a window in a bread truck. And so you really get a sense of the day-to-day with the citizens of New York. It's interesting, I think I used it to research a film I designed called The Master, because of what real people would be like in 1948. And you see that not everybody wears hats, it's only the older ladies. Like there's a lot of bareheaded men and a lot of bareheaded women. And I think it's going to lend reality to my work if I see what it was really, really like day-to-day in New York City. So, love it.

Let's see, what's this? La belle et la bête. Just beautiful, surreal, shot right at the end of World War II in France. Everybody was cold, everybody was hungry. Cocteau came down with la grippe, during the filming of it, but managed to have the most amazing, beautiful fantasy film. And, it's beautiful to this day. I love to watch it.

Let's see. Oh, someone, Sunday Bloody Sunday. Someone mentioned this to me last night. I currently have a film out, Maestro, and, it's, there's part of it in 1971. And someone asked me, "Oh, were you influenced by Sunday Bloody Sunday?" I said no, but I, I'd love to look at the movie. And here we are today getting a copy. I can't wait to look at it.

Excuse my back again, but oh, wait a minute. My Beautiful Laundrette. One of the first films I worked on in Hollywood, I was assistant costume designer to Richard Hornung on The Grifters, and it was directed by Stephen Frears, who directed this film. Also, I've done a couple of films, Phantom Thread and, There Will Be Blood with Daniel Day-Lewis. And I have to say, the whole time I was working with Daniel on There Will Be Blood, I never once related that that was the same actor that played this part. He's so perfectly in his roles that you never think, "Oh, that's the same guy." And I loved this movie when it came out, it affected me a lot, and then I ended up working with Stephen, and then I ended up working with Daniel. So, down memory lane we go.

Marriage Story. Beautiful, beautiful movie. Oh, oh, who did the costumes? Oh, I did. But it's a beautiful movie, and, directed by my friend Noah Baumbach, who is, I've done another film for him too, and it's always a joy. It's always a joy. He, he lets you do what you do and supports you all the way.

Oh, you have another one of my movies. Wow, Punch-Drunk Love. It was, it was our beautiful musical, not musical, beautiful love story. And, we, we were kind of influenced a little tiny bit by, Godard films in making this. And it's just sweet, and I, I highly recommend you see this if you get a chance.
I'm going to start with this one. This is a real classic: Stagecoach.
Red River.

Forty Guns. Sam Fuller, the master of pulp fiction movie storytelling. There's a great shot that starts the movie where she's riding hell for leather, leading her 40 men with their 40 guns. Barbara Stanwyck is really great in this movie.

The Gunfighter. I had my doubts, you know, about Gregory Peck in this role. He's, he plays a veteran gunfighter who was trying to leave that behind, hang up his gun and lead a more peaceful life. But it's a dark kind of psychological drama, and I, my doubts were at the start, you know, I guess I was thinking about To Kill a Mockingbird and other sort of upright roles that Gregory Peck had usually played, and I didn't know if he'd be dark enough psychologically, but I was wrong. He's great in this movie.

The Furies. This is another great Barbara Stanwyck role. She's not the boss, but she's pretty bossy. The boss is played by Walter Huston in his last role, directed by Anthony Mann, who's one of the icons among Western directors.

Let's see, the original 3:10 to Yuma. Delmer Daves, studio director, very capable, very efficient. It is a really well-paced movie, really well done. Another thing about this movie, 3:10 to Yuma, is Glenn Ford on a horse. He was at the time, you can see this in this and other movies, he was, if not the best, probably one of the top two or three horsemen among popular Western actors. I think he was probably the best. It's not just the way he rode, it was the way he would get on a horse or approach a horse, get off a horse, totally at home with it.

This is the newest of the Westerns I picked. It's McCabe & Mrs. Miller. It's, I guess you'd consider it part of like the New Hollywood in that the story is kind of messier than what you're usually getting from Hollywood until that point, and the stories don't resolve in a predictable way. Really good. Oh, I love the music in this movie, and it features primarily three songs by Leonard Cohen: "The Stranger Song", "Sisters of Mercy", and "Winter Lady". And these are beautiful, and he was listening to this music a lot when he was preparing and shooting this movie and editing it, but these songs are beautiful. It's, I can't think of this movie without thinking of Leonard Cohen. Songs are perfect.

film_title: The Ranown Westerns: Five Films Directed by Budd Boetticher
catalog_title: The Ranown Westerns: Five Films Directed by Budd Boetticher
quote: Okay, this is a great box set. I love these movies. These are Budd Boetticher, who made a series of B-Westerns. He teamed up with actor-producer Randolph Scott, who was a kind of a, he was in the vein of Gary Cooper, although he had kind of a Virginia twang as opposed to Gary Cooper's Montana lilt, you know, but a similar kind of, you know, tall, kind of strong, quiet person. Those are the characters he played, but I think they did seven Westerns together, but he did five under this label, The Ranown Westerns. That name Ranown comes from Randolph Scott, the actor-producer, the start of his Christian name, and the last name of Harry Joe Brown, which was his co-producer. These five movies are The Tall T, Decision at Sundown, Buchanan Rides Alone, Ride Lonesome, and the last one they made together, Comanche Station. They're lean and mean, and you don't think about how the camera is looking at the landscapes and the characters, you just see it, you get it, and you're into the stories. I think that the first one that he worked on with Budd Boetticher, John Wayne was supposed to play the part, and John Wayne actually produced that one, Seven Men from Now, and he said, "Well, I can't do it, I'm going to do something else, a little movie called The Searchers, and so I think Randolph Scott would be great, he's done a good job in lots of Westerns." And that was the beginning of the teaming up of Budd Boetticher and Randolph Scott. Legendary partnership.
box_set_name: The Ranown Westerns: Five Films Directed by Budd Boetticher

quote: Here is Targets, Peter Bogdanovich's first film. Peter had been my assistant on several pictures and shot second unit on a few. He was clearly very talented and I had a very strange commitment with Boris, Boris Karloff to do a few days on another film. The result was Targets, with Boris at a drive-in where one of his pictures was premiering, and there was a shooter on top of the drive-in. And the idea was to more or less combine fictional violence with real violence. It was a brilliant and is today a brilliant film.

Here is The Gunfighter, which was a personal film for me. I had just become a story analyst at 20th Century Fox. I finally got a script called The Big Gun. The Big Gun was about a famous gunfighter whose reputation precedes him wherever he goes. I wrote a number of notes on it and I suggested changing the title from The Big Gun to The Gunfighter. I submitted this to the story editor who recommended it to one of the producers at Fox. He produced the film and the film, starring Gregory Peck as The Gunfighter, was a giant success. The story editor got full credit for all the notes that I wrote. I said, "That's it for my career at 20th Century Fox. I'm out of here." So I applied to Oxford, was accepted and went to Oxford on the G. I. Bill. So I got something out of The Gunfighter.

Here is Fellini's picture Amarcord. This is one of the foreign films we distributed. I remember that Allan Arkush and Joe Dante, our trailer editors, had just finished editing the trailer for some wild exploitation film, and they said, "This is a different kind of film. How should we build the trailer?" I said, "With the same style you use for the exploitation films." They did it and Amarcord was the biggest opening film Fellini ever had in his career.

Here is the Russian film of War and Peace. This is one of the greatest film adaptations of a novel, in my opinion, ever made. The way Bondarchuk photographed those battle scenes going on into the distance in long shots and then cutting to individual shots, as you took in the concept of the grandeur of the forthcoming battle and the beginning of the battle and then brought you in to the terror of the real battle, is brilliant.

This is Raging Bull, directed by Marty Scorsese. Marty actually directed his first feature film for me. It was called Boxcar Bertha. I had previously produced and directed a film called Bloody Mama. The picture was a major success for American International. A little later, they wanted a sequel to Bloody Mama and they wanted me to produce and direct it. By that time, I had my own company and I said, "I'll produce it, but I don't want to direct for another company, but I'll pick a new director." And I picked Marty. They were somewhat dubious and I said, "I don't care. A good director can direct anything." That's more or less true. Anyway, I convinced them to let Marty direct it and Boxcar Bertha became a solid success, both critically and commercially, and it started Marty's career. And Raging Bull is a great example of the way he was able to combine violence and at the same time explore the life of Jake LaMotta, who was the Raging Bull.
[Translated] Oh, I just saw... There it is. The Age of Innocence, by Scorsese. To me, one of the most beautiful endings in the history of cinema.
[Translated] An Angel at My Table, by our friend Jane Campion. Magnificent film. This was a great discovery. The lead actress was wonderful, and the whole opening... A truly great film.

[Translated] Here I've spotted our friend Cristian Mungiu... 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days. - Magnificent. - This film was a wonderful encounter for us. And Cristian became a friend. So it's good to pick a friend's film, especially when this friend's film moved us so deeply. A great story about friendship. Yes, and also about the communist system in freefall. That's right, the communist catastrophe.
[Translated] Kieslowski's Dekalog... We saw it in the 80s, after '85. It really influenced our work. We were really inspired by him.

[Translated] A great discovery. Wanda, by Barbara Loden. I don't think I've ever seen such a profound loneliness depicted in cinema. She wants to change her life, and she isn't able to escape this terrible solitude. And by the end of the film, you want to be with her to have a drink with her. And smoke a cigarette. Definitely.

[Translated] - Oh, wait a moment— - There's another film? Yes, another film we thought about... A film we both saw— We both saw it in school, A film from our pre-adolescence... - Death of a Cyclist. - I never saw it again, and I think it'd be wonderful to be able to revisit it, given we haven't seen it since a long time ago.

catalog_title: 3 Films by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman
quote: [Translated] Let's stay in Italy, in a way. Scorsese, Rossellini. I just saw that there was a Rossellini... Rossellini and Bergman, films my brother and I watched over and over again, that we talk about often. And of the three, the one I've seen the least, is Journey to Italy. quote: This, Charles Laughton. Great movie, scary movie, and I was surprised that he was able to pull this off.

A movie called Yi Yi that you have, that, Edward Yang did, who didn't... Was a movie about so much and yet about so little at the same time. Like after watching it for two hours, three hours, I, it was a movie about nothing and a movie about everything. And when I finished watching that movie, first thing I did was call home and tell everybody that I love that I loved them.

Okay, well Antonioni was big for me. And stylistically I started getting into this when I was first a still photographer and liked Helmut Newton. And I don't know why, but they were cut from the same ilk and it just was stylish. This was when the time, more than narratively, I was into stylistic photography, and these were the movies that I would, there were a huge influence to me. Graphic, industrial... What else to say about that?

One of my favorite directors of all time is Kieślowski, and, Blue, White, and Red are amazing trilogy. I love, one of my favorite movies is the, it has a perfect opening where the family drives around the périphérique, I think it's called, Blue. And, they're going to their house in the country. The father is a composer, and, the child, they're driving all night, and the child, there's no dialogue really, in the beginning where you see the child, ask the mother to pull over so they could, she could use the restroom. So the car pulls over, you see the bottom of the car from the driver's side of the car, and the little girl's feet runs out and she sits in the grass and goes to the bathroom. In the foreground, the rack is focused to the hose, the brake hose, and you see the, brake liquid leaking, so you know something's going to happen. The car drives and there's a little boy, playing a, one of those games where the ball bounces into a cup, and he seems to not be able to catch it. And you hear the car, screeching like it's going too fast down this country road, and, you see a dog running, you see the boy, running after the dog, you hear an accident, the boy actually finally catches the ball, and you cut to a car against a tree with just a wheel spinning. And so much was told without any dialogue. I thought it was a perfect setup for a movie, you know, it was very powerful, and, that kind of blew my mind about making movies. It was the power of movie. Very powerful opening movie, and that changed my whole, way of trying to tell stories. Unfortunately I'm a cinematographer, my contribution isn't always narrative, but when I can, I think about that Kieślowski movie and how they set that story up.

And here's Brief Encounter, a movie that is just one of the most perfect of British mid-century film history that inspired and formed the sort of structure around my film Carol, and the performance, Celia Johnson's performance, and the cinematography, and Noël Coward's writing, and anyway, it's an amazing movie. And I don't know if I have it on, Blu-ray, so I'll just stick it in my bag.
Gus's My Own Private Idaho. This is a beautiful edition that I treasure in my collection.

Where's all the Sirks? And Ed Lachman, my DP, I think timed them for a Criterion, so Written on the Wind, All That Heaven Allows, and Imitation of Life, and I don't think Criterion has Imitation of Life, but they're just, and Fassbinder would agree with me, two of the most perfect films ever made, and they have to be seen by you guys, anybody, everybody.

Where's all the Sirks? And Ed Lachman, my DP, I think timed them for a Criterion. So Written on the Wind, All That Heaven Allows, and Imitation of Life, and I don't think Criterion has Imitation of Life, but they're just, and Fassbinder would agree with me, two of the most perfect films ever made, and they have to be seen by you guys, anybody, everybody.

Masculin féminin is an extraordinary Godard, that I also quote in my film I'm Not There. It evokes the '60s, and in some ways it's so exquisitely made, and it also is problematic in the depiction of women, I think, in the film, and it's something that I tried to actually bring into one of Dylan characters, the Robbie story played by Heath Ledger. And this film kind of embodies all of the contradictions of that time in a way that, of course, Godard can expose in himself.

Oh, Sunday Bloody Sunday. I return to it. It's maybe a lesser-known film. It's a John Schlesinger film with Glenda Jackson and Peter Finch, and it's just, and I looked at it a lot for my last film, May December, and it's just, an exquisite, mature, and complicated film, sexy and beautifully constructed. Notice how I just slipped it in my bag.

Okay, Night of the Hunter is just one of the mo— maybe the most important films that anybody should see, made outside of the Hollywood system with no money, and with a tone and with a nuance. It's Charles Laughton's only film as a director. It's just, it's been quoted and quoted, but it is an astonishment to watch every time.
Long Day Closes. Terence Davies just passed away. He was such an artist, so completely unique. Speechless.
Every movie I start to make, I rewatch Beau travail, and I'm ready for the next one.

Okay, and this, this film is by Irving Rapper, who's not, you know, a celebrated director as we're discussing, but something happened with Bette Davis at the prime of her career with this film, Now, Voyager. It is a perfect film.
Oh my God, my friend Kelly Reichardt made Old Joy. What a beautiful, beautiful version.

Joseph Losey's The Servant. It's probably the most well-known of Joseph Losey's films, but it's an amazing and strange and hypnotic, similar kind of lure of homoerotic subtext that you might project onto a movie like Persona, but with the Joseph Losey signature.

film_title: Beyond the Valley of the Dolls
catalog_title: Beyond the Valley of the Dolls
quote: Now there's a dispute among the queer world between Valley of the Dolls and Beyond the Valley of the Dolls, and I'm in the Beyond the Valley of the Dolls camp, so to speak. It's Russ Meyer. The soundtrack is incredible. It's twisted and funny and dark and surprising.
I'll just end with one of the most perfect films made by Nicholas Ray, In a Lonely Place. If anyone hasn't seen it, you're lucky, 'cause you get to experience it. Okay, cut.

Now The BRD Trilogy is somewhere, and this is one of the most coveted box sets. It's so beautifully designed. It includes three of the later Fassbinder female-driven stories: Marriage of Maria Braun with, Hanna Schygulla, Veronika Voss, and Lola. It is just an exquisite and perfect object, collection of three masterpieces, and the perfect gift, and I just, every time I see it, I want to repossess it. Thank you, but I already have two copies.

Here it is, On the Waterfront. Great film, and I loved his work. He, he, I, I, I think I worked a lot like him because he, he was honest, he was open, he, he wasn't making, playing games. He was just doing films and always did, told the truth. He was, he was an honest director. That's, that's the way I feel I am, I'm an honest director.

One of my favorites, 'Round Midnight. First of all, it's a film full of jazz, and the jazz, the music is sensational. But it's also a story. You don't usually get a story with jazz. They usually are documentaries and you see the musician, you know, wonderful music, but this is a really terrific story, and I loved it. I always loved it.

The Shooting. Now this, this is, a film that was written by, her name was Carole Eastman, but she took the name Adrien Joyce because it had more literary, indications that there might be famous names by that name, Adrien Joyce. And, it was, it's a low-budget film, and it's very well crafted by, Monte Hellman, who I got to be friendly with because of Carole, and she was also friendly with Jack Nicholson and, Warren Beatty. So there was a little group of people that I got to know because of them. And, I remember when Carole died, Nicholson did a, a speech talking about her, and it was just beautiful. I mean, everybody was crying, and a great loss to us.

She was so beautiful, and I was a fashion photographer and I'd see her photograph, and I'd see her come on the screen, she was so beautiful. And I think a lot of my photographs of women were copied from what I'd see, the photographs that were taken of her. Marlene Dietrich, which, that's right, yeah.

quote: I'm happy to take this Varda collection home. It'll take a lot of my time, that's wonderful. I remember we're going with the Bertrand Tavernier's wife and Agnès to a museum, in, I don't know whether it was in France or Italy. And, when we got in there, there was an artwork, a piece of art of a nun, and she was sitting on a chair. And Agnès walked in there and they just seemed to go together, and I took, a wonderful photograph of Agnès standing next to the nun in the chair. It's, and it's one of my favorite photographs. I'm sure if you look my name up, you can find it somewhere. And if you could get me a, a cheese sandwich, I'll sit down and start watching them.

quote: I know which one I want to find first, which I think is probably the best way to start this, but I have to find, where will I find The Night Porter? Oh, got it! This. Oh, oh I like the cover. Yeah, it's a beautiful cover, a new one. So I think we have to start with that, just because I don't have that on Blu-ray. No, I don't, well I'll have that one. When was the last time you watched? I'm not going to take it out, it's the first one. When was the last time you watched The Night Porter, would you say? Very long time ago.

A Room with a View, which was one of the first. I worked for Merchant Ivory in my youth, and it still holds up so amazingly well, that film. I saw it recently and Howards End too I saw, they're both really beautiful. They're much more kind of subversive than you end up thinking they are, do you know what I mean?
Oh, that's a good one.

Oh, this is a whole, this is If.... Wonderful. Oh yeah, wonderful film. Oh, that's great, I loved out that, yeah. Do you want that, one of them? Yeah. Do you have a DVD player or a Blu-ray player? Well, I don't have a Blu-ray player. Then you should take the DVD.

Now I should probably not admit to not having seen this film, but I have never seen Ivan's Childhood. Trouble with Tarkovsky, I always fall asleep. I think that's all right to fall asleep in Tarkovsky, I mean that's what I've been told. It's all right Charlotte, don't worry about it. You wake up and it's still going on and you know it's still, you fall asleep and then you wake up and it like invades your dreams. That's right.

Have you ever seen this film, Charlotte? Which? Ratcatcher, Lynne Ramsay's British film. It's beautiful, beautiful film. She is great. I like, when I was dreaming of being a filmmaker, I always used to watch Ratcatcher in the hope that I would be like Lynne Ramsay one day, yeah.

And you're not going to take Weekend? No, I got it. You gave it to me, you gave it to me. You insisted, I heard you insisted I see it. This is a really good film. It's a really, it's a lovely film, you should try and catch that one.
Watership Down, which I'm very pleased that Criterion released. Have you ever seen Watership Down? Oh yeah. Existential agony of life played by rabbits. Yeah, all right, can't beat it.

Black Narcissus, definitely one of my all-time favorites. Have you seen Black Narcissus? Yes I have. Incredible. They did it so well, didn't they? Just incredible, yeah. So much like repression bursting from every frame.

Bergman Island, which I have, but I went to Bergman's island. We showed 45 Years at a little tiny festival on his island, and it was incredible because you show like the film in his little personal cinema, and I watched Persona in his personal cinema, and they don't let anybody sit in his seat where he used to sit, and it's just incredible. And then you stay in this little kind of guest house which is attached to his house, and you can walk around and you can see his like desk, and they show you like his scribbles on the wall and all kinds of things. It was just amazing.

One of my favorite British films, Sunday Bloody Sunday. Very good film. That's a beautiful film, beautiful film, and so crazily modern it's almost like amazing that, I'll take that again. That's an amazing, just incredible film.

Symbiopsychotaxiplasm, in the bag.

Wilhelm Reich, W. R.: Mysteries of the Organism, bag.
Robinson Crusoe on Mars, Byron H. Haskin, bag.
Sid & Nancy. Oh my God, we love a tragic romance. Shout out Amy Winehouse, Blake, Bobby and Whitney, Sid and Nancy.
Ooh, Summertime. Well, it's got Katharine Hepburn. She's giving us this power lesbian energy, and I'm here for this shit, so I'm gonna see what it's about.
Oh, Ratcatcher. Yo, Lynne Ramsay is a total vibe. If you don't know, now you know. Watch this film, you will never see curtains the same way again.

Douglas Sirk, that's my dude. I love Douglas Sirk, he's one of my favorite filmmakers ever. I literally copy this man in my head all the time, you know, German weirdo, sis. We got Lauren Bacall, we got, we got Rock Hudson, you know, the original trade.
All That Heaven Allows. Jane Wyman is a whole mood in this movie. Like, this movie is basically like How Stella Got Her Groove Back, but with like white people in Connecticut.

Rashomon. This movie just does a lot for me. I'm very much into the idea of like reconciliation and conflict resolution, and also the kind of Rashomon effect, right? How people remember things from their own subjective points of view. And I think this is a movie that really makes that come alive for me, and I return to often when I write my movies, especially The Inspection. This movie played a lot, had a lot to do with how men spoke. It's not necessarily a direct reference, but it's something that I kept close to me while making the film.

Paris is Burning, the deluxe edition. I'm thrilled. Carmen Xtravaganza, we love you. R. I. P. To all the pioneers, icons, legends, and statements, femme queens, butch queens who paved the way for all of us butch queens to have this moment, so thank you so much.

Bamboozled. You know, the problem of the Black, the image of the Black in the Western world, you know, these cameras that we use were invented by, you know, these white men who had access to everything, and they had an agenda, you know, to create a world that could justify their perpetual dominance. And blackface and minstrelsy is a part of that agenda, you know. And I think Professor Spike Lee, who's my professor at Tisch, I think he really broke open a conversation and managed to help the whole world understand the damage those images did through this film. And, you know, Damon Wayans, Miss Jada Pinkett Smith, Tommy Davidson, again, another incredible, incredible talented actor that we need to see more of. I saw this movie in Philadelphia in a theater, and I remember sneaking in Budweiser and cigarettes and smoking during the film, because I was like, ain't no white man gonna tell me I can't smoke a cigarette while I'm watching this movie. So thank you, Spike.

The Battle of Algiers. You heard it here, folks. This is my favorite movie of all time. I personally don't see a difference between documentary and fiction. I think there are two paths to the same outcome of called a film, and this film proves it through Gillo Pontecorvo. Incidentally, this film also premiered at the New York Film Festival, and now The Inspection has closed the New York Film Festival. So I have, I've written about this film in schools many times, and I love this film, and now I finally have it as a physical object that will go into my studio. So thank you, Criterion, I love this movie.

Last but not least, Marilyn Monroe in Some Like It Hot. I think Marilyn Monroe is the greatest movie star that's ever lived. I think she is the most famous person that has ever lived, maybe aside from like Jesus Christ and Martin Luther King. I have this kind of world in my head where Marilyn had lived, and she got a chance to experience feminism, you know, and she never did, but she was a feminist. She was the first, I think she was the first woman to own a production company in Hollywood, you know, and it's, people play her to be some sort of like, shrunk back, some bimbo, and you know, you could be sexy and you could be smart, and you know, and that, and that is powerful. So we love Marilyn, and because we love Marilyn, we're going to take her home.

Melvin Van Peebles, it's a box of his work. Melvin is one of the architects of what can be called Black American cinema. We are all walking in his legacy. Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song is one of the most badass movies ever made, and also one of the most profitable movies ever made, people don't talk about that much, but now I get to see everything else he's done. I'm excited about that.

This is an amazing movie. Stanley Kubrick told me that when I was this age I should do a remake of this movie. It's an Akira Kurosawa movie called High and Low with Toshiro Mifune. And it's a story about a man who worked his way up from shoe factory, making shoes, to becoming an executive at the shoe company. And then his child is kidnapped, or so he thinks. The kidnapper took the wrong child. They kidnapped his butler, his servant, the person that works in his house, they kidnapped the wrong child. Soon then he's faced with the moral dilemma: what do I do? Do it's not, you know, it's a it's a great movie.

Where's Tanner? Robert Altman, who I had the pleasure working with three times. I did a play with him in London at the Old Vic, an Arthur Miller play, and I did one of the films that's in the Criterion Collection, Short Cuts. I'm not sure where that is, but Short Cuts. And I had the great pleasure of working with Julianne Moore amongst all the other brilliant actors that are in it. But this is amazing, this Tanner '88, because what Robert Altman did was follow the an election that was taking place, and the brilliant Michael Murphy, he pretended to be a politician that was running for office. I think at sometimes he actually felt that he really was running for office.

This is amazing. This is The Black Stallion. This is directed by Carroll Ballard. Carroll Ballard, I had the pleasure of working on a movie that Francis Ford Coppola, he produced this, Francis Ford Coppola, and he produced the movie that I made with him called Wind. And Wind is about the America's Cup, and I had the pleasure of working with the most amazing sailors in the in the world. And it was it's a it's a beautiful Carroll Ballard, this is a beautiful movie, The Black Stallion. And Carroll Ballard is best, he's the best filmmaker when the actors are not speaking. That he's like a documentary filmmaker that that captures moments rather than tries trying to create moments.

film_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
catalog_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
quote: Here's another film by my friend Stanley Kubrick, who I worked with on Full Metal Jacket. Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb. Stanley said that he told me that he wanted to make a movie that was a serious movie about the doomsday machine and about nuclear proliferation and nuclear warfare and the terrifying aspects of it. But the more he did research, the more he realized how stupid the entire thing was, and that you couldn't make a serious movie about this because the absurdity of human behavior and in human the industrial military complex was it was so ridiculous that the only way that you could really make a good movie about the nuclear war and nuclear bombs was to make a comedy.

Night of the Living Dead. My father was a drive-in theater manager, and I watched this movie in the projection booth of the drive-in. It was called the Highland in Salt Lake City, Utah. And I was much, much too young to have seen this film, and it damaged my at least 10 years of my childhood of just being scared to death that these zombies were going to come out and start consuming my flesh.

Midnight Cowboy. This played at my father's drive-in. This is directed by John Schlesinger, and Midnight Cowboy, when it came out, it was rated X, and it played at my dad's drive-in. So I told you we were living in Utah, and this movie, the Mormons threw my dad and our family out of Utah basically because of this movie.

Here's another Robert Altman title, The Player, that Tim Robbins was in with Greta Scacchi and an unbelievable cast of actors from show business that Robert, everybody wanted to work with Robert Altman because he was so cool, and working on his sets, that the freedom that he allowed actors to have, the experience was just like not working on anybody else's movie.

Well, this one, 8½, I mean, I think it became the film that every filmmaker, or wannabe filmmaker, said, "That shows you that you can make a film without knowing what it's about, you know, and try and find out while you make it." That's what he was trying to do. And then in the middle of the film, somebody says about the guy, Mastroianni guy, "Again, he has nothing to say." It was shocking. I said, "Wait a minute, I'm believing every second of this. What are you talking about?"

Another friend of mine, who was a friend of Hal, wrote this film. And I said to him, "How'd you come up with all that automobile nomenclature?" He said, "I made it up. I don't know shit, anything about it." I thought that was great. In fact, I spoke to him yesterday. His name is Rudy Wurlitzer.

quote: And you know about this guy, right? He was a friend of mine. He was one of the sweetest characters ever, and he was always interested in other filmmakers, Cassavetes. He always wanted to know how you were doing. And also Hal Ashby was the same way, another friend. And both these guys would be in heaven in this room. They wouldn't want to leave, you know.

Classic ehm film that I never tired of, Midnight Cowboy. I love also the song that is connected with this film, Everybody's Talkin'. So I like how eh is less cutey eh so you can actually up the space for you to...

Film and one of the few films that play in Hamburg, it's where I made A Most Wanted Man, so I watched it before I came. This is really nice when you use a city that people actually don't know. It's not someone's home, it's all new territory what you look at. And Dennis Hopper's in it, bonus too.

I believe that Robertson together for the DVD for Casino and Robertson's for the music and the musicians, ehm the uniqueness of it all and I think and Scorsese covers a lot cleaner the film is that...
Never made a film before you know that's not your language, it's so nice to be on a set of a proper filmmaker.

They used to show Italian movies with subtitles where I grew up in Schenectady. We had a big Italian-American population, I think it was some of the reason they did that. My father had been in Italy in World War II, and so I had some kind of ideas about what it was like. I actually understood the language a tiny bit from hearing it around the neighborhoods. And this was a kind of mind-blowing movie when I first saw it. Anthony Quinn was a filmmaker, actor from much more mainstream movies than I had ever seen, so it was interesting to see him in this really kind of stark story, very human, that Fellini made. There were a whole bunch of directors who I started tracking down their stuff, Mario Monicelli being one of them, and Ermanno Olmi, and certainly De Sica, and Fellini's movies were ones that I started tracking down. For one thing, the people seemed actually from the neighborhood, familiar in some ways, but also it was this interesting thing of a society rebuilding itself after everything had been bombed and knocked down.

This is a Mario Monicelli movie called The Organizer with Marcello Mastroianni. It's one of his greatest performances. It's set in the industrial north of Italy when unions were a pretty new idea up there. A wonderful cast, there's a couple great French actors, there's some of Monicelli's usual guys. He was very good at what I eventually figured out was Italian regional humor. So there's usually some Roman who's full of himself dealing with some Neapolitan or some Sicilian, and making wisecracks based on how awful each other's region is.

This is a movie, His Gal Friday, Girl Friday, that I had not seen many of these except on TV, and finally they showed them enough, these kind of fast-talking comedies. This is based on a play that Ben Hecht was one of the writers for. I'm a screenwriter for hire, and Ben Hecht was an everything for hire. He had his name on a lot of things, he did a lot of work on most of them, sometimes his name just got on them. And this is one of those dialogue-driven movies where the dialogue is so good that you forget that the filmmaking's actually pretty good too. That the director really realized what his job was, was about pace and physically keeping the thing moving, as well as the lines just coming one on top of each other. Yeah, I'd say it's one of the tightest comedies I've ever seen, and it's one of the very few times where I feel like a play worked perfectly for a movie. And some of it is the chemistry of the leads, and some of it actually is the directing. This is Howard Hawks, and he, you know, he made a bunch of good movies. He was good. One of the things that he was the best at was he was one of the first directors, American directors, to really capture that people often talked at the same time. And we had great group scenes where people would talk over each other and keep the energy going up. And so that this very written dialogue doesn't feel quite as written, there's a kind of spontaneity to it.

This is State of Siege. You know, I saw this, I had seen Z first, and the, you know, this is a movie in a very, very political time. You could actually, if you weren't an American, get away with making a very political movie. This was a filmmaker who had really a lot of political analysis about what was going on in the country, but managed to make these thrillers. And to a certain extent, you had to be careful where you shot these movies. You had to go to a place where, you know, it's not just are they going to stop us from shooting, are they going to threaten us, it's also what's going to happen to the people who collaborated and cooperated with us, that we are going to leave behind while we're shooting. And you have to think of that before you go. When we shot our movie Men with Guns, we didn't shoot in Guatemala because we felt like anybody who works with us, when we leave, is going to be on somebody's list. So we shot it in Mexico across the border.
Kwaidan. This is a Japanese folk-horror omnibus, and it’s very beautiful, deeply beautiful film. It’s long, but, you know, it’s in four segments, so you could break it up over a couple of nights.

Do the Right Thing. The ’80s, underrated decade, as far as I’m concerned. As far as I’m concerned, this is the best movie of the ’80s. It’s just as vital now as it was when it was made. It’s a great film. Do the Right Thing.
Hoop Dreams. I’m given to superlatives, but I think it’s the best sports movie ever made. I think it’s the best movie of the ’90s. I think it’s the best Chicago movie. Can’t lose with Hoop Dreams.

Berlin Alexanderplatz. This is 15 hours long. But you want to be a movie person, don’t you? That’s why you’re watching the Criterion Closet video. So I suggest, if you want to be a movie person, you turn off the streaming and you put this on and put on some pants and sit down on the couch and take your dissonance like a man.
Westerns, I love westerns. Winchester ’73. Anthony Mann western with Jimmy Stewart.
Red River. Howard Hawks, John Wayne, Montgomery Clift.

Jazz. I’m a jazz guy. ’Round Midnight. Dexter Gordon. You get to see a lot of great jazz musicians in this. Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Bobby Hutcherson, Cedar Walton. You get to see these guys play and play whole songs. It’s a movie that is about jazz and actually lets them play the songs.
And Thelonious Monk Straight, No Chaser. Great documentary. Amazing artist. Watch that.

Choose Me. Sometimes Criterion confirms me. This is a movie I’ve been toting around for twenty years or longer and trying to get people to watch, and then Criterion came out with the disc and I was like, “See, I knew this was a great movie.” Another great ’80s film. And some people think Alan Rudolph was just an Altman knockoff, but he wasn’t. He had his own thing going on, and that’s very apparent in Choose Me. It’s a lot of fun.

Love Jones. Sometimes Criterion introduces a movie to you. I did not know this movie at all. And I was just blown away. It’s such a… such a beautiful, tough… It’s a romantic comedy, but it’s also a really tough movie. And it’s a great Chicago movie, which is important to me. So Love Jones, a real discovery.

I want to say one more thing about… Where’s Mr. Arkadin? Mr. Arkadin, Orson Welles. This is an amazing thing that Criterion does. So, when I was a kid, different versions of this would be on TV and you might watch it, but you wouldn’t know which version you’re getting. There are different versions of it. You know, with Welles’s history, it was always chopped up and there were several different versions. Criterion, in this box, gives you three different versions and kind of a road map to how they each got put together and why they are the way they are. And they’re all great. They’re all different. They’re all the same. They’re all a great movie. But it’s just… it’s one of the great things about physical media. There’s no other way to kind of get the package of all three versions of Mr. Arkadin, if you’re the kind of person who needs that. And I am. I mean, he’s one of the greatest artists America has ever produced, and so we should absolutely have this kind of record of his work.

quote: And The Ranown Westerns, directed by Budd Boetticher and starring Randolph Scott. My wife and I watched these, we watched them one at a time, one a week for about five weeks till we knocked them all out. It’s just… The feeling I get when I put these on, it’s just – you wrap yourself up in a blanket on the couch and you watch these things and you just feel really good and very warm and comforted and safe.
