quote: Army of Shadows. This is a fantastic film. This is a movie about the French Resistance. And I think oftentimes we think that it was so dashing and romantic, the Resistance. This is a very bleak film, and I think a very honest appraisal of what it was like to be in a resistance movement in that time. But it is a beautiful film, and there are great character names. Le bison. Le masque.

Okay, here’s another movie that dabbles with the idea of fascism and what it does to us, but… Here’s what I want to say about Grand Budapest Hotel. I think Ralph Fiennes should’ve been nominated for an Oscar. And I think sometimes when actors are funny, they don’t get the same respect they deserve. And he was so very funny. And also, you know, deeply sad. It was real emotion to the character he was playing, who was trying to hold onto this thing, this past that wasn’t going to be part of his present or his future. And so those are the two real oversights for the Academy, I think, as far as comedy not getting Oscar, which is Ralph Fiennes and then Ted Knight in Caddyshack.

Miller’s Crossing. I mean, there’s not a bad Coen brothers movie for me, but this one, there’s just sort of a… an entirely new vocabulary this film teaches you in the first 30 minutes that you have to understand to appreciate the rest of the movie, and so it’s so much better on each rewatch. And let me tell you, not one of us, not me, not anybody who watched it, is ever gonna wear a hat as well as Gabriel Byrne wears a hat in this movie. Best hat work in cinema history.

Watership Down I’m only bringing up because it is truly– I think this is the scariest moviegoing experience of my life. My mother took me to see this movie when it came out. What year did this come out? So 1978– I was five years old. My mom thought it was an animated rabbit movie. And, guys, it is technically that. If you’ve got a five-year-old who loves rabbits and also dreams of just blood running through fields, run, don’t walk to Watership Down.

Okay, Lost in America. There’s a scene where Albert Brooks loses his life saving in a casino, and Garry Marshall runs the casino. And Albert Brooks is an ad exec and his pitch is that Garry Marshall should give him all his money back and then do an ad campaign about how Desert Inn is different than other casinos because they have heart. And Garry Marshall just impresses upon him that would be a terrible way to run a casino. But the special thing about this is I worked with Garry Marshall and I was in one of his movies and basically the main reason I did it was to talk to him about this scene. It was so funny because he was so frustrated by how many takes Albert Brooks made him do. They were friends. All these years later, I’m like, “It’s the best scene,” he goes, “We got it on the first take and he makes me do it again and again.” Perfect scene, Garry Marshall was complaining that Albert Brooks made him do a lot of takes. The movie I did with Garry Marshall was New Year’s Eve. New Year’s Eve… Where is the Criterion? Oh, out of print. The Third Man and New Year’s Eve are out of print due to popularity.

Withnail and I. The greatest movie about getting drunk ever made. And when it’s over, you either never want to drink again or you want to have a ton of drinks. I think that’s a good test to let you know which way you’re breaking. Richard E. Grant, he drinks in this movie like Gabriel Byrne wears a hat in Miller’s Crossing.

Okay, Long Good Friday. I love this movie. Just top to bottom. It’s just a British mobster over the course of one long Good Friday as everything falls apart. Helen Mirren is his wife and, you know, so fucking hot. Just Helen Mirren– and I say this as a friend of Helen Mirren’s. Just outstanding, and final scene in this film, greatest face acting you’ve ever seen. Just Bob Hoskins, not talking, telling you literally everything his character’s thinking. It’s…

So, Grey Gardens, the Maysles. Couple Maysles. Salesman. These are two fantastic films, both of which we used as inspiration for a show I created with Fred Armisen and Bill Hader called Documentary Now! Alex Buono, Rhys Thomas. I’m shouting them out because this is the sorta… this is the sort of thing they’re going to watch. John Mulaney. But we were lucky enough– Alex and Rhys actually talked to one of the Maysles, talked to them about using the right lenses, and the thing is, when we write one of these episodes, you know, I wrote both of these, I had to watch them so many times to see if there was stuff I could find as inspiration. And you just– the humanity that they managed to get, the way that they are present, but not in a way that gets people to be anything other than their true selves.

Salesman. These are two fantastic films, both of which we used as inspiration for a show I created with Fred Armisen and Bill Hader called Documentary Now! Alex Buono, Rhys Thomas. I’m shouting them out because this is the sorta… this is the sort of thing they’re going to watch. John Mulaney. But we were lucky enough– Alex and Rhys actually talked to one of the Maysles, talked to them about using the right lenses, and the thing is, when we write one of these episodes, you know, I wrote both of these, I had to watch them so many times to see if there was stuff I could find as inspiration. And you just– the humanity that they managed to get, the way that they are present, but not in a way that gets people to be anything other than their true selves. Also, a little bit of bonus, the Doc Now! Episode about Salesman, called Globesman, Globesman is available on this.

I'll comment on this for sure because it was, I saw Weekend of Godard with my mother and I was enraged by it. And I said, "This is the most horrible thing that I've ever seen. I hate it." And over the course of maybe two days it sank in on me, and I then decided that it was like my favorite movie that I'd ever seen in my life, and I... And it was prophetic. And it was prophetic. Yes, it was prophetic. It was a great, great film and I, I, and it was a big shock to me that that could happen.

I had a very interesting experience with Antonioni, which is slightly the opposite of what happened to you because I loved his movies when they came out, because he seemed again like a prophet. He was showing the shape of things to come. And then about 25 years later, I went back to see his movies and hated them because the world had already become what Antonioni was predicting. And then about 10 years later, I went back to them and again was just staggered by them, absolutely.

That's, I had an interesting experience with him. There was a screening of Red Desert, which is maybe my favorite of his films, a director's cut at MoMA, and somebody took us as a surprise and didn't tell us where we were going, because Antonioni is Cindy, my wife's, favorite filmmaker. And there were these little tables we sat at for dinner after the screening of the film, and strangely enough Antonioni was at the next table, and sitting all by himself. Everybody had left him, either because he only spoke Italian or French. And I went and sat next to him and said, introduced myself and I said, "This must be an amazing night for you." And he said, " no, I hated tonight." I said, "Why?" He said, "There are 14 frames in the film that I can't stand, and every time I see the film it breaks my heart, but I can't do those over again." That's a tragedy of film.

Goodness me, this is the late and very adorable Paul Bartel, Eating Raoul, a wonderful film from the time of My Dinner with Andre, by a wonderful filmmaker. Anybody who hasn't seen this... Well, I haven't, let me take a... I'm sure you did at the time.

Oh, this one. One of the most visual Japanese movies ever. I already have the DVD, but, it's more colorful and crazier than any Dario Argento movie or any Mario Bava movie. If there's one masterpiece in Japanese horror cinema from the 60s, this is the one.
I haven't seen it in a long time, Island of Lost Souls.
And this is the first, the first cannibal movie that is really a masterpiece.

quote: I'm doing a play on Broadway right now with Ben Foster who was in the film 3:10 to Yuma, but not this 3:10 to Yuma, so I'm going to take a copy of this film for Ben.
And oh man, what do I want for me? What do I want for me? I guess you can't go wrong with Bergman, so I'll go with The Magician on Blu-ray. Thanks.

I'm going to take this and I'll tell you why. My friend Jimmy Toback and I made a film about ostensibly the Cannes Film Festival, and we went to Cannes last year, 2012, and we shot the festival and the story, so to speak, is us selling a film we want to make, but really what it was an appreciation, kind of an homage to Cannes. And when we were there we interviewed Bertolucci, we interviewed Coppola, Scorsese back in the States, we interviewed Polanski and Bertolucci at the festival, and the film we made, which is called Seduced and Abandoned, is in the Cannes Film Festival this year, so we're at Cannes with the film. And, and while we were talking to, Bertolucci, he talked on and on and on about his debt to Pasolini. So I'm going to get this for Jimmy, and I'm going to get 3:10 to Yuma for Ben.
I'm a big food guy, I don't know if you've heard, but this might be the ultimate movie about a meal.
Stagecoach, I recommend to you. It's the Star Wars of its day.
Hitchcock. This is a great movie, Foreign Correspondent. Incredible, indelible set pieces, brilliant scenes in this movie, so much fun.

film_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
catalog_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
quote: There's never been a movie like this, Dr. Strangelove. I play this game: if there was a day and all your favorite filmmakers were opening a movie on that day, which filmmaker's movie would you see first? That tells you something, right? For me, it's this guy.

What's Overlord? Shot by Stanley Kubrick's longtime cinematographer John Alcott. See, if you don't pick it up and read it, you don't know what you got here. Now I have that. Who doesn't want to see that now?

What's Make Way for Tomorrow? The saddest movie you'll ever see? No thank you, I have enough. Life is hard enough, some things you know, yes I know. Would it be good for me to see the sad movie? Yes, probably, but today I don't feel like it.

This is easily one of the best, most influential comedies of all time, and it, you know, it's about, it's about comedy. If you can see any Preston Sturges movies, I think Criterion makes The Lady Eve also, that's fantastic. All of his movies were tremendously funny with rapid-fire dialogue and, and just brilliant. He used some of the same character actors in all the movies, so he had like this little company of players, and you love seeing them recur in the other movies. It's almost like he was doing a sitcom, but changing the story in each movie.

Here's On the Waterfront, and the cool thing about this one is all three aspect ratios that the movie was released in are in here. In 1.66, you, you see the gun on Rod Steiger's lap in the, in the taxi scene, but if it's cut in 1.85, you don't see the gun in his lap. Or when Brando is rolling the, the cue ball in the, in the, in the pool room scene, you don't see him doing it, you don't see the ball, you just see from here his arm going like this, you don't know what he's doing. The framing of something, sometimes it's everything. So you got to have that.
Never saw this. Everyone says this is a great scary movie, and I've never seen it.

I hate when people go, “Oh, what’s your favorite movie of all time?” “What’s your favorite Black movie of all time?” The best I can do for that question is a tie. Fortunately, both films are in here. Black Orpheus, exquisite in every possible way. I like to watch it periodically and go, “Oh, yeah, this is what I’m in the business, to make a movie– to aspire to make a movie as good as this one day.”

The other greatest Black film ever made: Killer of Sheep, Charles Burnett. When I was in college, I would put together little film festivals at school, and I brought Charles there, and I showed the movie and everybody in the film program was blown away. This movie was made– He’d worked all week, saved enough money to buy a roll of film, shoot that roll of film, go back to work. And thank God for Charles Burnett for making a true masterpiece. This and Black Orpheus, that’s where I try to live, somewhere between those two films.

Menace II Society by the Hughes brothers. Early in our careers, people would mix up the Hudlin brothers and the Hughes brothers. We laughed about it all the time because they would compliment me over Menace II Society, they would compliment them for House Party, and we decided we would claim each other’s body of work. So, if you see one of us, we’ll just say yes, and, you know, we’re all brothers.

Risky Business. There’s a couple of movies that really inspired House Party. Animal House was one of them. Risky Business was the other. You just go, “Wow, I can make a movie like that, about my life experiences.” I don’t know if we succeeded or not, but Risky Business is the business.
Rouge, great movie from Hong Kong in the ’80s, mixing all kinds of genres. It’s romantic, it’s scary, it’s all the feelings, it’s this extraordinarily beautiful, touching film. Yeah.

Melvin Van Peebles, the father of modern Black cinema. Sweet Sweetback, legendary film. What most people don’t know – and they’ll put it on and go, “Oh, wait, what’s this?” – it’s a completely experimental film. This movie is, wow, this is free jazz. And the irony of me saying that is the score is by this unknown group, which later figured out, “Oh, we should call ourselves Earth, Wind & Fire.” But Melvin Van Peebles acted, directed, produced, did every doggone thing. The true do-it-yourself guy with a revolutionary statement that Hollywood would try to duplicate but never properly imitate.

film_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
catalog_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
quote: Bruce Lee, what a great action actor. In one of the great fight scenes in Enter the Dragon, where he’s fighting Oharra, the guy who killed his sister at the beginning of the film, he fights the guy, the guy crosses the line and he takes him down and he stomps him out. Now, here’s what you see in that film that you’ve never seen in other movies like this. There’s a close-up on his face in slow motion where you see him go through this whole range of emotion. It’s: “I did it, I executed my technique. I got revenge on this guy who I’ve been driven to kill.” And then the regret and sorrow of: “I just killed a man.” That’s the brilliance of Bruce Lee amongst everything else he was.

My final win of an amazing visit is one of my absolute favorite filmmakers, Fellini. Fellini, postwar Italy somehow really resonates with me for working-class Black America. Something about, okay, we’re rebuilding our life out of the ruins and we’ve got so much flavor and we embrace the surrealism of our lives, and it’s comedic and it’s tragic and it’s heroic. It’s all the things at once. He’s always been a giant hero to me. When I was in film school, I remember writing a paper on 8½. I did not get the grade I deserved, but I got the life I deserved. Thank you, Fellini.

I’m going to start with what I think might be my favorite filmmaker: Robert Bresson, whose rhythms and stillness is a little bit like listening to Bach. And A Man Escaped is simply that. It’s somebody who’s in prison and who, bit by bit, using the materials of what’s in his jail cell, escapes from the prison. Think of it metaphorically, think of it in narrative terms, it’s one of the most beautiful films you’ll ever see. So in it goes.

I think I’m going to surprise you by picking something that looks utterly predictable. Citizen Kane has a connection to The New Yorker. It’s written by Herman Mankiewicz, along with Orson Welles, of course, and there’s a famous book by Pauline Kael, who was the great New Yorker film critic, about the controversy about who gets the credit for Citizen Kane, which many people think is the best movie ever made, certainly in English, whether it was Herman Mankiewicz more or Orson Welles. In any case, you have to see it.

I watch a lot of music movies. Thelonious Monk was one of the great composers and players during the bebop period, and Charlotte Zwerin’s film, Straight, No Chaser, captures his stage presence and his quirkiness and humanity like no other film I’ve ever seen. So Straight, No Chaser.

When I was a kid, just learning about films that were a little more than Daffy Duck, I started seeing Werner Herzog’s films, Aguirre, the Wrath of God, Fitzcarraldo, things like this, and I knew nothing about the absolute eccentric working life of Werner Herzog, why would I? But along came a documentary about Werner Herzog. It’s called Burden of Dreams, and it’s revelatory about the filmmaker’s art, especially on the more lunatic end of the spectrum.

I love French New Wave films, Godard, Agnès Varda, François Truffaut, Rivette, all of them. And one of the ones that I saw earliest in my life, when I was a teenager, was Shoot The Piano Player. I think I learned about it from Bob Dylan’s liner notes in an early album. A great, simple melodrama, and Charles Aznavour is absolutely wonderful in the title role.

So one of my dearest friends in the world is a guy named Richard Brody, who you know better as the film critic at The New Yorker, along with Justin Chang, and Richard is of the belief that the great revolutionary filmmaker is Jean-Luc Godard. But he would not choose Breathless or Masculin féminin as his greatest film. He will choose and he will tell you that King Lear, starring Norman Mailer and Molly Ringwald and Godard himself, is the epitome of Godard’s art. I don’t agree, but you should give it a shot.

film_title: The French Dispatch of the Liberty, Kansas Evening Sun
catalog_title: The French Dispatch of the Liberty, Kansas Evening Sun
quote: And I was really honored that he did a film that was kind of about The New Yorker called The French Dispatch, so Wes Anderson, the first 25 years. And if you have a sore back and can’t schlep around a big gift box: The French Dispatch, all by its lonesome.

film_title: By Brakhage: An Anthology, Volumes One and Two
catalog_title: By Brakhage: An Anthology, Volumes One and Two
quote: Now I’m going to blow your mind, probably somebody you’ve never heard of: Stan Brakhage. I came to him because I took a film course by the late, great P. Adams Sitney, and P. Adams Sitney– I think all the kids came to this film course thinking they were going to get an escape from academia and see The French Connection or The Godfather or something, and he put on a film called Window Water Baby Moving, which was the equivalent of seeing Jackson Pollock after a lifetime of seeing nothing but naturalism and realism. He is the godfather of experimental filmmaking, along with people like Maya Deren from an earlier age. Be patient with this. Don’t let it be all you ever watch, but it’s extraordinary in so many ways. Painterly is one of the words that you could put here. Give it a try. Stan Brakhage’s films.
box_set_name: By Brakhage: An Anthology, Volumes One and Two

film_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
catalog_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
quote: Far be it for me to be selling gift sets, but you might as well. It’s the first 25 years of Wes Anderson’s art. You have to say he has a vision. Within two seconds of seeing one of his films, you know who’s directing it. And I was really honored that he did a film that was kind of about The New Yorker called The French Dispatch, so Wes Anderson, the first 25 years.
box_set_name: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years

quote: Color of Pomegranates, by Parajanov. Parajanov is a really fascinating filmmaker who is really into recreating folk culture with a lot of detail. And he, you know, does these beautiful tableaus that are interpretations of the art from... From the world that he’s trying to articulate and bring us into. And it’s really spectacular.

Death in Venice, also costume designed by Piero Tosi. I don’t know, maybe my favorite Visconti movie? You know, obviously, like, Visconti and his collaborators’ attention to detail in creating the period world is something that I, shockingly, really love. You know, in The Leopard, when they open up the closet, at a ball, and it’s filled with, like, hundreds and hundreds of chamber pots, I’m like, “This is gold.” And, you know, anyway, I love Dirk Bogarde. His performance is incredible. It was also so brilliant to, you know, to make the lead character a composer instead of a writer. It just makes it much more cinematic. And a funny story that, like, Warner Brothers, when they saw the director’s cut, they were perplexed and also disappointed. But then one of the studio executives said, “The composer is amazing.” “I love this guy.” And Visconti said, “Well, it’s Gustav Mahler.” And the studio executive said, “Let’s sign him!” So that’s funny.

This is An Actor’s Revenge by Ichikawa, which I’ve only seen once. Kazuo Hasegawa was, like, a really illustrious kabuki actor, and he plays male and female roles, is, like, really powerful and really cool. And just the gender dynamics? Fascinating, you know, and... Anyway, I’ve only seen it once. I’m really looking forward to checking this out, and...

Related-ish is Demon Pond, which I actually have never seen, but I have seen clips of this, like, crazy parade of creatures. I just have to see this movie. I’m, like, desperate to see what’s going on here.

The Innocents is by Jack Clayton. This is one of my favorite films. I watch it, like, twice a year, probably. I love Freddie Francis, the cinematographer, like in, you know, his work with David Lynch, particularly The Elephant Man. But his work with Jack Clayton is, I think, his best work. I feel like they really pushed each other to have the most sophisticated and elegant staging that doesn’t draw attention to itself, but, like, just pulls you into the story. The studio wanted them to shoot it in Scope, they wanted to shoot it, like, in 1:33 or 1:37, and you know what? It ended up being one of the best-looking movies in Scope ever. And then they made a little vignette to do these sort of nighttime, hallway, horror-movie-set-piece scenes in a way that felt more like an Academy ratio. So, awesome movie if you haven’t seen it, like... Well, I mean, the screenplay, you just... Your imagination is on fire with, like, the disturbing shit that you don’t see. It’s awesome.

This is a heavy Pasolini box set, which is very exciting. I wanted to talk about Medea, but also happy to talk about Oedipus too. The worlds that Pasolini creates with Piero Tosi, the costume designer, and Dante Ferretti, the production designer, who, you know, was... Piero Tosi was older, Dante Ferretti was younger, and Dante Ferretti’s had this, like, insane career. But it’s amazing to see what Dante Ferretti does when, like, he doesn’t have any money and he’s just got to, like, go to a market and, like, grab some rugs and grab some baskets and still, like, create this incredible world. But one of the things about Medea is the music. Like, Pasolini is taking music from all over the place, you know, Bulgarian female choir singing, that has kind of been, like, a more popular thing since the ’80s, but he was putting it in films very early and lots of Middle Eastern music, and it’s really evocative to see what he does with it. So, look forward to exploring it more deeply.

film_title: Tod Browning’s Sideshow Shockers (Freaks, The Unknown, The Mystic)
catalog_title: Tod Browning’s Sideshow Shockers (Freaks, The Unknown, The Mystic)
quote: So this Tod Browning box set... This is just a recommendation. I own it. It’s awesome. Freaks is obviously, like, a major classic that a lot of people know. But The Mystic and The Unknown are movies that people know a lot less. I actually saw The Unknown, like, on TV when I was a teenager. And it’s this, like, amazing, transformative performance by Lon Chaney. Of course, it’s transformative, it’s Lon Chaney. Anyway, this is... And it’s, like, the special features are also, like, insane, so... Definitely, definitely check this out if you’re a Tod Browning fan, if you’re a Universal horror fan, if you’re a silent movie horror fan. It’s fucking cool.
box_set_name: Freaks / The Unknown / The Mystic: Tod Browning's Sideshow Shockers

quote: Well, this movie, Y tu mamá también, by Alfonso Cuarón, it’s a movie... That helped me discover these wonderful actors. One of them is Gael García Bernal, who I worked in three movies, is a wonderful actor and a great friend. And I really, really love this movie. When I saw it for the first time in 2001, it changed my head. It made me think and dream big. Because the movie made in Spanish that is so universal. And I keep it in my heart. I’m very happy to take it home in a Blu-ray.

The one and only Fassbinder. Berlin Alexanderplatz. Fassbinder is someone that had no... No affiliation. He did not respond to anything or to anyone. He only wanted to make the movie that he wanted. This movie is from 1980. It’s just like a master class on a city, on a relationship with a square. And the characters, and the way that the movie is shot, really... Just blew my mind. There’s nothing like this. And this edition is just wonderful and beautiful. Look at this.

You know, something that... That strikes me as a filmmaker is the chance of use of time. I think cinema might be the only and the most beautiful time machine that humans have ever created. And this movie is a very good proof of it. This is Boyhood from Richard Linklater. This movie is very important to me. It lives in my heart, and I admire everyone that did this film. It really, really hit me. And when I grow up, I would like to make a movie as good as this one.

Oh, here it is. Yeah, looking for great movies in our language, in Spanish, this movie by... It’s Señor Pedro Almodóvar. Todo Sobre Mi Madre, All About My Mother. Beautiful, beautiful film. And I think your Mother, anyone’s Mother, but your own Mother can always be a source of material for yourself. I have worked around the ideas and my experience with my own Mother in many movies, my Mother’s very important in my cinema, so I completely share Pedro’s necessity to make a movie that’s called All About My Mother.

This movie, Certified Copy, by Abbas Kiarostami. It’s a very particular and small story, but shows all of his power and all of his poetry. I had the chance to meet Mr. Kiarostami when he was doing this film, and it was very moving to see how he was expressing about this idea of certain things that can be copied and other things that should never be copied because they can be copied. If you have not seen this movie, have a look.

The master, Pier Paolo Pasolini. This is a beautiful collection of nine movies. The last one of this collection is Medea. I just made a movie about Maria Callas called Maria, and Maria Callas actually plays Medea in this movie. And I’m just, like, very curious for you to discover it, because Maria Callas really acting, she never made a movie before or after, and it changed her relationship with cinema. Pasolini was a wonderful writer, a filmmaker, and a poet. Teorema, which is also here, is one of my favorite movies. And it’s such a poetic, poetic film that ends with the most poetic ending ever, ever in filmmaking.

Krzysztof Kieślowski. The trilogy of the Three Colors. He did Blue, White, and Red. And specifically Blue, I think the use of music in this film has really changed me and educated me as a filmmaker. Music is very important in my world, in the movies that I do. And I think there’s something here, hearing in this film that I truly, truly value. If you have the chance to see it, look.

Fat Girl. I have never seen a film think it's one thing, like tell you it's one thing and then in the end reveal itself to be something else. The performances are amazing. Breillat is a queen. All of her movies are just unreal.

Definitely not the first person, won't be the last. Wanda, Barbara Loden, she made this brilliant film. She left the world way too early. This movie is such a study of womanhood. There's no glory in it, it's just the life of a woman who has reached the end of her rope. I could watch this movie over and over and over again.

Girlfriends, Claudia Weill. This movie is incredible. It actually reminds me a lot of Frances Ha, of Noah Baumbach's that he wrote with Greta Gerwig that she stars in. The relationship between the friends is super similar. I love Girlfriends, it's like a true New York City story. The dynamics are amazing, there's you know a little bit of inappropriate behavior by people who have more power than others, and friends who get pregnant versus friends who don't. I just love the way the story is told. It really feels like she just grabbed the camera and was like, let's make a movie, which I just love.

Interesting anecdote about Vagabond: I watched when I watched Maurice Pialat's À nos amours, To Our Loves Sandrine Bonnaire was in that. I think that movie is beautiful, but I also think it's really important in 2022 to be able to contextualize it, right? Sandrine Bonnaire was like 14 or 15 years old, there's like full frontal nudity, it's important conversations to have. And I watched Vagabond right after, that also has Sandrine Bonnaire, and I remember just in my head they're kind of linked, where I was like, oh she went from like that character is in Maurice Pialat's world and like little troubles and then she ends up like as a vagabond and that's what happens. Which is not true, but if I was ever asked to plan a double feature, I might put those two movies back to back.

Okay so, this movie for me is perfect. Truffaut made a movie that is so generous in spirit. He divulged all of his secrets, he let you in on what the process was. There's a huge montage in the middle of the film where they're setting up the day, I think, and the cranes are going up and the and the extras are getting into place, and this, and the score is unbelievable. It's also hard to find. I'm like, this I might frame it. I'll take the DVD out, but then I'll frame the box.

Okay, I'm just gonna pick one more and I'm gonna pick it at random. I'm just gonna close my eyes and, and my eyes are closed and I'm just going to turn around once. The Other Side of Hope. Couldn't have picked a better film, so thank you.

Oh well, this is a good place to start. I just remember, I mean, A Woman Under the Influence, amazing, Shadows, Faces, but Opening Night for me was just, there are scenes that sometimes I wake up in the morning and I think of them, like when they're on stage and I just, I love that movie.

I would be remiss if I didn't talk about Rohmer because I was kind of named after one of his movies. There's a softness to the way he tells stories that you know, the French filmmakers of the New Wave are just so incredible.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: And here, it's like I could be holding them up together, Varda. I really love her so much. You know who she reminds me of? There's that filmmaker, Alice Guy-Blaché, who was like the first, arguably the first fiction filmmaker of all time. She was French, but then she came over to the US and was living in Fort Lee, New Jersey, before Fort Lee moved out to be Hollywood, and I feel like Agnès Varda really picked, like lived in her shoes when she was alive. Interesting anecdote about Vagabond: I watched, when I watched Maurice Pialat's À nos amours, To Our Loves, Sandrine Bonnaire was in that. I think that movie is beautiful, but I also think it's really important in 2022 to be able to contextualize it, right? Sandrine Bonnaire was like 14 or 15 years old, there's like full frontal nudity, it's important conversations to have. And, I watched Vagabond right after, that also has Sandrine Bonnaire, and I remember just in my head they're kind of linked, where I was like, oh she went from like that character's in Maurice Pialat's world and like little troubles and then she ends up like as a vagabond and that's what happens. Which is not true, but if I was ever asked to plan a double feature, I might put those two movies back to back.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: Oh, I like so much that movie, An Unmarried Woman. It's so crazy. I like so much the actress, she's fantastic. I like so much the scene with the therapist inside. It's really, I like this. This movie is so perfect.

La vérité, the truth, La vérité from Clouzot. For me it's a very feminist, very feminist movie in a way. Also all the, what he invents with the shot, with the movement of camera, everything, it's so beautiful. And it's very, yes, very modern in a sense.

And Petite maman, so oh wow, it's so beautiful what you did for the poster. It's beautiful, Petite maman by Céline Sciamma. And my daughter is totally obsessed by that movie, she loved so much, so yes, so I took it.

Sex, Lies, and Videotape, you must see that. And I like so much the way he talk really with the language of movies, you know, all the movie is a mise en abyme of everything. And the way he's used the video in the movies was really, really so modern, so contemporary when he did it, of course. And I saw it really recently and I'm still really impressed by this movie. It's really simple, just a love story, a heartbreak, and I like so much the way the James Spader have very many, many problems to have sex with women and he resolve everything with the camera. So intelligent. This movie is the real masterpiece, of course.

Okay, La notte is the best thing to see when you want to break up with somebody, to split. And the last letter that he read to her is so, I don't want to spoil, but he succeed to summarize exactly the feeling when it's over with somebody.

I think Sacha Guitry is very important for me. I discovered him very late in a way. When I'm lost, I think I have to watch Faisons un rêve or Désiré. So modern, so intelligent, so it gave me some, you know, he blew me away each time. And in a way it's very interesting because it's very not expensive movie, you know, with nothing he's doing a masterpiece.

film_title: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King
quote: And oh, Allan King, oh so important for me when I was student, studied in art school in Paris and I discovered Warrendale. Warrendale, the way he's doing that movie, I don't understand how we can do this when we get inside that place, very special because it's like an orphelinat and the children doesn't want to wake up and so the idea just of the first scene is so incredible. I watched the Warrendale just before doing Anatomy and I show some scenes to Milo, my the child who are playing in my movie, and yes, it was very interesting. I love so much to mix, to show sometimes some documentary, sometimes some movies, yes.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 24: The Actuality Dramas of Allan King

quote: So this is An Angel at My Table. I love and Sweetie, the two of Jane Campion, the early films she made that I love so much. So sensible, so intelligent.
And Sweetie, the two of Jane Campion, the early films she made that I love so much. So sensible, so intelligent.

And then that, one of my favorite film, Kiarostami, The Taste of Cherry. Because you know the thing about the desire to die, and we know that we are dust, we'll come back to dust, but he made it in such a huge set of stone, dust, and the man trying to find his own way, and the way he tried to be helped, and then the strength of life, and the life, the Taste of Cherry wins over. I love that film, really.
Then I picked La promesse, one of the first les Dardenne feature fiction film. Beautiful. I remember when I discover it, I was impressed.
And my favorite Godard, one of my favorite Godard, Band of Outsiders. I love when they dance. I love I love Sami Frey and Anna Karina is so innocent too you know, I just pick those now.
Now, Tiny Furniture. Then I have to see it because I don't know. I know her series. I love Girls. I'm a fan of Girls, but this I want to know what she did as a fiction before.
And okay, I pick also that, one of my favorite, Le Mariage de Maria Braun, Fassbinder.
Look at this, there's two Rififis. There's one I bet is a Blu-ray and one is a, look at that.

And it goes 8½. I have a lot of these already so I can't touch them. 8½ is, you know, this is the film that is the first film that really convinced me that's what a film director, what his life and job is about. People like Truffaut made Day for Night, which is a wonderful film, but it's a lightweight version of what a director's life is. And this was before I even got into the business. And having now made films, I realized the honesty and the truth of 8½ more and more.

And here is the film that completely changed my view of what films are about. It was a Saturday matinee in the San Fernando Valley, and, all the kids were thrown in there by their parents to get out of their parents' way for the afternoon. And I was about 13 years old, and this film came on, and it completely changed my life because I suddenly realized films are about justice, injustice, the rights, the wrongs of the world. They're not just jolly entertainment. And I spent my life trying to combine jolly entertainment with very serious looks at the world we live in. Brazil, the shots through the clerks' pool, the tracking shots, are all my homage to Stanley and those wonderful shots going through the trenches. First time I'd seen, first film I saw that I was aware of the camera doing something, not just a static observer, but a participant in the whole process, the dynamics of the process.

film_title: Yojimbo / Sanjuro: Two Samurai Films by Akira Kurosawa
catalog_title: Yojimbo / Sanjuro: Two Samurai Films by Akira Kurosawa
quote: Look, next to Brazil: Yo- [ __ ] -jimbo, yes!
box_set_name: Yojimbo / Sanjuro: Two Samurai Films by Akira Kurosawa

quote: Here's a Tati complete, mine. This is, this is my revenge on all the great talents because I can do what I want with their work and they're not in the closet with me.

Now one thing that is interesting when I saw this Bergman stuff here, which I'm going to take, I'm going to open. Oh, this may break my back, I, but I'm going to put it in here because it's important to put in there. We'll sort out the transportation later. But when I made Brothers Grimm, and there was Bergman, one of my great heroes. Seventh Seal and Wild Strawberries, they all were wondrous films that I'd hoped one day to be able to make something even a fraction as good as that. But making Brothers Grimm, Peter Stormare, who plays a main character in the film, had worked with Bergman. He knew him really well. In fact, Bergman had directed, redirected him in Hamlet on stage. And he said to me as we worked on Brothers Grimm, "This is like working with Ingmar." Which is funny because everybody assumes Ingmar Bergman is a very serious, solemn man. And Peter said, "No, Ingmar, we laughed the whole time." And that, I thought, there's moments like that when you realize, oh, maybe I, I can do some, this kind of work. I don't have to be as serious as I thought you had to be. You can have fun and direct.

This one is just staring at me. Right when I walked in I saw Fast Times at Ridgemont High, and… I saw this way too young. And I’m probably going to push it on my son way too young. But this… Spicoli is as good as it gets, man.

Equinox. This is another one that maybe I’ll show my son solo someday, because he’s talking about movies and how movies are made and we talk about magic a lot. And this is some homemade magic right here. Maybe his next birthday I’ll give it to him.

I see you have Scorsese Shorts here. Big Shave, amazing. You don’t really need a traditional narrative to send a message. Martin Scorsese learned that early on, and we’re all still trying to catch up and figure that out, too.

Trainspotting. It’s energy, that’s all it is. It’s just energy for an hour and a half or two hours. And Danny Boyle’s one of these great filmmakers who… I love filmmakers that have a style or a signature. But Danny Boyle kind of doesn’t do that. He’s like the Ween of filmmakers. He just explores different genres and different styles whenever he wants.

Okay. Last one, last one. This is a big one. If.... By Lindsay Anderson. I found this on VHS at Kurvan’s Video in Alpena, Michigan when I was 18. And it was for sale. It was in the big bin where they don’t even line them up, they just throw them in a pile in, like, a garbage can, and it was the guy from A Clockwork Orange. It was Malcolm McDowell. And so I got it and it blew my mind because it was, like, angry but also kind of artsy in its own way. And it was one of the first, like, almost borderline experimental narrative films I’d seen. And it really stuck with me. It’s a film I try to talk about with my students, but it’s actually kind of heavy duty, because the end of this film is more relevant today than it probably was in 1969, I believe. Okay, I’m going to take this last one.

This is amazing. Three Films by Luis Buñuel. For me, the reason that Buñuel’s films work so effectively is that they don’t look weird. They don’t have that kind of Lynchian, dreamlike cinematography. They look very straightforward, which makes it so much stranger when a family sits around on toilets, talking about politics and things like that, and when they go to the bathroom to eat their dinner. Phantom of Liberty and Discreet Charm, two of my absolute favorite movies ever.
This is... Great Expectations, directed by the great David Lean. Exquisitely done, absolutely cracking movie. I'm going to stick that in the bag of tricks here.
There's a good one, Repo Man. We used to have this on our tour bus. When I was touring with Elvis Costello, we used to have this on sort of permanently. Yeah, nice to see that one again.

Another one of my favorites, One-Eyed Jacks. It's directed by Marlon Brando, who is the star along with his old mate, Karl Malden. Fabulous actor. This is from sometime in the early '60s. '61 or '62, I think it came out. It was directed by Brando and, apparently, it went massively over budget. But it's such a great story. And the acting, of course, is... Is brilliant, with the two of them. It's also got Slim Pickens in it, who's one of my favorites, in his familiar role as a sort of redneck bully. Fabulous.

This is a good one for a Sunday afternoon with your feet up, recovering from something. The Flight of the Phoenix. Fantastic movie. This tells the story of a rickety old transport plane which crashes in the Libyan desert. And the transport plane is carrying a bunch of oil rig workers. Nobody knows they've crashed or where they are. There seems to be no chance of them being rescued, but they have this plan to build another plane out of the wreckage under the direction of Hardy Krüger, this German aeronautical engineer. He says he's an aeronautical engineer. And the movie came out in... When was it? '65. So Hardy Krüger is playing the German aeronautical engineer as a sort of... As a kind of– He doesn't wear a monocle, but he plays him rather like a Wehrmacht officer, in this rather clipped, German, slightly sinister way. Don't let my explanation of it put you off. It's a fantastic movie. The Flight of the Phoenix.
I haven't seen Loves of a Blonde in a long time, and it's fun, I'll take that.

Paris, Texas. Okay. I think Paris, Texas is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen, and I think there’s not a lot of movies that can portray loneliness as good as this one. And by the way, the colors.

City Lights. Why? When I was doing Babylon, Damien Chazelle told me I had to study Chaplin’s eyes because he had the superpower of making the saddest expression and still have innocence as a kid. A classic.
8½. Well, movies about movies. Fellini and… I know I will never, but Marcello Mastroianni is kind of a role model for me.

After Hours. This is going to be a little weird, but I have an After Hours tattoo, because the first time I watched it, I got crazy. And it’s also my favorite Velvet Underground song. So After Hours is really important to me.

Japón. Well, first of all, the actor, who died, he was my father’s friend. And Reygadas is pretty controversial, but I think he’s one of the most interesting directors in Mexico right now. Carlos, you’re weird, man.
Well, I know Buñuel is from Spain, but for us in Mexico, he’s one of the greatest Mexican directors. The Exterminating Angel.

Another great– I really like Welcome Mr. Marshall! But The Executioner, Berlanga. I think Berlanga is one of the greatest from Spain, honestly. I don’t remember the name of the actor, this old guy… Berlanga’s, I think, cliché actor. He always worked with him. José Isbert. Wow, and this has an interview of Pedro Almodóvar talking about Berlanga’s movie. It’s going to be great.
One of the greatest rebel movies, in my opinion. This is the rebel dude right here. The 400 Blows by Truffaut. Amazing. Some nouvelle vague, why not?
Gummo. This was also one of my favorites. Before entering film school, I think this was one of the movies where I decided to dedicate myself to filmmaking.
Fish Tank, okay. Andrea Arnold. This is another… I think I’m obsessed with everything that is related to teenage and coming of age, so I think Fish Tank is an amazing film from Andrea Arnold.

Slacker. Another great, great movie. Once again, my teenage obsession. And what a dialogue. There’s a… There’s a moment where a guy tried to sell pubic hair of Madonna, Madonna’s pubic hair. Amazing movie. Can I show another tattoo? Teenage kicks forever.
Well, of course. Videodrome. Cronenberg. Amazing. I like this one. And if you have Crash…
And if you have Crash… This is probably gonna sound weird, but I think this is a sexy movie. Crash.
Another sexy movie, why not? From the king: Pink Flamingos. If you haven’t seen this, you should.
Okay, and for the last one, I’m going to pick Do the Right Thing, a Spike Lee joint. Another amazing movie.

And question: do you have any Gregg Araki? Teen Apocalypse Trilogy. Once again, my obsession with coming of age, weird coming of age. I think Doom Generation also changed my life. Amazing. But Mysterious Skin, Criterion, come on.

Make sure you see No Bears if you haven’t. Speaking of No Bears, I am actually going to take that as well. Sorry. Panahi is, in my opinion, honestly, if someone put a gun to my head, I’d say the greatest filmmaker alive at the moment. I know that’s hyperbolic, but I mean it. And, hey, I’m a filmmaker, hyperbole comes with the job, so, if you haven’t seen this, please, please, please see this movie. It is one of the greatest films of this century, in my opinion.

I'm also going to take Saint Omer here, from Alice Diop. This was one of my favorite movies of the last several years. It's just a beautiful, concise, powerful, emotional, heart-wrenching, and very, very aesthetically sophisticated film, from a filmmaker who has made many documentaries that I also love. But this is a very, very strong narrative and I'm taking it.

This is my very favorite movie of all time. I show this to a lot of actors when I'm making films, because I haven't made a film that isn't heavily stealing from Ugetsu. There's an opening shot of this film where he pans across the village. I actually was just told it got cut off one of the versions, which is terrifying. It's on this one, but this idea of a film that kind of operates almost as one continuous piece of movement has heavily influenced my filmmaking. I grew up dancing, and movement and physical movement and acting are important to me. And this is, in my opinion, a towering masterpiece, one of those films that you watch and you just think, "How on God's earth did he do that?" Hurrah!

Amazingly enough, I don't own this. This is one of my very favorite docs, it's one of the greatest documentaries ever made. It's Barbara Kopple's Harlan County, USA, and it is a film about a… a striking workers' skirmish that they embedded themselves into that got quite violent and terrifying. I think it speaks timelessly to the struggles of workers everywhere, but also to how documentaries can actually have something to say about society while being art. Because I make documentaries myself about political things often, I can tell you that's very, very hard to do. It's a high-wire act that Kopple wrote, in my opinion, the book on, in terms of modern doc cinema, so, can't say enough about that one.

The grand master of cinema, in my very, very humble personal opinion. There is no one above Luis Buñuel for me. He encapsulates surrealism, humor, the barbarism of society, the beauty of society. He's our Dostoyevsky, as far as I'm concerned, and Él is made during his Mexican period, which is… I have weird… We all do, but my affinities for Hitchcock's British period are similar to my… I have an affinity for Buñuel's Mexican period: Los olvidados, Él, the films he made in Mexico speak, I think, the most honestly and openly towards his worldview, aesthetic and social. I like the later movies, though they're a little, like, hang around the dining-room table with your bourgeois friends. They're great, but Mexico Buñuel, great Buñuel.

I'm going to end with Keaton, which is where I started. I was… I was about five or six years old, and my babysitter was a movie theater. It wasn't TV. My mother taught dance at a university, and they just socked me in the campus movie theater, and I discovered Keaton and Chaplin and Hitchcock and Fred Astaire and all the things that informed my early love of movies. And Keaton has remained for me the kind of… the great synthesis of performing arts and cinema. I'm an actor and I direct, and I've always synthesized those things, and I do not profess to be the towering genius that Buster Keaton is, but he remains probably my greatest influence, so, I'm very happy to walk out of here with The Cameraman, which is a masterwork, like all Buster Keaton.

I'm going to start here with the Kiarostami Koker Trilogy, which I'm absolutely going to take. Where Is the Friend's House? Which is my very, very favorite Kiarostami film, but I also love Through the Olive Trees. And he made other great movies, don't get me wrong, and we now have great Iranian filmmakers who are making incredible cinema to this day, so make sure you see No Bears if you haven't.

Withnail and I. Withnail and I is a very interesting film, and very personal to me because the character of Withnail was a personal friend of mine and he actually packed boxes for Paul Smith in my very first warehouse. His name was Vivian MacKerrell. People who pack boxes are normally… And then they get this brown tape, and then they… Like this, and they pack the boxes, and then there’s a stamp or a Sharpie that they write on. Not with Vivian. First of all, he had to have James Brown playing. Second of all, he had this tape, which was… The trade name of the tape was called NOPI. He had the NOPI tape and he used to stand there like this and go, “Beautiful, beautiful!” Anyway, the film is brilliant. It’s real. The music’s fantastic. You’ve got to listen to it.

Breathless by Jean-Luc Godard. I’m privileged to say that he wore some Paul Smith clothes. He bought a very beautiful brown leather jacket. It’s really inspirational for me for more than one reason. One is… I’m going to put this down. One is because of editing. Very fast editing. And the other thing is color. Incidentally, when I’m talking about the color of this, I’m talking about the color levels, because it’s black-and-white film, but it sort of goes into almost sepia. I worked on Men in Black, and… and they said to me when they came in, “Which black do you want?” I said, “What?” He said, “Well, there’s about 120 blacks,” so, black is black is black.

This is My Beautiful Laundrette and the reason I chose that is very personal. Of course, the film is… was, in my opinion, very ahead of its time for all sorts of things. Quite political. It was about race, it was about the gay community and that… how it was just starting to become something you dare to be open about. Hanif Kureishi is a really good mate of mine. I’ve known him for years. Sadly, he’s in a wheelchair these days after a terrible accident, but he’s still writing. He’s still doing amazing things. Stephen Frears, who directed it, his father was my landlord in my very first flat. And then, of course, the other person in it is Daniel Day-Lewis, who I’m a very, very close friend of. We go back a long way. We go back to this time. What I like about it as a film, it’s real. It’s a real film. You feel like you are part of it. So that’s another one I’m going to definitely steal.

The other film I’m thinking about, because I work in Japan a lot: Kurosawa’s Kagemusha. There’s whole areas of this film where most of the color is army, khaki color, and then these… these electrifying bursts of red. So as a fashion designer, you can imagine you’re like this, and then suddenly you’ve got a bright color suddenly sitting on top of a very neutral base. So, even if you don’t understand it, even if you switch the sound off, it’s amazing. But don’t do either of those things.

Well, for my last pick, I’m going to close my eyes and pick at random. I might not know the movie, so I’m sorry about that. The Kid Brother, with Harold Lloyd. Very interesting that so many cowboy-related movies are starting to become popular again now, and they’re… great.
All right, I’ve never seen Amores perros, I’m embarrassed to say. A bunch of shame all the way through this Closet.
Moonstruck I’ve never seen. Again, completely embarrassed.

Here’s another great choice here: Klute. As far as cinematography goes, this is a Gordon Willis project. This guy loves to, you know, keep the fill side real dark. He’s just a master at low-light photography, was, and is a big inspiration for me. You kind of have to watch the stuff I do at night and on your bigger screen, so it’s his fault. Send your letters to him. Alan Pakula is one of our great directors of the past. All the President’s Men is one of my favorite films. He did that one, too, as did Gordon Willis.

Stanley Kubrick is someone who, you know, is just a master at how he uses the frame and the symmetry of everything. So this is perfect: Barry Lyndon. This is, I think, all candlelight, I think. I think they had special lenses made for this. And so I’ll bet this particular version tells me all I need to know.

So there’s some danger and some crime and some violence in Black Rabbit, as there was in Ozark. I really… There’s a way that Europeans film violence and danger that I admire. I haven’t seen enough of it, and so I’m imagining that some of that is in here. Funny Games I have heard of as something that does it real well in a way that is a bit life-scarring. Michael Haneke. Apparently there’s nothing funny about this. As you can tell by the nice poster here.

Being There. Here’s something… Hal Ashby, Peter Sellers, you can’t go wrong. I haven’t seen this forever. Peter Sellers, one of the original kind of no-winking comedy guys. So there’s a lot of pure acting chops in what he does. He never asks for a laugh. You’ve got to pay attention. No jokes. It’s just characters that would be deeply offended if they ever heard anybody laughing at what they were going through and what they were doing or saying. Takes a lot of good acting to do this kind of comedy, the stuff that Hal Ashby did, and that Peter Sellers did. So a must-see-again for me.
Shampoo. Another great Hal Ashby, so I hear. I have not seen this one.

Here is something… I’m not even going to try to pronounce this brilliant man’s name. But I could get the Blue, White, Red part down pretty good. My father always told me about these films, as something that I need to see and should see. He’s the one that kind of inspired me to go into acting and directing, and he said that I need to see these films. I have yet to see them. I am going to see them now.

I was going to begin with Jane Campion, who I worked with and who I adore. And recently I saw– Well, not that recently, maybe two years ago, I saw one of her very first films, called Sweetie. Here. This is so wild, you can hardly believe it’s happening. And it’s got something of, like, the real New Zealand, almost happening on another planet energy about it. Completely singular. And I love Jane, so that’s going in the bag.

This film is very beautiful: A Canterbury Tale. It has this beautiful line in it about how disappointing life is. It’s such a tender, sad film. I’m going to take that. This is one of Derek Jarman’s favorite films. He loved this film.

And do you have Derek Jarman at all? I have never seen this Derek Jarman film. I love Derek Jarman, great British director in the ’70s, ’80s, queer, somehow managed to make strange art-house films in Thatcher’s Britain. How on earth he managed it, I don’t know. So I’m going to take that, too. Derek Jarman. Total genius.

Oh, yeah. So, Ira, when we were making Peter Hujar’s Day, Ira Sachs would show me and Rebecca Hall… rarely the whole of films, but he’d go, “Just look at this ten-minute sequence from a film and look at the images and look at the nature of the performances.” And it was a particular era of Godard filmmaking. Yes, King Lear. Not seen it. Seen a bit of it. But I’m going to take this so I can see what he was up to in the ’80s. Amazing guy.

L’humanité. This guy is extraordinary. Bruno Dumont. I mean, I don’t even know how to describe… They’re a bit like Bresson, but with a kind of more obvious, weird, dark humor. This film I’m obsessed with. He worked with a… with a nonprofessional cast. It’s very disturbing, but also kind of, again, a sort of strange tenderness. L’humanité. Bruno Dumont. I’m going to take that. I want to see everything by him.

I’m also going to take this, by my friend John Cameron Mitchell, because he’s extraordinary. And I saw this too long ago and I need to see it again. Amazing director. Amazing human. Going to take that.
We’re going to start with To Sleep with Anger, Charles Burnett. If you don’t know, ask somebody. Find out. It’s a classic.

Oh, on a similar theme, Devil in a Blue Dress, Carl Franklin. It’s not often that you see people go face to face with Denzel Washington and come out unscathed. Don Cheadle’s performance. Legendary one. Underappreciated. I think the film, just overall, underappreciated.

Okay, Memories of Murder, Bong Joon Ho. This is strangely difficult to find. And so part of the reason I’m drawing it here is so I always have access to it. Physical media is important. And really everything Bong Joon Ho does is brilliant. So, can’t go wrong there.

Spike Lee, Bamboozled. Saw this movie before I worked in Hollywood. Loved it. Terrified me. Having worked in Hollywood for more than 20 years, it’s scary how accurate and prescient it is. If you want to work in Hollywood, everybody should see this movie before doing so. Also annoyingly hard to find, so get the DVD.
4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days. Also topical. I’m not going to say anything more about the film, other than that it’s brilliant and everyone should see it, especially in this country today.

Tootsie, Sydney Pollack. I had the great pleasure of working for Sydney Pollack in the last year of his life. A legendary filmmaker with legendary… just a record of brilliant films. And also just a really good man, so RIP Sydney, RIP Teri Garr. Yeah, Tootsie.

Anatomy of a Fall, Justine Triet. It won the Oscar for a reason. If you haven’t watched it, do. It’s just a… I’m just very excited to see what she does next. And Sandra Hüller is just an incredible actress. Just doesn’t miss a moment. There’s an oblique 50 Cent reference, which you don’t really get in French cinema on a yearly basis.

Last but definitely not least, Alice Diop’s Saint Omer, one of the great new, exciting filmmakers on this planet. Anytime she does anything, I’m excited for it. This is another underappreciated classic, which I guess is the theme here. So watch this movie. But also watch anything that Alice does because exciting new voice. Not even new anymore, but exciting voice period. She’s got a lot to say about the world and we all should listen.

film_title: Paul Robeson: Portraits of the Artist
catalog_title: Paul Robeson: Portraits of the Artist
quote: I know absolutely nothing about this box set, but one of my holy grail projects is a Paul Robeson biopic. And if I can’t make it, somebody else should. So I’m taking this, mainly so I can ask everybody on Earth to seriously consider figuring out a Paul Robeson biopic or, more likely, a limited series because his life is so incredible over so many different eras and so long-term impactful that someone should figure it out. If it’s not me, that’s fine. Then I can watch it without having to make it. Very, very excited about this. Oh, featuring essays by Hilton Als, Charles Burnett, and Paul Robeson. So great reading in addition to film stuff.
box_set_name: Paul Robeson: Portraits of the Artist

quote: Or like that? Right, there we are. Battle of Algiers. Hugely influential film. Ennio Morricone’s first score. But that’s sort of beside the point because a film so incredibly good and so incredibly… Oh, yes, the… the true… freedom fighters are actually playing their parts in it. Whoever’s left alive, as it were. But it’s an extraordinary film.

Oh, God, I went for all the heavy ones, didn’t I? Night and Fog. The film that, to me, in its most unflinching way describes the Third Reich, the Holocaust and the concentration camps. So you have to have strong nerves to go and watch this one.

I think I need to get up to the step stool. Here we are. Favorite film my whole life long. Andrei Rublev, Tarkovsky. It’s inexplicably beautiful. It’s inexplicably profound. It’s shot in 65mm black and white, except for… But I won’t give it away. And… you have to be patient with it. I mean, look, how many films do you know where your main protagonist takes a vow of silence for a whole act? But it’s… it’s such an incredible, incredibly well-crafted and well-thought-out film which just deals with everything, everything that life is about somehow.

And, just to counter it, we’re going to go for Sid & Nancy. The history of that time, and I was very much part of that time and I loved that time, and I believe my friend Eric Fellner produced it. And… it’s, of course, the great Gary Oldman.

Now, I always… I always wonder what the best script written is, the best comedy. And if it’s not Lubitsch with Ninotchka, I go to His Girl Friday. Do you want to have a good time? His Girl Friday will show you a good time like you’ve never had before.

The great Les Blank, of course. This is a journey through different lives, which I love because we get so isolated these days, and especially because we’re sitting behind our little phones and our iPads and our televisions, etc. But sometimes there’s something you can put on that just rips right through the screen and takes you outside and takes you into the world, and there’s something more to see, to explore, something more to see than you ever imagined. So.

Story goes something like that: Nic Roeg was the second-unit cameraman on Lawrence of Arabia and the studio would get all these fantastic reports back about how beautiful everything looked. And Freddie Young, who was the main cameraman, started getting a little bit jealous and so Nic got fired. Nic was seriously down. He teamed up with his partner, Donald Cammell, and they made this movie about the London East End. But it’s really a movie about the ’60s. It’s really, you know… Mick Jagger and James Fox, and – I’m saying this for myself – a very big Moog synthesizer, and lots of orgies. I think people didn’t quite know what to make of it, in the best possible way. And I’m not sure if even now we know what to make of it. It’s a gangster movie with philosophy. So, what can I say? And of course it’s incredibly, immaculately shot. It was Tony Scott and my favorite film. We would talk about it all the time. So. Nic was the first director who taught me anything. And Tony, I suppose, was another one who taught me a lot. So there is that as well, you know. And so, for Tony and Nic, I’ll take Performance.

House. Know nothing about it other than that I sure would love the one sheet. Actually I had heard of it. But the ladies here have highly recommended it to me, which probably means they’re trying to go and pour acid into my brain and make my head explode or something like that, or turn me into a real composer. I don’t know what it is, but I’m pretty sure there’s a trick behind this whole thing. So if this is the last you see of me, I wish you all a good life because mine’s over.

I found another one. I found a true treasure. David Lean Directs Noël Coward. In Which We Serve, This Happy Breed, Blithe Spirit, and Brief Encounter. That’s going to be a really good weekend. God, my tastes are all over the place, aren’t they? But I think that’s what movies are supposed to sort of do to you. You know, you’re supposed to get excited about life.

Blue Is the Warmest Color is a French film about two women coming of age. It’s about lesbian love. It’s just one of those movies that, once you see it, it’s unforgettable. And it takes its time, it breathes, it allows the characters to live, so I’m going to put that one in there.

Oh, Fantastic Mr. Fox, this is a movie that I love, by Wes Anderson. This movie means so much to me and my family because every Christmas we watch this at least 15 times. It’s good for adults, it’s good for children. And it’s got Meryl Streep’s voice and George Clooney’s voice. And my daughter knows every line of Kristofferson’s – that’s one of the little Fox characters – she knows every line of his. And because of this movie, my kids have found a way to curse in the house with me, because this movie introduces the idea of saying, instead of saying, “What the hell?” or, “What the F?” They say, “What the cuss?” So now my kids and I go around the house saying, “What the cuss? What the cuss? Are you crazy? What the cuss?” And it always reminds us. And we named our kitty Bandit after Kristofferson and his bandit outfit, which you will see if you watch this movie.

Love Jones. This is a movie that has two of my dear friends in it, Larenz Tate and Nia Long. In this movie, they play characters Darius and Nina, and it’s set in Chicago and the city is sexy, it’s kind of a character of its own. It’s got lots of poetry and jazz and it’s about how these two characters come together through that medium and all the challenges that they face. So if you want a good date night and you want to experience Black love at its finest. It’s become a cult classic.

Oh my God, Bringing Up Baby. This is one of my favorites. This is Katharine Hepburn and Cary Grant, directed by Howard Hawks, and this is a movie I saw over and over and over in my childhood. It has such a fast-paced comedy that is really fun to watch and I know it’s very hard to do because I’ve tried to do this, and trust me when I tell you, this kind of comedy and physical comedy and intellectual comedy is really, really hard, and I had so much respect for this as a kid growing up and this movie is one of the movies that really made me want to become an actor.

Claudine. This is a favorite of mine too. Two of my all-time favorite actors are in this movie: James Earl Jones and Diahann Carroll. I’ve been such a big fan of Diahann Carroll my whole life. She was a mentor of mine. And again, this is one of those movies where we get to see Black performers living their slice of life. For me, as a young girl growing up, these weren’t movies that I saw very much so when I got to see myself reflected and I got to see my culture reflected, they were big moments in my life. And Diahann Carroll also was Oscar-nominated for this performance and, if you ask me, she should have won. She should have been– along with Dorothy Dandridge, they should have an Oscar far before I ever had an Oscar, and it’s heartbreaking that they did not.

Oh, Parasite. Also, another one of my favorites. It’s a movie about the haves and the have-nots, and how a family sort of infiltrates a rich family, and there’s one scene that lives in my brain rent free, when the whole family, the disenfranchised family, ends up under the table of the rich family and then, because the rich family is coming home and they find themselves stuck under the table and it is one of those scenes where you are just sitting… you are holding your breath and you’re hoping that this doesn’t all go awry. It won all the awards and… rightfully so.
Malcolm X. Spike Lee and Denzel, always did an amazing job.

Love & Basketball. Another one of my favorites. Gina Prince-Bythewood directed this. As a Black woman, this was huge for me, to see a Black woman direct a film. She was doing this before this was allowed to be done, so she was paving that way for us, as Black women in cinema and as directors. This dared me to dream that I could too one day direct my first film, which I did, and she was a huge inspiration for me to do that, so it’s… it’s one of those feel-good movies, that you just don’t… You want to pick that up.
Cure, this is what I want to see. I’m a big, huge fan of horror and it’s a Japanese horror film that I’ve heard about, and so I’m going to take this one because I want to see what this is about.

For my last pick, I’m going to see what the Closet feeds me. What am I drawn to? This feels like tarot cards. What should I see? Okay. Boom. Rebecca. I have never seen this Alfred Hitchcock movie, and, because I love the horror genre, I also love suspense, so that’s going to be good. I’m going to take it.

There is one movie by Béla Tarr, the great Béla Tarr, who unfortunately recently died. You see, Werckmeister Harmonies, and it’s a… a very eccentric individual who delivers newspapers in a Hungarian town and a crazy mob that rises in the town and makes development impossible, and the way the leading character in the movie resists, in a very personal and peaceful way, is a great inspiration, apart from the fact that Béla Tarr, of course, was one of the great directors of the medium.

Not everybody can master this peaceful, and, to a degree, very wise resistance. Some give into their more feral urges. But on an individual level, if committed by one of the most beautiful women that ever appeared on a screen, in this case, Catherine Deneuve, that’s Repulsion. It’s about a woman who can’t fend off the onslaught of sexual interest that she meets in everybody she encounters. It was a revolution in moviemaking and, to a degree, it still is.

Let’s stay with the female aspect of resistance and go back to the very peaceful yet strict resistance. There is a movie by Ozu and it’s called Late Spring. The main character resists the push from the outside to be married off. That told in the most delicate and sensitive details is a true… a true delight.

The 400 Blows. This is a kid who feels, like most kids do at that age, misplaced. He leads a life that doesn’t fit into the kids’ lives around him, it doesn’t fit into his parents’ lives, it doesn’t fit into the life in school, it doesn’t fit into the system that tries to press him into a decent citizen, so he escapes from the… I hesitate to say oppression because it’s not oppression, yet there are forces that are against the integrity and a life that we really… in which we can really gauge the relationship between us as an individual and the society as a whole.

And I start with Jacques Tati. Out of this complete collection, I would recommend Mon Oncle, because Mon Oncle shows the eccentric individual who clings a little bit to the past, without being obsessive about it, but he has difficulties coming to terms with what then made the modern world, and he does that by showing his nephew that there used to be another world that was more open to the childlike spirit. Yeah, so we’ll put that in the bag.

To get back a little bit on to the lighter side and, oddly, Ingmar Bergman, the majority of Bergman’s movies are really actually of lighter character. There is one that I specifically like, and it’s in this heavy and hefty collection: The Devil’s Eye. The devil has an eye infection and he always gets a stye if there is a… a virgin on Earth who shouldn’t be a virgin. So he employs Don Juan, who is in hell, and he says, “Go and seduce her.” The way this woman or this girl, rather, played by Bibi Andersson, resists Don Juan’s approaches and resists Don Juan’s seduction is extraordinary, because she does it out of conviction, out of joy. So Don Juan is actually completely desperate because it’s the first failure that he had to suffer through. And so I recommend it for the joyful private resistance of the leading lady.

How can we forget Amy Heckerling’s Fast Times at Ridgemont High? Had a little something to do with that. I was lucky enough to have my screenplay filmed by Amy, who really wanted to protect the authenticity of the high-school experience. Not a fantasized version of it, but an often raw and realistic, aching version of what it is to be young in the early ’80s. Thank you, Amy. I’ll take this with me.

film_title: The Worst Person in the World
catalog_title: The Worst Person in the World
quote: This is one of my favorite movies of the last years. This is Worst Person in the World, which I think really redefined the romantic comedy in such a beautiful way. The performances are incredible, the structure is amazing. And one of my favorites is the moment where “Healing” by Todd Rundgren takes over and you have a beautiful moment where time stops and our leading lady runs to find the true bubbling love of her life in a way that’s so original it took my breath away. And I revisit this movie a lot. Thank you for this copy of Worst Person in the World.

Yi Yi. Yi Yi is a movie that takes its time to bring you its magic. A moment in time where you are part of a family and an experience, and nobody’s rushing you, but they’re taking you to a place owned by themselves. The characters all kind of give you their lives in just the quiet moments in between the dialogue. And it’s my favorite kind of movie. An elixir that takes over.

Carnal Knowledge, for me… Right here. Carnal Knowledge had performances that I saw growing up, and it made me know that raw, personal filmmaking could be invigorating in a way that I was not aware. And also, once again, Mike Nichols will keep the camera on a performance and let you live through the character. You don’t have to rush things. You know enough about the character, all you have to do is watch the face and the face will tell you what they’re thinking. That’s so true of Nicholson, and Art Garfunkel’s performance is thrilling. And I always think about Carnal Knowledge as one of the great experiences in a theater. And this one lasts forever.

For my last pick, I’m going to pick out at random. Yes, Medium Cool. Medium Cool I have not seen for a very long time. My mom took me to see Medium Cool as a little guy, a film by Haskell Wexler. And I remember Medium Cool was a film that looked like a world I didn’t know and I wanted to step into that world. And thank you for reuniting me with a beautiful copy of Medium Cool.

I love Monterey Pop. In a world where a lot of people try and do period movies and try and imagine what it’s like to be in the ’60s and what an audience would be like in the ’60s, Monterey Pop is the best examination and the best kind of footage of real life at the time, and it captures that feel in the air. And also the faces are incredible. So Monterey Pop is a moment in time that lasts forever. I love it.

film_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
catalog_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
quote: And I am going to hold up this mighty collection and say I can’t wait to have this on my shelf. I first met Wes when we were both working in the same building, at Gracie Films. He was doing Bottle Rocket, I was working on Jerry Maguire. And I saw the first cut of Bottle Rocket, which had classical music in it. And the one thing I knew is that Wes had been listening to great rock in his office. So my one note that I gave to him is, “Why don’t you have a rock sensibility in this film?” He said, “I’m going to try it.” And he did. And Wes’s marriage of movie and music thrills me to this moment. This is a generous collection that I am so happy to have.
box_set_name: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years

quote: I’ll start with this. The last sequence in this movie has been an inspiration for me forever, the dance number. Beau travail is going in the bag.

I’m going to take Tampopo. Tampopo is hot and a really good food movie. I’m going to take this. I actually watched this when it was on the Criterion Channel during a Thanksgiving– Covid Thanksgiving, right after we made The Lost Daughter, oh, I got to say, as a double feature with Babette’s Feast, which was the first time I ever saw Babette’s Feast, and then we named my dog Babette.
I’m going to take this for my husband, who loves this movie and loves Dexter Gordon. I’m going to take this for Peter. ’Round Midnight going in the bag.
This is another film, which I have not seen, by the same director, so I’m going to take this and check it out.

Yeah, another movie that Fonzi recommended was I fidanzati. God, the first 20 minutes of that movie, and the title sequence. Definitely ripped off the title sequence for the beginning of The Lost Daughter.

I’m looking for some Bride! Movies now, like the beginning of Persona, and if you watch the reinvigoration sequence in The Bride! You’ll see the influence for sure. I was trying to think about… obviously we don’t have the science to bring people back to life, so what is the science? Maybe it’s something very, very, very simple, like the arcing in the beginning of that movie, of the lights, in the very, very beginning, mixed with something magic, so I… I was really influenced by that.

I want Trainspotting. Trainspotting… Okay. I was… I think I was 18 or 19. I was going to school in London, did an acting program in London for a couple of months one summer, and nothing like this had ever been made. I went to go see it by myself in a little theater, and it’s just one of those experiences that you have every once in a while where I was just completely stunned. I finished the movie and just sat in the theater by myself, and I really want to show this to my daughter, who’s 19, who I think will love it. We’ve been talking about it and waiting to be together to watch it. I haven’t seen it in so long.

I just watched Nouvelle Vague. I’m just looking at Breathless. I watched it with my 13 year old, who had never seen Breathless, but still really loved it. And I got to show that to her. All right, I’ll take it. I’ll take it, Breathless.
Vivre sa vie. I love this movie, too. A little… A couple of double Godard feature.
I love this movie, too, White Material.
Okay, close my eyes and pick at random. Okay. Let’s do that. Lone Star. I made a movie with John Sayles, early, early on in my career, called Casa de los Babys. Great, I’ll take that.

Actually, do you know what I want that I saw that you have is The Marriage of Maria Braun.
