I feel like that was one of the first movies that I saw, and I saw it in that same film class in college, that I was like, “That’s my taste.” Thank you. It really spoke to me. And then I did… I tried to copy her hair for Candy in The Deuce, or at least as an inspiration. So, going in the bag.

film_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
catalog_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
quote: [Translated] The Killing of a Chinese Bookie. This is one of my favorite among John Cassavetes's films. What I love about this film is its blend of raw, brutal realism and drama, which feels very fresh. It makes you wonder if this is a documentary or a gang film. I think this film is between the boundaries of both genres, which I love very much.

[Translated] Next one. Koroshi no Rakuin in Japanese, or Branded to Kill. This is the film that I have always recommended. Well, I probably shouldn't. It's not kind of the film you should recommend, but I personally love it. This is one of Seijun Suzuki's masterpieces. How should I put it? This is the kind of film that confuses you, but also haunts you. It's mesmerizing. I absolutely love this film. A well-made film doesn't always mean it's something you'll remember. So sometimes, it's worth watching a peculiar film like this. I heard that a studio fired the director because he made this. That's why this film is amazing.
[Translated] I happened to find this pre-war German film, M by Fritz Lang. This film is extraordinary because it's a culmination of German Expressionism. I'll take this, too.

[Translated] Wow, the Jacques Tati collection! This is great. I'm so happy! I discovered this, The Complete Jacques Tati. I'll add this to my bag, too. Jacques Tati is a French filmmaker. He makes comedy films, but they're not light comedies. It's hard to explain, but... It's like the characters in his films act cool rather than funny. Instead, it feels like they deliver jokes with straight faces. That style of humor influenced my work because I love that kind of comedy. I must take this home. Wonderful. This one... It says "Complete", so I think all of Tati's works are in the box. Am I right?

film_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
catalog_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
quote: [Translated] I'll take this too. Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits. I loved Bruce Lee since elementary school and he was a big influence on me. But I forgot about him in middle school. Then, in my mid-20s, there was a resurgence for Bruce Lee, for example, the Beastie Boys referenced him. That drew me back to him. I thought "They like Bruce too? He was my hero!" When I rediscovered his work, I found his philosophy really interesting and I was deeply inspired by it. In Cowboy Bebop, there is an episode that quotes one of his famous sayings.
Okay, next, Werckmeister Harmonies, Béla Tarr. We just lost Béla. I say adios, Béla, and thank you for what you’ve given us. I loved him.

Tarkovsky’s Mirror. Such an incredible film, sort of merging poetry and cinema in the most beautiful way. A masterpiece. I vacillate between that being my favorite Tarkovsky film and Stalker and Rublev, but I think The Mirror is it for me.
Film I love very much: Black Girl. It’s not exactly feel-good movie of the year. It’s a beautifully made film, one of the greatest, so thank you for that.

Okay. Close to my heart, of course, Love Streams. John Cassavetes, Gena Rowlands, two of my great heroes. I saw this film in the theater. I walked out after it ended and turned around and walked right back in and watched it a second time in a row, which I’ve rarely… I think that’s the only time, maybe, I’ve done that, but that film remains so deep in my heart, as do both of them.
Dino Risi, Il Sorpasso. Fantastic film. One I love. Beautiful.

On that note, I would like to find I Knew Her Well. This film, I Knew Her Well, oh, wow, Blu-ray. Stefania Sandrelli is fantastic. I think she was only nineteen when she made this film. There also– I don’t know if it’s on here, but there’s a beautiful screen test of her that is fantastic, of her doing a scene from the film just in a blank, empty room, but so beautiful. I just love her and I love this film. I always thought this film and Black Girl would be a good double bill. See the front.
Pickup on South Street. Richard Widmark and Sam Fuller together. A great classic. I love it so much. And Sam Fuller, he meant so much to me.
First off: boxset Pasolini. All the ’60s films. Incredible.

The first movie I’m going to bring up is… It’s right in front of me: Daisies. So my family moved around a lot, but in seventh grade, for one year, we lived in a place where I could walk to a video-rental store. They had Daisies, and I knew nothing about this movie. I just watched it as a seventh-grade girl and it blew my mind. I was like, “This is the best thing I’ve ever seen.” I felt so much freedom. I felt so absurd in the best way. I watched it over and over and over. So Daisies was my very first experience of the Czechoslovak New Wave, and after that I had to watch everything I could get my hands on. It was the best experience. I feel like I watched most of the weird movies in my life from that video-rental store with no consciousness of, “This is actually really special that I’m getting to watch this.” It was run by… a bunch of dudes in, I think, their 20s, who all had too-long hair, bangs over their eyes, very pale, and they… It turned out it was a very formative year for me, so thank you to the nerds.

Moonstruck. I mean, this is one of the greatest films of all time. But for me, it’s significant because it was the movie that started my journey of Nicolas Cage fandom. When I first saw him on screen in Moonstruck, I was like, “Is this a god? Who is this? This man is so… looks unlike anyone else I’ve ever seen. So magnetic.” I still believe that he’s someone who is meant to be on screen. There is no other profession for him. He can do other things that he likes, but he needed to be on screen. He has described his acting style as nouveau shamanism. I think of it as dream acting. I know realism and realistic acting has been very popular for a long time and that works in some contexts, but sometimes what I really want to see from an actor and a character is their inner world and how they feel, not just how they would react in the real world. And he does this beautifully. That’s my first access to Nicolas Cage, and I’ve been in love ever since.

For millennials and older, a big experience in the household was that you had a certain amount of videos and you just watched those over and over and over and over again. So, Breakfast Club was one of those videos, and I first watched it before first grade, way too early. I didn’t understand most of it. I didn’t know what a hot beef injection was, but I could recite it over and over. So, thank you to The Breakfast Club for creating a part of my mind.

Next one is The Piano Teacher. I can’t do every Haneke movie, but this one was right in my Q zone. This one, I watched it during a formative time when I was a teenager and it hit me right when I was in my phase of… cold, repressed sexuality. I don’t know if any other woman has gone through that. I hate to admit this, but I remember walking down the streets of New York with “Well-Tempered Clavier” by J. S. Bach in my ears and walking very severely down the street thinking of The Piano Teacher. Many will disagree, but I think Bach wrote the “Well-Tempered Clavier” hundreds of years ago just so it could be in this film. This film has one of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard. The use of music is so perfect in this, the Chopin, the Schubert, everything. And Isabelle Huppert is one of the best actresses, if not the best. The scene where she’s like, “If you want to hit me, hit me.” But in French, obviously. And in that scene, her face is so open and vulnerable, and you can tell, when she says, “If you want to hit me, hit me,” it’s what she really wants, and then he doesn’t give it to her and her face is just so perfect. So, anyway, this is a beautiful, beautiful film by Haneke.

My Own Private Idaho. I think, again, I watched a lot of art films way too young, and this is definitely not for children, but I remember– I think it was one of my first experiences of unconventional directing and acting. I still remember the scene where the actors are staying still. And it opened my mind to so many different possibilities. I thought movies were one thing, and then I watched this and I was like, “Movies are a lot of different things that I don’t know if I’m comfortable with yet, but… but this is going to stay in my mind.” And this was one of those. And it didn’t hurt that it was full of beautiful people.
This one. Henri-Georges Clouzot, and this film tells a story, which shows us what it means, fascism, and from where it came and how it destroyed society.

film_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
catalog_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
quote: Do you have Salò by Pasolini? I remember, I watched this film in… Soviet Union collapsed already. A famous scriptwriter, he made the scripts for Sokurov films, Yuri Arabov, he teach dramaturgy in our school and he show us this film like forbidden piece of art, and the door was closed, and I remember people in such a small room, they were standing, watching the TV. For Soviet Union, it was a revolution. I love this. Two brothers, these films, which I love: the films and directors who fight.

You have Arturo. Deep Crimson. Fantastic. I will send Arturo a photo with that. So, it’s a great… You know, this film inspired Tarkovsky, made a film, Nostalghia. The story, when somebody closes his family and keeps the family from the world outside, it’s from Arturo Ripstein.

film_title: Brief Encounters/The Long Farewell: Two Films by Kira Muratova
catalog_title: Brief Encounters/The Long Farewell: Two Films by Kira Muratova
quote: I have a relationship to Kira Muratova. So, this is her first film, which is named… -And The Long Farewell. -Brief Encounters. In Russian, it’s Korotkie vstrechi, “short meetings,” if translated direct. And she made this film in ’60s, and ’60s was, in the Soviet Union, a little bit a time of freedom. And after that, she continued… Another film, she made another film, Dolgie provody. It is here, so this is two films. And after that, she lost her job. And till 1988, she was a… member of studio in Odesa, but what she did, she cleaned the floor in the film studio and, after, she made… she made great film, Asthenic Syndrome, also, hook! Serious stroke, punch to all Soviet society. She lived in Ukraine, but it was a very strong voice, very strong voice, and she’s a very strong character. Great, great. Thank you very much.
box_set_name: Brief Encounters / The Long Farewell: Two Films by Kira Muratova

quote: Okay, it’s another great Soviet and Ukrainian director, Larisa Shepitko. Also very strong, like Kira Muratova.

film_title: Eclipse Series 29: Aki Kaurismäki’s Leningrad Cowboys
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 29: Aki Kaurismäki’s Leningrad Cowboys
quote: So, and another. I know this very good director, Aki Kaurismäki, the great person, the great director. I love his sense of humor and grotesque, which you can find in all his films. And it’s very sentimental and very distanced, at the same time. Good.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 29: Aki Kaurismäki's Leningrad Cowboys

quote: This is my lovely director, Luis Buñuel. It’s very difficult to read. It’s really not easy to understand his statement in his films. And from the other side, he’s very, very easy and his films are very simple. And I’m a friend with Arturo Ripstein. He was… first AD for Angel Exterminator.

Well, of course, one of the first movies I saw on the screen, in London when I was living on my own, was Battle of Algiers, Gillo Pontecorvo. Basically takes us through how Algeria found its independence through this gritty, incredible movie. Once you’ve seen it, you’re never the same again. No one’s ever made anything like it. It’s a classic, so we’re keeping that, thank you.

One of my favorites: Fellini, Roma. Why do I love Fellini? Fellini… All his films are like dreams. He used to write down his dreams, as soon as he woke up in the morning, because he wanted his films to feel… have that ethereal feel, and he said moviemaking and movies are the closest things we have to dreaming, and so all of his films are like fever dreams. And I just love this. Roma’s incredible. Every extra is a star in this movie. It’s fabulous. Okay.

Bob Fosse, All That Jazz. This is one of the great movies of all time. This guy only made a handful of films and they’re all just brilliant, and also kind of like a fever dream. Roy Scheider is going through terrible personal life and he’s trying to put on a musical at the same time and… Yeah, amazing film, beautifully shot.

The Hit. Yes. Stephen Frears. Oh my God. This is one of my favorite, favorite movies. Every time it’s on, I dare you try and flip the channel if it’s on TV. This is a beautiful film, and it’s about a guy who’s on the run. He’s in the witness-protection program, Terence Stamp, he’s sent to Spain and given a new identity, and then he has to deal with the fact that John Hurt and Tim Roth have been sent to kill him. And it’s fabulous. It’s a great look at the British underworld and gang life and… everything. It’s so great, and Terence is brilliant in this. As is Tim Roth, it’s his first role. John Hurt, can never go wrong with John Hurt.

Okay, one of the films that defined me growing up. First time I saw Carol Reed directing. All of his films are brilliant, but Odd Man Out is one of my favorites. I mean, James Mason, what a beautiful, beautiful film. This guy also on the run from the law. Belfast. Part of a robbery that goes wrong and he finds himself on the street, ends up with Robert Newton. God. This film is a film noir. It’s just beautiful. And Carol Reed was just one of my favorites. Just a beautiful, beautiful, beautiful filmmaker. Just extraordinary. Every film of his are classics. A keeper.
I’ll start with this one, Grey Gardens. Always a favorite. Yes.

Loves of a Blonde. Have you ever seen that? No, I’ve never seen it. It’s really cool. It’s an early Miloš Forman movie. Oh, really? Yeah, maybe you need to take that and see it. Great. I’d love to see that one. It’s great.
I have to have All That Jazz. I’ve seen All That Jazz probably 20 times.

film_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
catalog_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
quote: And The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant. You know how much I love this movie. The most incredible visuals. I don’t think I’ve ever seen it all the way through. Every frame is like a fashion image. It’s so incredible. I mean, I’ve seen Petra von Kant at least 20 times. I’m so excited I’ve never watched it all the way through.

Paris is Burning. I love that movie. So good. I’ve watched it a million times, I know, I want another Criterion. So a million and one won’t kill me. I thought Cosi needs to see that. Do you want to take this one? Well, do you have one? Yeah. You do? Okay, we don’t… I’m sure I have it. Here, you take that one for the girls. I’m so excited. Amazing.
You picked Female Trouble. Yeah, I did. Again, a classic, in a way.
Oh, and close by is Klute. Another classic. Another extraordinary fashion movie.
Look what I found. Another all-time favorite, The Virgin Suicides. I’m so proud… Have you ever seen it? I’m so proud to have a Criterion. Yeah.

Here’s your After Hours, I think. That was something you were interested in. I love this movie, but I haven’t seen it in a long time, so I’m really excited to revisit it. New York and big lofts in the ’80s.

Oh, this movie. Have you ever seen this movie? No. It’s a Bergman movie, Summer with Monika. It was just on the Criterion Channel one night and I thought, “We’ll just put it on to fall asleep to.” And then I couldn’t take her eyes off it. It’s kind of this love affair with this bad girl and it was really– I really love it.

I love this movie, I Knew Her Well. It’s Stefania Sandrelli at her most beautiful. It’s really good. It’s a young kind of model girl and the way it looks, it’s so stylish. It’s really inspiring. Okay. I love that movie, if you haven’t seen it. I’m glad to discover a new stylish film. Yes.

What about this one, Sofia? You pulled out… Oh, yeah. This one… I love these: The Apu Trilogy. I think I’ve seen the first one and the last one. It’s the same character through his life, and he starts as a little boy and then him as an adult. Do you want to take it? Yes. Another recommendation from Sofia Coppola, ladies and gentlemen.
Oh, there. Belle de Jour. Oh, yeah. We have a clip in our doc from that, for her style. There’s a… Yeah. Yves Saint Laurent, beautiful dressing of Catherine Deneuve.

And this one, which I love: Flow. It’s, like, my favorite movie. I haven’t seen it. You have to see it. I’m so excited. It was kind of the exception in my list because all the other ones were fashion inspiration… all inspired me in terms of fashion. But this one just is the most… Touching. Beautiful… I can’t even tell you how much I love this movie. Just so beautiful and sweet. Each of the animals is… They express themselves, but they’ve got the behavior of each of the animals so perfectly. It’s just incredible.

Oh, this I was excited about. I’m a big fan of Sakamoto, who I knew about from Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence as a teenager. Oh, yeah, Ryuichi Sakamoto. And they have… It’s his last concert that he filmed at the end of his life, which seems really beautiful, I haven’t seen.

Did you ever see all of these? It’s Totally F***ed Up, Doom Generation, and Nowhere. I’ve only seen Doom Generation. Should I see the rest of them? Yeah. I love that actor who’s in them. James Duval? Is that his name? Yes. I’m getting a thumbs-up. But it was so good about… Doom Generation, I thought it was so interesting and cool and strong, wild. And Nowhere was really good. Those are like period movies now. I know, I know.

Oh, I love The Heiress. I just watched this recently. I won’t take it because I have it. It’s Monty Clift as a grifter and an innocent heiress, Olivia de Havilland. I thought it’s ripe for a modern-day remake. I wonder if you’d be into it. It’s… You won’t like the clothes because it’s 1860s… Oh. …oldy-timey. But her performance is incredible because she goes from really innocent to… to not in a really cool way. So that’s cool, just for her performance.

This movie so disturbed me. Oh my God. That movie was so upsetting. It’s so, so disturbing. I wish I’d never seen it. Me too. We’re talking about Funny Games. It is terrifying. We’re talking about this. But don’t watch it. No. Unless you want to be terrified. Yeah. It is really upsetting. Really upsetting, and I… I’ve seen some pretty horrible movies, or horror movies, and they didn’t stay with me the way that did. Me too. I thought, “That could happen to me.” And it was so… It was just relentless, just… Evil. Evil. That was terrifying. I wish I could erase that from my memory. Me too.
But on a brighter note, Fast Times. Fast Times. Sean Penn as Spicoli, one of the best characters ever. Ever. It’s so cool that you guys have this one.
I love The Grifters. We don’t need to take it, but… Yeah, it’s so great. Anjelica Huston. Another great… Oh my God, I love her in it. It’s so cool. So good. I’ve seen that one many times.

Shampoo, written by Robert Towne and Warren Beatty and directed by Hal Ashby. Robert Towne was on the staff of Mad Men in the last season or two seasons and I got to hang out with him and I don’t know where I got the nerve to ask him out to lunch, but I did. I asked him how long it took to shoot and he said 75 days, which is, in modern filmmaking, that’s a lot of days. And I felt, “Was it Hollywood ten-hour days?” And he said, “No, it was… We’d do 50 takes.” At some point, they laid over the Nixon election over the story because Warren wanted… He knew he had a moment and he knew he could make what he wanted. Just knowing all that. Also Jack Warden would sing “Born Free,” which they couldn’t afford and Warren kept telling him, “Stop singing that song. We can’t afford it.” And he said, “I can’t help it, I’m nervous,” and he would just sing… Every time you see Jack Warden, he was singing ♪ Born free ♪ while he was showing up and… And anyway, a lot of funny stories and I love this movie.

Here’s a movie, No Country for Old Men, which I think… I worked with Mike Nichols once and he said that every stick of furniture, every piece of clothing, everything you put into the movie should add to the telling of the story, and I feel like this movie does that. The beginning, there’s an opening sequence where he’s hunting, Josh Brolin’s character’s hunting, and he takes off his boot and he puts it on the rock and then he aims at the… elk or whatever, and then he picks up the shell and puts it in his pocket, so you sort of get the idea that he’s either ex-military… Just every single thing about this film, I think, is just masterfully executed. These guys are at the height of their… their filmmaking abilities when they made this.

This movie here is maybe my favorite screwball comedy, of which I’m a great fan. Leo McCarey, The Awful Truth. Leo McCarey didn’t like the original script and rewrote it a bunch and had a piano on set that he would sit at when he wasn’t sure what to do and he would play, just to get creative, and he would think of what the scene ought to be. It was the first time that Cary Grant had improvised and Cary Grant offered to give his money back after the first week of production because he didn’t understand the way McCarey was working, and McCarey was like, “Just trust me. This is going to work out.” It was a very rocky early going and… and then they kind of fell into it. And it’s some of the most inspired acting, comedic acting that I’ve ever seen. There’s a pratfall that Cary Grant makes when he goes to see Irene Dunne singing an aria and tips the table over, and it’s one take and it’s incredible. Both of them are great in it.

Here’s a movie, by the great Stephen Frears, called The Hit. It starts out small. It’s shot in Spain. The production gets bigger and bigger. It’s sort of a chase. And it’s about a hitman who loses nerve and starts to examine his conscience. And it’s full of amazing performances. There’s a scene in it where Tim Roth goes into a bar and gets a couple of beers to take with him and gets made fun of by a bunch of locals. And he’s just sort of smiling, and he’s taking out his brass knuckles and his garrote wire and his knives and stuff, and he’s just going… And then he gets his beers, he puts them in his pockets, his four beers, and then he proceeds to beat the holy hell out of those four guys and then pull the whole bar to the ground before he runs and gets in the car. This is a great film. Really, really well done.

There’s a movie that I… go back to a lot. I directed a couple movies. One was called God’s Pocket and it was inspired by this, The Friends of Eddie Coyle. Peter Yates is a guy who, to me, is remarkable in his breadth of field. He did The Dresser. He did Bullitt. He did Breaking Away. He did this. And Mitchum is unbelievable. I come from Boston, so a lot of old Boston is here. He goes to the Garden and watches Bobby Orr play hockey when he was a kid. There’s an entrance that he makes through the… He steps up to the window of a diner, and that’s the first time you see the reflection in the window of Mitchum. That menace, when you’re in the hands of heavyweights who don’t have to prove it. It was so well cast that there’s so many people that are just conversationally saying stuff that is really pretty chilling. It’s a great film.

I’m choosing Merrily We Go to Hell, an incredibly daring film about marriage and the breakdown of a marriage. There’s so much more to say. This is such a complicated movie. And Fredric March and Sylvia Sidney are so incredible in it. Watch all of Dorothy Arzner’s films that you can, because she was such a fascinating woman and filmmaker and very important in the history of cinema.

Something Wild by Jack Garfein. This film really means a lot to me because I became good friends with him and I know this was a very personal film to him, starred his then-wife, Carroll Baker, and it’s a very… realistic depiction of the aftermath of rape and the surreal, anxious feelings that follow. Cinematography by Eugen Schüfftan, who did Eyes Without a Face, so there’s all these experimental elements to the film as well. Sheila O’Malley wrote a beautiful essay for this, too. I recommend that you read her essay on this.

Ellen. Ellen from Leave Her to Heaven. Farran Smith Nehme and I have talked a lot about the movie. She writes a lot for Criterion. We’re always discussing this film together because we feel, although she does many misdeeds, obviously, in an understatement, we have this feeling that she maybe, perhaps, is an artist herself and she’s not really happy with her husband’s book. However, do not dedicate a book to your wife’s sister. You will have Vincent Price defending you in court after you pass away. I’m summarizing it in the briefest way possible, so, please, you’ll get much more out of it when you watch it.

film_title: Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould
catalog_title: Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould
quote: Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould. I love movies that aren’t traditional biopics. I love that through the music– There’s a scene in here that I love where he’s at a diner and he’s listening to all the sounds, he’s listening to the people talking, and you can feel the musicality of that, and what Glenn Gould would incorporate, just in regular life, how musical he was, what a genius he was. More people should check out this film, and it’s just a beautiful… meditation on Glenn Gould. It’s not just directly telling you about him. It feels the way music makes you feel. There’s mystery still there. He allows the mystery, it’s so… such a beautiful film.

I love this movie, Punch-Drunk Love. I remember seeing this at a screening and just walking out… just kind of walking on air. I love that what Paul Thomas Anderson did with Adam Sandler, who, of course, in other work, I believe, showed that he had dramatic chops, and even in his comedy, the anger that he would show, you see it in here and he pulls it out of him, somewhat in a way that Hitchcock pulled out of Jimmy Stewart. It’s universal, but there’s something so American about Jimmy Stewart and Adam Sandler, just the way that he shows his… his sadness, his… his anger, and the edginess, right down to the score, the way that you feel constantly on edge, either with his happiness, as he’s walking through the grocery store and doing the little tap dance, or just the constant worry. It’s such a romantic, beautiful movie, all about the messiness, also, of love and all of the anxiety that it can produce. Unforgettable. Unforgettable.

So Kiss Me Deadly by Robert Aldrich. This was made in 1955. It’s a little bit late in the noir cycle. This film was so influential to the French New Wave, and then all the way to Quentin Tarantino with Pulp Fiction, with the suitcase, and Alex Cox’s Repo Man before that. But the movie is just, still to this day, I don’t want to use the word modern. I want to say timeless. If you have not seen the opening sequence of this movie, you have not watched cinema. You need to see the opening of this movie. And I love that Aldrich, he ranged from doing Ulzana’s Raid to The Longest Yard. A vicious, somewhat nihilistic filmmaker, in terms of this film, but also had a lot of heart and sensitivity towards men, women, and really saw the whole human condition. There’s a reason this film has endured and has inspired so many people and I love it so much. And I love all the Los Angeles locations. In fact, when I’m driving down Wilshire, I always point out Mike Hammer’s apartment building. It’s right on Wilshire. Every time I pass by. My friends make fun of me because I have to, like, take a picture and text them.

So I’m choosing The Killing. This is a seminal Kubrick film, and what I love about it is it moves like clockwork in terms of the heist, but then it ends with that suitcase. And I don’t want to just focus on the suitcase here, but he buys the worst suitcase, I must say. The absurdity of it is almost beautiful. In fact, it is in the way that Sterling Hayden, who’s so perfect in this film, says those great final lines, “What’s the difference?” Which you could read as very sad, and his life is over, or very Zen-like. I recommend this, but also get Barry Lyndon and Eyes Wide Shut, get all three. But I don’t want to be greedy, so… this in the bag.

So, Criterion kindly pulled these out for me. I wanted to show these in honor of the great Udo Kier: Flesh for Frankenstein, Blood for Dracula. Two of his greatest performances. I’m very partial to Udo. I adored him. Watch these movies and watch all of Udo Kier’s movies. He made many, and he always left such an impression. There was no one like him. No one like him.

So, Criterion kindly pulled these out for me. I wanted to show these in honor of the great Udo Kier: Flesh for Frankenstein, Blood for Dracula. Two of his greatest performances. I’m very partial to Udo. I adored him. Watch these movies and watch all of Udo Kier’s movies. He made many, and he always left such an impression. There was no one like him. No one like him.

I’m actually going to start with Secrets & Lies, Mike Leigh. Hello, England. This to me feels like… I don’t know if he’d appreciate this review, but his juiciest work. Sorry, Mike, if you don’t like that. There’s just something in him kind of utilizing naturalism for really heavy drama. He also doesn’t waste the character, which I think is, in my experience of being an acting person, quite a common pain you feel. I spent a number of years being “You need to be here by this time or this is going to happen”-guy, and I think that that guy in his films always is given a proper something to do, which I think is so generous, but also beneficial to the film. So, yeah, I love this one.

Celebration, Festen. Takes me back to the days where I tried to define myself as being the guy who liked Dogme 95 stuff. I’m still that guy, but I don’t define myself by it. I think that the… the amount of extra business that goes on when making stuff these days, it’s useful to remember that you don’t have to, and that the kind of obstructions that they created for themselves obviously ended up being insanely fruitful creatively, and the product is actually verging on soap-style drama. It’s really accessible and brilliant, and, actually, all that fat being trimmed out, all the kind of… Look, I love a cinematic light. Don’t get me wrong. But all that fat being trimmed out does leave you with this really horrible, amazing, cold, sinewy drama that I love.

These I picked because they’re three… they’re three contemporary performances that I think changed the way I want to act or inspired me to do better. Jeff Daniels in Noah Baumbach’s Squid and the Whale is taking a person in the world, via Baumbach’s incredible script, who is seemingly one-dimensional. He has no ability to introspect. I think it’s one of the funniest performances. But it requires so much introspection from the actor to get it over the line. And I think the idea of that horrendous guy being so watchable is such a testament to real skill from everyone involved.

Sandra Hüller in Anatomy of a Fall. Sandra Hüller, that year, with Zone of Interest as well, immediately became the person that I will see anything in. Feels like a classic from a million years ago already. I think her dedication felt like a new… It really felt like a new level of naturalism that I just… I just can’t fathom how she did what she did in that film.

And Paul Thomas Anderson’s Punch-Drunk Love. I think as time passes, people are becoming more and more obsessed with Adam Sandler’s performance in this, for good reason. On the surface, when I think about that film, I’m thinking that he’s playing the most anxious man in the world. But then, when you actually think about it, he’s the most confident character who’s ever existed. The things that he’s willing to do demonstrate that there’s no… there’s no simplicity, you can’t reduce it down to that. Anyway, love these three performances and films on the whole.

film_title: The Worst Person in the World
catalog_title: The Worst Person in the World
quote: The Worst Person in the World, a recent classic. Kind of demonstrates that cinema does have a future, despite my gut feeling that it might not. It’s really rewarding to see.

Okay, and to finish, I am going to blindly choose a film. Lovely stuff, of course. I’ve seen a million times. Loved a million times. I’m not sad that this, Being John Malkovich by Spike Jonze and Charlie Kaufman, is going in my bag.

Brief Encounter, which is just a classic. David Lean. The performances are beyond belief, and it’s very emotional and… it’s sort of gone in a big circle, where there was a time when it was considered to be really old-fashioned, but it’s sort of not that.

Le cercle Rouge. I did a version of this set in Hong Kong, which is going to come out at some point. Brilliant, brilliant, brilliant. Alain Delon, possibly the best actor maybe, certainly out of Europe, and wonderful film.

film_title: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
catalog_title: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
quote: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold, for me, it’s about Richard Burton, who was the most remarkable actor, born in Wales, son of a coal miner, fluent in Welsh. Drinker, fighter, all of those things. Brilliant actor. His story with Elizabeth Taylor was a movie in itself. And he’s the actor I would most have liked to have written for that would have reflected that sort of fire that he had in his soul.

Paris, Texas. One of my daughters, when she was three years old, became obsessed with… Three years old, became obsessed with Paris, Texas. And if we needed to get her to sleep, or if we needed to calm her down or anything, we’d just put Paris, Texas on and she’d just sit there. Not just listen to the music, but she’d watch it and sort of know what was coming next. There’s something hypnotic about it.

3:10 to Yuma is indicative, for me, of westerns… my dad used to take us boys to westerns, with usually John Wayne. But any western that was on… My dad was a farrier, a blacksmith, he’d shoe horses, he used to take us all out shoeing horses, so we knew about horses and my dad used to love to watch the way they rode, because the people who ride horses in westerns are amongst the best riders in the world. As well as the stories, the horses were quite important to us.

One-Eyed Jacks, I mean, Marlon Brando, so… And Karl Malden in this film, it’s one of the strongest performances. For me, this film introduced a sort of modernity to– Marlon Brando himself, a modernity to performance. You didn’t quite know if he was in it or not, if he was really in the character or not. But that was because the character who he always played was not really in the world, in my opinion.

Betty Blue. I love– Again, when I was a kid, me and my brothers, Saturday night on BBC Two… That’s not relevant to this film, but on Saturday night on BBC Two they used to play French films and they did have an effect on me. Anything when you’re little has an effect, and watching those films had a real effect on me, not because we were arty, but… All this stuff would be going on, everything would be happening, and then it’d suddenly go, “Fin,” and nothing had been resolved and the plot hadn’t really come together. They’d just done a series of scenes and then went, “Fin,” as if to say, “I’ve had enough of this, I’m bored.” And the French sensibility, I really miss it in films, because they didn’t care. Betty Blue was a great film.

Dont Look Back. I mean, God. Bob Dylan. When I see this, and see his interviews on telly, he looks like a time traveler who is from now who has been taken back in time, and he’s sort of bewildered by how weird everybody is. He’s actually more like us than them– Is that my phone? I’m sorry about that.
Citizen Kane hardly needs… explanation. It’s just so good.

So I’m going to start with just one of the greatest films ever made, A Woman Under the Influence. It doesn’t need to be sold to anybody, but it was definitely… not only this film, but all of Cassavetes’s films in general were a helpful point of reference in making my first feature, just in terms of the ethos of filmmaking and independent filmmaking and the way he prioritizes performance over technical precision. I think especially when you’re working with children, it’s really helpful to not think so much about how the actors can be blocked, but how you can block the camera to the actors, so, that was a huge point of reference for us and for every other filmmaker on the planet.

Watermelon Woman. It’s one of those films that you watch and you see, “Oh, wow, everyone has been copying this film. Everyone is inspired by this film.” Because it really does use the hybrid form in such an inventive way, in such a seamless way, in the way that… the way that she self-inserts, as a director, but as a performer, and brings documentary elements in without it bringing attention to itself. It’s just brilliant, and it really should be one of those films that every filmmaker has to watch at some point.

Not a Pretty Picture by Martha Coolidge. Made fifty years ago, another film that is extremely, I think, integral to the form of hybrid filmmaking and to personal filmmaking, but is an extremely formally intelligent film, the way that it marries documentary and fiction, and it’s incredible that a film like this exists. So I’m going to take that one as well.

So I did promise my dad that I would get him a film. My dad and my mom are both very cinephilic people. They watch a movie almost every night. They’ve had a big impact on the way that I watch movies and see the world. From the four movies that my dad sent me, I’m going to take Jules and Jim, because I had an interesting moment when I was making my short film Still Processing. My dad sent me all the home-video footage that he’d taken, or he sent me a selection of the home-video footage he had taken of me and my brothers growing up, and there’s a video of me as a two- or three-year-old, and he’s whistling a tune and I’m dancing to the tune, and it sounded familiar to me so I asked my dad, “What is this tune that you’re whistling?” And it’s the song that they sing in Jules and Jim. She sings and he plays the guitar. So it’s a special film.

I’m going to take Girlfriends as well. There are few films that show the complexity of friendships between women in a way that I think this film really, really nails, and this point in life where friendships can diverge because of different paths in life, and she does it in such a subtle but also very humanist kind of way where neither character is villainized, but is also quite flawed in their own ways, and it’s rare in, I think, its representation of women and the particularity of friendship between women.

Might as well start here. Okay, so this is Arsenic and Old Lace, Frank Capra, starring Cary Grant. I… Probably genre-wise, romantic comedy or screwball comedy, things like that, those are my go-tos. And this one I actually haven’t seen. And Frank Capra, of course, is one of my favorites, as is Cary Grant. There’s no one like him. I wanted to choose mostly films that I haven’t seen, but there are a couple… It’s hard not to get the ones that are your favorites.

So, anyway, speaking of, here is Swing Time. So my kind of introduction to film, one of the first films I remember seeing was Swing Time and Top Hat, Fred Astaire, Ginger Rogers films. Holds a special place in my heart.

The Cameraman. Another one I have seen, Buster Keaton, but haven’t seen in a very long time. This is a just… I mean, obviously classic. I’m probably talking to film buffs here. I don’t need to explain these movies to you guys. You know more than I do. But this, for me, was definitely one that I watched in my revival-house days. I worked at the Silent Movie Theater in LA for a while, and obviously that was a very cool, romantic job. Not the cleaning of the bathroom so much, but the… And even if it’s a revival house and a silent film, people still throw their popcorn all over the floor, which I don’t understand. But it was my opportunity to see a bunch of beautiful, silent films like The Cameraman.

So this I’ve actually never seen, which is crazy. Holiday. Again, Cary Grant. Katharine Hepburn. Come on. The greatest of all time. I love The Philadelphia Story so much, and this is another classic from George Cukor.

Also a film that is very much wrong that I haven’t seen. This is Sweetie, Jane Campion. And I got the opportunity to work with Jane on Top of the Lake seasons one and two, and become friends with her, which is a great honor and privilege. She’s an even better friend than she is a director. And she’s a very good director. But don’t tell her, but I never saw this movie. I just kind of went with her other films when I wanted to work with her. But this is one I haven’t gotten the opportunity to see, so I’m excited.

Okay, here is another one that I could not help but choose because… Well, it’s All About Eve. Starring Bette Davis, who was my kind of first idol as an actress. I don’t… How do you describe why with Bette Davis? Just is. And All About Eve is such a great film about theater and about acting and about an actress, and this is when they knew how to write. The scripts. They do that now. They do it now. But it is not as frequent as it was then.

The ultimate: Broadcast News. I mean, James L. Brooks, just… How do I– I mean, I get chills talking about him. I think he’s somebody that if I met, I think it would break me. I truly… I would be so– I don’t know, I can’t even speak about it, I would be so incredibly starstruck. My admiration for him knows no bounds, and his work and his films are my favorites. So this is obviously one of the best movies ever. Speaking of dialogue and writing. Oh my God. And Holly Hunter, calling back to Jane Campion, Top of the Lake, I had the opportunity to work with her. She is so nice, so cool, and so funny and just the most beautiful actress.

So given that this is a sort of comedic theme, I have to go with the ultimate in screwball comedies, which is Don’t Look Now. I know that I need to watch it. I know that it’s really good. But I also know that it’s dark and I know why it’s dark, and I think that it will be something I will just have to buck up and get through. And perhaps it’s punishment for all of the times that I have made extremely dark material about children and made other people watch it. So this is my… this is karma.

No better place to start than at the beginning, and the first movie that I saw was a little movie called The Daytrippers, which is directed by Greg Mottola. Greg’s a dear friend of mine. He directed me in Fletch. He also directed me… Confess, Fletch, not the original Fletch, which I was not in. And this is a fabulous movie and the heyday of independent cinema in the ’90s. So check it out.

This is one that I’m thrilled that is in here. It’s a little number called WALL·E. This movie makes me cry every single time I see it. It is a brilliant piece of storytelling, almost silent movie. It is so well told. Prescient, you might say. A very, very good one.

This movie means a lot to me. It’s a movie by Lasse Hallström called My Life as a Dog. It is a coming-of-age story, Swedish movie. It is breathtakingly beautiful and heartbreaking, and if you have children or you like children or you are a child at heart, see this movie. It’s a beautiful, beautiful film.

This is kind of a weird one: Videodrome, David Cronenberg. A crazy Canadian genius. The reason I saw this movie again, I’d seen it back when I was young in the ’80s, was because the Criterion app had a little collection of movies, a themed collection of movies, called VHS Forever, and it was basically movies that had VHS as a big plot point. Also Blondie is in this, so it’s very cool. And a very young James Woods. Very cool movie.

film_title: How to Get Ahead in Advertising
catalog_title: How to Get Ahead in Advertising
quote: This is a movie that’s a very interesting film. The only reason I pick this is because I used to be on a TV show called Mad Men. It was about advertising. This is a movie called How to Get Ahead in Advertising. The title is a pun. I love a pun in a title. How to Get Ahead in Advertising. It’s about a guy who grows a head that has really interesting opinions. Bruce Robinson, from Withnail and I. Maybe you know that one. A lot of people like that movie. I like that movie too, but this is equally spectacular and weird.

This movie, this is maybe one of the scariest movies I’ve ever seen. It’s called The Vanishing, and it’s about a couple who go on a trip and they stop in a rest stop, and one of them goes to go to the bathroom and never returns. I saw this movie in the cinema. I was shook by it. See this one. It’s deeply disturbing.

Man Bites Dog is a very, very, weird movie that I saw, again, in the cinema in the ’90s. It is… I hate to keep using this word prescient, but this is about media and manipulation. If a dog bites a man, then that’s not a story, but if a man bites a dog, that’s a story. That’s what this is. It predates our fascination with reality TV and all those things.

Jim Jarmusch. Great movie starring Roberto Benigni, as well as Tom Waits and John Lurie. Super vibey and definitely picks up the mantle of people like John Cassavetes and all of these incredible independent filmmakers. This is a good entry way into Jarmusch.

This is Tootsie. This is, I think, and I’m not the only person to say this, a perfect comedy. Deeply funny. Very, very heartbreaking. Incredible performances up and down the line: Bill Murray, Teri Garr, obviously Dustin Hoffman, Jessica Lange, young Geena Davis is in this. You’ve probably seen this, but it’s really good.

All right. Last one, the one that I have to… Oh, boy. All right, I said I’m going low. I’m going low. All right. This is what I’ll do, because this one started off a pretty great career. This is Wes Anderson’s first film, called Bottle Rocket. All three Wilson brothers are in this movie. This is a great movie for aspiring filmmakers to look at because it proves you just need a fun story and talented people to make a great movie. You don’t need a bunch of money. They certainly didn’t have it, but they made a great movie and he has a great career because of it. And this is how it all started.
Oh, yes. Thank God. Chamber piece. That's my speed. One room, one set of characters. "Let's get to the bottom of this dilemma." Boom! 12 Angry Men.

Ice Storm. Simple. Grounded. No lunatics. It's not absurdism. I say all that because all that stuff is not really my speed. I have an appreciation for it, but I think it's important to know your speed. And maybe my speed will change. But my speed is something like this. Ice Storm.

Heater. Just beautiful. The party scene makes me want to be at that party. That's the type of party I want to be going to in my forties and fifties, and those are the type of conflicts I want to be getting in with my wife. La notte is going in the bag.
To Sleep with Anger. This was a banger. Watching it unravel was an absolute pleasure.

Heater. Never seen anything like this. It even takes a second to get your bearings and understand what's going on, but by the end you're like, "Wow, this is a wonderful piece of art." Never seen anything like it. Close-Up going in the bag.

Come on now. Come on now. This my life right here. I was like, "Well, that's my fault." The scene where broski is in the crib with all 12 of the women he's ever dealt with. Only dream sequence I've ever enjoyed, I'll tell you that. 8½ going in the bag.

Fail Safe. Saw it for the first time last year at the Roxy. I love Sidney Lumet. I already put 12 Angry Men in the bag. You know, it's funny. I peeped how this came out around the exact same time as Dr. Strangelove. And Dr. Strangelove feels like it has a little more notoriety, but I actually slightly prefer this to Dr. Strangelove. It's more grounded. It's more serious. I love that they're different movies, but this is my preference. I love this movie.

Saw this with a woman. It was A Man and a Woman in the theater watching this, and maybe I just saw it at the exact right moment in my life as I was falling for somebody, but it's a touching movie. I recommend you seeing this with somebody you love.

Six Moral Tales, Eric Rohmer. It feels like a perfect way to start, because I love seeing characters sitting around talking about love. Very little action, just conversations on camera that felt organic and genuine and unscripted, so, big inspiration.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: Agnès Varda. I would call this a discovery pick for me. I'm taking this home to educate myself, because I've seen Le Bonheur and I would say that movie inspired the song "My Winter" on my new album. I love that movie, and I'd like to see more of what she's done, so I'm going to take this home and find out.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: Scarface. Old movie. Some of the old movies are funny because they’re unafraid of just wallowing in tropes, and this one is one of those and great fun to watch. Paul Muni, Boris Karloff, George Raft, a Howard Hughes production directed by Howard Hawks.
Uncut Gems. Do you know how great this is? Do you know how great Adam Sandler is? Adam can do anything, and he’s one of the nicest guys you’ll ever meet.
The Big Heat. I’ve never seen it. I like a noir film.
A Man Escaped. Haven’t seen it. Can’t wait to see it. Frenchies working at it. They’re the best. They love it.

Do you know Quadrophenia? This is a movie that used all that French filmmaking coming out of the New Wave, but it’s a British film, using the music of The Who to tell the story of a youth who is rebelling, but he doesn’t know what he’s rebelling against. And it’s kind of got just an incredible vibe.

film_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
catalog_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
quote: Gotta go up here. I’m getting the higher shelves because no one goes there. This is a movie called Salò. It’s one of the great films ever made by a human being. It’s horrifying. I’m putting it back. I’ve already seen it. One time, that’s enough. Never need to see it again. And yet it says so much about people and power and how it corrupts.

This is called The Red Shoes. This is a beautiful film. I caught it on TV when I was young. They did all kinds of clever camera techniques to make it come alive. It’s just… It’s just a beautiful, romantic, visually stunning film.

Here’s one of my favorite films of all time: My Life as a Dog. Anybody who’s writing or even acting, if you want people’s… the viewer’s heart to break, don’t have the characters cry. This is about a little kid who is deeply sad for reasons that are presented to you, but he doesn’t really know how sad he is. And it is heartbreaking and beautiful.

In a Lonely Place. I just saw this. I saw this on the Criterion Channel. This a good movie. Somewhat of a complex, psychological noir. It’s not an obvious story. And Nicholas Ray directed it. He did a good job. The story and the complexity of the story and the delicate nature of the story is to be appreciated.
Jackie Chan, Police Story is a movie that I shared with my kids when they were young. It’s just fun, clever action. I love it. I love Jackie.

film_title: Jackie Chan: Emergence of a Superstar (box set)
catalog_title: Jackie Chan: Emergence of a Superstar (box set)
quote: Since we’re talking about Jackie, the Criterion Collection has this. These are his early films. It’s called Emergence of a Superstar. It has six films. If you ever wonder about the connection between Buster Keaton and Jackie Chan, watching these movies will show it to you. Set pieces one after another after another. Clever as can be. Physical comedy. Brilliant.
box_set_name: Jackie Chan: Emergence of a Superstar

film_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
catalog_title: Bruce Lee: His Greatest Hits (box set)
quote: I’ve never seen Bruce Lee films. Never seen one ever in my life. So I’m taking these.

film_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
catalog_title: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story
quote: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story. BBS was a group of producers who were making cool movies in the late ’60s, early ’70s, and these are movies that Nicholson’s in, Hopper’s in, Peter Fonda’s in, the Monkees are in. They were aiming for cool, thoughtful stuff, but also trying to be very realist. Get this box set and you can hang out with them.
box_set_name: America Lost and Found: The BBS Story

quote: This is Last Temptation of Christ, which I don't have on Blu-ray. This, I remember the hysteria that happened when this came out. And I grew up in this evangelical household, so I remember being in the video store, walking with my dad and then him seeing this on the stand and him just smacking it. But now I get to pick it up. But then he and I did watch it years later and he was like, "That's a very amazing movie about Christ." It really is a real meditation on the actual… what it cost Christ to make this sacrifice. And I just love it, and I love Willem in it, and it's hard to beat Harvey Keitel as, like, a Judas from Brooklyn. "Hey, Jesus! Come on, I got a deal for ya."

Rushmore. I mean, this was right before I went off to do my actings, this Wes Anderson film… I loved Bottle Rocket. I thought it was incredible. And then when Wes did Rushmore, it kind of blew up into this whole other level of incredible expression. And Jason Schwartzman and Bill Murray in it. Bill Murray is so funny and sad. I just love this movie.

The Fisher King, Terry Gilliam movie. Love this movie. It's so wild and so out there. Robin Williams and Jeff Bridges just at their most electric and dynamic. And I remember watching this… I was quite young when I watched it, I probably shouldn't have watched it when I watched it because it was a weird psychedelic experience for an 11 year old. But, yeah, what an incredible movie.

Bob Dylan, Dont Look Back. I had seen this before doing Inside Llewyn Davis, but this was one that I went back to. All the stuff that Llewyn Davis wasn't experiencing in his life, watching from afar, was this. Such a fun movie.

Okay, cabrón. It's my guy. Pan's Labyrinth. I had just done a film and was in Toronto and… Toronto, the film festival, and Guillermo was there as well for Pan's Labyrinth, and that was our first introduction to each other. I remember him punching me in the shoulder and being like, "Hola!" and… I remember I cornered him and I was like, "We should do something about Federico García Lorca." And he's like, "I kind of just did in Pan's Labyrinth, in some kind of way." I was like, "Yeah, you're right." But I was so moved by the way that he uses fantastical expression to talk about something very real and very painful, like the Spanish Civil War. And then, of course, these quintessential, iconic creatures that he created that feel like they've always been a part of our psyche and somehow you're like, "Oh, yeah, of course, the guy with the eyes in the hands. Somehow I know that figure, even though I've never seen it before." And it's just such incredible visual poetry.

Well, there's this little movie called Inside Llewyn Davis that I guess I should probably mention. Yeah, this was a movie that I was in. And it was the first time I got to play a lead part in a film, and it happened to be this incredible masterpiece that I got to be a part of, and getting to see the bros work and the way that they work and the kind of effortless ease that they have with it and the flow and the… the fact that it really felt, for the first time, like we were all a team building something together, and also getting to play music and getting to live in that time and that place, it was one of the great blessings of life. So funny and sad, which I guess is my jam, I'm realizing.

Kurosawa's Dreams. This was so wild. I mean, granted, I was very high when I watched it for the first time. But I think I would have gotten high just watching it, with how wild this thing is. Still the image of those men on the mountain in the snowstorm, so thrilling and bizarre and mournful. And then Marty as Van Gogh. That's pretty great. I've watched this so many times. So high.

Throne of Blood is my favorite Shakespeare on film and, ironically, it has none of Shakespeare's dialogue in it. But there's something about the way that he cracked open Macbeth and, of course, setting it in feudal Japan and just all of that imagery, it just… it all makes sense suddenly. The witches, the supernatural element, the idea… and Toshiro Mifune at his absolute most vicious and incredible, and the gravity that he has in this, it's astounding. I've watched this so many times and I can never get enough of it.

The Tree of Life. God, I love this movie. This movie made me weep uncontrollably. I love Terrence Malick, of course, but there was something about this, and my dear friend Jessica Chastain, what she did in it was so incredible, and the Book of Job is my favorite book of the Bible. No, it's such a… Some say it's the most ancient book, and it's so powerful. And the way that Terry approached it, in setting it in the '50s, and I know a lot of people saw it at the time and were like, "And dinosaurs now?" when it suddenly goes to that, and that's the feeling of reading the Book of Job, when this guy's suffering and asking, "Why, why?" And then God shows him creation and says, "Why not? You're a part of creation. You're not separate from creation." And the way that he weaves that into this beautiful dream of this boyhood… these boyhood memories, it's so powerful. I remember walking out and… and calling Jessica and saying, "Oh my God. I'm so proud of you. This is incredible."
La Llorona, Jayro Bustamante, a fellow Chapín, Guatemalan, incredible director and I've not seen this Criterion version of the film yet. Really excited to see this.
Pinocchio. This is the… It's the double-header: Pinocchio, Frankenstein, they're telling similar stories about really fucked-up dads. What a marvel of artistry, again from Guillermo del Toro.
Raging Bull on 4K. What can one say else about Raging Bull, other than I need to have it?

You Can Count on Me. You guys have this on 4K? That's crazy. Mark Ruffalo in this, it's a perfect performance. And Kenny Lonergan, This Is Our Youth, his play, was one of the first plays I did, in Florida, in a little, small theater, and I couldn't believe someone could write that truthfully. It was so funny and acidic. And then to see him do that on film here. Laura Linney's incredible. Rory Culkin. As someone who loves his sister so much, to have that relationship so beautifully portrayed, it's great. Mine.

I'll just talk about this briefly because I've– this is a very early purchase that I made. This Cassavetes is fundamental, particularly A Woman Under the Influence. And Peter Falk in this is incredible and heartbreaking and so funny as well. The energy of this thing is something that I'm always… I always get inspired by watching this.

Richard Linklater, Slacker. It’s, like, here I am, this suburban kid, I listen to the radio, the top 20 songs, and you go to the movies and you watch the movies that everybody else watches, and then I remember I went to see my first… The first movie, I don’t even know if you’d have it… Oh, Straw Dogs. The first movie I went to see that was an independent film that kind of changed the way I started looking at things was Birdy. So then I started walking… I started going into Blockbuster and not getting The Outlaw Josey Wales for the 15th time and watch it with my friends, I started going, “What’s– What is that?” Richard Linklater, one of the greatest filmmakers of our time. Period.

Let me stay on this Slacker… which then turned me to: “Hey, what’s this?” Really an amazing experience that I had as a young person watching this for the first time. Oh, and so I’m going to keep Mystery Train.
Here’s another one. Paris, Texas. I mean, it’s such a great… You know what’s also great? You got to listen to the soundtrack, Ry Cooder. It’s one of the best.

Miller’s Crossing. That’s… These are people that I’d love to work with at some point. Maybe… I don’t know. You know how sometimes people show up in movies after you’ve kind of washed out a little bit? People get bored of you and then you go into hibernation for ten years and then some great filmmaker goes like, “Hey, I wonder what so-and-so’s doing?” Maybe that’ll be me. Maybe I’ll just go fish for ten years and have people be like, “What happened to Steve?” And then maybe the Coen brothers would be like, “Maybe we should just put him in a really cool movie?” I’m just throwing it out there, guys.
Some Like It Hot. This is genius. This is great comedy. I would put this up at, like, top five.
Being There. I got to have… Peter Sellers is frickin’ genius. Sometimes it’s crazy, I’ll forget who the director is. And then you’re like, “Of course, of course! Hal Ashby.”

Oh, yeah, I do have Night of the Living Dead. That’s a real… This was, also, as a young person watching, watching something that was just off-kilter. Think about that. That’s really interesting, too, that 1968, Vietnam, right before the Tet Offensive, and this cat makes this movie. It’s kind of interesting.

Okay, I’ve got to go here to Happiness by Todd Solondz. I remember first seeing this when I was at university. It kind of blew my mind. It’s very hard to sum up the plot of this. Bunch of misfits shuffling their way through life in really sort of very dark and very, very idiosyncratic ways. Some of the storylines, some plot lines, I couldn’t believe. It was very much a sort of artistic coming-of-age film for me, in the sense that I didn’t quite realize that film, TV, all these kinds of things could go to these depths. There’s a particular scene in it, which I won’t take us through, where I remember watching it, and actually the kind of sweat and the tingles went up the back of my neck. But this goes to some shocking places, but it never, ever loses sight of the human life behind it all. So that goes straight into the bag.

Memories of Murder, Bong Joon Ho. Parasite’s a ten out of ten for me. But this, somehow, it was a 10.1 out of 10. It was just incredible. When I describe the plot of Memories of Murder to people, it’s a detective trying to solve the crime of a serial killer, and a lot of people sort of feel like that’s a plot they’ve seen before. But the way he does it, the frustration you feel emanating out of the camera, it’s got huge satire at the heart of it: corruption in the police force, the damage that incompetence does to victims. So one of my favorite films, one of my favorite directors, that goes straight into the bag.

Trainspotting, probably my most favorite film of all time. I remember when I sat down to do Baby Reindeer, I really wanted to have voice-over in it, and so I almost watched every film that had voice-over, of prominence, and Trainspotting gave it this exhilaration, this pushing forward in time. It takes you from one scene and it throws you to the next, and it all feels like an adrenaline rush, it all feels like you’re on drugs when you’re watching it. It captures the euphoria in amongst the degradation. I think there’s a version of Trainspotting that a lot of directors would take, and it would be social realist and it would be bleak, but Danny Boyle keeps that sense of play alive. But it’s all earned. It’s all borne out of character, like the famous bit where Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day” plays and he sinks into the carpet. All of that is just… It’s directorial vision at its very best, and none of it’s cynical. I think a lot of new directors, I feel like they come in and they put the trickery onto a show that doesn’t call for it. But every single piece of flair in this film is earned. What a film.

I can’t not go to a Scorsese film and I’ll go to… I gotta go to Raging Bull. I don’t think this is too controversial, but I think De Niro as Jake La Motta is the best on-screen performance of all time. And of course, you can’t forget Joe Pesci in this film as well. All the acting is top-notch. You realize you’re kind of… That’s the beauty of acting when you actually get lost and you think you’re watching real life. That’s what those two do the best. There’s the scene where he’s punching the wall and he’s going ballistic, and you feel everything in your own hands as you’re watching it.

I gotta bring out another Scorsese: The Last Waltz. The thing that I love most is, it does have talking heads and it does have… it does have all the band speaking about why they decided to call it a day and all that kind of stuff, but really he just lets the music play. That’s the thing with Scorsese: I never, ever feel like he gets in the way of the story he’s about to tell. I never feel he put something on to it. I feel, everything he does as a director, which is why he’s the greatest, is that he pulls… “How do I pull this story out and honor it in the correct way?” And with this, I think it would have been so easy to splice it up and have talking heads every two seconds. But really, he just lets the music play and, in a way, I watch it and I feel almost… I almost feel quite emotional, just watching this, this exquisite band play their last. And that’s the beauty of Scorsese. He had all this footage in the world and he just lets it breathe in all the most beautiful ways.

Oh, is this Gimme Shelter? Is this that Rolling Stones one where the… Yeah. Oh my God, this is another amazing music documentary. I’ve realized doing this that I’m a sucker for a music documentary, actually. I think it’s often spoken about as being the end of the ’60s and peace and love and all this stuff, this horrific act happening at the very heart of one of the… of one of the gigs of one of the bands that made the ’60s what it was. It’s so much more than a music documentary in that sense. And it’s an absolute must-watch, so Gimme Shelter, check it out.

Easy Rider. I’ve seen this film so many times. Jack Nicholson, he comes in close to the end and I always remember the tragedy of the performance. I always remember him doing… Every time he takes a drink, he goes… For some reason, every time I’ve taken a drink in my life of anything, I always feel the urge to go… So that’s always stayed with me. It’s very interesting, you see tripping on TV a lot, but you never see it as realistically well done as this, where you feel the characters are actually going through quite a lot of personal anguish and pain. These prejudices are still prevalent in today’s society: this fear of anyone who’s different or carries different opinions, and it’s just a timeless piece of work. And I always remember the way it ends. I don’t want to give it away, but sudden suspension and then credits.

The Vanishing, George Sluizer. This is an oft-recommended horror film. This premise of someone being taken in broad daylight, whilst pumping gas on a road trip and then ultimately meeting who that killer is, who that psychopath is, in such a chilling way, is just… It’s a masterpiece.

Iñárritu’s Amores perros. The thing that I think about when I think about this movie is the Control Machete song, “Si Señor,” it is such a dope moment in the film. It’s such a punk-rock movie. And really the sort of explosive way that his career began. I love this film.

David Fincher’s The Game. I feel like no one talks about this movie in the way that they should. This idea of an immersive game that sort of challenges you and you think is… someone’s chasing you or someone’s after you. It’s this very elaborate ruse that Sean Penn’s character gets for his brother in the movie, played by Michael Douglas. It’s awesome and surprising and, yeah, one of my favorite Fincher films.

Antonioni’s Blow-Up. Herbie Hancock, the way I came to this movie was actually through its music. There’s a great song on this that is very identifiable from the Deee-Lite song “Groove Is in the Heart.” So that opening bassline… …that comes from a song from Blow-Up. This movie’s great. It’s… was later sort of remade as Blow Out. In this case, this was not about sounds, it’s about footage. It’s about a photographer that accidentally captures a murder, and this sort of world that he descends into in trying to decipher what that was. It’s awesome.

Thelonious Monk Straight, No Chaser. I didn’t even realize this was on Criterion, so I’m very stoked about this. This movie’s great. An incredible, intimate portrait of Thelonious Monk. Fly-on-the-wall revealing of one of the great artists in jazz. The footage is gorgeous. And if you want to get into jazz, even if you don’t care about jazz, that’s the beautiful thing about documentaries, is it doesn’t matter if you have a preexisting interest in a subject, you just immediately dive into a world that’s not your own. And you might have come out the other end having learned something, certainly, or be invested in something. In this case, it’s Monk and his incredible piano playing. So good.

Jonathan Glazer. I mean, every… How can every movie be such a masterwork? Jonathan Glazer’s… Birth I’m talking about. So, Jonathan Glazer got his start in music videos, as many great filmmakers do. Certainly filmmakers from the ’90s and the early 2000s. And this film is like… It’s sort of got a real Polanski-meets-Kubrick vibe. It’s chilling and haunting, and it keeps you guessing. It’s such a great film. I adore it.

Speaking of Kubrick, Eyes Wide Shut. It’s one of those films that, if it’s on TV, I have to watch it. There’s an atmosphere to this movie that’s so special. Even the way that characters speak, the way that Tom Cruise speaks in this movie, everything’s a question. Everything gets repeated. It’s rhythmic and fascinating. And, yeah, I’ve seen it innumerable times and I still can’t get enough. It’s really awesome.

This is not a happy movie. Todd Solondz’s Happiness. I’ll never forget seeing this in the theater and being really deeply disturbed by it, but also utterly moved and impressed by the skills of the cast. It’s such an extraordinary cast, particularly Philip Seymour Hoffman. It’s one of his great performances, and that’s an amazing cover as well.

Speaking of disturbing, Haneke’s Funny Games. That is not a party. The opening credits sequence is such a great indication of where you’re at. It’s a family on a drive to their country home, and it gets interjected with super-intense metal, punk rock. And you kind of go, “Right. I’m not safe here.” It is so upsetting and so wonderful, but it’s not for the faint of heart. It’s funny, I don’t get really freaked out by horror movies. Horror doesn’t scare me because it’s often so of the imaginary world. The horror that freaks me out are the things that humans do to other humans, and they don’t necessarily have a reason for why they’re doing them. And this is certainly a representation of that.

I mean… Right, just literally… pin the tail on the donkey. Oh! It’s On the Waterfront. I have never seen this, so… I’m letting you into my shameless now. This is a legendary classic. Now I’m motivated to see it. Thank you, Criterion.

film_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
catalog_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
quote: This Wes Anderson Archive, ten films over 25 years. What a fascinating and amazing career, especially watching someone develop their identity over the course of this many years. And with Bottle Rocket, it hasn’t quite started yet. The Wes Anderson that we’ve come to know is not there, but is there in many ways. That’s still one of my favorite films. I love that movie so much. The relationship that Luke Wilson has with the housekeeper at the motel is the most charming thing that you root for as an audience. It is such a great caper of some real average dudes that don’t know what the fuck they’re doing. And then it’s been just an absolute joy from that moment on. So, The Wes Anderson Archive. This is dope. It’s so cool.
box_set_name: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years

quote: Black Girl. My mother took me to see this maybe when I was ten. I know I thought it was boring a little bit at the time. You know, you're ten and there's no action happening right away. But by the middle of the film, even as a ten-year-old, I was totally engrossed.

True Stories. As I mentioned, I come out of music, and a lot of what I do is just an expansion of what my creative process in music was. This was something that early on, for me, showed me that there weren't boundaries that I had to be stuck to.

Election. This has influenced me maybe more than I've ever talked about. The way the music is used to cut on shocking or explosive things. The... You know. The twists and turns. The characters that are slightly larger than life, mixed with people that he cast in here that were non-actors.

I'ma get this, The Hero. I don't know much about this movie. People keep dropping the name, saying I should check it out. And I like the cover. Nothing wrong with liking the cover. If you're a filmmaker, make your cover and your font really good.

Come on now, we got to do The Princess Bride. Let me say this. It's got two of the most stand-up actors you could have in a film: Wallace Shawn and Mandy Patinkin. You gotta check out the shit that they say, in Wally Shawn's case, the stuff that he writes. I don't want to put labels on them, but they're comrades of mine, whether I've only met them a couple times or not. And they're in this movie, which is one of the greatest movies on Earth.
Almodóvar. I love all of his movies. I love All About My Mother. There's a purposeful artificiality to things that feels really true. It feels the way you wish you express yourself.

film_title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
catalog_title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown
quote: Do you have Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown? Yeah, we do. You can see by the cover what I'm talking about. This pops out at you. It pops out of your life, it... Says something, it magnifies things. Hopefully, your life is as fun, but not as terrible, as the things that happen in Almodóvar movies.

film_title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters
catalog_title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters
quote: Mishima. So this is a movie about a super right-wing artist told in a few ways. One in which this artist decided to take over a military base. The other is happening in his childhood. The other part that's really interesting takes these sequences from his writing and re-enacts them and does them in these fantastical stage play-like things. And Paul Schrader is a persnickety, grumpy dude sometimes. And I've been on... You can find stuff with me and him bickering on panels. And I love this movie. It's one of my favorite movies ever.

film_title: Three Revolutionary Films by Ousmane Sembène
catalog_title: Three Revolutionary Films by Ousmane Sembène
quote: Ousmane Sembène. And I haven’t seen any of these films, but what I have seen, it’s…
box_set_name: Three Revolutionary Films by Ousmane Sembène

quote: Melvin Van Peebles. I also do music, and he's somebody that started coming to Coup shows. Obviously, I also already was a fan. Anyway, so he came and one day he sent me a CD. He was like, "These are some songs of mine, could you remix them?" And I listened to it. It was perfect. It sounded old school, sounded like something he would have done in the '70s. And I was like, "Why would I want to remix...? Nobody should touch this." Hung up the phone with him. About eight or nine months later, he calls me up and says, "Can you send me back that CD-ROM?" I was like, "What?" He's like, "Yeah, I accidentally sent you the master and there's no other copies." He was like, "Man, you got to find that!" I hope that he found another copy of it because I didn't find it and I didn't talk to him since then, and he was a good guy.

The Qatsi Trilogy. Let me tell you a little secret. Pitch a movie to a studio, play a Koyaanisqatsi score behind you while you're pitching them your movie. Sold. Little trick I'm giving to you. I'm doing it so I don't do it again.

I need to watch more Fellini. I don't know a lot about Fellini. I don't know a lot about movies. I just kind of bumble along and find stuff that I like, and I try not to make rules about it. And I just watch what I like, and steal what I like, too. But somebody said that my stuff is Fellini-esque, and so now I gotta watch this stuff to see what I'm doing.

I want to start with this movie, Midnight Cowboy. It’s one of the first movies that I watched as a… actress, in the sense of thinking of myself as an actor. And I just remember watching Dustin Hoffman’s performance, and Jon Voight, of course, but Dustin’s performance in this was just mind-boggling to me. I couldn’t believe that someone could commit to the craft to that extent, and so vivid, so alive. It’s one of the most alive performances I’ve ever seen. And obviously that led me to Sunday Bloody Sunday and led me to all these incredible films by this director who I adore. John is one of my favorite directors of all time, and he just has such an honest view of performance and understands dialogue in a sensorial, cellular way. I don’t know, it’s just amazing when a movie can move you so much.

I grew up in Mexico and my reach to cinema was very limited because I grew up in the ’90s and we just had, like, cable and what we had on TV. And when I moved to the US, my education started expanding. And then I went to Strasberg here and I had amazing teachers who… I had this Shakespeare teacher who dressed like a cowboy in Strasberg, and he would tell me his favorite movies and this is how I discovered Klute. The cinematography was so unique. It looked all like a photograph. And the performances, and it was so quiet. Someone can feel so much in such a silent type of performance. This movie started my passion and awakened my love for film noir. Devil in a Blue Dress, The Killing, Orson Welles and some of the best movies you’ve ever seen. I wish we did more film noir, stylistic-type movies. We don’t have enough, so if you’ve never seen this movie, incredible. Also, this director does amazing other movies, so you should watch.

This movie, La Maman et la Putain, is so good. The Mother and the Whore. Perfect, perfect movie. I keep going back to it, and there’s something about going into mixed relationships and the complexity of relationships, and the complexity of the analysis of the man zeitgeist, of understanding what they want versus what they need, and vice versa. But it does it in such a darling way, and it’s so entertaining. You’re laughing when you don’t think you should be laughing, and it’s sexy. It’s one of the sexiest films. And those women are so hot. I may have doubted my sexuality for a second with them in this movie and their performances. I mean, really… Françoise, just… bomb, I love her.

In the Mood for Love. I know that everyone picks this, but the most beautiful film to ever be shot. Small and contained, and you kind of can’t breathe in these rooms when you’re watching them. And you see these perfectly gorgeous human beings.
