This movie is just all about passion and desire and building up that sort of feeling underneath, and you’re sort of palpitating while watching the movie. Let’s bring back yearning. The biggest pleasure on earth. I recommend it. Go watch it.

And then maybe I’ll just do a little… I love when I watch people close their eyes and pick a movie, so… Charles Chaplin, Monsieur Verdoux. I’ve never seen this movie. This makes me excited because who else could I learn more from than him? So.

Fanny and Alexander. As a girl that lost a father, and then finding this movie, it connected to me in such a profound way. These kids, their feelings, their sensations, sort of reconnecting with life, the loss of joy and the portrayal of the joy. If no one’s ever acted with children, you’d realize how complicated that is. It’s really hard to get a child to perform and keep the authenticity. But also when you hit lightning and you find a talented kid, it’s just the most amazing thing. Obviously Bergman has some of the best movies of all time. But if you’ve not seen it and you have five hours spare, you should watch Fanny and Alexander.

Pierrot le fou. My favorite film ever. My favorite filmmaker ever. It’s not true that you become a movie buff at the age of 13 or 14. Little genius, I don’t believe in that. No, when you are 18, 20, and you put the cinema you used to see back in your past and you start a new life in cinema. I started my new life in cinema with Pierrot le fou, and it’s a film I could see every day.

My friend, Bertrand Tavernier, ’Round Midnight, with a wonderful scene between Marty Scorsese, and Dexter Gordon. Every music is registered live, and especially the concert homage at the end, with Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Tony Williams. And in this DVD box, we have a wonderful bonus material: the making-of, made by Jean Achache, which is… which is very good.

Il Posto. Ermanno Olmi. My second year in Cannes, we had About Schmidt by Alexander Payne. Jack Nicholson came and we had a restored print of Il Posto. And I remember Jack Nicholson… I was quite scary about him, welcoming that great artist. And I said, “Hello, Jack.” And Jack said, “Hello, hello. Is it true that you have Il Posto today screening in the festival?” I said, “Yes!” “I want to see it.” Because Jack Nicholson is a great, great, great movie buff. And it’s wonderful how at the time a big movie star like Nicholson was focused on the film of Alexander, but also in watching the new restored print of Olmi’s movie.

La vérité by Clouzot. Two things. First, Clouzot… François Truffaut didn’t like very much Clouzot. He was destroyed by the Cahiers du Cinéma. But Clouzot was a great filmmaker. Le Corbeau, about the French occupation, is a masterpiece, and this film is a masterpiece. Brigitte Bardot. Brigitte Bardot, especially in this movie, she’s extraordinary, and the movie is very good, not only for the movie itself, but for what the movie says about French society at that time.

film_title: The Ranown Westerns: Five Films Directed by Budd Boetticher
catalog_title: The Ranown Westerns: Five Films Directed by Budd Boetticher
quote: I could take that because Budd Boetticher, because in France I’m always fighting against schools: “If you like that, you can’t like this.” Yes, I can like that and I do like this. And I like… Me, I’m the kind of spectator, I love Chantal Akerman and Jean-Marie Straub, and I love comedies, French popular comedy. I don’t take one from the other. But if you like cinema, you like everything. So all those westerns of Budd Boetticher with Randolph Scott. All masterpieces. Films of… Everyone can see that, because… even in… at lunch, because it’s one hour and ten minutes.
box_set_name: The Ranown Westerns: Five Films Directed by Budd Boetticher

film_title: Eclipse Series 12: Aki Kaurismäki’s Proletariat Trilogy
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 12: Aki Kaurismäki’s Proletariat Trilogy
quote: I wanted to find some… some maybe… Yes, some Kaurismäki films. He’s one of the greatest poets and greatest geniuses of the history of cinema. He used to say, “In my country in winter, days are short, it’s all night, so we are sad, so we drink. But in summer, days are long, we are happy, so we drink.”
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 12: Aki Kaurismäki's Proletariat Trilogy

quote: Godzilla. And of course, King Kong vs. Godzilla and so on. It’s a great.

Big Deal on Madonna Street, terrific movie. I mean, it’s been so many years since I saw it, but it was just terrific. There was another Italian movie, Mafioso, and that was also terrific, with Alberto Sordi. Marty and I also talked about doing a remake of that.
Divorce Italian Style. Yeah, this was a terrific movie. Terrific.

Blow-Up. As I remember, it was kind of… Because I think he shot it with… Who’s the young English actor? David Hemmings. But it was another– almost another style, it seemed. It was a more popular movie, I think. It was, in those days, an ‘art film,’ but more people saw it. It was a terrific movie.

film_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
catalog_title: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda
quote: And Agnès Varda’s film. And I knew Agnès and her husband, Jacques Demy, a little bit. We did this, and the toughest thing I remember was speaking French with Catherine Deneuve. It just drove me crazy.
box_set_name: The Complete Films of Agnès Varda

quote: This is the best of Fellini. Yeah. Well, La dolce vita. And I think– I remember I was… a premiere of it on Third Avenue at the Baronet or the Coronet, and I was there watching him come in. Of course, big fan.

And Withnail and I is right at the top of that list. I was about 22 years old and a friend of mine had a videotape and said, "I think you'd like this movie." And I watched it, and then I rewound it and watched it again. I'd never done that before. It's proof that you can make one of the funniest movies ever and it's tragic, it's sad, and heartbreaking. And everyone in it is brilliant.

Boyhood. I think Richard Linklater is the great American director. We have many of them, but I don’t think people take as many big swings as Richard Linklater. I also think that maybe the greatest thing that’s ever been put on film is the Michael Apted 7 Up series, and Boyhood is like that in narrative form, in a fictional movie. And I saw it at Sundance and it destroyed me, because to focus on all of the connective tissue between major events in people’s lives, and you see it unfold over the course of many, many years. It’s stunning, and I’m a massive fan.

I know people have picked this before, but Defending Your Life. Four movies that Albert Brooks did in a row, starting with Real Life, which was incredibly prescient, to Modern Romance to Lost in America to Defending Your Life, is maybe the… is a murderers' row, it's Meet the Beatles! To Sgt. Pepper. But Defending Your Life I'm picking because it might be the most high-concept comedy that I know of. And all of the performances: Rip Torn is amazing, Meryl Streep is unreal, but every single minor actor that has maybe one scene: the guy in a sushi restaurant or the comic on stage. You know, Albert Brooks uses this stable of actors. They're all perfect. He can take a joke that's hilarious and then make it even a little bit better. It's amazing to see Shirley MacLaine pop up in the Pavilion of Past Lives. But then to hear just, "Oh my God!" coming from the Wings, who thinks of that? Albert Brooks. That's why he's a genius.

Secrets & Lies. I do love Mike Leigh. I love his films. But there was a moment in this film from Timothy Spall where he has such an emotional outburst after sitting on emotions throughout a lot of the film, I thought. And when he did this, I burst into tears and I thought, "I don't know of a performance that was so restrained that just exploded." I've thought about that moment for years, and the power of restraint.

This is a concert film. It's Ryuichi Sakamoto | Opus. I must say, I actually haven't seen Opus. I have wanted to, but I wanted to bring this up because Ryuichi Sakamoto's someone I actually kind of share with my son, who is a massive fan and actually the one who really showed me the light. My son heard Last Emperor and said, "Wait a minute." And he was young. A little kid. And it kind of set him on a direction. And because of him and because of that, I then went down the Sakamoto rabbit hole, to YMO and all of the things that he did, including acting and scoring Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence. He's an exceptional artist. Everyone should know who he is. It's a tragedy that we lost him recently. But what a treasure that we get to experience him through Opus, Coda, and every other incredible piece of art that he created.

I just saw this one. Fast Times at Ridgemont High. I was, I think, maybe in sixth grade, seventh grade when I saw it. But Amy Heckerling, who I adore and made the movie Clueless, also made this, and I can't think of another person who has their finger on the pulse of what kids are going through and what they're saying. And it's easy, actually, to almost overlook how talented she is and how brilliant this movie is. People think in terms of comedy or drama, and life is all of that. And you have a scene where Sean Penn is ordering a pizza at a class, which is a big, funny sequence. And then you also have a young girl in high school getting an abortion, and this exists in the same movie. And it does so with care and dexterity and elegance that Amy Heckerling really captured. She should be doing whatever she wants.

So Hedwig and the Angry Inch. First of all, this is a drag queen staple. I actually did not know much about this movie until I moved to New York City. Shout out to my friend Adam Siciliano who actually taught me about Hedwig. He’s what they call a Hedhead. But John Cameron Mitchell kind of created this character and the New York City cabaret, theater scene. It’s been played on Broadway by, my God, Taye Diggs, Andrew Rannells, Neil Patrick Harris. Don’t know why they didn’t call me. It’s kind of crazy. But I guess I’ll take this home for a little bit of research purposes.

film_title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling
catalog_title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling
quote: So, okay, I do not know this one. Let me read this real quick. “One of the greatest comedians of all time, Richard Pryor” – I guess we agree on that – “gets raw and real in this brutally funny and lacerating self-portrait, following the notorious incident in which he caught on fire while high on cocaine, nearly losing his life.” Well, sign me up. Hook, line, and sinker. I’ve been doing stand-up comedy for 17 years and I don’t think there’s a comedian who has not been inspired by Richard Pryor. He’s been in everything from musicals, The Wiz, to, apparently, Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling. I don’t do cocaine, but if you do, go to your bathroom right now and flush it. And I know it’s expensive. You’ll get the money back.

Okay, I have Pee-wee’s Big Adventure. I don’t know if you know this, but Pee-wee Herman didn’t actually start as a kids’ show. It started as, like, a live theater thing that was actually for adults, and then somehow it morphed and it made its way to my desk as a small child. Contributed so much to the culture. Paul Reubens, wherever you are, I don’t know what you believe, but much love to you.

The movie Network. Have you ever seen those things online where they’re like… they take a monologue and then they overlay what’s happening right now? The fact that this movie came out in 1976 and the stuff they’re saying in this film makes even more sense today is sign that progress is slow, if at all. “The moral arc of the universe is long, but it bends towards justice.” Will we all be there for the justice? I don’t know. I probably won’t. I’m probably older than some of you watching this, but I’m definitely younger than some of you.

Okay, this is actually a really controversial movie because it was kind of a flop in its time, but it ended up being a cult classic. Diana Ross was cast as Dorothy in The Wiz, which is kind of crazy because Dorothy’s, like, a 16-year-old girl, Stephanie Mills was actually pretty young when she did… Is this, like, the butchest lean you’ve ever seen? But yeah, I mean, this movie, it’s got Michael Jackson, it’s got Nipsey Russell, it’s got Diana Ross, it’s got Mabel. There’s so many amazing actors in this film. Quincy Jones did a lot of the music for this. This is an absolutely brilliant, brilliant film. Richard Pryor! Richard Pryor’s in the bag twice. Okay, good.

Okay. A Black gay guy chose Paris is Burning. Shocker. That being said. What ended up happening to the subjects, like, a lot of them died in abject poverty. This movie has secrets that aren’t even revealed in the movie. There is actually a dead body in this movie, and they didn’t even know there was a dead body in the movie, which is crazy. Do you know about this? One of the main subjects of the film actually killed a man by her own admission, through a note that she wrote. And then she mummified his body using pleather and put it inside of a trunk in her closet, and it was there till the day she died. And the body had been missing for, I think, 20 or 30 years. There’s a note that said stuff like, “This poor soul tried to rob me.” Her name is Dorian Corey. And it has one of my favorite quotes of all time, which is: “If you shoot an arrow and it goes real high, hooray for you.” You don’t have to bend the world to make a change. You change the world just by existing and living through it. This movie really changed the way that queer people speak. It changed the way that ballroom was respected. It changed the way that Black and brown people are seen, through creativity and expression and culture-making. Paris is Burning is probably one of the most important films of all time.

Now, this is something I remember very well as a kid. Cooley High was a staple for us, especially Army kids. We loved this film and it was a hit. The other one that was a huge hit was Mother, Jugs & Speed, around the same time, and Car Wash. So I will be grabbing that.

Moonage Daydream. Of course, I’m wearing David Bowie today, and I’m going to be doing a David Bowie tour this year in Australia, so I have to get Moonage Daydream, which I still haven’t seen. I know I’m supposed to see it in IMAX, but this is just as good or next best.

I should get my favorite musical, really, which is All That Jazz by Bob Fosse. The film probably most responsible for the freedom of style in the Hedwig film was this film, Bob Fosse, an autobiographical classic.

You know, I never saw Multiple Maniacs. I think I need to get that one because John Waters is a friend and I feel terrible I haven’t seen this. He feels terrible that people have to watch it. He always jokes about grandma saying, “I love your work.” And he’s like, “Did you see Multiple Maniacs?”

A great film by Kore-eda, a Japanese filmmaker who I met right after this film. He loved Hedwig. He was a little bit scared of Shortbus. But recently I met him and Noah Cowan, our friend who ran the Toronto Film Festival, passed away, and I was there when someone told Kore-eda that the last film that Noah wanted to watch was a film that he helped, which was this. And Kore-eda just started weeping, A beautiful film about a possible afterlife that really is a metaphor for filmmaking. So I’ll definitely be taking After Life home, which will prepare me for my impending end.

This is Shampoo. Now, this is a classic ’70s comedy. Funny as hell. I find the women funnier than Warren Beatty, but that’s just me. Julie Christie, Goldie Hawn, Lee Grant, brilliant. Also, the great Jack Warden. I love Jack Warden.
My own film. I really don’t know what to do with that. Actually, I need an extra copy. Ha! We are independent filmmakers, after all.

Network, which is the world we live in now. Sidney Lumet’s one of my tops, along with Altman and Cassavetes. And people forget about Lumet. He worked in very different styles. He came from the theater. But people like you to do the same style. It’s called a brand. But we theater people change depending on what the subject matter or the script is. And this is a perfect example of a highly theatrical screenplay done brilliantly.

And then the last one, Pee-wee’s Big Adventure. Combination of two geniuses, Paul Reubens and Tim Burton, making something absolutely unique, and yet somehow weirdly familiar, with a little bit of B-52s thrown in, maybe. And queer undertones. Just so damn good. And I can’t wait to see the extras on here, too.

film_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
catalog_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
quote: I might have to get The Wes Anderson Archive, which is like a boom box of things, with the great Rushmore, of course.
box_set_name: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years

quote: The Cassavetes box set. I mean, the greatest independent filmmaker in America ever. And probably my favorite film ever is A Woman Under the Influence. There’s also an incredible doc about– like, a three-hour doc about how he worked, which was very singular, with the great Gena Rowlands, maybe the best film actress of all time.

All right, Pasolini, a queer icon, an intellectual icon, a Marxist icon in Italy. So moving, The Gospel According to Matthew. He was Catholic, but in the deepest way that is much closer to socialism, when you think about it. And that film– I remember Lazarus coming out of the tomb to the sound of an old American ancient blues song, and it somehow worked. Teorema, one of my favorite films, with Terence Stamp playing a guy who seduces everyone in a Milan family, and to their chagrin. Of course, Mamma Roma, the great Anna Magnani. Brilliant performance. Yeah, so this is great.

First one is All About Eve. I saw this when I was, like, a pre-teen and was just blown away by the intelligent way they spoke. The dialogue is unbelievable. My funniest line in this, to me, and this is my sense of humor. Anne Baxter is Eve. Do I have to tell you what the movie’s about? All About Eve. Bette Davis is a theater actress who feels like she’s aging out of ingenue roles. That’s not true in the theater because it’s so far away. You could be my age and playing 20, I think. Anyway, Anne Baxter is a young, up-and-coming actress that everyone just adores, and she turns out to be a big, fat liar. So, George Sanders plays Addison DeWitt, a critic. She gets mad at him because he threatens her with some– you know, exposing her as a fake. And she just says, “Get out!” Really theatrical. “Get out!” And he just says, “You’re too short for that gesture.” It’s so easy to hurt people without hurting them. That’s what I got out of it. Anyway, it’s really good.

Right next to it. Okay. It’s Now, Voyager. This was my mother’s favorite movie. She told me. So, I made sure and watched it. And, again, it’s Bette Davis, who was one of the most interesting women. Really strong. Just sort of knew who she was and put that in all of her characters. It was really important to see, I thought. I also thought, when I was young, “What happened to women?” Isn’t that funny? They had barely any rights. Right? Not barely. I mean, they could vote. Just. And I thought, “Wow, they’re so much stronger.” That’s how it felt. And then, of course, I started on Friends, went out to the Stage 24, when we were on that stage, and looked at the plaque at Warner Brothers, and they shot some stuff from Now, Voyager, it was on the plaque, and I was so excited to tell my mom. Yeah, that was thrilling. Private Benjamin shot there, too, and that was exciting.

Another important movie for me when I was young: Philadelphia Story, Katharine Hepburn, Cary Grant. I mean, talk about just throwing lines away. They were so effortless, while performing, but effortless and sharp, bright dialogue. And also just what it’s about was really interesting to me. And every time I saw it, I sort of changed my mind depending on who I was. But that’s art, right? Depending on who you are when you’re experiencing it, you have a different experience. So love this. You have to see this. Come on! Katharine Hepburn was in the play and she needed to boost her career, so smarty-pants optioned it to make it a movie and got George Cukor to direct it. That’s a big deal. Phenomenal. Everyone’s great.

This movie, Defending Your Life, Albert Brooks. I had already seen Modern Romance. Fantastic. Right, that was before this? Yeah, yeah, that was before this. He did Real Life, which was one of the first mockumentaries. Thank you, Albert. But anyway, Defending Your Life, with Meryl Streep, no less. Another one where, every time I see this movie, I realize something different. There are some things that a writer, it comes into them and gets expressed. And this movie has a lot of insight, I think, into how the universe works, in a way. Fear is the opposite of love and the cure for fear is love. So it’s a fearful guy, so afraid of himself, and it isn’t until he surrenders to love that he can get where he’s going. As if it’s a big mystery and surprise, “You’ll see!” Yeah, you probably have already seen it, because who hasn’t?

When I was a kid, I saw 12 Angry Men on TV. Phenomenal actors. And it was a play, and it’s all shot, basically, in a jury room. And one juror who’s the holdout, Henry Fonda, who’s pointing out to everybody, “You’re making some biased decisions. Not all the evidence adds up.” And so everyone’s getting so mad at him. It’s really hot. They’ve got something else. No one really even wants to be there. For me, it really, really highlighted the fact that, ooh, juries are problematic and might not always get a fair trial. Anyway, 12 Angry Men, so good and true.

And the first one that did is this movie by Jim Jarmusch, Down by Law. "I scream, you scream, we all scream for ice cream," the famous Roberto Benigni line. But also this was in the early days of my obsession with Tom Waits when I was in college, that's when I discovered Tom's music, and he's such a good actor. And you can tell he's improvising these weather reports from the prison cell, and it's just a real formative movie for me. I'm still trying to get in a Jim Jarmusch movie. No luck so far, but at least we have this movie. I saw it at the Biograph Theater in Chicago on Lincoln Avenue, and that one's going in here.

film_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
catalog_title: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie
quote: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie by John Cassavetes. Timothy Carey, one of the great, bizarre character actors. He was in Stanley Kubrick's The Killing. Anyway, he plays one of the goons, and there's this whole showdown scene where he's been assigned the job to kill Ben Gazzara, and he starts to get the sense, "This guy is tougher than I realize. This guy…" And then Ben Gazzara's sort of like, "Get out of here, man. You're an amateur." This is just a great, great movie. And it's also kind of a travelogue of Los Angeles.

This one's kind of random. I haven't seen this movie since it came out in the theater when I was a child, and I snuck into the movie theater, the Marquette Theatre on the Southwest Side of Chicago, which is no longer there, to see David Cronenberg's The Brood. It really upset me. A woman has a… she bites open this embryonic sac and these babies– these monster babies come out. Anyway, terrifying movie. That weird moment. Be careful what movies you sneak into, kids. I also saw Jaws way too young. Way too young. It made me afraid of the bathtub.

So, moving right along to some comedy: this movie, Defending Your Life by Albert Brooks, might be the hardest I have ever laughed in a movie. I was laughing so hard I thought… it felt like I was tripping on mushrooms. All of it, from top to bottom, is– it's just a brilliant, brilliant movie. And Albert Brooks is one of the all-time American greats of comedy.

On the Waterfront, by Elia Kazan. Of course, one of the canon, right. I went to boys' Catholic high school, and we had this whole year of junior year where they would show us movies that had ethical issues, and then we would discuss afterwards. I remember seeing Billy Budd and Rebecca and On the Waterfront. I pick it out because it's one of the great misreadings of lines in history. So Rod Steiger and Marlon Brando are in the back of the car, right, and he says… The misconception is the line goes like this: "I could have been somebody, Charley." But what he actually says in the movie is: "I could have been somebody, Charley." It makes me cry because it's, like, "My life could have had meaning." And began probably my lifelong love of Karl Malden. Every time Karl Malden showed up, you knew he was going to be standing on the side of righteousness, and when he stands up for the people on that waterfront, it's a beautiful thing.

All right, one more. Like, a nostalgia movie, okay? And that is The Great Escape. It makes you punk rock, this movie. It teaches you how to resist the system. How do you… What do you have to do to trick the guards? And I kind of took that through my whole life, growing up on the South Side of Chicago and going to Catholic school. And Steve McQueen in this one, it's just one of the all-time great performances. It's full of amazing actors, actually. Donald Pleasence is so great in it. And it's just got that catchy… It's got a very catchy theme song.
Oh, Grey Gardens. That is a great– That’s a great one, just as an observation of humanity alone. Worth a look. But not on my list.

Oh! This is my number one: Withnail and I. As an actor – it’s about two out-of-work actors, and obviously that’s something I can relate to very easily. Bruce Robinson himself was an actor, and a lot of this– a lot of his life is in this movie. I would hasten to say that it is Richard E. Grant’s finest film performance. And the beautiful Paul McGann. The two of them together are as heartbreaking as they are hilarious. But Richard Griffiths as Uncle Monty, with some of the most quotable lines you will ever find in a beautifully made picture. In you go, my dearest thing.

Now, where would I find – hang on – The Princess Bride? This is probably the film that I have watched most. It was a great point of honor for me to show this to my son about a year ago. And what I delight… Excuse me, I’m getting emotional. What I delight in the fact was that his ability to pick up the right quotes from the entire film left me with one of the greatest senses of pride I’ve ever, ever felt. It transports you, enchants you. It makes you cry and laugh. It thrills. It has real intrigue. You’re forever going, “What is going to happen now?” I would say a perfectly made film, and I don’t often say that. Inconceivable.

Now then, where would I find Do the Right Thing? How could I miss it? Ooh, Spartacus. “I’m Spartacus.” See, this is very difficult. All of a sudden you get sidetracked. Sid & Nancy, another classic. Traffic, of course. But I am going to stick to my guns on this one, and I’ll tell you why. As a young boy growing up in Wales, I just remember it felt like I was being slapped around the face the first time I saw it and just introduced to a world I had no idea of. And that’s what great films should do, and it did. And it was this introduction to Spike Lee’s Brooklyn or America that made me… made me want to come here, certainly made me want to come to Brooklyn. I fell in love with Rosie Perez, and I kind of still am. But keep that to yourselves. 1989. I am clearly a child of the ’80s. Two ’87s and an ’89.

This being one of them. That was another one. In the same way that Do the Right Thing blew my head off, that blew my head off, because I went, “You mean people make films like this? Who made this?” A man called Martin Scorsese. What’s incredible about Mean Streets, now that you have his body of work, is to kind of begin here and keep going through and then finish with the documentary about him. That is a real treat. A time commitment, but one not misspent. Like a religious icon. You should take it. No, I won’t. I can’t. I shan’t. I want to hand it on to some younger kid, throw that in his bag or her bag and say, “Watch this.”

♪ The babe called Brian ♪ Another movie that I mercilessly destroyed, a VCR tape, rewatching and rewatching and rewatching. Also a movie in my formative years. My family back home in Wales went, “Would you please, for the love of God, stop quoting Life of Brian?” There’s one glorious moment when the Roman centurions have to search a house and then they all come out and they go, “Did you find anything?” And he goes, “We found this spoon.” And my mother went, “If you say that line one more time, I will take that spoon and club you to death with it.” And also directed by Terry Jones, a Welshman. The only Welsh Python. Was he? Yes, the only Welsh Python. So we take great pride in this. Classic.

So I’m torn about my final because two great classics, obviously. I have a friend who says, “I hope to one day lose my memory so I can watch The Great Escape every day and not know how it’ll end.” It’s a remarkable piece of filmmaking as well. And it’s worth it just to see McQueen on a motorbike alone. However, good old Dickie Attenborough is also in The Great Escape. Another of the true great filmmakers. So… I’m about to escape this small closet with a great classic in the form of The Great Escape.

However, twenty-five years– twenty-seven years ago, I did a stage version of The Graduate in London’s West End with Kathleen Turner, and I played Benjamin Braddock. Obviously, I watched… foolishly, watched this film a lot prior to making that in the vain attempt that I would somehow imbue the magic of Dustin Hoffman, and maybe it just turned into a poor impersonation, I don’t know. But I’ve always loved, well, almost everything of Mike Nichols. I shall put The Graduate back.
I will start here with Tampopo. The egg? Crazy.

I’m seeing this here. Paper Moon. Peter Bogdanovich, Mr. Swag. Mr. Glasses and Scarf. Kind of an icon. Yeah, I love this movie. It’s incredibly heartwarming, and I feel like I, as sort of a– kind of disgusting phrase to say, but daddy’s girl. Sorry. It’s, like, I love my dad, and so this is a movie that is kind of about loving your dad. Shout out to you, Dad.

Thelma & Louise. Ever heard of it? Look at this art right here. Is this a Criterion…? Yes. Exclusive art right here. Shout out to Susan Sarandon, the god, by the way. Oh my God, Geena Davis. Schwing! This is, like, a beautiful love story about female friendship, and… Hey, look, I’m familiar with that.

Hey, look, I’m familiar with that. The Philadelphia Story. Cary Grant was on my dorm-room wall, and I held up his black-and-white photo with a Bernie Sanders bumper sticker. You want to know about me? There it is. There it is.

This reminds me of my favorite Cary Grant performance, which is His Girl Friday, which I didn’t know was here but is here, and it was plucked for me by my friends here at Criterion. “Give it here, Svengali!” I love these freaks and the way that they talk. Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell, comedic geniuses. Two of my absolute– on Mount Rushmore, no question. This is extremely Hacks-coded in that they bond… their love is connected to their work and their work together, and their work also gets in the way of their love. But they still do love each other and they can’t quit each other. The two Cary Grant hits right here. Freaking awesome.

film_title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders
catalog_title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders
quote: Okay, so Valerie and Her Week of Wonders is, like, really a nightmare. It’s really scary and disorienting and surreal and freaky in a way that is so Eastern European. Watching this movie made me reflect on my experience of being a young girl and being sexualized externally before I in any way identified with my own sexuality, that perhaps I hadn’t totally processed or thought about, and so I think that’s good for a movie to, yeah, make you kind of do that, in addition to just being visually unbelievably dazzling. And I’m so happy to have it.

This is Crash by David Cronenberg. I believe that this film should be played on the floor of the US Senate. I think it could help people to expand their minds and understand that they’re wasting so much time trying to tame the untamable, which is the human being and their liberation. Just watch this and don’t feel weird about your shit, basically, I think. You know what I’m saying? Consent, and then you’re rocking. You know what I mean?

Lost Highway. Something that’s really beautiful about… about cinema, in my opinion, is it can change the way that you view the world. For instance, David Lynch changed the way I see roses. And I’m a proud Los Angeleno, I’m born and raised in Los Angeles, third generation, and I feel like David Lynch loves LA in a way that I think is so cool. I think people like to hate on LA. But LA rocks hard, and Lost Highway’s scary. My brother Spike showed it to me. Spike’s fiancé was the guy with the camera for Halloween, and it was really scary accurate. Maybe when this comes out I’ll post a pic of Eric in that.

Defending Your Life rocks. There’s a scene in a comedy club in that movie, and it’s shot at The Comedy Store, and having started at The Comedy Store as a stand-up comedian before I was ever an actor, yeah, that’s what purgatory’s like, okay? I can tell you it is on the way to hell. This movie makes me laugh and makes me feel really warm. And Meryl Streep is a god, and so is Albert Brooks.

Oh, one thing that I know is in the Collection and I do want to mention, and I asked about it and I guess it’s not yet in print, is High Art, which, if you like Bound and you’re sad and gay or both, you would really love High Art. And so I just want to say honorable mention to High Art.

The Before Trilogy. You know sometimes when a film is a poisonous mirror and you look at it and you’re like, “No!” It is a bisexual text. I don’t feel like I need to elaborate on that. That should be… The reasons why that’s true, I think, are evident if you’ve seen this stuff.

And… with Face in the Crowd. It’s the most wonderfully insightful insight on celebrity and the cult of celebrity and Andy Griffith, who you’d probably only know from The Andy Griffith Show, playing small-town sheriff of Mayberry, you have no idea the depth and breadth of this man’s talent, and he puts it all on display in this movie. His character of Lonesome Rhodes is one of the great film characters of all time. Absolutely love this movie. Going in the bag.

Forty Guns, Sam Fuller, starring Barbara Stanwyck at her most ferocious. Sam Fuller, for those of you who don’t know, is one of the most resourceful filmmakers. This guy could stretch a dollar farther than anybody. There’s a great story I heard from an actor named Perry Lang once, who was in a movie of his called The Big Red One, and he said to Sam Fuller, “Sam, I saw Steel Helmet the other day and it still holds up.” And Sam Fuller said, “Griffith Park, eight days,” which is how long it took him to shoot it and where he shot it. Forty Guns has got a great opening shot of literally these 40 gunmen riding past the camera on their way to do Barbara Stanwyck’s bidding.

Repo Man, Alex Cox. This made a huge impression on me when it came out, like it did a lot of young men. I saw Emilio Estevez in this movie and I saw the sort of irreverence of the humor and the punk-rock vibe to it and just thought, aesthetically, this is so me. Love this movie.

Eating Raoul, directed by the great late Paul Bartel, also a dear family friend. Wonderful black comedy, highly recommended. Almost got me suspended from high school when I accidentally had the misfortune of recommending that they show it during Arts Week at my high school.

Speaking of people that I knew, my stepmother’s father was John Sturges, the great film director, and this is one of his great movies. If you haven’t seen The Great Escape, John Sturges was one of the great directors of male ensemble movies. He did The Magnificent Seven and he did The Eagle Has Landed and he did Ice Station Zebra and he did The Great Escape. True story about a POW escape from World War Two. Highly recommend it. And has that famous motorcycle jump that Steve McQueen does over the barbed-wire fence, which was really Bud Ekins, terrific stunt driver.

’Round Midnight. Dexter Gordon, and takes place in Paris at the end of this fictitious musician’s life and it’s about a young Frenchman and his daughter who befriend him and have a real appreciation for his life and music. Just a really wonderful movie.

Seconds. This is sort of a science-fiction movie. It’s really– I think it’s John Randolph who wants to get remade over and he becomes Rock Hudson. So it’s an older man going through a procedure to become a younger man, and it was shot by James Wong Howe, who is one of the great cinematographers of all time, so the photography’s really excellent. And it includes this really crazy scene where he’s out stomping grapes and sort of discovering his youth and sexuality again. It’s really quite wonderful. James Wong Howe, also the DP of Sweet Smell of Success and Hud, I believe.

These two are really great. Which one do we start with? Let’s start with Trouble in Paradise. For those of you that don’t know the great Ernst Lubitsch, this is one of his most sophisticated comedies. This stars the great Herbert Marshall, who is so dryly wonderful in this movie, and Miriam Hopkins, and they both are competing pickpockets who meet trying to basically con the other, and it turns into a great love story. And then the two of them go off and try to enter into the big con. But the dialogue is so witty, as is all Lubitsch dialogue. And the Lubitsch touch, how do you describe it? There’s an opening shot in this movie that takes place in Venice, Italy, and you could open a movie in Venice, Italy, anywhere. You could open it on the Grand Canal. You could open it on the end of a gondola. You could open it anywhere to recognize it. He opens it with garbage being dumped into a garbage scow in the back side of a hotel. So he takes you to the most unromantic place to enter into the most romantic of stories. That’s the Lubitsch touch.

film_title: The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp
catalog_title: The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp
quote: Life and Death of Colonel Blimp. This is one of my favorite movies. I saw this movie not that long ago and I was so knocked out by how contemporary the cinematography felt, how sharp the dialogue felt. I just thought sometimes you come across an old movie that holds up so beautifully because it speaks to a contemporary rhythm, and I highly recommend this one, it really does.

Documentary. Or is it? F for Fake. This is Orson Welles’s break with traditional form, unabashedly taking an audience on quite an adventure. You go to Ibiza, Spain, you get to learn about art forgery, you get to learn about the guy that forged Hitler’s diaries, and you get this unbelievable story about Picasso, which I won’t ruin for you, but F for Fake is terrific.

As is Pickup on South Street. I love this movie. We’re back to Sam Fuller again. This stars Richard Widmark as a pickpocket. As you can tell, I like movies about pickpockets, I guess. This guy inadvertently picks the pocket of a woman who has some microfilm in it that is being sold to the Commies. This is high Red Scare, Cold War-era drama. Thelma Ritter. I don’t know if she was nominated for this or not, but she gives one of the most heartbreaking performances. She plays a woman who sort of gives information to the police, and her cover is that she’s a tie salesman. She sells neckties. And there’s the last scene in this movie where she… I’m not going to ruin it for you, but it’s her last scene and she will break your heart with that.

Medium Cool, speaking of documentaries that aren’t really documentaries. It’s a great time capsule of Chicago in 1968, and a wonderful sort of coincidence of events, where they’re making a movie about making a movie and then the events that they are depicting actually become more intense and more explosive than they anticipate. Riots are actually breaking out during the Democratic National Convention and they’re there filming it. And that great chant, “The whole world is watching. The whole world is watching,” comes from the end of this movie, as this is all being put on display for the world to see.

This Sporting Life, Lindsay Anderson. It follows the rise and fall of a professional athlete, in this case a rugby player, and it’s just blistering. The performance is so raw. Richard Harris is so young and dangerous and unpredictable in this movie. And he had a really interesting relationship with Lindsay Anderson, and the two of them made some unbelievable things together, but this is my favorite by far.

Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence. Nagisa Oshima. This movie knocked me on my butt. It’s about British POW… prisoners of war in a Japanese prison camp. Came out in 1983, and the soundtrack is Ryuichi Sakamoto, who we just lost a couple of years ago, and I used to play that thing over and over and over and over again. I thought it was so beautiful. David Bowie gives a great performance in this. If you don’t know Tom Conti’s work from Reuben, Reuben or so many other great films, he’s just wonderful. This made a huge impression on me. Definitely worth watching.

This is a terrific documentary Terry Zwigoff made about the animator R. Crumb, Robert Crumb, who was extremely popular back in the ’60s. His cartoons made it into… You know, Fritz the Cat and his animation. He did the cover art for, I believe, Janis Joplin’s Cheap Thrills album. Fascinating guy from a fascinating family, and this is like Grey Gardens in a way. It’s a look into his upbringing and into what informed his art and his style, which is very specific, including his kinks and peccadilloes, and really a kind of honest look at an artist.

Last Picture Show. You almost have to watch this movie just to see Cloris Leachman’s performance and the performance of Ben Johnson and Ellen Burstyn. Those three in particular will kill you. Ben Johnson will kill you as Sam the Lion. I just love this movie, and I love that performance, almost– I’d put that up against just about anything.

I wasn’t going to talk about him because apparently everybody talks about him, but John Cassavetes’s Shadows. There’s a great story that I heard about this movie, that he shot in the location that was underneath Arthur Murray’s Dance Studio, and so the sound was terrible. It kept getting all this noise bleed, and he spent all this money trying to clean up those soundtracks and was ultimately unable to clean up the sound, and so they had to release it as was. And one of the earliest reviews praised it for having one of the most authentic sound designs in cinema history. So a good lesson to all you young filmmakers out there that sometimes the happy accident is the thing that makes it special.

film_title: A Whit Stillman Trilogy: Metropolitan, Barcelona, The Last Days of Disco
quote: For those of you that… that don’t mind a little glimpse into upper Manhattan, this trilogy – Metropolitan, Last Days of Disco, and Barcelona – I just find them to be like candy. The dialogue is so perfect. The characterizations are so specific. It’s such a razor-sharp look at a particular time and place, done with a really deft touch. It’s very elegantly done. It’s sort of… I don’t know how to describe it other than to say when I watch – especially Metropolitan and Barcelona – they just feel like… like home movies of a time that I wasn’t in and people that I didn’t know that I felt like I could have known. That says probably more about me than it will about you, but I hope you enjoy them nonetheless. I’m going to enjoy watching them again.
box_set_name: A Whit Stillman Trilogy: Metropolitan, Barcelona, The Last Days of Disco

quote: [Translated] I'll start with a Spanish film that I feel needs to be vindicated, which is up here. It's El Sur, by Víctor Erice. I think Víctor Erice is a master and he's one of the main reasons why I make films. People always talk about The Spirit of the Beehive but I think El Sur also deserves a mention. It's a beautiful film, with incredible photography. Especially the relationship with the father, that mystery of the father... I think it really speaks to how children see the world.

[Translated] Here's another film that deserves more attention: Wanda, by Barbara Loden. Unfortunately, it's the only film that this director made. She was the wife of Elia Kazan. For me, it's about seeing someone— she plays the lead because she was an actress— Seeing someone manage to just be in front of the camera. Watching this movie, you feel like you know this woman in all of her complexity, and in all her fragility. I think it's a deeply feminist film, and it's one of the stories that truly made me think about what feminism really is, and where it can be approached from.

[Translated] There's another film up there that fascinates me, which is Walkabout by Nicolas Roeg. This film, which I think is from the 70s— there was a lot of experimentation in the 70s, so the editing in this film is crazy. It's an incredible story about an encounter in the desert between two characters from very different worlds. Well, three, actually, because there's also a child. I don't know, I found it fascinating. I actually discovered it very recently. My editor recommended it to me.

[Translated] There's a lot of very interesting Italian Neorealism here. And since it's always been a great influence for me, I'll try to choose one, although it's hard. Umberto D. I think it's a beautiful film. Actually, I really like everything Vittorio De Sica does, but this film is so tender, and I think it expresses very well the whole spirit of Neorealism, and of Italian films of that period.

[Translated] Well, since we're in Italy, I'm going to pick up this masterpiece, which is Ermanno Olmi's The Tree of Wooden Clogs. This film mesmerizes me. It talks about rural life in a beautiful way. It's filmed throughout the seasons, and it's also an ensemble film, with a lot of characters. I think it's very beautiful.

[Translated] Actually, there's a film here that I saw very recently... I saw it earlier... And I think it's like a sister film to The Tree of Wooden Clogs. It's this one: Vermiglio, by Maura Delpero. It's about what happens during the war in the villages — what happens to women, especially. How they experienced the war, from their homes and villages. It's shot in the Alps, and I recommend it as well.

[Translated] Another film I consider a masterpiece, is Beau travail, by Claire Denis. I'm passionate about Claire Denis, but among her films, this is one that affected me the most. There's something about the way she relates to the male body, in particular, and this sensuality that she sees in all of her characters, that I think is really fascinating. And that last dance scene... I think it's also really epic.

[Translated] Another director who's been recommended me, though I haven't seen her movies— and it's wonderful that I can discover them in a box set— is Mai Zetterling. Well, this is the perfect opportunity to meet her.

I wasn’t planning on picking this one, but I’m just going to choose the movies I really love and Tootsie, motherfucking Tootsie. It doesn’t get better. Has music ever contributed as much to a movie? It would be great without the music, but that score—I still listen to it. I listen to… there’s a song on the soundtrack which is, like, ♪ Go, Tootsie, go ♪ and she’s marching through the streets of Manhattan. It’s this very ’80s shot of Dustin Hoffman in drag marching, and I will listen to that as I walk around Manhattan thinking about, “Maybe I’m Tootsie.”

Moonstruck. Boy, this is a movie that made me fall in love with movies. This is a movie that made me say, “I want to make magical, romantic, uplifting, funny, human things.” And God damn it, why isn’t Cher acting? That really pisses me off.

The Fisher King. If you had asked me what the best movie ever made was when I was 13, I would have said The Fisher King. I used to analyze all the Best Actor and Best Actress nominees. I wrote a long analysis as a child about, even though I knew Anthony Hopkins was going to win, that if I were voting, I would have voted for Robin Williams in The Fisher King. I thought it was the greatest performance I’d ever seen. It’s very of its time, but I loved revisiting this movie.

I am going to probably be… Well, I don’t know this for a fact, but I don’t know how many people have walked into the Criterion Closet and chosen Barbra Streisand’s The Prince of Tides. Barbra has always been like a North Star for me, and I think for anyone at all unconventional trying to make it in show business, because she was the epitome of unconventional when she started and she succeeded in every way. And the more she tried to branch out, when she went from a singer to actress and then director, screenwriter, producer, and star, like in this movie, the more flak she got. And yet she did it. She stayed true to the courage of her convictions. I went to see The Prince of Tides with my parents, and I would… at the Continental 3 movie theater in Forest Hills, and I remember that the weekend it came out, we couldn’t wait to see– Everyone else was like, “Oh, The Silence of the Lambs.” There was a countdown in my house until The Prince of Tides came out. This movie had a lot of feeling and a lot of romance, and it doesn’t end with a big, tidy bow and a happy ending, but it makes you feel something. It stays with you. And I think today we’re a little bit afraid of leaning into that old type of sweeping, glamorous, tortured Hollywood romance, right? And I miss that and I love it, so proud to recommend The Prince of Tides.

This is a movie that means a lot to me: My Beautiful Laundrette. This stars a young Daniel Day-Lewis, before he was a really big star, and it’s about him having a gay relationship, a gay romance, with a younger, closeted Pakistani man in London. I am eight years old at that point and my aunt said, “You should watch My Beautiful Laundrette,” because we had read about it. It had gotten good reviews. Stephen Frears directed it, the great Stephen Frears. I do believe it ends up getting nominated for Best Original Screenplay at the Oscars. So it wasn’t an obscure film, but it was definitely an art-house film and a rare gay film to get as much attention as it did at the time. And my parents, Jay and Debbie Eichner, they went along with everything I wanted to do. They let me watch very adult things, and I don’t mean pornographic, obviously, I mean sophisticated things that were about adults that weren’t intended for kids necessarily. And I said to my dad, one Saturday afternoon in 1986, I said, “I want to watch My Beautiful Laundrette,” and we went to our local video store, Video Joe, up the block, in Queens, and we rented My Beautiful Laundrette on VHS, around the same time as we were celebrating the 1986 New York Mets winning the World Series, because they played near our apartment, and we watched this gay film and we loved it. And my dad treated it like any other film. There was no special conversation about it. There was no discomfort around it at all. And not to make a shameless plug for my book, but it’s really… I wrote my book because it’s a tribute to my parents, because they always, always, always, going way back, let me be me, and that gave me as a gay kid, coming of age, a real confidence and a self respect that I wish all gay kids had, and part of that was exposing me to movies like this and, like I said, treating it like any other movie. And I’m so happy it’s here because it had a real impact on my life.

film_title: A Whit Stillman Trilogy: Metropolitan, Barcelona, The Last Days of Disco
catalog_title: A Whit Stillman Trilogy: Metropolitan, Barcelona, The Last Days of Disco
quote: Metropolitan. I grew up in New York City. This came out when I was a teenager and really getting into movies, and I wasn’t ready for Metropolitan when I was a kid because it’s a bit muted, you know? It’s really sophisticated and chic, but on a different level. Now I love it. And the movie that Whit Stillman made, which I saw – I saw all of these in the theater – that I finally said, “Okay, I get this,” because I had gotten a little older, was Last Days of Disco. They have it. They have it. It’s a whole Whit Stillman box set. These are really wonderful movies to revisit. Not that Whit Stillman needs to hear that from me.
box_set_name: A Whit Stillman Trilogy: Metropolitan, Barcelona, The Last Days of Disco

quote: And I wanted to talk about My Life as a Dog. Directed by Lasse Hallström. And I happen to speak Swedish, so I watched it in Swedish. The Swedish title is Mitt liv som hund. So I love this, such a good movie. I forgot. I can just put it in my bag. Yes!

I’m a huge Elaine May fan, so I found this movie that she wrote and directed called Mikey and Nicky. I’m excited to see this because I never have seen it, but I adore Elaine May and I’m very much looking forward to this.

Only I can reach the top shelf in the Criterion Closet. This is His Girl Friday. I’m sure you’ve heard of this and maybe you’ve seen it. A classic. It’s so fabulous, and Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell. Love it. Love it so much. And all that sharp language they had in those movies back then. That’s going in my bag.

I found another classic movie, which I have right here, which is Some Like It Hot. If you haven’t seen this, you have to see it. It’s directed by Billy Wilder and it’s got Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon and Marilyn Monroe. What could be better? So funny and fabulous. So high energy. I love these old movies.

And then finally, I might get this movie. I don’t know. Little thing called Thelma & Louise. Great cover. But it’s got all the extra stuff in here, right? All kinds of fabulous behind the scenes and commentary and everything, so ought to check this out.

Look at that cover, Time Bandits. Terry Gilliam was one of the Monty Python crew, team. Still is, I guess. It’s not a club that you leave. And Time Bandits I think was probably the first film of his I saw. It’s just got this extraordinary imagination. There’s just nothing really like it. It sees the world through Terry Gilliam’s brain, which is fascinating and very pleasing. Some great performances in this. David Warner I remember being very good. Sean Connery. That’s right, Sean Connery’s in it. Ralph Richardson. Ian Holm. Anyway, a great film.

This, The Importance of Being Earnest. I’ve always loved this play. I’m probably never going to be in it now. I’m a little bit too old. This, I suppose, is the… was kind of the acme of productions of it. It’s got the famous line, “A handbag?” Edith Evans delivering that famous Oscar Wilde line and having it captured forever on film. Michael Redgrave as well, right? A perfect telling of a great bit of writing.

His Girl Friday. Cary Grant, there’s something sort of otherworldly about Cary Grant. You can’t imagine he was a human being who walked amongst us. He was the perfect, ultimate movie star, and he just did his thing. He didn’t ever do anything else, really. He just was Cary Grant. His characters had names that weren’t Cary Grant, but he was always Cary Grant and it was a glorious thing to witness. He was like a sort of perfect cocktail. And him and Rosalind Russell in this movie are two perfect cocktails.

12 Angry Men might be my very favorite film of all time. I remember – I would have been 16, maybe – and this came on the TV at Christmas time, late one night, my parents had gone to bed and I sat and watched this film, not really knowing anything about it, and being absolutely enthralled. So it’s about the mechanics of an actual case, which is fascinating in itself, but then, of course, it’s also about all our inbuilt prejudices. It’s about relationships between father and children. Henry Fonda is magnificent, glorious. Titanic performance. Lee J. Cobb. That’s him. It’s one of the great… great performances of all time. But they all are. Just like when I was 16, if you’ve never seen this, give yourself a treat. It will transport you.

David Lean Directs Noël Coward. So there’s… Oh, there’s four movies on here. Brief Encounter is probably the one that I am most excited about here. It’s a love story, and it’s about people having an affair, an illicit affair. And yet all told through the micro-gestures and moments of eyes darting, hands touching. Beautifully shot. The sumptuousness of the black and whites and the billowing steam from the train engines, and just as a study of humanity, it’s a really beautiful film. Surprisingly subtle and intelligent and… But then it’s David Lean, so maybe it’s not that surprising.

Now. A box set here of Olivier’s three Shakespeare adaptations. As a drama student, these are the kind of things you kind of think, “Well, what… what did the greatest Shakespearean actor of all time, how did he do it? What were his choices?” Obviously, they are slightly from a different time. Expectations about acting were slightly different, and Olivier himself was a kind of grand man of the theater. So these three – Henry V, Hamlet, and Richard III – they’re a little dated now, in some ways, and yet there’s something in the essence of what he did and how he uses that language. And he made it… For his time, Olivier was doing new things by speaking that verse in a very naturalistic way, by making it kind of sexy and raw. And I feel very lucky that we have these three movies, because, of course, most of that work that he did was on stage, was live. It disappeared on the night that he performed it. But we have these to get a glimpse into what that was, to why Olivier was regarded as the greatest Shakespearean of all time. There are moments in these films where the clouds part and the light pours through and you see something very, very special.

The first thing that I’ve picked out is A Hard Day’s Night. This is really one of the first things I kind of remember watching with my dad. Sometimes you watch a film that you liked and there’s the scene you love and then there’s other stuff, and then four scenes later, there’s like, “Oh, there it is.” And this is sort of back-to-back magic. The second or third scene is them on the train and they’re like, “Who’s the little old man?” And he goes, “It’s Paul’s granddad.” And then he goes, “He’s very clean. He’s a clean man.” The Beatles’ music is totally the most important music in my life. And for some reason, I was, super, super anxious and filled with a sort of unfounded guilt as a child, and I think other people that I’ve spoken to that I didn’t even know growing up also felt this kind of “They’re going to come and get me”-feeling as kids, but this made me feel safe and comfy. So I’m excited to have this physical media now.

This is Eyes Wide Shut, the Stanley Kubrick film. From a music perspective, the reversed choral, like… thing that plays during the sort of seance/ritual scene, one of the scariest pieces of music I’ve ever heard. I watched it a couple years ago right before Thanksgiving, and then I remember being at the Thanksgiving table, meal had already been eaten, pie had already been eaten, and I was sitting there with Billie and my parents, and we were, like, on the Sonos, and I remember pulling up that piece of music from that sequence. And Billie was like, “Why are you playing this? Why are you playing this right now?” I think it was so jarring and unsettling to her, which is the whole… whole point of that piece of music, but it’s pretty fantastic, so excited again to have this in hi-fi and listen to that disturbing piece of music to my heart’s content.

This is Sound of Metal. This is a film I’ve only seen the one time, but I was really moved by this film. I was also haunted by it. It was a new fear… new fear unlocked, as kids love to say these days. And the sound design is fantastic. His gradual deafness is amazingly designed. And then he gets a cochlear implant toward the end of the film. Then his world is this kind of lo-fi, degraded thing that he’s hearing through his cochlear implant that is really beautifully conveyed in this film. And then there’s a sequence at the end of it – I’m spoiling the whole movie. Whatever. – at the end of it, he takes his cochlear implant off and it just goes to complete silence, which is so effective and haunting. I have goosebumps. I really think this movie is fantastic. If you haven’t seen it, I recommend it.

I’ve picked out WALL·E. I really loved this film, seeing it in theaters at whatever young age I was when it came out. I will admit it seemed like a more distant future than it seems like it is now. But it’s so funny and it’s romantic, and I did rewatch this very recently and it really does hit. It’s aged fantastically. Actually the thing I wanted to do before I wanted to make music for a living was be an animator, that was the thing that I was the most obsessed with, so I think that that is really the core of why I’m happy to talk about WALL·E.

Punch-Drunk Love. Paul Thomas Anderson, one of my favorite directors. Punch-Drunk Love. I really think that Adam Sandler is the GOAT. He’s especially great in this. And I’m highlighting this specifically because of Jon Brion’s music in this. I just think that it’s spectacular. Jon Brion obviously has done film scores that I love and also done work on the albums of pop stars and hip-hop artists and I’ve been equally inspired by that. So I think that, as I have tried to get as good an education as I can in film score and soundtrack, Jon Brion has been a North Star for me because of how the music in the movies that he’s scored makes me feel.

We have Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma. My backstory on Alfonso is that, pre-Roma, Billie and I played a show in Milan, we got word that Bu Cuarón, Alfonso’s wonderful daughter, was coming to see our show. We were playing really small venues at the time, little clubs for 250 people, and we would kind of say hi to everybody before the show and Bu was there and we got to meet her and she was a total sweetheart. Alfonso had brought her to the show. And, you know, I have also… during that period of time, Chris Rock brought his daughter to a show and walked up to us and was like, “I don’t know who you are, but my daughter loves you.” And I was like, “Great, fantastic. That’s all good. Nice to meet you.” And so I was pretty prepared for the same story to be true of Alfonso. So I just walked up to Alfonso and said like, “Thanks for coming. Thanks for bringing your daughter.” He was like, “The sound that is at the end of the song ‘hostage,’ that go like… what go like that?” And I was like… I was so surprised that he had taken the time to listen to the music and had ideas about it and opinions. And so we talked about music for the 30 minutes before we played, then we played a show, and then we kept talking afterward. And he was like, “Will you send me a playlist? I will send you a playlist.” And so we started sending each other tunes, and he sent me a bunch of really great stuff. He kind of hipped me to… I knew about FKA twigs, but he hipped me to a couple FKA twigs songs that I loved. And my pride and joy was I sent him “Ponyboy” by the artist Sophie, who has been a big influence on me. And so I really credit Sophie and “Ponyboy” for him offering me the scoring gig for Disclaimer. I was in London, on tour with Billie, this is now many years later, it’s 2022, I guess, and I went to visit the set of Disclaimer, and it was like an episode of a TV show or a scene in a movie about filmmaking, if that makes sense. It was, like, sets rolling in and out of frame. And in between setups, Alfonso would be like, “Come with me to the edit bay.” He would show me these scenes in the edit bay, and then a PA would run into the edit bay and she’d be like, “You have to see the hospital set. You have to come check out the hospital set,” and we’d go check out the hospital set. He’d be looking around and he’d go, “Has Chivo seen this?” And Chivo would come and he would just be like, “Have you seen this?” And Alfonso goes, “No, but the… the blue on the walls and the blue on the floor are all wrong. The wrong blue.” And Chivo’s like, “I was thinking the same thing.” They were so immediately aligned about this stuff. And then the PA came back over and was like, “The dogs are here.” And he was like, “…” And we went over and there was a… there were, like, six dogs sitting lined up. And he looked at all the dogs. And he loves animals, he’s very sweet to animals, and so he’s being sweet to all the animals, and he goes, “The fur is too white on this dog. Could we make the hair darker on the dog?” And the owner was like, “No.” And he was like, “We’ll need to find a darker dog.” And I remember saying to one of his producers on set, I said, “What day of production are we on?” Because he was operating the way that I operate on, like, day one. And she said, “75.” And I think that it reminded me that that is the goal, ultimately, is to just care about the thing you’re making and every detail of the thing you’re making as much as possible. So, a great lesson in passion and focus and investment in the project that you’re working on. I have learned just as much from standing over his shoulder as I have from watching his amazing movies.

Oh, The Piano Teacher, Michael Haneke. I know French people say, “Michael Haneke,” and I met him once and he was, like, six-foot-something tall. He was older and I tried to impress him and I was speaking to him in French, and my French sucks, but I was like, “Je… Je t’aime.” But I was like, “I love all your filmmaking.” And I do. I love White Ribbon, I love Funny Games, I love Time of the Wolf, Caché. I mean, White Ribbon is one of the great films of all time, but… And Amour, of course. But The Piano Teacher, this film is so incredible because it’s so daring. I mean, talk about dysfunction. I love dysfunction because I came from a dysfunctional family, thank God, because I think the most interesting people I’ve met in my life all come from very dysfunctional families. So this is so dysfunctional. She’s so twisted and sick, and Isabelle Huppert is fearless. And sick, but in a good way, because they’re not sick for gore’s sake or to get a manipulative reaction out of you. It’s more to tell you that we all carry some sickness in ourselves and we don’t know how it’s ever going to manifest itself. And the film is so dangerous that way. And I think he’s one of the great filmmakers, might be one of my favorite modern filmmakers of all time.

Oh, Roma! Roma, Alfonso Cuarón. This film was so powerful. Those shots that… The 360 in that room was insane. I don’t even know how he did that. And coming out of the water where she saves the kid, which was such a powerful scene because the camera starts in the water and then it comes out and follows her into the… Insane. The shots are so phenomenal. And he puts politics in it, and… It’s so full of Alfonso Cuarón.

A Man Escaped. J’aime beaucoup ce film. J’aime beaucoup cette cinéaste, Robert Bresson. C’est magnifique, formidable, en plus, bordel, salope. My kitchen French, because I worked in a bakery in Paris. I wrecked so many croissants for people. Vous êtes mauvais. “You’re bad.” Robert Bresson is one of the great filmmakers. Au Hasard Balthazar is a beautiful film. But this film is exceptional because it all takes place in one room, and you can’t believe that he can create such drama, such tension. If you’re an indie filmmaker, you gotta study this. And it’s such a powerful political piece. One of the brilliant filmmakers of all time, one of my favorites as well. Can you say favorite about everybody?

Do the Right Thing. Do the Right Thing and see this movie. That is the right thing to do. When this film came out, Spike Lee’s Do the Right Thing, it was such a powerful moment. To have Rosie Perez, a Latina, opening up the film, it was huge. And it was political and it was angry, and it was owning the anger that we people of color have, and especially Black people in this country have, in this country, of being erased and being in spaces where you frequent and you put your money in and they don’t represent you and they don’t like you, but they’ll take your money. And he was fighting against that. He’s one of the great filmmakers. He’s also a huge Knicks fan. Did I mention that I’m a huge Knicks fan? Did I mention that this is the Finals and we made it? It’s been 53 years, people. Anyway, this is such an incredible film. I love Spike Lee as a man. I love him as a filmmaker. I love his politics. I love what he did for all of us people of color to understand that we can make our own films, and we should. All right.

El Norte, this is such a beautiful gift. You know, immigration, seeking a better life, sort of the erasure of Indigenous culture. Because, you know, we Latin people, we come from a colonized society where, you know, our religion was destroyed, our history, our language, and yet we’re thriving. We contribute $4.2 trillion to the US GDP. That’s our buying power in America. And yet, you know, we’re virtually invisible, but especially Indigenous Latino people get no love, and Afro-Latinos. So, when this film came out, it was… it was mind-blowing to see how beautiful an Indigenous face, how cinematic, how photogenic it could be. That just reversed all the self-hate that I had. It was like an antidote. I want to see more from Gregory Nava.

Oh, Gold Rush! Charles Chaplin. Oh, man. I mean, I started out as a comedian, doing comedy, and watching Gold Rush was so powerful. And when I was in Latin America, in Colombia, as a little kid, and I used to go to parties, they used to play… I mean, I’m not even that old, but they would play Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton films in people’s homes for children’s parties. And I’m talking about– I was eight years old. But I would watch that, and I guess that’s where I got my love for Charlie Chaplin. I love this movie. This movie makes me laugh out loud. I showed it to my kids and it didn’t… it didn’t have the same effect. I don’t know why. Maybe I showed them too many films. I also made them watch the silent four-hour Abel Gance Napoléon when they were four or five. So maybe they were just too cinematic for The Gold Rush by that point.

This one right here. Starting strong. The Great Beauty. This is one of my favorite films. I love Paolo Sorrentino so much. I don’t know what it is about watching a 65-year-old man contemplate his life and sort of have an existential crisis. I don’t know what it is about that that just really resonates with me. I feel like maybe deep down I’m a 65-year-old man. Jep Gambardella is his name. And I kind of love films that are essentially about nothing, but they’re not about nothing. They’re about so much. The themes are so deep, but nothing really big happens. You’re just kind of watching a character experience life. I really get a kick out of that. And I think this movie’s also secretly very funny.

Triangle of Sadness, another one of my favorites. Ruben Östlund is a director I would love to work with one day. Ruben, if you’re listening to this, please, I’m a big fan. The fact that it’s sort of three films in one, three different parts, three different themes, and I was along for the ride the whole time. And then there’s that iconic sequence when they’re eating on the yacht, and all the elite are eating sort of what’s essentially Michelin jello. I just couldn’t believe my eyes when I watched that sequence. And also the first part, the back-and-forth between a man and a woman talking about gender roles, and this really nuanced dynamic that is so interesting. I mean, I think that’s what he does so well, is explore the social contracts that we have with each other and what happens when all of that disappears.

Oh, Nicole Kidman in The Others. I remember watching this… I had just got out of the shower in middle school, maybe, and my mom was watching it in her bedroom, and I just sort of sat on her bed in my towel and couldn’t take my eyes off the screen. I don’t like anything that’s remotely, like, horror. I get really scared. I’m a big scaredy-cat, and I was really creeped out by this film, but I couldn’t look away. And the plot twist. Alejandro Amenábar, he’s so good at creating suspense. There’s a lot of tension in the film and curiosity and, yeah, I think he’s very talented.

Tótem. I recently watched this film. I was doing research for a project that we’re developing at my company, Honor Role, and… Wow. Lila Avilés, she does slice-of-life so flawlessly. You just feel like you’re living in someone’s family dynamic the whole time. And this little girl that she discovered. There’s something so amazing about watching the discovery of a young actress, a child actor who is just so tuned in to their instincts. I think that’s so impressive to see that as a kid. I feel like Dakota Fanning had that when she was a kid. And still has it. But to have it as a kid is just something extraordinary. You’re watching this little girl navigate the world and sort of start to understand grief and death. I recently worked with a Mexican filmmaker, Carlos López Estrada, and he was telling me, because our film has a lot to do with death, how, in Mexican culture, you start learning about death at a young age. It’s something you start to process in a way that is enlightened and sort of seeing it as a positive thing and just, like, the cycle of life. And it’s really beautiful to watch this little girl start to understand death and grief. And an illness, dealing with illness. So, this one’s definitely going in. She is one to watch.

The Before Trilogy. Before Sunrise, of course, is my favorite. And what Richard Linklater captured in Before Sunrise is so hard to do. You’re just watching two people walk and talk for an entire film, and you’re not bored, you’re so in it, because everyone knows what it feels like to have that feeling– I mean, I hope everyone gets to experience what that feeling is like, but to have that feeling of falling in love in real time and sharing intimate moments with a complete stranger, but you have that sense of familiarity where you feel like you’ve known them your whole life. I really feel that from this film, that there’s this beautiful chemistry between these two souls who are just being drawn to each other. This movie is just so, so beautiful and captures the nuance of falling in love perfectly.

This is an incredible movie: Anatomy of a Fall. I love this film because it answers the age-old question of: did this woman murder her annoying husband or not? I was about to say Sandra’s performance as though she’s my good friend. I’m gonna call her Sandra, like we know each other and we text. Her performance is so good. I actually wasn’t aware of her. It’s exactly the kind of thriller that I like, a domestic thriller.

Next is the classic Love & Basketball, directed by the iconic Gina Prince-Bythewood. This is one of those movies that made me want to write for TV and film. And what I like about this romantic movie is that it kind of proves that competition can be foreplay. That is the kind of romance I like, when two people are ambitious people gunning for the same thing, and that’s what the two leads in this movie are. Also, I do a TV show about basketball, basketball is hot. Okay? We all know it. And this movie is one of the first movies that showed us all how hot basketball could be. Also, these two leads could not be better looking. So this is going to go in the bag as well.

All right, I’m really excited about this one. This is a movie that is very special to me: Frances Ha. Do you ever have that film where when you meet someone new and you like them so, so, so much, and you want to hurry up and get to that point where you know everything about each other and you want to show them a movie that really encapsulates who you are? To me, that is Frances Ha. This movie is so special. When I first saw it, I thought, “This has so beautifully captured what it’s like to be broke, underappreciated, and just longing.” But instead of romantic longing, it’s longing for close, intimate female friendship. And Greta is luminous in this movie, and I’m not throwing around the word luminous.

Oh, this is such a blast from the past. This is A Room with a View, and it’s a Merchant Ivory film, which, if you’re Indian and you were around in the ’80s and the ’90s, Ismail Merchant was so huge for us because he was one of the people we could look to as really making it in the business and being successful, and, for someone like me, that was so meaningful. But it was also one of those movies where… I think up until then my favorite movie was, like, Sister Act 2, and this was, like, a grown-up movie. And there’s actually a very grown-up scene in the movie people who know the movie will know, which is Julian Sands and another actor are running fully naked around a pond in this joyous scene, and I don’t think I’d ever seen a man’s penis before that, so I’m going to say that was very imprinted on me as well.

My next choice I think is going to be a surprise to people, which is The Shape of Water. I love Guillermo del Toro because he has this way of making monsters seem human and humans seem terrifying. And when I saw this, I was like, “Is that amphibian man hot?” Like, you understand why Sally Hawkins falls in love with this man. And the relationship between Octavia Spencer and Sally Hawkins in this movie is one of the most tender friendships, I think, in any film. And Michael Shannon as a psychopath is unforgettable. So I love this film. It’s really strange. It’s incredibly romantic. And like all of Guillermo del Toro movies, there’s just surprising violence that devastates you and you can’t stop thinking about. And a couple of images that I just have seared in my head forever. So I’m going to take it home with me.

This is Mississippi Masala, directed by the iconic legend Mira Nair. Before she was the mother of New York’s mayor, she was a legend for my people. Mira Nair has made so many amazing movies, but this one, to me, really sticks out because of how ahead of its time it is. Not only are Denzel Washington and Sarita Choudhury the best looking that they’ve ever been, or the best looking anyone has ever been, the movie is about immigration, displacement, and how marginalized communities can feel prejudice towards each other, and, like I said, I just think it’s incredibly ahead of its time. And most importantly, it’s romantic and the story is so gripping.

Okay, so for my last pick, I’m just going to see what the Closet wants me to watch. Kind of like the Sorting Hat in Harry Potter. So I’m going to close my eyes and then just blindly move my arms around. Pickup on South Street. Hey, this looks hot. I think I did a good job. I can’t wait to see that, so that’s going to go in my bag.
For All Mankind, Al Reinert. That is a phenomenal movie. I do already have it. I suppose I could steal a second copy, but I think I’ll leave this here for somebody else.

So this one is great: Mr. Arkadin, a. K. A. Confidential Report, written and directed by Orson Welles. It’s a film he made all over the world in the scrappiest, most sort of homemade, put his friends together, grab some costumes, find an interesting location kind of way. But yeah, it’s got all the different versions that were ever released in different strange forms. It’s a very, very peculiar piece of work, but really speaks to Welles’s genius, absolutely.
