Fritz Lang, Testament of Dr. Mabuse. Amazing mastermind criminal. We looked at Dr. Mabuse a lot, my brother and I, when we were doing The Dark Knight, for the character of the Joker.
Scorsese Shorts. I’m going to have to grab that. I’ve seen The Big Shave, but I haven’t seen the other ones, so that’s pretty exciting.

Yeah, Spike’s Malcolm X, I’ve been meaning to revisit that. I saw it on 70mm film when it came out and I don’t think I’ve seen it since, so going to check that out. I think John David Washington has a little cameo as one of the children at the end saying, “I am Malcolm X.”

Lost Highway. That’s one of my favorite David Lynch movies. When I first saw it, I cannot say that I enjoyed the film. I found it quite laborious to sit through. I thought it was quite heavy going, quite hard, but I found myself thinking about it weeks afterwards and remembering it like I was remembering one of my own dreams, which just speaks to the way that Lynch figured out how to take dream logic and the experience of dreaming and make a sort of cinematic proxy for that for the audience. I’m very keen to revisit this one.

Going to have to pull out The Player. For me, Altman’s masterpiece. I don’t think it’s generally considered to be his greatest film, but possibly I’m biased because I work in movies, but I just think it’s an incredible thriller and it’s an absolutely incisive satire of Hollywood. Hugely influential on things that have come since.
Yeah, I got to take Linklater’s Boyhood. What an incredible concept and to actually pull it off in such a moving way, really something.
One False Move. Terrific movie. Carl Franklin directed it. It’s a great performance by Bill Paxton, Billy Bob Thornton. Really great neo-noir.

The Black Stallion, Carroll Ballard. Absolutely beautiful film. Saw it when I was a kid. It stayed with me. Incredible photography by Caleb Deschanel. Very, very influential visually, and just a beautiful kids’ film.
And I got to finish with Citizen Kane. I mean… I love that packaging, too. Just says it all.
Got to get a little Don Siegel, Killers.
Definitely want to get the Cassavetes box set. Shadows, Faces, Killing of a Chinese Bookie, Woman Under the Influence. Incredible work.

And The Apu Trilogy, Satyajit Ray, one of the great Indian filmmakers, The trilogy, starting with Pather Panchali, which is an absolutely incredible film and just blew my mind, but I have not yet seen two and three in the trilogy, so pretty excited to get this one and complete the story.

film_title: Martin Scorsese’s World Cinema Project No. 3
quote: And on the subject of Martin Scorsese and The Film Foundation, which I’m a part of, I’m going to grab the box set from the World Cinema Project. It’s part of Marty’s project to really take what he’s done with The Film Foundation for American cinema and do it with different film industries around the world and really try and look at films in desperate need of preservation. And he dedicates himself and the Foundation to it, and they do incredible work and bring all sorts of amazing voices onto the Blu-ray format, so that they can be seen and enjoyed by future generations.
box_set_name: Martin Scorsese's World Cinema Project No. 3

quote: Definitely have to pull out The Qatsi Trilogy. Koyaanisqatsi, in particular, of the three, that is my great favorite. Extraordinary music by Philip Glass. No dialogue, just imagery. An emotional experience. It’s just one of the great pieces of pure cinema.

So Purple Noon, the same source material as The Talented Mr. Ripley, so I never saw Purple Noon because, as famous as it is, I stayed away from it to do Ripley. I didn’t want to see it, and Anthony Minghella didn’t want me to see it, and I never watched it after. But it is a classic, and so I’m going to pick this one up.

The movie that he did have me see for that, for Ripley, was actually Knife in the Water. It was to get a sense of the aesthetic and the boat work we were going to do. But I remember it being wonderful.

I wanted to grab one of Soderbergh’s movies. They have Traffic here. I like Traffic for a very special reason. So I’ve done, I think, ten movies with Steven Soderbergh. I absolutely adore him. I love working with him, for so many reasons. I mean, he cuts in camera. He is the editor, he’s the director, he’s the cinematographer, and he’s the camera operator. And he cuts the work you do the day you shoot it and he sends it to you, so you can watch the movie develop as it’s going. When he won the Oscar for directing this movie, he kind of scoffed at the idea that he would do anything like it ever again. It’s a remarkable movie, incredible performances. Benicio. Everybody in this movie is great. Benicio is absolutely out of this world, he’s phenomenal. But I’m taking it as a reminder to, when things go really well in your life creatively, never protect your beachhead. And that’s a conversation that I’ve had with Soderbergh many, many times. You want to keep pushing. You do not want to just do the same thing over and over and over.

This movie is impossible to find. So if you can get a Criterion edition of You Can Count on Me, you should definitely do that. This was my introduction to Kenny Lonergan. Casey Affleck and I went and did a play in London, one of Kenny’s plays. I ended up producing Manchester by the Sea that Casey was in. And that all happened because I saw this about 27 years ago and was like… It’s just a beautiful, beautiful little movie. I’ve been looking for it to show it to my kids for years, and I’ve even called Kenny and he’s like, “I don’t know, I don’t know what… I can’t find it either.” So, Criterion Collection.

Gus’s movie Drugstore Cowboy. I’ve got a couple of Gus’s to point out. Drugstore Cowboy, first Gus Van Sant movie I ever saw. I saw it in the Harvard Square Theatre, which no longer exists. Matt Dillon quite famously said to Gus that he would never talk to him again after he saw the rough cut. And that was why Gus was nervous to show us the rough cut of Good Will Hunting. It’s a phenomenal movie and Matt Dillon’s amazing, and they obviously made up once the movie came out and was a wild success.

All right, One False Move. Ben and I loved this movie when it came out, and this is what turned us on to Carl Franklin, the director. We’ve been a fan of his since. And it was the first time we saw Billy Bob Thornton. Billy Bob Thornton, obviously, went on to play a larger role in our lives. We both worked with him. Love him. And Billy Bob wrote this, I’m pretty sure. That was why he kind of… He was in the movie and he wrote it, and it was while we were trying to do Good Will Hunting, and so another one of those signals that we might be on the right track.

This one might not be surprising to anybody: No Country for Old Men. But I… when I worked with the Coen brothers when I did True Grit, the accent that I was doing, I was basing it on Tommy Lee, and the monologue that ends this movie, I probably… I don’t know how many times I’ve watched it, because I was watching it for work, but I enjoyed watching it. The final monologue that Tommy Lee has in this movie is so devastating. He is one of the great actors who has ever lived. And this movie is pretty damn near close to perfect.

Oh, yeah, Double Indemnity. One of my favorite little exchanges, I think, ever in a movie: Barbara Stanwyck is being a little coy and… and Fred MacMurray says something to her that’s, like, a little racy, and she says, “I wonder if I know what you’re talking about.” And he responds, “I wonder if you wonder.” Wonderful film. And of course, Edward G. Robinson’s in it.
Sex, Lies, and Videotape. That would be a good way to go through here is find first films for directors, because there are some really good ones.

That’s another great first film: 12 Angry Men, Sidney Lumet. That’s a hell of a way to introduce yourself to the world. This one was groundbreaking. And this one is just so… It’s so beautifully directed and taut, and acted, written, paced, everything. Brilliant.

So I’m going to close my eyes and see what the Closet feeds me. Hopefully a movie I have not seen. Maîtresse, I’ve never seen it. “A young provincial in search of adventure stumbles into the subterranean world of sadomasochism when he is implicated in the burglary of a Paris apartment. Barbet Schroeder’s Maîtresse examines the line between fantasy and reality, decadence and deprivation, and the distance one will go for love.” All right, Barbet. 1976. So I guess I was five when this came out, and it’s about S&M, so it’s not a mystery why I didn’t know about it. But I’ll check it out.

I do think it makes sense to start here because of what happened last night: Hoop Dreams. It represents everything I love about basketball and everything I kind of find to be deeply sad about basketball as well. It was one of the first documentaries I ever saw, and it was something that my mother showed me. And in light of how well the Knicks are doing and the incredible comeback that happened last night, and how much of a fan I am of them and basketball just in general – it really was my first love – this movie kind of encapsulates all of that.

This is a polar-opposite movie: Come and See. It is the movie I watched before shooting The Long Walk, that Francis Lawrence told us to watch, and it is because I think he wanted to replicate the fact of how you go into things and how you come out of them. I think it does a really good job of showing, in a very intense way, of how much kids want to grow up and then realize, as they grow up, how kind of more difficult it gets. This movie’s incredible.

I’m going to go with two together. And it’s because my girlfriend showed me both of these. Or didn’t show me both of these. Sorry. This is her favorite movie, and I love this movie: Paper Moon. Another great director showed this to me, Paul Thomas Anderson, and I was blessed to watch it in a screening room with him and my family. Tatum O’Neal is someone that I’ve always loved. This and also Come and See are two child-acting… It makes no sense. But when you watch it, you feel all of the things.

And then Thelma & Louise, it’s something I just watched. Also incredibly exciting. And my girlfriend showed this to me and we watched it together, and she has much better movie taste than I do. This movie’s fantastic.

Okay, we’re going to pivot. We’re going to totally pivot. But, you know, who the hell cares? Happiness. This movie… You know, not everyone gets to see their father jerk off on-screen. I did, in this, and it was something that really shocked me. And, you know, maybe I didn’t like it at the time, but I’ve recently rewatched it in the theater. And Todd Solondz was one of the first directors I ever asked to go meet when I got an agent, because I love this movie so much, because I think it’s an incredible testament to how imperfect humans are and how much empathy Todd has for them. And I think that’s a testament to also my father’s acting in this, and everyone’s acting in this. But yeah, this is one of my faves.

Punch-Drunk Love is a movie I just recently rewatched. It’s not my favorite Paul Thomas Anderson movie. My favorite Paul Thomas Anderson movie is The Master. But this movie is… feels like lightning in a bottle in a different way that I can’t totally describe, but when I watch it, I just want to keep watching it.

I haven’t seen this movie, Hud, but I want to take it with me because Paul Newman is one of my favorite actors of all time. He is unbelievable. Cool Hand Luke, The Sting. I could go on. He is remarkably handsome, and yet loses none of his empathy, his sadness, his depression, his guilt, his hilarity. He’s someone that I will never be but admire watching. And it’s really nice with an actor like that, where you aren’t striving to become them and you can just watch their work and be happy that they’ve done stuff.

Mean Streets. This movie is something I also just recently rewatched and it’s… not in the same way, but it feels like, with Paul, with Punch-Drunk Love, and with this – and by the way, also, these are two fantastic directors and this is just my opinion – but it feels like they were both trying to figure something out, and it worked so well. And I really enjoy the fact that both… Mean Streets feels like something that… it feels, even though it might not be, tangible for me and my friends to go make. And that’s really exciting as a young person who’s trying to make stuff with their buddies. And also, by the way, Robert De Niro in this is just a godsend. It’s crazy.

Love Streams, Cassavetes. My friend told me to watch this. James, shout out to you. And actually, hold on, we’re going to do a little twofer because he also told me to watch Salesman because I was shooting a movie called Wildcat, where I had to play a Bible salesman. Let’s talk about Love Streams first. Love Streams is one of those that I wish I had a more interesting take on, but it just felt so natural and kind of almost the feeling that I got watching, like, Y tu mamá también, where it’s a little bit, like, you just want to… you just want to be the camera and you don’t ever want it to shut off. And I think that that’s really sometimes hard to do because I have so many annoying critiques about things at times, but I don’t have any for this.

Okay, let’s go with another person that’s incredibly good at dealing with very dark subjects and creating humor and light out of them: Gregg Araki. This is a little controversial. I haven’t seen The Doom Generation, I haven’t seen Nowhere, but I’ve seen Totally F***ed Up. I want to watch both of these. I need to watch both of these. But Gregg Araki, I just worked with him, he is as funny and fun as his movies are, even though they deal with very intense subjects. You can’t lose your sense of humor. It’s something that my mom always taught me, and I like when movies have it, too.

You’ve seen Being There, right? Where did it go? You’ve seen it already. But that’s okay. I would love to have it. Peter Sellers, Being There. It’s a beautiful movie. He was a genius. He really was. Yeah. Not that you need convincing.

This is going to be really jock-like of me, but you know I’m really into basketball right now, so I’m going to give you Hoop Dreams, which is an amazing documentary. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it, but I’ll take it. Okay, jeez. I love Hoop Dreams. It’s a beautiful film. I love it. Except I didn’t realize until now it was basketball.

There’s something that’s kind of… it’s kind of obvious in a way: Sid & Nancy. At the time, when it came out, I was so thrilled to see it all happen. But now as I get older, I just love the end of it more and more. I’ll hand this to you. Okay.

Let’s see. I’ll pick one that is like this one for me for you. You’ve seen Moonstruck, right? Yes. Okay. But it’s been a really long time. Okay. This movie, it’s peak Nicolas Cage. There’s great lines in it. He’s like, “I lost my hand. I lost my girl.” Remember how he doesn’t have a hand? Yeah. And then he’s like, “Johnny has his hand, Johnny has his girl.” There’s so many good lines in this. It’s Cher at her best. I would say this movie is a movie I have watched more than any other film. I suggest a rewatch. This is a really good experience. Because you’re learning about me. Because– Yes. Because I didn’t know that about you. Yeah. Which is humiliating.

Female Trouble is a masterpiece. I know that John Waters is one of your favorites. Yes. And this is my favorite of his. But Divine really gives everything, just really is full-performance all the way through for what at the time was probably, like, an underground film. Okay, thank you. I appreciate it.

Let me give you a Portland film, which is Drugstore Cowboy by Gus Van Sant. What I love about this movie, aside from the amazing acting and the way it’s shot, is it… there are so many parts of Portland that no longer exist that have been, like, captured. And by old parts of Portland, what do you mean? Like Old Town, just things that have been gentrified or torn down. They’re all preserved in this film. And same with My Own Private Idaho. I love watching that. There’s just these diners and things in Old Town that just aren’t around anymore.

I see a movie that we both love: After Hours. Right? Yeah. Do we want to give each other this movie? Yeah. Okay. Thank you. Here you go. Okay. Thank you. I love the momentum of it. It’s propulsive. It’s funny. It’s just, like, there’s… It’s specific. That version of New York, too. There’s this one scene where he’s going off on a rant. This is towards the end. And he ends up in this guy’s apartment, this stranger, and they changed the subway fare, and he’s going off about it and he’s like, “Did you know that they changed the subway fare?” And the guy goes like this: “Mm-hm.” That’s so New York. It’s so New York that someone is freaking out about it and that someone else is like, “Yeah, I totally knew about it.” And also Teri Garr. Teri Garr. I… I mean, Tootsie, there’s so many… I miss Teri Garr. I miss her. I do, too. What?! To me, one of the best.

To let people know that we have seen a foreign film we’ll both pick Bergman’s collection. One of my favorites, though, is Through a Glass Darkly, a terrifying and dark film about a woman who has mental illness, and it’s tragic, but it’s beautiful. Ooh. And it’s just… There’s not a lot of films, to me, that are about mental illness that are from that era, I guess, but even now, that just lay things so bare and uncomfortable things in it, for sure. But I think that discomfort is part of it. The Seventh Seal is in this, and that’s my mom’s favorite movie. Really? Yeah. She used to describe it to me when I was a kid. Do we get to keep this? Ooh. Oh, wow. Man, that is awesome. I’m so happy about that. Thank you.

I'm going to start with Modern Times. When I was three years old – I'm an only child – and my parents, they put me in the living room with a VCR and a Modern Times Betamax tape, they taught me how to press play and rewind, and I basically brainwashed myself. And I think it was really the start of my love for Charlie Chaplin, and also, I think, my obsession with the relationship between mankind and human and technology and alienation and society and how modernity is really interacting with us. So Modern Times, it's really the beginning.

Sisters, Brian De Palma. At 12 years old, I was obsessed with Brian De Palma. With Guy-Man, from Daft Punk, before we started to make music, every Wednesday I would go to the video store and pick up a film and bring it. I was mostly also obsessed with Phantom of the Paradise, and Sisters is as close as you can get to Phantom of the Paradise. It's the film that he directed just before. It has William Finley, the same actor, that plays this time a very scary character and great Bernard Herrmann's score as well. So, it's a classic for me.

This is Spike Jonze's first feature, Being John Malkovich. Thirty years ago, a few blocks from here, we were with Spike when he shot the first Daft Punk music video, "Da Funk," with Lance Acord as the cinematographer. And a few months, a few years after that, Spike directed his first film. It's an instant classic. I love it and I highly recommend it.

Martha Graham: Dance on Film. I haven't seen this, but I was born and raised in a family of dancers. My mother was a ballet and contemporary dancer. My aunt was a dancer. My uncle was a choreographer. My wife is an actress and a dancer, Élodie, and she's the biggest Martha Graham fan, and I can't wait to bring it home and watch it with her.

The Color of Pomegranates, Sayat-Nova. I think it's the most beautiful film ever made. Music for the eyes. Every shot is a poem. The closest would be, like, a film adaptation of Carl Jung's Red Book. You go into this medieval symbolism of Armenian troubadours, and Parajanov is a genius. This is really a masterpiece.

Okay, this is David Fincher, The Game. It's probably my favorite David Fincher movie. I still have that on Criterion laserdisc, actually, that I purchased in the '90s. I really feel it was a big influence for me on this relationship between fiction and reality, because with Daft Punk and the robots and the narrative, that's, I feel, what we were exploring also for all these years, especially when it utilizes almost a lot of extras and production techniques from film, and that's pretty much what we did, going with special effects shops and creating props and integrating them in reality where you don't really understand where actually fiction ends and reality begins.

This is Thomas Vinterberg, The Celebration. I think I've picked a lot of silent films, in fact, films with almost no dialogue where the power of cinema goes to the imagery and the music. And here's a movie with dialogue, and here's a film where it's probably the most visceral and powerful experience I've ever had in filmgoing, in a theater, when it came out. The audacity of speaking up and breaking the silence and breaking the cycles of abuse, it's just a masterpiece. And I love it, Celebration.

The Qatsi Trilogy. Koyaanisqatsi, I saw Koyaanisqatsi when I was fifteen years old. This was a big inspiration, I think, when we directed Electroma with Daft Punk and I did the cinematography, because it's the most beautiful example of available-light cinematography. And Philip Glass's score is just a masterpiece. I think this is, again, like this visual album. I can't stop watching it. And also what I love is sometimes just taking a few minutes and just watching it in the middle and getting the best from it.

All right, this next one is Hollywood Shuffle. If you’re a Blacktor, like me, or even a half Blacktor, this is mandatory, mandatory reading. It’s a bit meta as a movie. It’s a movie about the Hollywood industry, but it’s a movie about what Black actors go through. I saw this when I first moved to Los Angeles and then, twenty-three years later, I finally got a job.

Okay. I’m glad you have Uncut Gems, not only because it’s a great movie. I befriended Josh, and he is the one that told me at the beginning of quarantine, I was, like, drinking all day and watching movies, and I was, like–...

The very first movie Josh Safdie ever recommended me is Sorcerer, and I love William Friedkin. I think this is actually perhaps his best movie, and that’s saying a lot, because I think French Connection and The Exorcist are two of the best movies ever made. I don’t like hyping a movie up too much. I like when you stumble upon something like… I like that Josh was just, like, “I don’t know, watch… watch Sorcerer,” because I was going into it with no expectations, knowing nothing about it, and I… Some people are so good at making movies, they, like, piss you off. It’s like, “Fuck you, William Friedkin, you fucking talented motherfucker.”

Okay, we got Bob Fosse, my man. All That Jazz. And I heard Bob Fosse in an interview said he smoked five to six packs of cigarettes a day, so he smoked 100 to 120 cigarettes every day. And he was a professional ballet dancer. He’s just such a fascinating guy.

film_title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling
catalog_title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling
quote: The only other auto-biopic I can think of is Richard Pryor made Jo Jo Dancer. He’s the architect of modern comedy and he was so brilliant and vulnerable and tortured and he had a really tough life. But he had an amazing, prolific… We’re all his kids. So I love both these movies. These guys were both tortured geniuses. And I used to have romantic notions about being tortured for your art, but there’s nothing cool about it. You want to keep your sanity if you can.

House, I think this is one of the greatest movies ever made. There’s not a single movie like it. Every lore I’ve heard about this movie is, like, one mind-explosion after the next, and it’s the great… it’s one of the greatest movies.

Is this Battle of Algiers? This is like City of God or the Safdies would cast – they call it street-casting, casting real people – this guy cast actual Algerian separatists, literally people that would, like, bomb French discotheques. He would cast to play versions of themselves in this movie. And this movie is, like… I think it’s like one of the best movies ever fucking made.

And Les Blank, total ledge. Les Blank goes into parts of Louisiana where people… He’ll find some 114-year-old Black grandmother who… not only is French her first language, she never learned English. He finds all these subcultures, in America and documents them, and they’re just some… they’re beautiful and they’re fascinating, and he, like, stays out of the way. Whenever I can’t think of things to watch, I’ll just put on Les Blank.
Okay. I’m done. I’ll get Malcolm X. Yeah. Come on, Spike. Knicks in five, baby. This one’s for Spike.

I’m not, like, a Cassavetes expert, but I love his movie Shadows, because it’s hanging on by a thread. It feels like it’s edited like a Ornette Coleman saxophone solo. It’s completely atonal, if that term made sense for filmmaking. If you ask me about A Woman Under the Influence or another Cassavetes film, I’m gonna stare at you with a blank stare. I’m not an expert, but Shadows rules. It rocks. Period. On God. No cap. For real, for real.

Jackie Chan’s the most talented living human being on the earth. He can do martial arts comedically and he’s, like, a multi-platinum-record-selling singer. Police Story. And I’m glad you guys got this, I’m excited to see his early stuff. He’s a ledge.

film_title: Jackie Chan: Emergence of a Superstar (box set)
catalog_title: Jackie Chan: Emergence of a Superstar (box set)
quote: Jackie Chan’s the most talented living human being on the earth. He can do martial arts comedically and he’s, like, a multi-platinum-record-selling singer. And I’m glad you guys got this, I’m excited to see his early stuff. He’s a ledge.
box_set_name: Jackie Chan: Emergence of a Superstar

quote: I just saw… I don’t know how I just saw this. I think it was on… on a flight, and I think they had this, and I was like, “Oh, this is interesting.” It’s an interesting short film, called Black Girl, and it’s just really interesting, intriguing to me. I thought it was shot beautifully. Of course, it’s about racial politics of this young woman coming from… I think she came from Africa, then to keep house in… France? Yeah. But I just wanted to study this. This is one of those films you want to study. It’s really awesome. And she’s great.

Check this out: Ermanno Olmi’s Il Posto. I’ve heard a lot about this film. “When young Domenico ventures from the small village of Meda to Milan in search of employment, he finds himself on the bottom rung of the bureaucratic ladder in a huge, faceless company. The prospects are daunting, but Domenico finds reason for hope in the fetching Antonietta.” I heard it was a great film. I’m inspired to see what I get out of it.

I saw this, Claudine. James Earl Jones, Diahann Carroll. One of my favorite films that I’ve watched over and over again, just about Black life, 1974. Woman really trying to find her way through, and James Earl Jones is a garbage man. James Earl Jones is like… this character is like my pop. I think maybe that’s why I relate to this character so much. I’m like, I see that dude, that dude who was, like, too cool, blue-collar dude, but who became a man and laid down some rules for the new family. And there’s comedy and drama that ensues. And romance.

Mean Streets. Come on now. 1973. I feel like I’m leaning more towards early ’70s movies. Scorsese at his best. Rough, raw. Another movie you want to study. Study frames, look at the way the storytelling is rolled out. I’m into it.

Purple Noon. Another film I saw on a flight. This is a theme that’s happening. I see a lot of films on a flight. And now– I built a little cabin on my property, and I think that’s the place where I’m going to really watch films like this. Alain Delon, one of the most beautiful men that has ever graced a screen. And it’s all complicated, and it’s all about being someone else and aspiring with the wealth, wealthy, and doing dastardly things, and looking like this.

I have to take this with me: Moonstruck. One of my favorite films. It’s great. 1987. I think everybody won an Academy Award for this: Cher, Olympia Dukakis. A fantastic film. I think I’ve seen this maybe fifty times. Now it’s going to be another fifty times, now that I have this.

Okay, what I’m going to do right now is see what the Closet wants me to walk away with. Let’s see. All right. Okay. You want me to do something from here. Coup de Grâce. “Latvia, 1919: the end of the Russian Civil War. An aristocratic young woman, brilliantly played by Margarethe von Trotta, becomes involved with a sexually repressed Prussian soldier.” All right. “When she is rejected by her would-be lover, the young woman is sent into a downward spiral of psychosexual depression, promiscuity, and revolutionary collaboration.” This is dope. And… “A startling tale of heartbreak and violence, a powerful film that explores the interrelation of private passion and political commitment.” I’m down with this. This is great.

I am going to take this with me: Wong Kar Wai, someone who really has inspired so many people. I know that Barry Jenkins was very inspired by this man, and he’s really someone for filmmakers to take a look at and see how he composes frames and tells a story, sometimes with just… Very minimal. How to make really smart decisions and storytelling decisions with lighting, with framing. I want to watch everything.

This is one of my favorite films of all time: Badlands. Young Martin Sheen, young Sissy Spacek, directed by Terrence Malick. The style of this movie was very influential to my friends and I when we were just getting into filmmaking. Loved the naturalistic performances, the simplicity of the script. It's just awesome. It's a killer film. Badlands.

Bob Rafelson's Five Easy Pieces. This film also very influential on me. I loved that this movie just had such an unlikable protagonist. I think that really influenced a lot of the kind of characters I like to write stories about. And oddly enough, the end of this movie actually inspired the end of the first season of Eastbound & Down. Kenny leaves his girlfriend coldly and, not to ruin anything, but something very similar happens at the end of this film, and it's exactly where we pinched that idea. Five Easy Pieces.

Here's one I love: A Face in the Crowd. Andy Griffith gives an insane performance here. It's awesome. We were actually inspired by this movie when we were writing the… was it the fourth season of Eastbound? We were watching a lot of A Face in the Crowd. You know, he's this sort of southern guy who gets put onto the main stage and is, like, milking that sort of down-home vibe. But he's a fraud. And we kind of took Kenny Powers on that same journey in the fourth season of Eastbound. It's funny how much of Eastbound is actually inspired by classic films, but it is.

This is a nightmare-inducing film: Fantastic Planet. When I was a kid, this used to air late at night, I think on, like, the USA Network. I'm not really sure why, but it would always seem to be playing on a Friday or Saturday night, and I would watch it and it's so odd, so strange. The soundtrack is honestly incredible. I listen to the soundtrack often. Yeah, what a cool movie.

Another visually stunning film: I Am Cuba. I used to watch this film all the time when I first moved out to Los Angeles. I had a projector in my house. I didn't have a TV. And I would literally just project this movie on the walls of my house. The cinematography is nuts. They pull off all these oners that are sort of unbelievable. I don't really understand how they did it at the time. Cameras flying over alleyways, down elevators, underwater. Yeah, pretty incredible movie.

I for sure have to shout out my boy, David Gordon Green's George Washington. I actually worked on this movie. I was the second-unit director. We shot this movie the day after I graduated from film school. I think we shot it in two weeks. It was so much fun. It was the very first time I worked on a production. It's what sort of launched David's career. We shot it in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. George Washington.
After Hours. Think this is one of my favorite Scorsese films. Griffin Dunne is amazing. It's a fever dream. This one's killer. I did not know that y'all had released this, but killer.
All right, let's just start picking blindly in here. Let's do it. Let's go. Right here. What's this? Rashomon.

film_title: Manila in the Claws of Light
catalog_title: Manila in the Claws of Light
quote: How about this right here? What's this? Manila in the Claws of Light. Sure. Let's do it.
What's this? Come on, big money, big money. Yes! Night of the Living Dead. Yeah, that's strong. Great.
Here we go: Fellini’s 8½. Just got done working in Italy for three months, where the ambiance is exceptional, and a lot of this man’s inspiration, what he did here is still around.
The Great Beauty. I enjoyed that. Going to stick with that too. We’re still in Italy, aren’t we?
Oh, I’m going to get Tootsie because this movie makes my mom so happy.

Oh, I’m going to do The Big Chill because I remember when I was young and I felt so adult appreciating this Lawrence Kasdan sort of melodrama. And I believe it still holds up. Always remember that scene, Kevin Kline goes jogging in some short shorts, he’s going into town for his morning jog, and the way he jogs into town – it’s a wide shot, he’s going away – you’re like… It’s the first time I’d seen someone that went jogging that– “Oh, they’re not trying to be in great shape, they’re just– morning to get the blood flow.” Why I remember that scene, I don’t remember. Thank you, Mr. Kasdan.
I’m going with the guy’s first film who put me in my first film: Mr. Linklater, Slacker. Austin, Texas. Madonna’s pube, still worth money.

Look at that. Speaking of. Sticking with Linklater. I’ve never seen this cover either. Well, I wouldn’t be standing here without… Walked in the right bar in Austin, Texas, met the right guy, Don Phillips, who introduced me to Mr. Richard Linklater, auditioned for a role, three lines turned into three weeks’ work, went back to school, graduated, drove out to Hollywood with a couple thousand bucks and the role of Wooderson in Dazed and Confused. Didn’t know if it was going to be a little hobby I would tell my kids about one day, “Hey, there’s this movie set I got to work on for a couple nights in Austin, Texas, when I was a junior in college.” Turned into a career. Thanks, cat.
Oh, yeah, Two-Lane Blacktop. Back to Dazed and Confused, Lee Daniel, the one-arm DP on Dazed and Confused, turned me on to this in 1992.
John Sayles. Yeah. Matewan.

Thelma & Louise, Ridley Scott. Doing that for sure. I remember loving that, as a big-screen sort of metroplex movie while I was in film school, I believe. And I remember in film school, all the film directors and everybody would go see… go to the art house only on the weekend. And they’d come back and talk about the Eisenstein, black and white, or what have you, and I’d listen, and I would always go to the multiplex and go see, like, this or… or Die Hard or something. I’d come back on a Monday and I’d tell them about it, and they would always bitch and moan, like, “It’s garbage.” “What are you talking about?” So I started to think, “Oh, man, I gotta go to the art house only, if I’m going to be an artist.” And then one day I was like, “Bullshit, I like these movies.” I went and I started talking about– They were like, “Oh, that’s bullshit.” I was like, “Okay, why? Why is it bullshit?” And they were like, “Well, I don’t know. I mean, we didn’t see it. We’re just saying, because it was, you know, big studio stuff.” Anyway. Like Thelma & Louise. Thank you, Ridley.
I want me some Mean Streets. Yes, I do. Thank you. My bag’s getting nice and full too.

Did a… film with him down in Piedras Negras, Lone Star. I remember the audition for that. It was at a time where I was not getting the role. I would get the second, third, or fourth callback, but never get the role. I was getting a little heady about things, and I met him and he hadn’t quite cast me in it, but he was, like… met to tell me he kind of wanted me in it. And we were talking about this character, Buddy Deeds, and I was talking to him about it, he was like, “Yeah.” He goes, “Now just kick back and talk to me with your feet up on the table, like this is your place.” And I did. And whatever I did, he goes, “That’s it. Want to do the movie?” And we did. It’s also the set where, at 1 a. M. Full moon night, I got a phone call during a break in scenes, and it was Joel Schumacher and John Grisham calling me to say, “Do you want to play Jake Brigance in A Time to Kill?” And I said, “[beep] yeah.” And I took off running into the desert until I broke a sweat, dropped down on both knees and put a hand up to shake the moon’s hand to say thank you. And right next to that we have Lone Star. We know that one, with Mr. Sayles. We already got Matewan of his.
Basquiat. Just because I’m a fan.
Election, Alexander Payne. One of my favorites of his. Good to see you there, Reese.
Amores perros, please. I’ll do that real quick on the way out. We like that.

film_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
catalog_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
quote: Dr. Strangelove. I saw this film first run when I was a young teenager, 1964. I was 16 years old. My parents took me to it in downtown Chicago, which was very odd for them, they rarely took me to a film, let alone would go to a film downtown, but I guess it was a big hit at the time or something, I don’t know. And I just loved it. I mean, I thought Peter Sellers was so great. Everybody was great. Sterling Hayden. At the very end, when… I mean, is that the darkest ending of any comedy I ever saw. And Kubrick, who’s the master of music, I think, among other things, in his films, puts in this great Vera Lynn song, this really beautiful song. She sings “We’ll Meet Again.” It’s playing with these beautifully edited shots of atomic bombs going off in just the right way. It was very powerful to me, that counterpoint of that music and those bombs. The lights came up and I looked around, nobody got up in their seats, this packed audience, mostly middle-aged couples, and I’m looking, like, “How come they’re not getting up?” And they were just stunned. They didn’t know what to make of the film. There’s my personal story about it, anyway.

Jean-Pierre Melville, Army of Shadows. This is probably my favorite film of all time. This was actually brought to this country for the first time in 2006 by Bruce Goldstein, the guy that flew me out here for this Film Forum retrospective of my own films, so I just… eternally in his debt. The color palette on this film is so obsessive. It’s so meticulous and controlled, it’s great. And my friend Robert Crumb came to visit me from France a few years ago, and he’d never seen this. I said, “Oh, you got to see this film.” So I put it on for him. He’s got unpredictable tastes in film. He’s a very fussy guy. If there’s, like, one mistake in a film, it’s unforgivable, ruins the whole film. So, as soon as I put it on, there’s an early scene, “Haircut’s wrong. That haircut is not the same period.” I said, “You know, ignore the haircut. It’s got a lot of other things going for it in this film, perhaps.” No. Didn’t like it. Oh well, you can’t please everybody.

The Asphalt Jungle. This is a perfect film. It’s one of my favorite films of all time. Marc Lawrence really stood out to me in this film. He plays Cobby, the sort of nervous, sweaty criminal guy who’s trying to arrange a loan or a deal for this heist, and I couldn’t help but thinking, the entire time I saw this, that this had to inspire Francis Coppola to cast Fredo in The Godfather. Again, they’re so similar. Either he cast him and thought of it that way and wrote it that way or the actor thought of it and just sort of channeled that. Marc Lawrence, great actor. Incredible.

All About My Mother. I’ve never seen this film, but, when I was in pre-production on Ghost World, my producer said, “Have you thought about a DP yet?” And I started listing DPs that I thought might be good, thinking what she thought, and her answer was, on each one, “Too expensive, too expensive.” I said, “All right, well, let me think.” And she said, “I got to go make a phone call. It’s going to take me two hours, I’m going to be on this phone. I’ve got a bunch of VHS tapes in here, if you want to watch movies, whatever. Maybe you’ll find a DP among these movies.” I come across this film. I don’t know anything about it. Put it in, put it on, see the opening. The colors look absolutely right for Ghost World, I don’t know why. Fast forward, “Oh, it’s still perfect.” I don’t know, just hit me. It was like, “This is… This is the perfect look. Who is this cinematographer?” Affonso Beato. So Lianne gets off the phone, comes in, I said, “What about this guy Affonso Beato?” She says, “He’s a friend of mine. I can get him.” And he was great. He was a great artist and helped me a lot, really taught me a lot about film. So, I still think Lianne may have planted that VHS tape in there, hoping that I would think that it was my idea, but it was actually hers. I don’t know. She won’t admit it to this day. So, All About My Mother. I’m going to go watch this now, and thanks so much.

Here’s a great film: Robert Siodmak’s The Killers. Opening of this film, the first couple scenes are so great, I remember. These killers come into this diner and menace this diner owner. I realized that, watching No Country for Old Men, in the scene where Javier Bardem goes into the gas station with the actor Gene Jones as the proprietor, where he makes him flip the quarter and he doesn’t want to call it, it’s the exact same dynamic. They must have had that in mind, at least subconsciously, I don’t know. But, you know, steal from the best. It’s good advice.

Rouge. This film is so romantic and tragic, and it's a story of a ghost being stood up in the afterworld and coming back to find the lover that they had made a promise they were going to swallow opium. It's Anita Mui's best performance. So beautiful. These two actors are so beautiful. They're no longer with us, but they are here. Immortality. Put it in your bag. It's yours. Oh, it's mine!

Mulholland Dr. And of course, I also worked with David Lynch, and I love his dreamy, atmospheric, complex way of telling this narrative, never straightforward, and you can't explain a David Lynch film at all because you have to watch it, because it's cinema. Yeah. So great.

Body Heat. I just arrived in the United States in 1981, when this came out, and this was, like, the first film that I saw in the United States, and I was absolutely shocked. I came from a communist system and we were a culture of hero-worshipping. And when I saw this, I was like, "What? You can make a film of such morally dubious characters?" I mean, Florida, the subtropical, kind of humid, it's, like, part of the decay, part of the corruption. And first time in a film: Kathleen Turner, so hot. And Kasdan's first film, too. You should see it.

My God. Kieślowski, Three Colors. I think I watched Blue, like, five to ten times. It's, like, my film school. The grief, the blue that represented an emotion and feeling. I remember the chandeliers, the swimming pool. It's a difficult way to tell a story because you're telling an inner world. And he externalized it just so perfectly. So perfectly. And, of course, also there is Red. Warmer, much warmer, the connectedness between people, compassion, and also something whimsical, of a retired judge always listening to the neighbor, and the encounter with the beautiful model. Also the red is in the billboards, in the light, the crimson. I don't have words for it. You have to see it.

World of Wong Kar Wai. And he's really my favorite director, my favorite Chinese director. I will just say my favorites: Days of Being Wild. I remember the last shot so well, that probably has nothing to do with the film, but it's absolutely unforgettable. Indelible. And then Chungking Express. I loved Chungking Express. And that… In Chinese, Chungking Express is actually Chungking Forest. So it's that urban jungle, that loneliness, isolation, and longing to connect. Again, so atmospheric, so beautiful. And Faye Wong was so unique. I don't think I've seen other female characters like that. But so happy. This is, like, gold.

I'm going to start with Defending Your Life. Now, this movie, I know a lot of people pick it, and rightly so. There's, like, three movies I did this with, where I went and saw this movie and then I went back the next day and saw it again. I think it's incredibly moving. The performances are great, but Albert Brooks, his... He's such a beautiful writer and such a disciplined, simple director that he leaves all of this room for the comedy, but while he's leaving room for these big comic moments and set pieces, he's also ushering in all of this emotion and all of these big, big questions. This is an incredible movie. It's one of my very favorite movies.

The Irishman. Okay. This is one of the other movies that I went back the next day and saw again. Certainly one of Scorsese's most underrated, I feel like it's underappreciated. I mean, it's about death and it's about coming to terms with... With your life ending. One of the great De Niro performances. That phone call he makes at the end is... Is heartbreaking. And it's a Martin Scorsese mob movie with no rock and roll in it, and I think that is significant. And there's no movie that feels like this in his filmography. And I'm not joking, I've probably seen it... I saw it those two times, like I said, but I've probably seen it at least 12 times since then. I think it's an extraordinary movie.

Sex, Lies, and Videotape. I would say this is in my top three movies ever, probably. This blew my mind when it came out. I grew up in the '80s, so it was all, like, Amblin and... Still is, those are... Temple of Doom is my favorite movie. Those are the movies I grew up on and love. And then when I was around 16, this came out, and this and Do the Right Thing came out the same year, and then from those I was, like, Scorsese – I kind of discovered this whole new world of movies. You know, this is when I realized people in a room talking is all you need. And James Spader's performance in this is... I've stolen from him so liberally.

On that note, Do the Right Thing. Incredible. I remember I used to read Spike Lee's journals. He would publish them for each movie back then, he wrote a journal while he was making the movies. And Giancarlo Esposito had those glasses that made his eyes bug out, and I remember reading that he had contact lenses to reverse the glasses' prescription so he could actually see, and just thinking that was the coolest actor move ever.

The Big Chill. Again, child of the '80s, so when this came out, I was a pretty little kid, and just watching the adults in my life react to this movie and watching the movie, not quite understanding what these grown-ups were talking about and what their problems were, but loving their clothes and their cars and not understanding their sorrow and all the stuff they're talking about and feeling. So I feel like this movie had this weird influence on how I put the world together for a while. You know how you kind of... When you're too young for something, you kind of reach for it and sort of put your own version of why this is happening together. Anyway, as I got older and understood the movie, as I was watching it, I realized just what a great movie it was. And I can say that I do understand The Big Chill now. Incredible group of actors here.

Yeah, Blue Velvet. I love the David Lynch-Kyle MacLachlan kind of mind meld they had for a few years there. There's a certain amount of audience surrogacy a leading man needs to do, and Kyle MacLachlan did that really well, but he also left enough room for weirdness. He wasn't particularly weird, but he was able to really carry a movie that was ushering in kind of a new era and showing the audience a lot of new things that they hadn't seen much in American movies before, in a new way.

Oh, His Girl Friday. I did a reading of this once, like a live reading in front of an audience. I played the Ralph Bellamy role, I believe. The script for this movie is, like, 200 pages. It was so long, we sat down and started reading it, they talk so fast. The movie is, what? 92 minutes. I remember when I got a small role in The Aviator, the Martin Scorsese movie, I went up to... To Montreal to shoot the movie, and when I landed, someone picked me up at the airport and they said, "Mr. Scorsese would like you to see something in a screening room before we take you to set." So from the airport they brought me to a screening room and I watched His Girl Friday by myself in a movie theater, in a screening room. And then it ended and they brought me to set and took me to video village where Scorsese was, and he was like, "Do you see... You watched the movie? Did you like it?" And I was like, "Yeah, I love His Girl Friday. It's so good." And he's like, "Great. Yeah, talk like that. That's... Get it? That's good, right?" And I was like, "Yeah, sure. That sounds great." And he's like, "Okay." And so that's kind of what I did in that movie was this. It was simple enough.

Okay, I love this movie so much, The War Room. It's a documentary about the 1992 election. I watch this every election season, every single one, because it's just people in a room with a white erase board trying to figure it out, beating their head against a wall, and you watch them, little by little, just hack away, just, "Okay. Cross that off. Let's try this. Now let's try this: 'It's the economy, stupid.'" Just trying everything they can. And they win the fucking election, they win the presidency. Just a great movie. Always worth watching again.

All right. Okay, my eyes are closed and I'm just picking at random here. Two Days, One Night. Marion Cotillard. I know that this movie is beautiful and she's always incredible. I look forward to seeing this. I have not seen this movie and I am now the owner of this movie. Thank you very much.

Oh, yeah, The Before Trilogy. I love these movies so much. I remember when the first one came out, Before Sunrise, it was 1995 and I went to see it by myself and loved it. And Ethan Hawke was so important to me in that era because I was just getting started in LA, trying to audition for stuff, and Ethan Hawke was just, like, becoming a giant star and was really good and really... I just started trying to emulate him because I was searching for an identity and not knowing– I was doing background work and then trying to get guest spots, and Ethan Hawke was– it was like, "That's what I want to do." But now looking at them, and them as a trilogy, it's timeless, and we've kind of moved through... Through the decades with these three people, and I would love to see another one. I hope they do another at some point. This is a really important trilogy.

film_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
catalog_title: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years
quote: The Wes Anderson Archive. Holy cow. I love Isle of Dogs so much. It's one of my favorites. My son, he was a little kid when that came out, and we used to listen to the soundtrack. It's kind of a sad soundtrack, so, he always wanted to listen to it, and it worried me, like, "Is he sad? Why does he want to keep listening to this music?" But I think it's just because it was beautiful and because the movie is beautiful. And the movie, if you're a dog lover, the movie is really a joyful experience, but also an emotional experience. I love these films, as does anyone with a head on their shoulders.
box_set_name: The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years

quote: I'm going to do The 39 Steps, Alfred Hitchcock. We know this movie. It's a reliable, standby classic. It's gonna play.
This one, my daughter loves this movie. This is one of my favorite movies ever made. Michael Powell, Emeric Pressburger, two of my favorite filmmakers of all time.
Lubitsch, Heaven Can Wait.
Also Lubitsch: Design for Living.

You know, I didn't pull The Lady Eve. Where is The Lady Eve? I just thought maybe I should have pulled that one. You guys know exactly where everything is. That laser pointer took me right to The Lady Eve. Henry Fonda, Preston Sturges, Barbara Stanwyck, one of the greatest actresses in the history of the cinema, as everybody knows.
Stagecoach, John Ford.
Tootsie. We know how good this cast is, but, remember, Bill Murray is in there and he's great.
I'm going to take Flow. Everybody in the family has seen this one, but it's a crowd-pleaser. They'll watch it again. They'll thank me for bringing it.

Okay, this is a good one to end on. This is one of the best of Satyajit Ray's films, maybe the best of Satyajit Ray's films. I stole many things for my own movies from Ray, and this one, this woman... Charulata, they translate it as The Lonely Wife, she spends much of her time looking out from the rooms in her house with binoculars. And for my film Moonrise Kingdom, which is out here somewhere, we've got a lot of binocular shots, only because of Satyajit Ray, one of my favorite great masters of cinema. And in fact, here at the Hollywood Bowl, we're playing some music that he wrote.

I’m gonna start off: my favorite Stanley Kubrick film, Eyes Wide Shut. I saw this movie in the theater. I understand it a little bit more now. I mean, I understand, like… I understand the beginning, middle, and end, but what… what it means to me, I am still trying to figure it out. I think this movie rocks. Scary as it is sexy as it is interesting as it is smart as it is weird as it is just special. One of my all-time favorite movies, and I love that Criterion has…

You can get Eyes Wide Shut, you can get, you know, Fellini, or you can get House Party. Watched this recently, actually, with my kids. The kids love it. The dance sequence, this moment right here between the guys and the gals, is thrilling. Gave me goosebumps when I was a kid, gave my kids goosebumps, gives me goosebumps as an adult. Love having that in the mix.

Again, one of my absolute faves: A Face in the Crowd. Andy Griffith, who everybody thinks of as just being from his show and the whistling and the country bumpkin, but he is such a mean son of a gun in this thing. If I could remake any movie, it would be this movie right here. So if anybody at Warner Brothers, if several other people pass, come my way. I would love to take a crack at that, but I wouldn’t try to screw it up too much.

Two of the most lovely people ever to maybe be on Earth, but also do acting: Cary Grant, Audrey Hepburn, having a fun little Charade, this movie, stylish as hell. You’d think it’s a Hitchcock movie. It’s not. And that may be the idea. But Stanley Donen, come on. You can’t go wrong with that guy. He knows what he’s doing.

One of the all-time great film noir movies: Double Indemnity. I mean, Billy Wilder, genre meant nothing to him. It’s him and William Goldman. What story they want to tell, they just told. It’s, like, “Is that a William Goldman?” They don’t care. “Is it a Billy Wilder?” He doesn’t care. This movie is based on a real-life story of a woman who… her and her boyfriend killed… killed her husband and then got the insurance claim. That woman was then executed. The New York Daily News ran a photograph of it. A photographer snuck into the… when they did the electrocution, had a camera strapped to his ankle and the whole wire coming up his leg, and then had to hold his leg perfectly still because it was a glass negative, and captured it, and then they ran it the next day. Fun fact: the guy that took that photo, named Tom Howard, my great-grandfather. So, we’ll take this.

I mean, look, Love & Basketball, I think this thing is beautiful. I mean, I rewatched it with my kids, actually, and with the exception of only two scenes that I had to, like, “Okay…” You know, they’re nine and 12. So I was like, “All right, all right, all right.” I think the nine year old was probably looking like this. The 12 year old wants nothing. The little boy, he was like, “Let’s just get back to the basketball. Enough with the love.” But the fact that it starts with them as little kids, they were hooked. They love it. Great soundtrack. I’ve seen Gina from across the court at a few Sparks games, and I’ve yet to make my way over to her, but big fan.

One of the best… Actually, speaking of sports movies, here we go, this one, another one: Bull Durham. Ron Shelton is basically, in my opinion, the Nora Ephron of sports films. And to write and direct and this be your first one, it still holds up, and it’s… it’s so funny. Because we would always talk about– Ted Lasso, this used to be our comp, so we used to… I remember recommending Juno Temple watch this, and she fell in love with it, as I think any guy or gal does when they get to see it for the first time. But I come back to this movie all the time. So between Love & Basketball and Bull Durham, those are two of my all-time favorite sports… They’re all about the love, all about the people, not about baseball, set in baseball, not about basketball, set in basketball, about everything else.

Okay, Dazed and Confused. Come on. Classic. Now, first time I saw this movie, did not like it. And here’s why: because I failed English my first semester of senior year and my second semester because I just never… I never handed in homework, and so, yeah, I had to go to summer school, and I remember they showed this in summer school, and a lot of the kids in summer school were a lot like a lot of the characters in this thing. So I was like, “Oi yoi.” It just felt like too much. I remember the one day that I was the only one at summer school. It was, like, a Thursday. And it’s because there was, like, a Pink Floyd cover band in town. Funny first time, to think that… whatever that teacher was thinking, “How do I connect with these young kids in summer school? I know: I’ll show them Dazed and Confused.” It worked.

Speaking of, hold on, my night-school movie. Look, when people ask me what my favorite movie is, I genuinely say Citizen Kane. And it’s not… I’m not a cinephile, by any means. I have friends… Golly, Bill Hader’s episode of this, when he’s going through, he’s, like… he knows this whole thing, and I love people like that, but for me, Mr. Zinger showed this at night school, and, again, I mean, black-and-white movies when you’re 17, 18, and failing English, I remember looking around and I’m just riveted, following this movie, looking around, everybody’s asleep. This was the first movie that I feel I saw that I understood it that movies were art, as corny as that may seem. The fact that that guy did all that, at that age. That guy being Orson Welles. It’s so subversive, it’s so clever, it’s so funny, it’s so heartbreaking. Yeah, so my summer-school movie and now my night-school movie are all part of the Criterion Collection. So, you know.

Martin Scorsese, After Hours. This movie was absolutely the inspiration for an episode of Ted Lasso we did, season two, where the character Coach Beard, played by co-creator and star and dear friend Brendan Hunt, is our little nod in celebration to this film. But it’s just great storytelling, great performances, and yet, you know, any cynic could watch it and just go, “Just walk north, man.” It’s, like, “Hey, sometimes life isn’t that easy, all right?”
Pickup on South Street by Sam Fuller. I don’t know this one. I’ve never heard of this movie.

You got one that you’d already seen, just close your eyes and grab from the back wall, so you get your… The Devil’s Backbone by Guillermo del Toro. I haven’t seen this. I don’t know anything about this. Awesome. That’s fun. That’s the way to do it, because, yeah, I have picked a bunch of movies that I’ve seen, and here are two that I hadn’t even heard of. And those will get viewed probably before anything else.

All right, oh, here we go, The Before Trilogy. I have not seen the third one yet, and I only watched the first two in the last few months. It’s nuts to watch something that you feel like you’ve seen and have always wanted and then it’s existed, then you catch up with it. That’s what these first two movies felt like. And these would have come out when I was working at Blockbuster Video, and this is something that I would have gravitated towards. I love the movie Leaving Las Vegas, and this is in that… genre, if you will. Just two people, just great dialogue, great performances, and you get to be a fly on the wall and you kind of, like, romantically hope to seek out one of those… one of those moments in life. There’s a great line in the book Leaving Las Vegas: “the unspoken anticipation of conversations yet to be had.” This… The first two of these movies are living example of those things. I mean, this is getting heavy.

Okay, I’m going to start off with The Last Waltz. The greatest concert film ever made. The Band, the greats. And my favorite director, Martin Scorsese. The great thing about Scorsese is he went back and forth between narrative movies and documentaries, and he’s music-obsessed. Marty, I love you.

Written on the Wind. This is a Technicolor dream of a movie. Douglas Sirk, one of my all-time favorite filmmakers. I feel like melodramas kind of get a bad rap by a lot of people, but they’re, like, post-modern. They’re purposely overly emotional, and that’s what draws me into this style of movie. They lean into everything that makes cinema great.

The Celebration. Dogme. The first Dogme movie. And the way that this movie is shot is hugely inspiring. It’s kind of shot like the Criterion Closet. It’s just, like, they would put a camera in the Closet and actors would go in there, and they wouldn’t pick out DVDs, but they would have these really intense emotional scenes. It feels like you’re being injected into these people’s lives. It’s an OG.

Godard, Pierrot le fou. Jean-Paul Belmondo. Is there a better, more charismatic actor in the world than this guy at the peak of his game? I don’t know that there would be Brad Pitt if it wasn’t for Jean-Paul Belmondo. Is that a hot take? Has anyone ever said that before? He is dripping with charisma, the playfulness. This is, like– You know, Godard’s films can be kind of hard to reach. This one is very, very accessible. It’s romantic, it’s cute, it’s flirty, it’s fun, it’s a joy to watch. And it’s also just beautiful. The colors in this movie pop off the screen. I love this movie. I’m excited to rewatch this.

Love Affair will grip you. The romance, the heartbreak that happens here. This movie is so good, it’s been remade probably 100 times. It’s every romantic film you’ve ever seen, it’s based off of this movie. I also love these old movies with ships. 1939, it’s, like, people were taking these grand cruise ships across the Atlantic Ocean. There’s that story in here. If you haven’t been able to tell up until this point, I’m a romantic. I love romantic movies. This is one of the best.

film_title: The Worst Person in the World
catalog_title: The Worst Person in the World
quote: Worst Person in the World. Joachim Trier, who I discovered relatively early on, before he made this movie. I think the first one that I saw was Reprise, which is about a group of teenage, high-school-age friends as they’re getting older, what’s happening to them. He made another movie, Oslo, August 31st, that I saw in theaters, and ever since those two I was waiting for him to make new films, and whenever there was even, you know, looking online, “what’s he gonna be–?” Hearing the first news he’s working on this, I remember telling my friends, “This is gonna be… I’m telling you this movie’s gonna be incredible.” The rest is history. And I was lucky enough to get to meet Joachim for Track Star. And he is not only the coolest guy, not only was he a professional skateboarder and world-champion skateboarder of Norway, he’s also just the nicest, sweetest guy ever, coolest guy. Incredible filmmaker. Cuts through, hits you in the heart. He’s the best. All of his movies are amazing. Joachim, love you.
Now, Voyager. More boat stuff.
One more: Mildred Pierce. Again, I don’t know why I came in here with such, like…
Oh, there’s one more: Leave Her to Heaven. These are also incredible melodrama movies.

film_title: Eclipse Series 12: Aki Kaurismäki’s Proletariat Trilogy
catalog_title: Eclipse Series 12: Aki Kaurismäki’s Proletariat Trilogy
quote: Aki Kaurismäki. I saw this – The Match Factory Girl and a bunch of these – when I was in college, and they’re hilarious, but they’re uniquely hilarious. There’s nothing quite like these movies and the deadpan nature of the humor. But besides the humor, they’re beautiful. There’s colors in this movie that are super different than what you typically see. The performances are amazing. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry. Kaurismäki, always a winner.
box_set_name: Eclipse Series 12: Aki Kaurismäki's Proletariat Trilogy

quote: And there’s one more: Rainer Werner Fassbinder, Marriage of Maria Braun, Veronika Voss, and Lola. Again, to tie things up with my whole melodrama thing, I mentioned Douglas Sirk and Written on the Wind earlier, Fassbinder was someone who was hugely inspired by Sirk. He is someone who is hugely inspiring to me. His movies are weird. They’re beautiful. They are playing with emotion in a way that’s unlike any other director that I can think of.

Okay, so the first one I'm going to grab is Grey Gardens. I first watched this, I think, when I was at NYU. My advisor, Rahul Hamid, introduced me to so many of these movies, actually, and we would do these independent studies together, and we did a documentary one, because I love documentaries maybe the most, honestly. I'm so fascinated by anything that is real and specific, and I don't think there's anything more specific than Big Edie and Little Edie in Grey Gardens, and I found a lot of sweetness in them, too, aside from the outrageous, funny things that they say and the sort of quirky aspects of the two of them, but I actually found their relationship to be quite beautiful in its endurance.

On the Waterfront, I'm… I don't know that I have anything groundbreaking to say that hasn't been said before, but the moment with the glove, when she drops her glove and Marlon Brando picks it up, it obviously wasn't scripted, and it was just a moment that happened that to me says everything about the kind of actor I aspire to be, which is present and in the moment and not getting so locked in to what's supposed to happen and being free enough to go with something unexpected, and sometimes you can really create something extraordinary from just being present and listening, and I guess I'm always attempting to be Marlon Brando when I'm acting.

Okay, next: Hedwig. I will never forget, I had heard about this movie Hedwig and the Angry Inch, and the person that was telling me was like, "I can't describe it to you. You just have to watch it. It's something that you just have to see." And I've never seen anything like it. And I don't even know what kind of genius you have to be to come up with this character and this story, but John is insane. When these songs come on, they're on a playlist in my car, and there's nothing better than blasting "Tear Me Down" on a summer afternoon, which I do often.

Okay, I'll go with this one next: Anatomy of a Fall. I have never been more star-struck from meeting an actress than I was when I met Sandra Hüller. And I was watching an interview and they're like, "How do you prepare for a movie like that?" And she was like, "Well, I just learned my lines." I was like, "I love that," you know? Because you can… It's sort of what I was saying about On the Waterfront, she's in the moment. She's present. I don't even know if I have an opinion on what the plot of the film is and it doesn't even matter. I just… I love… I just love watching amazing actors living in the story. And I think that she is the ultimate version of that. One of my favorite movies.

Maybe my favorite one of all: Sentimental Value. Obviously, my sister is in Sentimental Value, and my sister and I are super close, very, very close. She was filming Sentimental Value at a time where she was also in New Zealand filming a Predator movie, and then she was… she was back and forth. She was all over the place. Keeping track of what she was doing was really difficult during this time. So I knew she was doing a movie in Norway with Joachim Trier, and didn't really know what it was about. I didn't really know anything. I knew she had an amazing experience and really loved doing it, and I was like, "Oh great, great, great." I watched the movie at a screening in LA and was so blown away by the movie, so blown away by my sister, obviously. I would have been, regardless if I loved the movie or not. I always love her. But this is the kind of movie that I like to watch. Whatever magic is captured in Sentimental Value, that's what I want to see. The scene with Renate and Inga towards the end, on the bed, when they're talking about their lives and their sisterhood and the difference between an older sister and a younger, I could get emotional talking about it right now, which I don't want to do, but seeing those feelings translated into words that Joachim and Eskil wrote and then seeing them performed by Renate and Inga was really powerful. And then seeing my sister playing this character that could have become, like, kind of the butt of a joke, in a certain way, which I don't think would have been Joachim's intention, but, I mean, it's, like, she's playing this American actress and whatever, and it could have been one-dimensional, and seeing Elle make her a real person that you're completely with and that you completely understand, it was just amazing. And then Stellan Skarsgård is just the greatest of all time to me. And I'm getting to work with him at the moment. We like to keep things in the family. Sentimental Value is really next level.

I’m looking for The Ruling Class. It’s Peter O’Toole, doing what I think is probably the best performance any British actor has ever done in anything. He’s amazing and way ahead of his time. To me, he was a premier actor.

Midnight Cowboy. Just what I consider a perfect film. There are no flaws in this movie. This movie has incredible performances from everybody, especially Voight and Hoffman. But more than that, it’s full of incredible characters. It’s a very New York movie, which is weird because it was shot by an Englishman. The editing, the cinematography, and the performances are so raw and real. It’s amazing.

Man Bites Dog. So this is a film… The reason why I’m picking this is because it starts as a documentary and unfolds into a brutal movie about a serial killer. It shocked me when I first saw it. I’m curious to see if it still holds up, but I imagine it does, because I imagine that… All I know is that I’ve seen a lot of these types of movies, with this kind of genre. The best bits of those movies, I’m reminded of what this film did first.

Divorce Italian Style. I’m a huge Marcello Mastroianni fan. He was way ahead of his time as well. I remember seeing him in a movie for the first time when I was very young, and I could follow his thinking just through his eyes, and nobody has done it better than him, even to this day, I think, where sometimes there’s no dialogue and you’re just watching him think and he’s sort of acting and not acting simultaneously, and it’s just beautiful.

This speaks for itself. It’s Cassavetes. It’s just a great movie. It’s so raw. It’s so emotional. The idea that… that they were actually able to get away with this film is just… If you like to watch raw films where you can hardly tell if they’re acting, this is the beginning of something here, and only Cassavetes could have pulled it off.

Okay, I have this on laserdisc: Down by Law. I remember seeing this with my friends, and I was in LA doing a movie at the time. I remember three of us watching this film together and just thinking, “What is this? Is this… what we can do? Are we allowed to do now? Can I be in a movie like this?” we were all thinking. And then, not long after that, I met Jarmusch, just hung out with him one evening at the Viper club, Depp’s club that he used to have, in the office in the back, got to hang out with Jim Jarmusch. It was pretty awesome.

So I was handed this just now because I came in and very selfishly asked if I could have a box set of all of Bergman’s classics. Almost all of them, I hear. Almost all of them. But my first love, from afar, was Liv Ullmann. And so she, in a way, turned me on to… indirectly turned me on to Ingmar Bergman’s films. I’ve… I will never forget seeing her act for the first time, and I remember thinking, “I wonder if I could ever get away with the kind of acting that she’s getting away with,” in these films, being directed by Bergman. That led me to the rest of his movies, which I’m sure you all know out there. They’re incredible. So, this is now mine. Thank you very much.

We got Elevator to the Gallows. This soundtrack is on heavy rotation in our household. One of my favorite pieces of music Miles Davis ever did, and he improvised it to picture for this. Jeanne Moreau walking the streets. Oh, that sequence. Unbelievable. “Je t’aime,” like… Doesn’t rain come down at some point? Yeah, she’s just walking through, and everything’s going wrong. She’s waiting for this guy. Absolute magic. That’s going in the bag.

I’m going to go for this, Woman in the Dunes, because, interestingly, it was our first date movie, which is pretty fucked up, because it’s very weird and it’s very intense and it’s very erotically charged, and I invited Karen round to my house and said, “Do you want to come see this movie?” And she was like, “Sure, yeah.” And I was sold from that point on.

film_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
catalog_title: The Bitter Tears of Petra Von Kant
quote: Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant. This film has one of the most astonishing transformations on screen. It’s kind of the equivalent of seeing David Jones and then, over the next 20 minutes, him methodically making himself up to become Ziggy Stardust or David Bowie. It’s, like… The way that it starts off, she’s, Petra von Kant, is waking up. After that point on, she’s basically, like, a Mesopotamian goddess for the rest of the film. As someone who’s, like, in the rock sort of heritage, it’s been a pretty major moment for me.

Eraserhead. All right, we have to do this because we are both a) obviously lovers of Lynch. Yes. Devotees. B) When Karen went on tour recently… He left the earthly plane right before it. Yeah, and she integrated something for him into her music. It all goes back to Eraserhead for me. It’s just, like, this is the perfect summation of a person’s… Inner world. …artistic vision. This is it. It just, like, all starts here and ends here, and you can see it in every one of his films, and it’s just… it’s just beautiful and really funny as well, so we’re gonna laugh all night long watching Eraserhead. I would say that I’ve seen this clip going around about… where David’s complaining about having two days to shoot something that he wanted to shoot, and he’s really pissed off. He’s like, “If I had more time, the amount of magic I could make…” He’s just really upset about it, because I feel like, with Eraserhead, he had, like, ten years to really make all that magic and go into his world. Simmer in his world. And I wish he had ten years for every film that he wanted to make. We all wish we had that much time. I’m sure you do.

Night Porter. A friend of mine messaged me, saying, like, “Hey, do you know that Barney looks a lot like Dirk Bogarde?” I was like, “Who’s Dirk Bogarde?” And so I was like, “Oh, let’s watch some Dirk Bogarde films,” and Night Porter was one of the first ones. Quite the film. I would say that adept language of interiority and subjectivity. There’s a lot of brutality in it. The experience of these two people kind of going into oblivion. Like, they need each other like fish need water to breathe. Yeah, quite erotic and quite subversive. And I love all of those things, so.

Want to grab that? Night of the Hunter, yep. This is my favorite film of all time, but… Karen was like, “I don’t know if I can talk about this, I love it so much.” It doesn’t really feel like anything else. It’s, like, this self-contained universe. And it’s got Robert Mitchum, which is, like… being just terrifying in it. It’s very fairytale-like, and it almost feels like a musical to me. There’s this incredible, magical sequence where the kids are floating down this river, and this beautiful song is being sung. Yeah. Charles Laughton, so it was the only film he ever made, and I think because it was a big flop, and… but now it’s lauded as one of the greatest films, of course. But what a film to be the only one that he ever made. Absolutely. Good one, Charles!

I’m going to choose this for you because I think it’s incredibly beautiful, and I think you… Jean Cocteau, Beauty and the Beast. Yeah, yeah. Fantastic. So that one’s for you. Thank you. It’s, like, visual poetry. Yeah, exactly.
I’m going to grab Videodrome for Barney. He has a shirt that says, “Cronenberg for President,” so that’s going to go in the bag. If only. Yeah. Perfect. Thanks. Cool. Thanks, my love.

I’m going to start with… because I came in here looking for it, and you said it was in here: The Red Shoes. Because, I mean, isn’t that everyone’s favorite movie? Where is it? Got it. All right, so that’s a must. The Red Shoes. Powell, Pressburger. It’s, like, you… Everyone who is an artist has to see this movie. Everyone who’s a ballerina has to see this movie. Everyone who is just anyone should see this movie, because it’s all about how scary it is to be an artist. It’s amazing.
Oh my God, you have… you have a few Visconti pictures, right? You have The Leopard, which is amazing. Just the costumes in The Leopard, right?
And The Damned. Actually, the costumes in The Damned are really beautiful too. But that’s not the only reason we see Visconti, for costumes, but we see him also for, like… crazy, crazy…
Wait a minute. Except maybe we’re throwing in one French picture, which is Jules et Jim. Truffaut, darling. Jeanne Moreau. Where is the Jeanne Moreau festival? Where is that?

Here’s a kooky, kooky movie that I like that I see every once in a while. It’s called Dance, Girl, Dance, and it’s kind of a Damon Runyon tale about New York in the ’40s with a bunch of people, including… including Maureen O’Hara and Lucille Ball. Anyway, I’m going to go and watch that again. It’s really crazy, that movie.

And then there’s this. I mean, wow, I really limited it, did I not? I really have it narrowed down, okay. But this is the greatest. Everyone knows this is the greatest, sort of gayest documentary ever made. This is the Pennebaker documentary of the making of Company, which is the play with Elaine Stritch and Dean Jones and all these kooky people. It’s amazing. That’s coming in the bag. Wow, my bag is getting heavier and heavier, I like it.
Can you pass up Claudine, with the most gorgeous Diahann Carroll? I mean, if there’s anyone more beautiful… Okay, that’s coming with.
