Wait, both of these. This is the greatest western: My Darling Clementine. This is the one western that I actually… Well, there are a few. There’s, like, three westerns I really like, and this is one of them.

Wait a minute. And then there’s this. This is, I think, literally my favorite western ever made: Destry Rides Again. Who knew I would be coming to this Closet and picking westerns, right? I thought I was coming in to pick Bette Davis pictures.
You know what? Now, Voyager is something so great and it’s so underrated because I guess it’s long and it’s melodramatic, but what would we do without a long, melodramatic Bette Davis picture, okay?
All About Eve. I mean, really? Can you? Can you, please?

Wait a minute, excuse me? You have Polyester in this Closet and I didn’t know about it? How did I not know about this? Who is responsible for not telling me you had this movie in the Closet? I’m taking this. Sorry. Too many pictures. What am I going to do? All right, that’s it. I better stop right now.

You do have Show Boat. Watch at your own risk, but it is the most magnificent thing in the world, the 1930s version. Not the ’50s version. The ’30s version with Irene Dunne and Paul Robeson. I mean, you’re kidding. Tragic, divine movie.

This is some kind of compilation. This is Pasolini. Oh, that’s Pasolini. Are we talking about, like, Italian movies right now? Because Pasolini, I mean, this… You have Mamma Roma, you have Oedipus Rex, you have Teorema, which is the greatest movie ever made, and has been referred to a thousand times by everybody else, and they never say it’s Teorema, do they? Terence Stamp, he just comes in and just has sex with everybody. Okay, so that’s coming. This is a fabulous thing. Pasolini. I forgot all about Pasolini. So maybe that’s it, right? Maybe it’s an Italian film…

Oh, and then, of course, look, darlings, if you leave here without this, you’re just being crazy, because a Fellini compilation, you have And the Ship Sails On, which is very underrated and so incredible. Right, the chicken standing on one leg for the entire thing. That’s so funny. It’s hilarious.
And then, of course, darling, how could anyone leave the Closet without the Jacques Tati? This is– I mean, I don’t even know what movies… Does it matter? You just put a disc in and you will be happy.
So I’m going to start with the Kubrick movie that I first fell in love with. This is The Killing, from 1956. It’s his third movie. It is the nearly perfectly planned heist. Starts it off.

Now, second on the list is another Kubrick film. This is not because I’m overdoing Kubrick. This film would be on any list that I made at any time: Paths of Glory, which I was introduced to by John McCain, who came on TCM and picked the movie during the Iraq War. It aches with humanity, which leads to outrage, which I can barely control every single time I see it. Certainly the greatest World War One movie ever made. I think the greatest war film ever made. And that Kirk Douglas photo is… that’s really something. And Kubrick, you see all the magic of Stanley Kubrick in Paths of Glory.

So Humphrey Bogart’s best film, obviously Casablanca, because it’s the greatest studio film ever made, but it’s not really his best performance, even though it’s amazing. So that’s In a Lonely Place. He’s a down-and-out screenwriter. Things aren’t working out. Falls in love with his neighbor in this apartment complex they live in Hollywood. He’s broken and he is dangerous and he’s violent. And yet the magic of Humphrey Bogart keeps us on his side. I can’t get enough of this performance from Bogart. And if you want to know why Nick Ray’s a great director, you watch In a Lonely Place and you understand it.

The next film I’m going to choose is Louis Malle’s first movie, Elevator to the Gallows. Again, we’re rooting for criminals here. Bad criminals. The movie opens, they’re plotting a murder. But this is, like, a movie that reminds me what I think everybody should pay more attention to: how much luck there is in life, or bad luck there is in life. Man, it is random. Things happen, and then it’s how you adapt to these unforeseen circumstances that you could never imagine. But this is as good a crime movie and as good a bad-luck movie as there is.

So, my grandfather was a screenwriter, Herman Mankiewicz. He wrote a film called Citizen Kane. It’s not a big deal. And I wasn’t going to include Citizen Kane because I talk about it a lot. And then I imagined the conversation after I did the Criterion Closet if my dad was still alive, Herman’s son, and if he said to me, “What’d you pick?” And I’d name the movies and then he’d go, “Did they not have Citizen Kane?” And I was, like, oh, man, I wouldn’t know what to say. So for my dad and for my cousin John Mankiewicz, my cousin Nick Davis, filmmakers, my brother, I’m picking Citizen Kane. But it is a reminder that we give Orson Welles all the credit for Citizen Kane, and he deserves it, it is his film, but this is a collaborative art. He had help from my grandfather. He had help from Robert Wise. He had help from Gregg Toland, shooting the film. He surrounded himself with experts. And that enabled Welles to be his best self and make this amazing, unforgettable film.

Nobody lightens things up better than Preston Sturges, who wrote and directed Sullivan’s Travels. It has maybe the line in movies that I use most in life: “I’m not a scientist. All I know is I’m hungry.” And when people question you about things that they have no business questioning you, answer them with, “I’m not a scientist. I just want to lie down on the couch.” Whatever it is, you’re okay, man, and you don’t have to defend your actions. And Veronica Lake, we’re still hungry.

I did plan to end this with four movies from the greatest ten-year period in the history of American films, 1967 to 1976. I want to start with the Martin Scorsese film Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore, with Ellen Burstyn. She was coming off The Exorcist, had tremendous power in Hollywood. She got to pick her director. She called Francis Ford Coppola, asking for a… “Who’s a hot young filmmaker who could understand this?” And he mentioned this guy Martin Scorsese. And it has a great soundtrack, because it’s a Martin Scorsese film, and it opens with “All the Way from Memphis,” Mott the Hoople.

Okay. So, continuing from that era, my favorite actor might be Gene Hackman. So I went with Night Moves, Arthur Penn’s film. Plays a former football player who’s a private eye, and he is reflective of the times. He has grown incredibly cynical about the world, about institutions. This is a very post-Vietnam and certainly post-Watergate film. And it has as good an ending as you can have in a movie.

Continuing with crime, apparently. I really– that was not my intent, but it seems pretty clear that’s where we are. Friends of Eddie Coyle, man. I discovered this movie while at TCM. This isn’t a big-crime film. This is a little-crime film. These are… These are Boston low-level gangsters. There’s a scene in this film with… with Mitchum and… and the woman who plays his wife, an actress named Helena Carroll, and it’s a beautiful moment that gives you a look at a marriage that you don’t really see in the movies that often. It makes me emotional just thinking about it. I love, love, love Friends of Eddie Coyle.

You know, I spend a lot of time trying not to be hyperbolic. And I get in this Closet and I get enormously hyperbolic. But this is the best documentary, certainly I’ve ever seen: Barbara Kopple’s Harlan County USA. This plays like a political thriller, an action movie, a tense drama. It has high-profile murder. It has danger. It has menace. And then it has just the… the drudgery and the commitment and the compassion that these miners and their families have for each other. It’s a great, great, great American film.

So that’s ten movies. But I am going to add one more. This Is Spinal Tap. Now, so smart, but mostly what it is uproariously funny. But I wanted to include Spinal Tap because this, this bag goes to 11.

I was just peeking around, and I see Yojimbo up here, Kurosawa movie that is absolutely amazing and very inspiring. Has a good bit of sword work in it, but there is sort of, like… there's something in the essence of this film that is definitely worth seeing. It's beautifully shot, so well acted, and an absolutely wonderful film. So I'ma actually put this in my bag. And the music in this thing is incredible too. For those who like to sample, there are some samples in here.

Hoop Dreams. Picking Hoop Dreams because some of you may know that I used to be a basketball player. I went to undergrad on a basketball scholarship, and when this film came out, I was sort of in the throes of that journey and really had Dreams of potentially playing professional ball, and I really love sort of the honest portrait of the difficulty around that journey. And it really focuses on two young men in Chicago, who are star athletes with real aspirations of playing in the NBA. This is a wonderful movie. It's a great documentary, one of the better documentaries ever made.

Short Cuts. This film I really love and appreciate because it did something that… For me– it was right before I started acting, or was really even thinking about acting, but my father and I watched this movie on laserdisc, and this was one of the films that he exposed me to. And what I remember being profoundly moved by was how Robert Altman was able to stitch together 22 different characters and their lives sort of were able to weave together in a way. And I had never seen that accomplished in a story before, and I thought it was really fascinating. So, Short Cuts. It's a good one.

The legend. Hollywood Shuffle. Robert Townsend, what a filmmaker. Oh, man, I really appreciate this film. There were so many things that were funny to me in this film before I started acting that are so much funnier now, and also a little painful, too. But just as a Black actor navigating and trying to traverse this terrain, I think that there are so many things in this film that are absolutely hilarious that Robert Townsend gets spot on, and this film should be talked about even more than what it is, so, Hollywood Shuffle.

When I saw this film in, I don't know, the '90s, or whatever, I wasn't familiar with Jean-Michel Basquiat, but I had seen Jeffrey Wright do Angels on stage. What an actor. And so to get to see him in this film, the work in this, how sort of left-handed this movie is, on a certain level, it's just a little off-center, and this is the kind of work that I, at least, aspire to do. And I just admire him as a human being, Jeffrey, in general. As a human being and as an actor, he's just remarkable. This is my jam. Basquiat.

film_title: Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai
catalog_title: Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai
quote: One more, one more, one more, one more, one more. Ghost Dog. The man, the myth, the legend, Forest Whitaker. What I would give to work with Forest Whitaker. And this performance, a man trying to live by a code in modern times, a code that is probably dated for the era, and also working in sort of a criminal element, and I feel like Jim Jarmusch created a really wonderful world.

I’m gonna go for this one first because, Princess Bride, which was the incredible Rob Reiner’s beautiful family fantasy. I mean, he was just one of the greatest filmmakers of all time. I think about the breadth of stuff that he made. You know, Spinal Tap and Stand by Me and A Few Good Men. That’s what I would aspire to be, someone who just doesn’t make the same film many times over. And The Princess Bride is so funny. Incredible set pieces and comedic characters that you remember forever, and it’s so full of heart, but it’s not sentimental in any way at all. And amongst all those family films, it was a huge stand out and it makes me think of my girl, so I’m gonna… This’ll be the first one.

Loves of a Blonde. This is a bit of a cynical choice because I haven’t seen it. I know it’s a Miloš Forman film and I know that it inspired Ken Loach a lot in his filmmaking. All those Czechoslovakian filmmakers of that era were a huge inspiration to him. And I’m going to pop this in the bag now. I got it because I went looking for it the other night with my boyfriend, who’s a proper film buff and who would kill to be here.

Because of Kes, which I think is… Yeah. Here. So we went to Karlovy Vary, which is this incredible film festival in the Czech Republic, and it was, I think, the 60th anniversary and it was coinciding with Ken Loach’s 90th birthday, and he had won their big prize when Kes first came out. So I watched it on the big screen there, just, like, a couple of months ago, and to say I was destroyed afterwards is an understatement. I couldn’t… I couldn’t speak. And it’s mad because I think if you ask anyone who watched Kes when they were young, it is one of those films, even if you watch it when you’re a really, really young kid, it just stays with you, it gets under your skin, and it’s because I think he’s removed any sort of block between the filmmaker and the audience. It’s not, like, “Here’s your wide, here’s your mid, here’s your close-up.” He’s just observing, and I think that brings a real freedom to the performances and it feels like you’re watching a living, breathing thing.

Okay, so I watched this very recently, Velvet Underground. I love documentaries, and I especially love music documentaries. And I think there’s nothing better or more relaxing than putting on your favorite music and hearing about how the members of that band kind of tore each other apart in the course of… in the course of making that sort of life-changing music. So, I’m gonna have that.

Okay. So, The Graduate. I’m choosing it for a bunch of reasons. It was my daughter’s twenty-second birthday recently and we took her to this little cinema that plays film. It was the most glorious thing watching my daughter watch it for the first time. And I think it sort of changed my life, or it changed what I thought about cinema. Just how it was shot, those mad, extreme close-ups and that sort of hidden-observer thing, shot behind doors, and it feels like one of those films that has a bit of a Hollywood story. Like, I think they were going to offer it to Robert Redford, and Mike Nichols didn’t believe that he had ever had any trouble with women. I think he asked him, “Have you ever been rejected by a woman?” And Robert Redford said, “What do you mean?” So he was like, “No.” And then the music. Music is so important to me in everything I do, and I think maybe that all was kick-started by watching The Graduate and seeing how the Simon & Garfunkel soundtrack told the story.

film_title: It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World
catalog_title: It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World
quote: Okay, so for my last pick, I’m just going to see what the Closet offers up. What the hell is that? So I got It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World. It looks mad. But never heard of it, so that’s exciting.

The Before Trilogy. I adore all of these films made by Richard Linklater. But Before Midnight stayed with me the most because there was something about the representation of just a real marriage. And the argument at the end, which I’ve tried to recreate in other shows of mine, actually, but never could. But that argument that they have in that little hotel room, that starts off as lovemaking and just becomes the most violently brutal argument you could have as a married couple, is just an extraordinary thing. And it was quite an inspiration for Catastrophe when Rob and I were writing it.

film_title: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse
catalog_title: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse
quote: The Red Balloon by Albert Lamorisse. I mean, this is just such a simple premise, and it just shows you the magic of film, really, how it can take something like a red balloon, like this little boy’s relationship to a red balloon, and for an inanimate object to become something that you really care about. I’ve had my daughters get emotional about a paper bag that was in the shape of a… a doll, get thrown away. They… It’s that gorgeous childhood thing of… like, putting a personality onto it. And I… I mean, spoiler alert, but, when they burst the balloon, I cried.
box_set_name: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse

quote: Another story that… that I loved when I was growing up was The Black Stallion books. I grew up with a little feisty Shetland pony, horses, and, you know, that always was part of my… In fact, I thought I was a horse. I pretended I was a horse until my mother told me to stand on my own two feet. But I loved horses. So The Black Stallion I first knew as a book by Walter Farley. So when the movie came out, I was really nervous because, a book, you can fill everything out with your imagination, a movie, it’s all there. I think it’s a spectacular movie. I think it really, really captured the essence of that book. Again, the relationship between a child and a wild animal. So Caleb Deschanel shot The Black Stallion and Caleb Deschanel shot The Natural, that I was in. A great cinematographer. So that’s The Black Stallion.

film_title: In the Heat of the Night
catalog_title: In the Heat of the Night
quote: Another movie that I absolutely love is In the Heat of the Night. And I just watched it again recently, and it is one of the great, great performances of Sidney Poitier. And of course, the moment in the movie is when he slaps. Rod Steiger plays the police. There’s one moment at the very end that I wished hadn’t happened. When Sidney Poitier gets back on the train and he looks back at Steiger, he smiles. And when I last saw it, I thought, “He shouldn’t have smiled.” Watch it. See what you think. Should he smile? Should he not smile? Oh, my gosh.

In The Comfort of Strangers, Chris Walken, Natasha Richardson, Rupert Everett, Helen Mirren. Gosh, I gotta watch this again. But I remember this moment: out of the blue, Chris Walken, with all his might, punches Rupert Everett in the stomach, and it’s like, “Oh!” And it’s so powerful. It’s so shocking. Watch it. And that moment will either shock you or you’ve gotten so inured that it won’t shock you. But it certainly shocked me.

Oh, I’ve got Big Chill here. The Big Chill was my second movie. Larry Kasdan, this incredible cast. And the unusual thing was that we rehearsed for a whole month. And we would riff, we would sometimes change parts, we certainly talked about everybody. And that was such a luxury. Nobody did that at that time. Rehearse for a month? It was unheard of. But what Larry was trying to formulate with all of us was a sense of long-term friendship, and it was all fomenting, this incredible comradeship. Kevin and Jeff Goldblum shared a house and every night we would… JoBeth and Mary Kay Place and I would go to their house and have dinner, dance to Michael McDonald and Linda Ronstadt and play a game that I had brought down from Canada that had been invented in a bar there called Trivial Pursuit. It was an incredible experience. And those people of course have remained my friends. We have lost Bill, unfortunately. But, yeah, life moves on.

Images that stay in your mind forever: Amarcord, a Fellini movie. In Montana, where I live, there are cottonwood trees, and in spring, it’s like cotton is flowing through the air. It’s kind of an amazing… And it gathers in the streets and there is, at certain times in Amarcord, that same thing of floating cotton in the air. There’s also another incredible image of a peacock on a wall in the snow. A movie full of images that just communicate in a way beyond words, obviously. I mean, that’s what great filmmaking is.

I had the great pleasure of filming a version of Hamlet. Alan Bates played Claudius. First of all, he was the most beautiful man, in every way. But I also remember vividly, and will always remember vividly, this, Women in Love, that he was in. There’s a famous, famous wrestling match: Alan Bates and Oliver Reed, naked, in front of a fireplace, wrestling. There’s also a very famous – again, the images that stay in your mind – of eating figs, and it was incredibly sexual and nothing had to be said. It was just eating a fig. So if you haven’t seen Women in Love, you should. Just for those two moments, if nothing else.

Cries and Whispers is one of them, because I remember the scene… My memory is it’s mostly of this woman’s face and she’s basically mutilating herself. I remember thinking, “I can’t sit in this seat. I can’t stay in this theater.” I did stay and I watched till the end of the movie, but, wow. And what a wonderful job of direction and acting, of course, of cinematography, because it went straight to my throat, to my heart, to my gut. A gift from Ingmar Bergman.

film_title: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse
catalog_title: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse
quote: So I started watching movies, I think, in the late ’50s, where you could go down to the library on main street in Greenwich, and that’s the first time I saw a movie called White Mane. And it’s actually in the Criterion Collection, along with The Red Balloon. A little boy on a white stallion being chased and they end up… I don’t know if I should tell you the ending. It’s in France, in the Camargue, and they end up going into the ocean and just swimming away.
box_set_name: The Red Balloon and Other Stories: Five Films by Albert Lamorisse

quote: The first thing I’m seeing is Tanner ’88. Way before The Sopranos, way before Larry Sanders, even, there was Tanner ’88 from Robert Altman and Garry Trudeau. Truly my inspiration for The West Wing, actually, it was… it was one of the first pieces of original programming on HBO. It followed a fictional campaign around New Hampshire, around the country, during the primaries, the primary that our fictional guy would ultimately lose to Michael Dukakis. But great show. Largely improvised. Very much in the Robert Altman style of long Steadicam shots, and it is terrific.

And here is Broadcast News. This was really the movie that reminded me that people write movies. I was a young playwright sitting in a movie theater watching this movie and saying, “Jeez, I wish I had written that. That must have been a lot of fun to write. I want to write things like that.” The whole cast is great.

Well, The Graduate is on my top five. I wrote the last movie Mike Nichols directed before he died. Just let me be clear: one didn’t have anything to do with the other. He didn’t die because I wrote the movie. But we would have these work sessions at his apartment on Fifth Avenue, and it would always take twice as long as it needed to because I couldn’t stop asking him questions about The Graduate. I asked him how he landed on that score, the Simon & Garfunkel score that’s so memorable. He said the two of them, Paul Simon, Art Garfunkel, came in to play him some songs that they had written and nothing was really clicking. So Mike said, “Okay, it was a good try, but thanks a lot, guys.” And Art whispered something to Paul Simon and said, “Let me just play something else.” And they played him a couple of verses of a song they had written called “Mrs. Roosevelt.” Only right there on the spot, they changed the lyrics to “Mrs. Robinson” and history was made. This movie is so phenomenally well done.

Network, Paddy Chayefsky. You should watch this movie, you’ll feel like it was written last week. And I’d give anything if Paddy was alive today to write a movie called The Internet. If there’s one moment in it that’s worth the whole movie, it’s not “I’m mad as hell, I’m not going to take it anymore.” It’s the woman who’s the head of the domestic terrorist outfit shouting, “Don’t fuck with my residuals!” Network.

The Princess Bride. The Princess Bride gives me a chance to talk about two people who were important to me coming up: William Goldman and Rob Reiner. William Goldman, who, in addition to writing The Princess Bride, both the novel and the movie, won an Oscar for Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, won an Oscar for All the President’s Men. When I was in my early 20s, I had written my first play, A Few Good Men, and it was a couple of months away from going into rehearsal, we were just casting, so people were reading the script, and I got a phone call from him one day that he had read the script and he wanted to meet me, and he took me under his wing, and he made me a screenwriter and, right up until the day he died, just a few years ago, he was always the first person I sent pages to, and he was incredibly helpful, a great mentor. And Rob, Rob gave me my first job. Rob directed A Few Good Men, produced it, and then my next movie, The American President, so I spent a lot of time with Rob, who was a wonderful, very friendly big bear of a man. He told some great, funny stories about The Princess Bride. André the Giant liked to drink. He liked wine. But to get a little buzz, he would have to drink, like, six bottles of wine. Also, there’s a scene, if you’ve seen the movie, remember the scene at the end, where they all ride up on white horses and they take Buttercup away, and that’s how the movie ends. They couldn’t have André the Giant sitting on a horse, there isn’t a horse alive that could handle André the Giant, so they had to come up with a kind of harness thing that had André the Giant just sitting about an inch above the saddle, being held by this harness. One night on the studio lot, in Culver City, they were testing out that harness, and Rob was asked to come on over to stage two, “We’re working the harness now,” and what Rob didn’t know was that on that particular day, the new Beaujolais or something had just come out and André the Giant had had a couple of cases of this wine. And so Rob walked onto the stage and just sees André the Giant swinging from this thing, “Hey, Boss, how you doin’?” That sounds like that shoot was a lot of fun. By the way, if you’ve only seen the movie and haven’t read William Goldman’s novel of The Princess Bride, immediately read the novel. You’re in for a real treat. It’s everything you love about The Princess Bride, there’s just… there’s more of it. The Princess Bride.

I did see something when I walked in here – where is it? – that I’m going to have to go with, because it’s about passion, and we can’t really forget about passion in this world, because it’s dying. I’m going to go with… As my first choice, I’m going to go with Moonstruck. And then Nicolas Cage is phenomenal. He’s like, “The hand! This hand!” And Cher was so beautiful in the movie. And the moon, and then you have the streetlamps, and her father’s walking the dog, and shouldn’t life really just be like that? So anyway, I’ll go with that to start with.

I see Hud, which is a very, very particular Paul Newman movie, and it’s an amazing performance. Martin Ritt directed it. I just remember watching this and thinking to myself that I need to play a character like this at some point. I also just love Paul Newman because he never, ever stopped working on himself. No matter what, he was always determined to be three-dimensional in his characters, and this is a very three-dimensional performance that he got nominated for.

Oh, my God. I mean, okay, well, you know, I’m just going to do it. I know it’s been talked a lot about, Paris, Texas, okay, but this is an unbelievable movie and a great performance by Harry Dean Stanton. I love it so much because it’s about memory and how inaccurate it often is, and how much we want to remember people and things that have happened a certain way, and reality is often very different. And Nastassja Kinski was so beautiful, and I love that shot, there’s one shot where she’s leaning in the glass and he’s coming in and you see his reflection with her hair and her all around his face, and it’s pretty great. So I’m going to go with that.

To Die For, because Nicole Kidman was so unbelievable in this movie. And how can you watch this movie and not fall in love with her? I mean, I just remember going like, “Yeah, I get why Joaquin Phoenix is just going to do everything this woman says, because I would.” And Matt Dillon, of course, is the husband and the victim. And it’s also got that structure where there’s the… they talk at the camera, very When Harry Met Sally... But obviously very different. But I just think she’s timeless. It’s a timeless, timeless performance.

Being There. I always loved Peter Sellers. I loved all the Pink Panther movies and everything, and I love Hal Ashby. We maybe are in the movie Being There right now, in some ways. So, if you are wondering what that means, go watch this movie, because it’s very much about what we want to believe rather than reality, and it just shows you how flawed we are as human beings. We want so desperately to believe in something or someone to come save us.

I think I’m going to have to go with Shampoo as well, because it’s another Hal Ashby movie. There’s something very interesting about the way this movie ends that always kind of leaves me weirdly feeling unsettled and kind of content at the same time, because, you know, you really can’t have it all. And if you think you can, you may actually miss out on the things you could have. And that’s how I sort of feel about Warren Beatty’s character in this movie. And it’s great. He rides a motorcycle without a helmet and, like, fixes hair, I mean… Also he answers the telephone by a bedstand, you know, the old days, before or after a cigarette. Important stuff.

Well, of course, Cristian Mungiu would be here. I’m going to have to go with Beyond the Hills, which is one movie that really made me want to work with him. Again, about how blind we can be as people sometimes, when we just… we just see only what we want to see, and this movie is scary to me as it is funny at times, because it’s really about absolutism and how it can be devastating and quite dangerous in mindset. And the two what I would think lead performances from the two women are spectacular. So, anyway, Cristian Mungiu, thank you for your ambiguity and terrifying realism.

I have to do a Michael Haneke movie, I have to, because that was the first thing that I ever… the first set I ever was on was 71 Fragments. I didn’t even know who Michael Haneke was. I was ten years old. Oh, it’s Michael Haneke: Trilogy. Oh, dear. Oh, 71 Fragments on this! That’s so crazy. I don’t think I knew that. All right, so there you go, 71 Fragments. A Romanian orphan in the subway system, that was me. I can’t get him to cast me in anything, so that was… This is going to be as close as I get to Michael Haneke, is right here.

I’m going to start with Do the Right Thing. So Spike Lee always had this thing where he said that he never ripped off directors, he paid homage to them. And I have paid homage to this film so many times in so many of my films. His more important film to me, on one level, was actually She’s Gotta Have It, because that was the very first film that I went… very first Black film that I went into a movie theater and bought popcorn and was able to buy popcorn and a soda to watch it. Normally, Black movies, you see them in a university or an educational setting, or you see it in an art house, or you see it in an art museum. This was just a straight-up movie theater. Spike Lee gave birth to so many Black filmmakers you wouldn’t believe it.

Saint Omer. I mean, it’s dealing with a mother who kills her child, and it’s not even up for debate. It’s not a whodunit. It’s a courtroom, you know pretty early on that she murdered her child. And as a mother watching it, it’s, like, you want to hear some big reason that she did it, and you don’t get that. She’s not a sympathetic character. But she is, as well. It’s a very confusing film, and yet it stays with you, and it makes you think about your relationship with your mother, what being a mother is.

Oh, goodness, Raging Bull. Talk about unsympathetic characters that you can’t take your eyes off. And it’s so beautiful. I mean, I read at the time that he’s, Martin Scorsese isn’t a sports fan, and I think that did something to it, because it’s brutal and it’s absolutely a sport– it’s a boxing movie, but it’s also really balletic, and he makes it feel very operatic. That opening sequence where he’s… I’m not going to do it because I’m not that graceful, and it was in slow motion when it was done, which helped, but where he is in the ring, by himself, shadowboxing. It’s black and white. It’s absolutely beautiful. And yet it’s absolutely brutal at the same time. It didn’t turn me on to boxing, but it is a classic.

I mean, there are so many classics in here. Talking of classics, Imitation of Life. So, I… I saw this when I was really young, and I related to it so much. Two single women trying to raise their kids, if I remember rightly. But obviously I was locked into the story about the Black woman who has a child that passes for white. And there’s a scene quite early on where it’s raining and so the mother goes to the school, and the daughter hasn’t told anyone at the school that her mom is Black and she’s Black, and the mother comes in, and it’s just this moment that just takes over. It’s really visceral because the child is so upset, so ashamed, the mother’s so heartbroken. You feel for both of them. You’re angry at both of them. You’re angry at the system. It’s so moving. So I must take that one as well.

This, Black Girl, it is the most beautiful film that’s ever been made. So it’s about a woman from Senegal who is chosen by a white French family to come back with them, to work for them in Paris or somewhere. It’s such a story about colonialism and the aftereffects of colonialism and what the relationship… because she thinks by leaving Senegal to go there, she’s going to get a better life, and she ends up essentially in indentured servitude. And they brought back a Senegalese mask, and it’s hanging on the wall, and there’s a scene where she’s trying to talk to it. It’s so… It’s so beautiful, but it’s also really sad. Ousmane Sembène. He’s the godfather. He’s the godfather of African cinema.

So this is me being greedy, taking an entire box set. In the Mood for Love is one of the most sexy and beautiful films. The locations, the costumes, the interactions, this forbidden love. You want to push them together, but you don’t. The rain… I don’t know how he makes everything… I have seen In the Mood for Love maybe six or seven times. It’s almost like an album that I just put on sometimes. And I haven’t– There’s so many on here that I haven’t seen, so this is going to be… I’m not going to leave the house for about ten days or something. I might just sit in there watching all this stuff.

I love Spike Lee. Spike Lee is, like, the patron saint of the neighborhood that I live in. I live in his neighborhood. Malcolm X and Bamboozled are my two favorites of his films. This performance is just unparalleled.

And this movie, I saw in college for the first time, and what he’s doing with genre here is so fascinating, what he’s doing with the history of Black people in white entertainment and then also the history of Black people’s self-generated Black entertainment and the intersection of those two things. I love art that makes the viewer aware of themselves in a different way, and I just can’t recommend Bamboozled more highly.

Paul always makes fun of me because– My partner, Paul, always makes fun of me because, like, I’ll often… Someone will bring something up and I’m like, “That’s my favorite movie.” And he’s like, “You say that about, like, 100, 200 movies.” It’s true. But this is one of my more recent favorites: Petite maman. It’s like a… a very intense piece of chocolate or something. It packs so much in. And it literally will take you as much time as it takes you to watch the average episode of television. I also read this piece about Céline Sciamma and one of the things that she said is that she makes a list of all the scenes that she needs to tell the story, and then a list of all the sort of, like, inchoate images, songs, moments that she knows that she needs at, like, a psychic level to tell the story, and she sort of does it like a word finder and matches them up afterwards. And then anything that doesn’t have one of those delicious bits attached to it, she just cuts and doesn’t film, which I find… or even write, which I find completely fascinating. So, watch this.

Koko: A Talking Gorilla, a film by Barbet Schroeder. So Barbet Schroeder was an adult in my life when I was a child. He directed a film that my father wrote called Reversal of Fortune, and he used to come over to my house and wear my tutu and let me put makeup on him, and was just a complete delight to have as an adult around when I was a child. Because we knew Barbet, my parents showed me this when I was very little, and I completely fell in love with Koko. And I recommend it. I think it’s also great for kids.

All right, Personal Shopper. I cannot stress enough what a life-changing experience I had going to the movies and seeing this. Now I’m a spooky girl who grew up, like, seeing ghosts and believing in the unknowable parts of life. And this traffics in that. But it’s also this rumination on loneliness and on what is terrifying about being a woman. And Kristen Stewart is extraordinary in it, and her relationship to the camera in it is really interesting. Highly recommend.

Pandora’s Box. I love this film. It is silent. Please don’t let that scare you, if you are not a person who watches silent films. What Louise Brooks does in this film is unparalleled. This is about a woman who does what she needs to do to get by. Through her interactions with men, we see the kind of kaleidoscopic portrait of who she might be or might have been if she hadn’t… if she didn’t have to please men in order to get by. Especially if you love performance, it’s worth watching. And then she wrote a beautiful book about her life, which is really worth reading.

It Happened One Night. Watching this film with my parents is one of my earliest childhood memories, and the image of Claudette Colbert jumping off of the yacht is, like, one of the first things I remembered. And then they rented it again, probably, like, eight years later when I was, like, ten or something, and it was like that meme of Leonardo DiCaprio pointing at the screen, I was like, “Oh! That’s what that’s from.” Anyways, it’s just delightful and I love a romantic comedy, so.

Notorious is one of the first films that my parents bought on laserdisc. We watched Rebecca first, which was another one they bought on laserdisc, which is right next to it. But when I saw Notorious, my mind was blown. I think it’s one of the great film performances of all time. Love this.

We watched Rebecca first, which was another one they bought on laserdisc, which is right next to it. But when I saw Notorious, my mind was blown. I think it’s one of the great film performances of all time. Love this. Love Rebecca.

Then as a teenager I saw In the Mood for Love. I’ve felt this way since I was a kid, I don’t really care about seeing people kiss on screen. What I care about is people wanting to kiss each other on screen, the moments before people kiss on screen. This one speaks for itself. Everyone loves this. I’m not the first person to pull this in this Closet, but I have to.

Then I saw Don’t Look Now when I was 16, maybe 17. My dad loved scary movies, and I grew up being the most afraid child of all time. Some switch flipped and I started to be curious about how scared I was and it led me here. It’s one of the sexiest films of all time. It’s one of the saddest films of all time. The direction, the sense of something happening both at the surface and also deep underneath it. It’s so much a film about what’s unseeable, too. Anyways.

In college, I obsessively watched When We Were Kings. It was the way that I bigged myself up for anything that was hard. I love being allowed to enter into a different time. This is a time capsule. It’s a portrait of an artist. I love it.

In my 20s, with my partner, Paul, I saw both of these for the first time. All That Jazz, Brief Encounter, Notorious, these are, like, top-five films for me. I love these two middle-aged people falling in love. There’s something really quotidian about the way that they love each other, even though they are not allowed, because they’re having an affair, to have anything quotidian between them. They exist only in stolen spaces. There’s no dailyness to their life.

And I love Still Walking. Still Walking was a movie that Paul was shown in a film class that he took in college. He showed it to me for the first time and it was like… it was like I had waited my whole life to see this movie. The way that this film reaches out in the most generous possible way to any viewer that might encounter it. I really, really love it, and it’s very sensual and it’s very simple, and it’s so much about what isn’t being said.

I’m going to end with Wildlife. Paul and I had been together maybe six years when he found Richard Ford’s book Wildlife. He started adapting it on his own, and then he asked me to read his script, and I was like, “I don’t know how to give you notes on this. I think I just have to rewrite you,” which is terrible of me. But this is a book that is told through the child’s perspective. He’s looking at his own parents. His mother is unknowable to him, and I think I felt this surge of protectiveness for her, where I felt like I wanted to understand her in a way that her son could not. And even though our film is told from his perspective, I felt like, actor to actor, I had to provide an actress with a roadmap that was full of understanding and not just mystery. Our dear friend Carey Mulligan I think gives one of the performances of her career in this. Jake Gyllenhaal’s also really special, and this kid, Ed Oxenbould, who is an Australian… at this time teenager. I’m really proud of this. So it’s deeply meaningful to us to have this film in this company, and, you know, I think that there’s something really relatable here, so maybe watch it. But, also, I’m just glad it’s here. I have enough copies of this, though.
Actually, this is a great one. This is My Beautiful Laundrette. When I first saw this, I became madly in love with Daniel Day-Lewis. This is a must.

film_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
catalog_title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
quote: Salò, I think I… has been a massive inspiration on me. I worked with this woman, Manuela Pavesi, and it was her favorite film. I think the wedding sequence can make you fall in love with irises. A must.
Every time I talk to Luca Guadagnino, he always tells me about this film, over and over again, and he has made me look at it in a completely different way.
Here’s– I’m going to do two at once. I’m going to do Room with a View, I think probably one of my all-time favorite films. I could watch it over and over again. I’ve never got bored of this film, so.

Burroughs. I had to watch this several times when I was doing research for Queer, for Luca, and there are characters within characters, and I think he is someone that, still today, we… we have so much to research into, as a person. So, this is definitely coming with.

Paris is Burning. Everyone has to watch this. Everyone has probably seen it, but it’s the most beautiful depiction of people. Every time I watch it, I find it so poetic, so emotional, but terribly funny, terribly, terribly funny. And the best one-liners that you will see in a documentary. This is, like, a genius film.

Trainspotting. Fantastic soundtrack. The best performances by all. It’s, like, visceral. It’s sort of… it will suck you in. I love this. It’s… I’m glad I saw that because I haven’t watched that in a while. So this is… Trainspotting. Classic.

Hairspray. Fantastic. I actually remember watching this in the middle of summer. It reminds me of summer, even though it’s not about summer. Dark. Silly. Funny. The best comedy. And it has Ricki Lake in it. And obviously Divine. But Ricki Lake is in it.
Sex, Lies, and Videotape. Yeah, this is one… This is another one to add to watch, because I feel like this is kind of a great combination for a weekend. It’s, like, all emotions.

And then Kubrick, because… this is the complete set, which is insane. I don’t know, when I first saw Eyes Wide Shut, I became obsessed by every painting in the… in their house. And it’s something that, every time you watch a Kubrick film, you find something in the corner of the film that you never saw before. So this is definitely a must.

So there’s another one. I’m just going to do box sets, I feel, because then you’ve got days to cover. This is a Pasolini box set, which is another great one. He has a way of showing a kind of curation of characters that I find is not seen today in cinema. It’s obsessive.

Néstor Almendros was a wonderful, wonderful cinematographer, somebody who really influenced my work over the years. I studied him. He shot many films, for Eric Rohmer, for Truffaut, for Robert Benton. He really got around and, you know, the thing I like is that they all feel different, like Terry Malick’s Days of Heaven is a fabulous tribute to his sense of the light, of the mood of a scene. It just really stayed with me as a story and it’s certainly reflected in the photography of Days of Heaven.

Visions of Eight is a wonderful, wonderful film. It’s an interpretation of… of the Olympics through the eyes of eight wonderful and very diverse directors. And there’s some of the most brilliant, brilliant photography, including really ultra-slow-motion studies of athletes. The directors are, you know, Lelouch, Forman, Penn, John Schlesinger. You know, it doesn’t get any better than that.

So Elaine May is a wonderful, wonderful writer and great director, and this film with Peter Falk and John Cassavetes, Mikey and Nicky, is just a wonderfully constructed script and story about… about two fabulous characters kind of on the run. As it happens, I worked on it briefly, just because John Cassavetes actually directed some scenes and I helped him photograph them. And I’ll never forget, they played out their lines and then they walked off screen and the camera operator, you know, cut the camera. And Elaine said, “What did you do that for?” Said, “Well, I cut the camera because they left frame.” And she said, “Well, they might have come back.” And that was kind of the way she directed much of the movie. We did shoot quite a lot of film on that movie, and it did take a little longer than the studio envisioned, but… but it’s really quite a wonderful film.

I love the film No Bears. It’s a fabulous study of a small town. It’s just brilliant in the way scenes unfold. And the director and cinematographer are not afraid to just hold and hold and block a scene in such a complicated way that they keep you, the audience, so involved every inch of the way. It’s a great drama.

So this is a favorite, Solaris is a favorite of mine. You know, I put myself through… through college as a projectionist, and in the projection booth, most movies come on 2,000-foot loads, so that lasts about 18 minutes or so on the screen. Well, the Russian film came to the projection booth on 10-minute rolls, instead of 20-minute rolls, and it’s all labeled in Russian. So I think accidentally I did a little editing in the projection, because some of the reels I know came up slightly out of order when I rewound them. So there was an audience that saw a version of Solaris like no other that evening because I… I messed up in the projection room.

film_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
catalog_title: Dr. Strangelove, or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
quote: One of the main, though last, selection: Dr. Strangelove is just such a brilliant film. It’s just fabulous. And it makes me laugh and smile every time. You know, I visit these films from the early ’60s, this one stayed with me better than any of the rest, I think. I just love it.

Miller’s Crossing, I discovered this movie in high school, and it’s become such a comfort film of mine. I’m a big rewatcher. There’s something about the score of this film that’s very warm and cozy. The production design, the wardrobe. It’s where I discovered Albert Finney. I wasn’t familiar with Albert Finney at all until I saw this film, and I was so glad for this particular introduction to him. Maybe my favorite John Turturro performance ever. Gabriel Byrne is, like, as cool as it gets. I love this movie so much. I had this baseball cap that I wore for six years, and I was walking in New York five years ago, and it was a very windy, rainy day in New York, and the cap flew off my head and I wanted to go chase it, but this film is so ingrained in me, I think of Gabriel Byrne saying, “There’s nothing more foolish than a man chasing his own hat.” So I just let the hat go. But I love this film. I’m going to take it home with me.

This is Melville, Le Samouraï. Very meditative. Very sparse. The performance is so nuanced. You could tell that he really trusted himself. He trusted that the camera was going to find him, find his eyes, and read what was going on. There was no pushing. There was no forcing. Really, really beautiful. And I’m very grateful for that.

Mike Leigh’s Naked. I watched this one when I was in high school and going through a particularly, like, high-school time in my life. I was mad at the world. And there was something so punk about this film, watching Johnny just make his way through London, after running away from Manchester. He’s, like, a really putrid, putrid man, but somehow he gets you. You’re invested, you’re interested. You can see all the pain in him. I did a TV show, Shameless, for a long time, and I remember seeing this performance and… and trying to instill a little bit of Johnny into… into my character, into Philip Gallagher. Mike Leigh’s a legend, and… and, yeah, this performance stands up.

On to Linklater. Dazed and Confused. I watched this movie in high school and continued to watch it until I graduated and left New York and moved to Los Angeles. It’s, like, about the end of innocence, the fear of growing up. It makes you want to stay this age forever. It’s about, you know, the idea of peaking and fully realizing yourself as a young person, as a teenager, but also about maybe not having found yourself entirely yet. It makes me think about having grown up in Park Slope, even though Park Slope’s very far away from Texas.

Okay, I’ve talked about this movie so much. I went to see this movie in theaters. It’s the only time I’ve left a theater, I’ve looked up at the showtimes, saw the next showing, waited around for a couple hours, went back into the cinema to watch it again. Just fills you with… with hope. You’re following this guy, Jep, he’s such a cynic, or you think he’s such a cynic, but he, over the course of the film, remains incredibly hopeful and open to… to the beauty of the world. And it’s, like, very… it’s very romantic. It’s a man looking back at his past and wondering if maybe he’s lived his life the wrong way. And I think when I saw the film, what struck me is the reminder to look back and make sure you’re living your life the way that you want to. The Great Beauty is coming with me. It’s going to go in the bag.

Virgin Suicides. One of the greatest debuts. It’s so confident. It’s so beautiful. It’s so stylized. The colors are remarkable. It’s very sad. It’s very sweet. It’s a very perfect movie, and it’s coming home with me.

Thief. Me and Chris Storer talk about this movie a lot. Chris created The Bear. Michael Mann, Chicago guy. Cool as hell. Beautiful. I’m so glad I have this one in my hands because there was a period where it was just impossible to find. You couldn’t stream it anywhere. You couldn’t buy it anywhere. So I’m glad I have it.
Okay, for my last pick, I’m just going to pick one at random and watch it later today. Okay. Can’t even pronounce it. We’re going to watch it.
